location.summary: Adamgarh hill near Hoshangabad (Narmadapuram), Madhya Pradesh, in the Narmada valley on the northern edge of the Satpuras, roughly 30 km south of Bhimbetka.

periodLevel.summary: Lower and Middle Palaeolithic in the basal levels, overlain by a rich Mesolithic horizon that passes into the Neolithic-Chalcolithic; excavated by R. V. Joshi.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the few sites in central India to preserve an unbroken sequence from the Palaeolithic through the Mesolithic into the food-producing stage.
points: The lower and middle levels yielded Acheulian core tools of quartzite; the upper levels produced an enormous microlithic industry of chert, chalcedony, jasper and agate, with geometric microliths and potsherds dated to about 5500 BCE.

Bones of both wild and domesticated animals were recovered, which, with Bagor in Rajasthan, gives Adamgarh the earliest evidence for the domestication of animals in the Indian part of the subcontinent, around 5000 BCE.
The rock shelters of the hill carry paintings, linking the site to the wider Vindhyan rock art tradition of Bhimbetka.

location.summary: Located in the Potwar region (West Punjab, Pakistan), lying between the Pir Panjal and Salt ranges along the Sohan (Soan) River Valley.

periodLevel.summary: Lower Palaeolithic (associated with the Sohanian / Sohan Valley pebble tool tradition).

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The site yielded characteristic Lower Palaeolithic core tools, including handaxes, choppers, and edged pebble tools.
points: It is one of the localities of the Soan terrace sequence surveyed by H. de Terra and T. T. Paterson in 1935, who identified five tool-bearing river terraces in the Potwar and attempted to correlate them with a four-fold glacial cycle in Kashmir; most of those correlations are no longer accepted.

The dominance of choppers and chopping tools over handaxes is the defining trait of the Soanian, long contrasted with the Acheulian handaxe traditions of peninsular India, though sites such as Ghumarwin where the two occur together have weakened that sharp division.

location.summary: Situated in the Thar Desert region around Ajmer and the Budha Pushkar / Hokra lake basins in Rajasthan.

periodLevel.summary: Multi-layered sequence covering the Lower, Middle, and Upper Palaeolithic phases.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The Budha Pushkar and Hokra basins provide a continuous sequence of prehistoric human occupation from the Lower Palaeolithic onwards.
points: Excavations revealed Middle Palaeolithic working floors at Hokra and Baridhani, situated close to ancient, now dried-up freshwater lake beds.
Small factory and camp sites in this region indicate a cooler, wetter, and more humid palaeo-environment with abundant surface water during the Middle Palaeolithic phase.

location.summary: Anangpur, in the Badarpur hills of the Aravalli quartzite ridge immediately south of Delhi (Faridabad district, Haryana).

periodLevel.summary: Lower Palaeolithic, with both early and late Acheulian assemblages.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Excavations revealed thousands of early and late Acheulian tools together with traces of several palaeo-channels of the Yamuna, marking this as a large Lower Palaeolithic habitation-cum-factory site.
points: A systematic survey of south Delhi and adjoining areas by Chakrabarti and Lahiri (1986) identified 43 stone age sites ranging from the Lower Palaeolithic to the microlithic, including finds on the Delhi Ridge near Delhi University and a late Acheulian handaxe on the JNU campus in 1983.
The site is a standard illustration that stone age sites are not remote curiosities but lie under areas that are today densely urbanised.
The same village later carried early medieval fortifications and a stone masonry dam associated with the Tomara king Anangapala, giving the place its name.

location.summary: Attirampakkam, in the Kortallayar river basin, Tiruvallur district, about 60 km north-west of Chennai, Tamil Nadu.

periodLevel.summary: Lower, Middle and Upper Palaeolithic in sequence, with a break in occupation after the Middle Palaeolithic; discovered in 1863 and excavated off and on since, most recently by Shanti Pappu and Kumar Akhilesh.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the richest and best-dated Palaeolithic sites in India, whose Acheulian levels have been placed at roughly 1.5 million years BP by cosmogenic burial dating, among the oldest Acheulian occurrences outside Africa.
points: Acheulian tools were recovered from a 4 m thick clay deposit; the artefacts, mostly bifacial handaxes and cleavers, were made of quartzite not available locally, and the near-absence of debitage shows they were manufactured elsewhere and carried to the site. A quartz tool of non-local origin was also recovered.
A set of animal footprints was found along with Acheulian tools: 17 round impressions of 15-20 cm together with a set of hoofprints, the first discovery of its kind in South Asia.
Three fossil teeth, probably of a horse, water buffalo and nilgai, indicate an open and wet landscape in early Palaeolithic times.

location.summary: Bagalkot district, northern Karnataka, in the Malaprabha-Ghataprabha basin of the Krishna system.

periodLevel.summary: Lower to Middle Palaeolithic, part of the stratified Lower-to-Upper Palaeolithic sequence identified in the Malaprabha-Ghataprabha valleys.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: An early-to-middle Palaeolithic tool zone dominated by Acheulian handaxes and cleavers, with pebble tools such as choppers and chopping tools occurring alongside them.
points: Kavalli nearby is an open-air factory site, where tools survive in successive stages of preparation close to the raw material source.

The co-occurrence of pebble tools with handaxes here helped overturn the older view that the southern Lower Palaeolithic, then called "Madrasian", was distinct from the pebble-tool traditions of the north-west.
The same district later became the heartland of Chalukyan temple architecture at Badami, Aihole and Pattadakal on the Malaprabha.

location.summary: Baghor I, II and III, Sidhi district, Madhya Pradesh, in the Son valley on the fringe of the Kaimur hills.

periodLevel.summary: Upper Palaeolithic, the shrine dated to about 9000-8000 BCE; excavated jointly by G. R. Sharma of Allahabad University and J. D. Clark of the University of California, Berkeley.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Baghor I has yielded the clearest evidence of an Upper Palaeolithic shrine anywhere in the subcontinent, and so of organised religious activity among hunter-gatherers.
points: A roughly circular platform of sandstone rubble about 85 cm across carried at its centre a natural stone with concentric triangular laminations ranging from light yellowish red to dark reddish brown; nine further fragments found on or near the platform join into a triangle about 15 cm high.

The Kol and Baiga people who live in the Kaimur hills today build similar circular rubble platforms and worship such triangular stones as a symbol of the female principle, an ethnographic parallel of unusual directness.

A microwear study of Baghor III (Sinha, 1989) identified boring, scraping and whittling associated with craft work, and cutting, slicing, piercing and chopping linked to food processing and hunting, with polish on some tools showing they had been hafted onto handles.

location.summary: Bhandarpur, in the lower Narmada basin of eastern Gujarat, in the tract where the Orsang and Karjan join the main river.

periodLevel.summary: Middle to Upper Palaeolithic, with a microblade horizon.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The microblade assemblage recovered here belongs to the class of evidence used to trace the dispersal of anatomically modern humans out of Africa into South Asia.
points: Microblade industries of this kind, dated across western and central India, are central to the debate on when fully modern human populations entered the subcontinent and how that relates to the Toba super-eruption of about 75,000 years ago.

Gujarat's Lower Palaeolithic is otherwise known from the valleys of the Sabarmati and its Orsang and Karjan tributaries, and from the Bhadar valley in Saurashtra, so Bhandarpur extends that record into the later Palaeolithic.

location.summary: Bhimbetka, Raisen district, Madhya Pradesh, about 45 km south of Bhopal and 30 km north of Hoshangabad, on a sandstone and quartzite hillside of the Vindhyas overlooking the Narmada; brought to notice and excavated by V. S. Wakankar, and inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003.

periodLevel.summary: An exceptionally long sequence running from the Lower Palaeolithic through the Mesolithic to the historic period, across hundreds of rock shelters.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The single most important prehistoric site in India, combining the longest occupation sequence with the richest body of rock art.
points: Most tools were made of a yellowish quartzite available locally, with a grey quartzite obtained from further away; five floors paved with flat stone slabs belong to the Lower Palaeolithic. No bones have been found, probably because of the acidic soil.

Cave III F-24, the "Auditorium Cave", stands on the borderline of the Lower and Middle Palaeolithic. A large rock in the middle of the hall carries seven cupules up to 16.8 mm deep, and a second rock has a single large cup mark with a meandering line; these were most likely made deliberately as part of a community ritual.
A chalcedony disc was found in an Acheulian context, and ostrich eggshell beads about 6 mm across came from an Upper Palaeolithic burial, lying at the neck of the skull of a buried man.

The Mesolithic paintings, executed in green and dark red, show hunters in red and dancers in green, along with large animal figures of bison, elephant, tiger and rhinoceros and geometric patterns; the shelters were attractive because of three perennial springs, about 30 plant types yielding edible fruits, tubers and roots, and abundant game.

location.summary: Chittoor district, southern Andhra Pradesh, around Renigunta in the Velikonda and Nagari hills of the Eastern Ghats.

periodLevel.summary: Lower, Middle and Upper Palaeolithic, with continuity of occupation into the Megalithic period.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The area shows an unusually complete cultural sequence from the Palaeolithic to the Megalithic, making it a standard reference for long-term continuity in the southern Eastern Ghats.
points: Acheulian tools occur together with Lower, Middle and Upper Palaeolithic material; two sites have been identified, one of them clearly dominant.
Finds include handaxes and pebble tools of varying sizes; the large number of tools and the distinctive flaking suggest a source of raw material close at hand.
Upper Palaeolithic artefacts were recovered from a cave at Renigunta, one of a series of such finds along the east coast of peninsular India dated between about 25,000 and 10,000 years ago.

location.summary: Chopani Mando, in the Belan valley on the Vindhyan fringe of the Allahabad (Prayagraj) and Mirzapur tract, Uttar Pradesh; excavated by G. R. Sharma of Allahabad University.

periodLevel.summary: A habitation site with a cultural sequence running from the Upper Palaeolithic (Period I) through the Mesolithic (Periods II and III, with geometric microliths in Period IIB) to the Neolithic; the Belan Upper Palaeolithic is dated between 25,000 and 19,000 years ago.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The classic Indian site for the transition from hunting and gathering to settled food production, set within a valley whose sequence runs unbroken from the Lower Palaeolithic to the Neolithic.
points: The Palaeolithic levels yielded tools of chert, a stone available in the nearby Vindhyas.
Period III produced handmade pottery with cord-impressed patterns, among the earliest pottery known in India, along with querns and mullers for processing wild grains.

Wild rice was recovered, though whether it was domesticated remains debated; the huts were beehive-shaped in the earlier phase and oval, clustered and wattle-and-daub later, evidenced by burnt clay bearing reed impressions.
Bones of sheep and goat, animals not indigenous to the area, suggest either contact with the north-west or an early stage of animal domestication.

location.summary: Dari-dungri, Sambalpur district, Odisha, in the Mahanadi basin.

periodLevel.summary: Lower and Middle Palaeolithic.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Explorations here recovered a large number of Lower and Middle Palaeolithic tools, making it one of the richest surface concentrations in the Mahanadi system.
points: Tools of all three phases of the Palaeolithic have been found at many places in Odisha, and Lower Palaeolithic material also occurs along the valleys of the Budhabalanga and Brahmani rivers.
Together with the river valleys and foothills of the Chhotanagpur plateau, these finds establish continuous Palaeolithic occupation across the eastern Indian uplands.

location.summary: Didwana, Nagaur district, western Rajasthan, on the eastern margin of the Thar desert beside the Didwana salt lake; the principal localities are Singi Talav and Amarpura. Studied in detail by V. N. Misra and S. N. Rajaguru.

periodLevel.summary: A stratigraphic profile extending from the early to the middle Palaeolithic. The Lower Palaeolithic is dated 390,000 BP by the uranium-thorium series method, and the Middle Palaeolithic has two thermoluminescence dates of 150,000 BP and 144,000 BP.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the very few Indian sites with absolute dates for both the Lower and Middle Palaeolithic, and the anchor for reconstructing the palaeo-environment of the Thar.
points: Finds include handaxes, cleavers and choppers in stratified deposits.

The study shows that the present environment of the Thar is very different from that of the Pleistocene: except for a phase in the upper Pleistocene between 25,000 and 13,000 BP, surface water was always available in some quantity and the flora and fauna were far more abundant than today.

Sediments of the salt lakes record a significant increase in rainfall in the mid-Holocene, about 6000-4000 BP, precisely the period to which the most widespread prehistoric occupation of the area belongs.

location.summary: Gudiyam cave, in the hills of the Kortallayar basin, Tiruvallur district, not far from Chennai, Tamil Nadu.

periodLevel.summary: A sequence of Lower, Middle and Upper Palaeolithic tools.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The cave has yielded a complete Lower-to-Upper Palaeolithic tool sequence, one of the few cave stratigraphies available in South India.
points: The small number of tools and the absence of other remains suggest that the site was occupied only for short periods at a time, a transit or seasonal shelter rather than a base camp.

With Attirampakkam and Pallavaram nearby, Gudiyam makes the Kortallayar basin the classic stratified Palaeolithic region of Tamil Nadu, giving a sequence from the early Palaeolithic to the Mesolithic near Chennai.

location.summary: Ghumarwin, Bilaspur district, Himachal Pradesh, in the Siwalik foothills of the Sutlej basin.

periodLevel.summary: Lower Palaeolithic, with Acheulian and Soanian material occurring together.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The association of Acheulian and Soanian tools at one locality argues against treating the two as separate and mutually exclusive cultures, and points instead to continuity between them.
points: Finds include bifacial handaxes, cleavers, scrapers and Acheulian choppers.

Fossil remains of Sivapithecus, one of the "God-Apes of the Siwaliks" and an ancestor of the orangutan, have been recovered here; such Siwalik apes, including Ramapithecus and Brahmapithecus, were dated between 10 and 14 million years ago.
Vertebrate and invertebrate fossils together with the fossilised tuber of a tree allow the ecology of the period to be reconstructed.

location.summary: Hathnora village, on the northern bank of the Narmada about 40 km north-east of Hoshangabad, Sehore district, Madhya Pradesh.

periodLevel.summary: Middle Pleistocene, in a late Acheulian to Middle Palaeolithic context; estimated dates for the hominid finds range between 0.5 and 0.2 million years ago.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The only well-authenticated Pleistocene hominid fossil locality in India, which places the subcontinent within the global story of human evolution.
points: In 1982 Arun Sonakia of the Geological Survey of India found a fossilised cranial fragment embedded in thick, closely packed sandy, pebbly gravel, along with fossils of proboscideans and bovids and a few late Acheulian tools.

The skull fragment belonged to a woman of about 30. Sonakia named her Homo erectus narmadensis, treating her as an advanced variety of Homo erectus because of the larger cranial capacity range of 1155 to 1421 cc; other scholars regard the cranium as that of an early or archaic Homo sapiens, and its date remains disputed.

In 1997 A. R. Sankhyan reported a hominid clavicle from the same boulder conglomerate deposit, together with animal fossils and several middle or late Palaeolithic tools, following the Anthropological Survey of India's intensive search of the central Narmada valley between 1983 and 1992.

location.summary: The Hiran river valley in Saurashtra, Gujarat, draining the southern flank of the Gir hills.

periodLevel.summary: Lower Palaeolithic dated between 190,000 and 69,000 BP, and Middle Palaeolithic dated 56,800 BP, both by the uranium-thorium series method.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the very few sequences in Gujarat to carry absolute dates for both the Lower and the Middle Palaeolithic, giving Saurashtra a securely fixed Pleistocene framework.
points: The dates place the Hiran valley alongside Didwana in Rajasthan, the Son valley in Madhya Pradesh and Nevasa in Maharashtra as the small group of Indian localities where Lower Palaeolithic contexts have been dated absolutely rather than by typology alone.

Lower Palaeolithic tools elsewhere in Gujarat come from the Sabarmati and its Orsang and Karjan tributaries and from the Bhadar valley, so the Hiran dates supply the chronology for that wider regional record.

location.summary: The Hunsgi valley, Gulbarga (Kalaburagi) district, Karnataka, on the banks of the Hunsgi, a tributary of the Krishna; investigated by K. Paddayya from 1982 onwards.

periodLevel.summary: Lower Palaeolithic (Acheulian), with Middle Palaeolithic occupation at the associated site of Isampur, where prehistoric occupation goes back to between 500,000 and 600,000 years ago.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The classic Indian demonstration of Acheulian settlement patterns, where the size and composition of sites have been used to reconstruct how hunter-gatherer bands used a landscape.
points: Sites with very few artefact types represent places where specific activities such as tool-making or killing game were carried out; sites with tools in larger number and variety were probably temporary camps; the largest sites, with tools in great profusion, were places where groups lived for longer periods.

The tools were made of limestone, sandstone, quartzite, dolerite and chert, some of which were not locally available; in one excavated area huge granite blocks were arranged around a 63 sq m space, probably to support temporary shelters of branches, grass and leaves.

At Isampur, covering about 7,200 sq m, siliceous limestone slabs were quarried and worked: the Acheulian material consists mainly of cores, large flakes and debitage, with chopping tools, knives, handaxes, cleavers and scrapers, and hammer stones of quartzite, basalt and chert in very large numbers. Unfinished tools far outnumber finished ones, marking it as a centre of stone tool manufacture and also a habitation site.
The area today supports about 40 types of wild edible plants and plenty of small game, which helps explain the density of occupation.

location.summary: Kalpi, Jalaun district, Uttar Pradesh, on the southern bank of the Yamuna, where the finds lie embedded in a 20 m thick cliff section.

periodLevel.summary: Middle Palaeolithic; the tool-bearing level has been dated to about 45,000 years ago.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Kalpi preserves the earliest trace of human occupation in the Ganga plain, a region where deep alluvium normally conceals or destroys Palaeolithic evidence.
points: Vertebrate fossils recovered here include an elephant tusk and shoulder blade and the molars of Equus and bovids.

The stone tools include pebble tools, points and side scrapers, and were found together with bone tools such as end scrapers, points and burins, an uncommon association in the Indian Middle Palaeolithic.

periodLevel.summary: Middle Palaeolithic, with a later microlithic or Mesolithic presence at the same locality.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the type localities for the Middle Palaeolithic flake industries of southern Karnataka.
points: Finds include handaxes and guillotine chisels.
Mesolithic tools of quartz have also been recovered, showing that the locality continued to be used into the microlithic phase.

location.summary: The Kurnool cave complex, including Muchchatla Chintamanu Gavi and the Billa Surgam caves, Kurnool district, Andhra Pradesh, in the limestone hills of the Nallamalai range.

periodLevel.summary: Upper Palaeolithic, with two electron spin resonance dates of 19,224 BP and 16,686 BP.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Kurnool and Muchchatla Chintamanu Gavi are the only places in the subcontinent where tools made of animal bone have been found in an Upper Palaeolithic context; in one of the caves as many as 90 per cent of the excavated tools were of bone.
points: Animal teeth found in one cave have grooves suggesting they were strung and worn as ornaments; ash deposits show familiarity with fire, and painted rock shelters occur alongside the naturally formed caves.

The faunal list is exceptionally long, including bat, nilgai, four-horned antelope, gazelle, chital, sambar, barking deer, mouse deer, wild boar, tiger, leopard, jungle cat, spotted hyena, civet, freshwater fish, mongoose, sloth bear, porcupine, hare, grey langur, horse, ass, rhinoceros and giant pangolin.
Besides recording the animals that Upper Palaeolithic people shared their landscape with, this range indicates that thick forests and far more humid conditions prevailed in the area than today.

location.summary: Lakhudiyar, on the bank of the Suyal river about 20 km from Almora on the Almora-Barechhina road, Uttarakhand - a rock shelter in the Kumaon hills. The name means "a hundred thousand caves".

periodLevel.summary: Rock paintings assigned broadly to the Mesolithic and later prehistoric periods, with some figures argued to be Chalcolithic. The shelter carries superimposed layers in three colours, the black generally earlier, then red ochre, with white over both.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The principal prehistoric rock art site of the central Himalaya - the northern counterpart to Bhimbetka.
points: The paintings show stick-like human figures holding hands in rows, read as dancing or as a group ritual, along with animals - long-snouted quadrupeds, foxes, lizards - and geometric and wavy patterns.

Human figures greatly outnumber animals, which is the opposite of the pattern at Bhimbetka and in the Vindhyan shelters. That difference is the site's analytical value: Indian rock art is usually discussed through the central Indian material, and Lakhudiyar shows a distinct regional tradition with its own subject preferences.
The three-colour superimposition allows a relative sequence to be worked out even without absolute dates, which is how most Indian rock art is dated.

Other Kumaon and Garhwal shelters - Falseema, Petshala, Kasar Devi - belong to the same group, so the region has a cluster rather than an isolated site, and it should be read with the Garhwal Neolithic settlement at Thapli.

location.summary: Lingsugur, Raichur district, Karnataka, in the Krishna-Tungabhadra doab, close to Maski.

periodLevel.summary: Palaeolithic surface finds, in a tract better known for its Neolithic ash-mound settlements.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: In 1842 Dr Primrose reported stone implements from Lingsugur, the earliest recorded discovery of a prehistoric stone tool in India, some two decades before Robert Bruce Foote picked up the Pallavaram handaxe in 1863.
points: Primrose's find attracted no scholarly follow-up, which is why Foote's Pallavaram discovery is conventionally treated as the starting point of systematic Indian prehistory.

The same tract, at Maski, later yielded the minor rock edict that is one of the very few Ashokan inscriptions to name the emperor as "Ashoka" rather than only by his titles, and the Raichur doab remained a contested frontier between Vijayanagara and the Bahmanis.

location.summary: The Luni valley of western Rajasthan, draining the western flank of the Aravallis towards the Rann of Kutch, across the Nagaur and Jodhpur tract.

periodLevel.summary: Stray finds of Lower Palaeolithic tools, a well-represented Middle Palaeolithic, and a thinner Upper Palaeolithic.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The valley gives its name to the "Luni industry", the term used for Middle Palaeolithic assemblages west of the Aravallis, contrasted with the industry of the Berach and Chittorgarh region to the east.
points: Middle Palaeolithic artefacts are markedly more abundant here than Upper Palaeolithic material.

The decline in the number of Upper Palaeolithic sites reflects increasing aridity in the Thar during the late Pleistocene, when occupation contracted towards permanent water such as the Budha Pushkar lake.
With Didwana and the Budha Pushkar basin, the Luni valley defines the Palaeolithic record of the Thar desert.

periodLevel.summary: Palaeolithic surface finds, in a district whose exposures range back to the Mesozoic Gondwana and Lameta formations.

location.summary: Mandsaur district, western Madhya Pradesh, on the Chambal-Malwa plateau; the Palaeolithic evidence comes from the Daraki Chattan cave in the Indragarh hill.

periodLevel.summary: Lower Palaeolithic, the rock art dated to between 200,000 and 500,000 years ago; the site is also a major non-Ashokan inscription and fort site of the historic and medieval periods.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: At Daraki Chattan more than five hundred pieces of rock art, cup-shaped depressions pecked into the quartzite, have been found together with hammer stones, making it among the oldest rock art sites in India and in the world.
points: With the cupules of the Auditorium Cave at Bhimbetka, these petroglyphs push the origins of symbolic and ritual expression in India back into the Lower Palaeolithic.

Mandsaur, ancient Dasapura, later carried the sixth-century Sanskrit inscription of Yasodharman marking his victory over the Huna king Mihirakula, and a fifth-century inscription of the time of Kumaragupta recording the migration of silk weavers from Lata to Dasapura, who organised themselves into a guild and built a sun temple.
The fort was built by Hoshang Shah of the Malwa Sultanate, was occupied by Rana Sanga in 1519, and was the place where the treaty of 1818 bringing Malwa under British control was signed.

location.summary: Nashik, on the Godavari in northern Maharashtra; the Palaeolithic material comes from the Gangawadi area on the river bank.

location.summary: Nevasa, Ahmednagar district, Maharashtra, on the Pravara river, a tributary of the Godavari; the associated living and factory site of Chirki lies close by. Excavated by H. D. Sankalia of Deccan College.

periodLevel.summary: One mound with two widely separated occupations. The deeper levels carry a stratified Middle Palaeolithic industry, with a uranium-thorium date of about 350,000 BP; above them lies a Jorwe culture Chalcolithic settlement of roughly 1400-700 BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The type site of the Indian Middle Palaeolithic, and one of the principal sources for Chalcolithic burial and belief in the Deccan.
points: Sankalia found Middle Palaeolithic artefacts here in a stratified context for the first time, and the "Nevasan" is accordingly the name given to the Middle Palaeolithic of central and peninsular India. The industry is flake-based, dominated by scrapers of every kind - convex, concave, side, end and angle - with points and borers.

The tools are worked in fine-grained agate, jasper and chalcedony rather than the coarse quartzite of the Lower Palaeolithic, and that shift in raw material is the diagnostic marker of the Middle Palaeolithic in India. Chirki nearby yielded some two thousand tools from a living and factory site.

In the Chalcolithic levels, children were buried in twin urns set mouth to mouth beneath house floors - the characteristic Jorwe practice of keeping the dead within the home rather than in a separate cemetery.

Some child burials at Nevasa and Chandoli carry copper necklaces while others have only pots, a difference read as emerging social inequality. Baked and unbaked female figurines point to a fertility or mother-goddess cult, the unbaked ones apparently made for a single ritual use.
Cotton and semal silk threads from the site show cloth manufacture in Chalcolithic Maharashtra.

location.summary: Odai, Villupuram district, Tamil Nadu, near Tiruvakkarai in the South Pennar tract.

location.summary: Paisra, in the Kharagpur forests near Munger, Bihar, on the northern fringe of the Chhotanagpur plateau; excavated by Pant and Jayaswal (1991).

location.summary: Pallavaram, near Chennai, formerly Madras, Tamil Nadu.

periodLevel.summary: Lower Palaeolithic (Acheulian).

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: In the summer of 1863 Robert Bruce Foote, an officer of the Geological Survey of India on routine survey duty, noticed a stone embedded in a gravel pit here: a seemingly unremarkable piece of brownish quartzite with one end chipped off, which he recognised as a handaxe. It was the first Palaeolithic tool discovered in India.
points: Foote went on to find and study many more stone tools and made major contributions to research on Indian prehistory, earning the title "Father of Indian Prehistory".

The Pallavaram handaxe was not strictly the first prehistoric tool found in India; in 1856 Le Mesurier, a railway engineer, had found a small chert arrowhead near Nyagurhee in central India, and in 1842 Dr Primrose had reported implements at Lingsugur. Foote's find, however, was the one that was followed up.

He travelled to England in 1868 to inform the scholarly community of his work, and in 1873 some of the tools he had discovered were displayed at the International Exhibition at Vienna, so that within two decades the foundations of Indian prehistory had been laid and internationally recognised.

location.summary: Patne, Jalgaon district, Maharashtra, in the Tapi valley.

periodLevel.summary: A stratigraphic sequence of Middle Palaeolithic, Upper Palaeolithic and Mesolithic tools; the ostrich eggshell from the Upper Palaeolithic level is dated to about 25,000 BP.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Patne is the single most important Indian site for Upper Palaeolithic art and personal ornament.
points: A piece of ostrich eggshell engraved with two panels of criss-cross designs was recovered here. Most patterned eggshell fragments from India turn out under the microscope to be naturally weathered; the Patne fragment is clearly engraved by human hands.

Four perforated beads and one incomplete bead of ostrich eggshell, about 10 mm in diameter, came from the Upper Palaeolithic level. Such beads are known from about 41 Indian sites in Pleistocene contexts ranging from 39,000 to 25,000 BP, and from Siberia, inner Mongolia, China and Africa, linking India to a wider Upper Palaeolithic world of bead-making.

A gradual reduction in tool size can be traced here from the late Pleistocene onwards, with microliths of that age, documenting the technological drift from the Upper Palaeolithic into the Mesolithic.

location.summary: The Peshawar valley, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan; the principal site is the Sanghao cave in the hills of the adjoining Mardan district.

periodLevel.summary: Middle and Upper Palaeolithic; occupation is commonly cited at about 30,000 years ago, with radiocarbon dates from Sanghao ranging from 41,825 +/- 4,120 BCE to 20,660 +/- 360 BCE.

Peshawar, as ancient Purushapura, later became the Kushana capital, where Kanishka I is said to have enshrined the Buddha's relics in a stupa that became the centre of a major monastery.

location.summary: The Soan or Sohan river in the Potwar plateau, between the Pir Panjal and the Salt ranges, in the Punjab province of Pakistan.

periodLevel.summary: The Soanian pebble tool tradition of the Lower Palaeolithic, contemporary with the Acheulian, with abundant Middle and Upper Palaeolithic material; Riwat near Rawalpindi has given a palaeomagnetic date of 2.01 million years ago, Dina and Jalalpur in the Jhelum basin about 700,000-500,000 years ago, and site 55 at Riwat 45,000 BP for the Upper Palaeolithic.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The type region of the Soanian industry and the setting of the first systematic palaeo-environmental study in Indian prehistory.
points: In 1935 H. de Terra and T. T. Paterson found a large number of tools here, mostly of the Middle and Upper Palaeolithic with some of the Lower Palaeolithic, and identified five tool-bearing river terraces. The assemblage is dominated by choppers, chopping tools and edged pebble tools rather than handaxes.

They tried to correlate these terraces with a four-fold glacial cycle in Kashmir and further with a four-fold European glacial cycle, and extended the framework to the Narmada and the area around Chennai. Most of their correlations and conclusions are no longer accepted, but the study marked an important stage in the development of Indian prehistoric research.
Fossils of gazelle, rhinoceros, crocodile and giraffe from the region help reconstruct the Pleistocene environment of the north-west.

location.summary: Bagor, Bhilwara district, Rajasthan, on a sand dune beside the Kothari river, a tributary of the Banas - in the eastern Rajasthan plain below the Aravallis.

periodLevel.summary: Three phases excavated by V. N. Misra. Period I, c. 5000-2800 BCE, is Mesolithic; Period II, c. 2800-600 BCE, adds copper; Period III, to c. 200 CE, adds iron. The sequence is continuous, which is unusual and is the site's main value.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The richest microlithic assemblage in India, and the best evidence that Mesolithic communities kept domesticated animals long before they farmed.
points: Some fifty thousand microliths were recovered, in quartz, chert and chalcedony, predominantly geometric - trapezes, lunates and triangles. Finished tools are relatively few against the debitage, which suggests tools were made here and carried elsewhere.

Bones of domesticated sheep, goat and cattle appear in Period I alongside wild fauna. Herding without cultivation is the key point: it breaks the tidy progression from hunting to farming that the three-age scheme implies, and Bagor is the standard citation for it.
Stone-paved floors, hearths and five extended burials with grave goods show a settled or repeatedly reoccupied camp rather than a transient one.
Copper arrowheads in Period II indicate contact with the Chalcolithic settlements at Ahar and Gilund a short distance away - foragers and farmers exchanging goods rather than one replacing the other.

location.summary: Birbhanpur, Barddhaman district, West Bengal, on the left bank of the Damodar river a little west of Durgapur - on old alluvial terraces at the edge of the Chhotanagpur plateau.

periodLevel.summary: A Mesolithic microlithic site excavated by B. B. Lal in 1957-58, generally placed in the earlier Holocene, roughly the 5th millennium BCE, though it is undated by radiocarbon.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The type-site of the Mesolithic in Bengal, and an unusual case of a non-geometric microlithic industry.
points: The tools are blades, points, scrapers and burins on quartz, chert and chalcedony, and are largely *non-geometric* - lacking the trapezes and lunates that dominate at Bagor and in the Ganga plain. Regional variation in microlithic form is the site's main analytical contribution.
It served as both a habitation and a factory site, with cores, debitage and finished tools together, so the whole production sequence is present.
No pottery and no burials were found, which distinguishes it from the Ganga plain sites and suggests either a shorter occupation or a different way of life.
The site was found on a terrace that formed under drier conditions than the present, and it is used with other eastern Indian sites to reconstruct the Holocene climate of the lower Ganga basin.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 2; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; B. B. Lal, *Birbhanpur: A Microlithic Site*

location.summary: The Bundi region of south-eastern Rajasthan, in the Vindhyan sandstone hills of the Chambal basin - rock shelters scattered along the Chambal and its tributaries near Bundi town.

periodLevel.summary: Rock paintings assigned broadly to the Mesolithic and later prehistoric periods, with some estimates of 10,000 to 15,000 years for the earliest layers and historic-period work over them. More than fifty painted shelters have been recorded in the district, many documented by the local researcher Om Prakash Kukki.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The largest concentration of prehistoric rock art in Rajasthan - the western counterpart to the Vindhyan shelters at Bhimbetka.
points: The paintings use red ochre and dark red pigment, with white in later layers, and show hunting scenes, human figures, animals, dancing rows and geometric designs. Superimposition allows a relative sequence even though absolute dates are lacking.
Horse-riders and weapons in the upper layers place some work in the historic period, so the shelters record continuous use across many thousands of years rather than a single prehistoric moment.

The Chambal basin joins the Vindhyan belt at Bhimbetka and the Kaimur shelters to form the largest rock art province in India. Bundi extends that province west and is the evidence that it was not confined to central India.
Microlithic scatters occur in and around the shelters, tying the paintings to the Mesolithic occupation of the region.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 2; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; ASI

location.summary: Damdama, Pratapgarh district, Uttar Pradesh, beside a former oxbow lake in the Ganga plain - the third of the great Mesolithic sites of this tract, with Sarai Nahar Rai and Mahadaha. The record is filed under the spelling *Damdana*.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by J. N. Pal and V. D. Misra. Radiocarbon dates cluster around the 8th-7th millennia BCE, making it among the earlier Mesolithic settlements of the plain, though as at Sarai Nahar Rai the chronology is debated.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The largest Mesolithic cemetery in India, and the site with the best evidence for plant food processing.
points: Forty-one human burials were recovered - more than at any other Indian Mesolithic site. Bodies were laid extended in oblong pits oriented broadly east-west or west-east, singly and in groups, some with elaborate grave goods including an ivory pendant, bone ornaments and antler.

Querns, mullers, anvils and hammer stones were found in quantity, together with charred wild grains and burnt floor plaster. Grinding equipment on this scale shows systematic processing of plant foods by people who were not farming, which complicates any simple line between foraging and agriculture.

Claims of domesticated rice at the site have been made and are not securely established; wild rice in the Ganga plain is well attested, and the honest position is that the grains show intensive use of wild cereals.
Animal bones indicate hunting and fishing across a wide range of species, matching the broad-spectrum pattern of its neighbours.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 2; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; J. N. Pal, *Mesolithic Cultures of the Ganga Valley*

location.summary: Kuchai, Mayurbhanj district, northern Odisha, near Baripada on the Chhotanagpur plateau fringe - lateritic upland between the Subarnarekha and the Baitarani.

periodLevel.summary: A Mesolithic settlement with a Neolithic phase above it, the later levels placed around 1750 BCE. It was the first Mesolithic site reported in Odisha and remains the reference sequence for the region.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The site that established Mesolithic-to-Neolithic continuity in eastern India - a transition visible in one stratigraphy rather than inferred.
points: The lower levels carry microliths on quartz and chert; the upper add ground and polished stone celts, shouldered axes and pottery, without a break in occupation. Communities adopting new technology in place, rather than being replaced, is the point the site is cited for.
The pottery is handmade reddish-brown with a slip and incised decoration, of a kind found across the eastern Indian Neolithic.

The shouldered celts link Odisha's Neolithic to the north-eastern group in Assam and Meghalaya and beyond to Southeast Asia, rather than to the Gangetic or southern Neolithic traditions. That typological link is central to arguments about Austroasiatic-speaking populations in eastern India.
Mayurbhanj's earlier Palaeolithic sites, investigated from the 1870s by V. Ball and later by N. K. Bose and D. Sen, give the district one of the longest investigated prehistoric records in India.

location.summary: Langhnaj, Mehsana district, north Gujarat, on a sand dune between seasonal marshes in the semi-arid plain north of Ahmedabad.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated from the 1940s by H. D. Sankalia and the Deccan College - among the earliest scientific excavations of an Indian prehistoric site. Three phases run from a Mesolithic microlithic occupation of roughly the 3rd millennium BCE into levels contemporary with the Harappan and later periods.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The type-site of the Gujarat Mesolithic, and the standard evidence that foragers and urban societies were in contact rather than sealed off from each other.
points: Fourteen human burials were recovered, laid in crouched position, along with a large geometric microlithic industry in chert, agate and chalcedony, and ring stones and hammer stones.

The faunal assemblage is unusually rich - rhinoceros, wolf, nilgai, blackbuck, chital, mongoose and fish - and shows a wetter environment than the region has now, which is the principal palaeoclimatic evidence for Gujarat in this period.

Copper objects, a Harappan-type ring and wheel-made pottery appear in the upper levels. Hunter-gatherers acquiring metal and urban-made goods is what makes Langhnaj important: the Harappan world is best understood as surrounded by foraging communities it traded with.
Sankalia's work here established the methods and the stratigraphic approach later applied across western India.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 2; Thapar, *Early India*; H. D. Sankalia, *Prehistory and Protohistory of India and Pakistan*

location.summary: Loteshwar, Patan district, north Gujarat, on a sand dune - locally a *tekri* - rising above the plain near the Rupen river, in the semi-arid country between the Little Rann and the Aravalli foothills.

periodLevel.summary: Two periods, excavated by P. Ajithprasad of MS University, Baroda. Period I is Mesolithic, roughly the 6th-5th millennia BCE; Period II belongs to the Anarta tradition, c. 3700-2000 BCE, overlapping the Harappan centuries.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The type-site of the Anarta tradition, and the clearest sequence anywhere in Gujarat from foraging to herding.
points: Period I has a microlithic industry and hearths; Period II adds gritty red ware, fine burnished ware and Anarta pottery, with pits, post-holes and two burials. The two periods on one dune let the shift be watched in a single stratigraphy.
Bones of domesticated sheep, goat and cattle from the lower levels show animal keeping starting early here, as at Bagor and Tilwara in Rajasthan.

The Anarta tradition is the indigenous Chalcolithic of north Gujarat, named from the region's ancient name. Its pottery occurs alongside Harappan wares at sites such as Nagwada and in the later levels here, so Anarta communities were neighbours and trading partners of the Harappans rather than their subjects - the key point for questions on Harappan Gujarat.
Period II pottery shows affinities with Amri-Nal wares of Sindh and with Surkotada in Kutch, tracing the contact routes.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3 and 4; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; P. Ajithprasad, in *Indus Civilization Sites in India*

location.summary: Mahadaha, Pratapgarh district, Uttar Pradesh, on the edge of a silted oxbow lake in the Ganga-Gomti doab, a short distance from Sarai Nahar Rai and Damdama.

periodLevel.summary: A Mesolithic lake-side settlement of roughly the 6th-5th millennia BCE, excavated by G. R. Sharma, J. N. Pal and V. D. Misra. Three functionally distinct areas were identified across the site.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The clearest evidence anywhere in India that a Mesolithic camp was deliberately organised into zones for different activities.
points: Excavation separated a habitation area, a butchering area with concentrated animal bone and burnt patches, and a cemetery. Most prehistoric sites are known only as undifferentiated scatters, so a site where living, processing and burial spaces can be told apart is exceptional evidence for social organisation.

Twenty-eight burials were recovered, including double burials of a man and a woman placed together. Grave goods include microliths, bone arrowheads, antler and bone ornaments, shell beads and ochre - the ornaments suggesting distinctions of status or role.

The skeletons show tall, robust people with excellent dentition and little caries, consistent with a coarse, low-carbohydrate diet, but with osteoarthritis in the joints, pointing to heavy physical labour. Bioarchaeology of this quality is rare in Indian prehistory.
The microliths are geometric, on chert and chalcedony carried in from the Vindhyas, with bone and antler tools worked on site.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 2; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; J. N. Pal, *Mesolithic Cultures of the Ganga Valley*

location.summary: Ratanpura, north Gujarat, a low dune site in the semi-arid plain of the Rupen and Saraswati drainage, in the same sandy tract as Loteshwar and Nagwada.

periodLevel.summary: A Mesolithic and Chalcolithic dune settlement of the Anarta tradition, broadly the 4th-3rd millennia BCE, investigated by MS University, Baroda, as part of the north Gujarat survey programme.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the cluster of north Gujarat dune sites that define the Anarta tradition - the indigenous culture of the region before and during the Harappan period.
points: Note that in the working notes for this book, Ratanpura carries the description written for Loteshwar. The two are separate sites in the same survey region and should not be conflated; Loteshwar is the excavated type-site, Ratanpura one of its neighbours.

The north Gujarat dune sites share a pattern: seasonal camps on *tekris* above the flood plain, microlithic tools continuing alongside Chalcolithic pottery, and bones of domesticated sheep, goat and cattle with wild fauna. They represent mobile herding communities rather than settled villages.

Their significance is regional: Gujarat's Chalcolithic was not simply Harappan. The Anarta tradition, the Padri ware of Saurashtra and the Harappan settlements coexisted, and the dune sites are the evidence for the non-Harappan component.
Systematic survey rather than single-site excavation is what established this picture, which is worth noting as a methodological point.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3 and 4; *Indian Archaeology - A Review*; MS University Baroda, north Gujarat survey reports

location.summary: Renigunta, Tirupati district, Andhra Pradesh, on the Swarnamukhi drainage below the Seshachalam hills - the gap in the Eastern Ghats through which the routes from the Tamil plain reach the Deccan plateau.

periodLevel.summary: An Upper Palaeolithic industry with a Mesolithic phase above it, investigated by M. L. K. Murty. The Upper Palaeolithic of peninsular India is generally placed between about 40,000 and 10,000 years ago, with the microlithic phase following.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A reference site for the Upper Palaeolithic blade-and-burin industry in south India, and for the transition into the Mesolithic.
points: The assemblage is dominated by burins, blades, scrapers and points struck from prepared cores on quartzite and chert - the blade-and-burin technology that defines the Upper Palaeolithic and replaces the earlier flake industries.

Murty's work in this region, including the Kurnool caves nearby, established the south Indian Upper Palaeolithic as a distinct stage, which had been poorly recognised before. Bone tools and ostrich eggshell from related sites in the belt strengthened the case.

The overlying microliths show the technological shift to composite tools with hafted geometric elements. Because both stages occur in one locality, Renigunta is used to argue for local continuity rather than population replacement.
The site sits in the same hill tract as Tirupati, so the entry pairs usefully with the later history of the region.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 2; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; M. L. K. Murty, *Pre- and Protohistoric Andhra Pradesh*

location.summary: Sanganakallu, Ballari district, Karnataka, on granite hills near the Tungabhadra in the Raichur doab - the ashmound country of the southern Deccan, close to Kupgal and within sight of the Hampi hills.

periodLevel.summary: A long sequence from a Mesolithic microlithic phase through the South Indian Neolithic, c. 3000-1200 BCE, into a Chalcolithic overlap. Excavated by B. Subbarao in the 1940s and re-investigated from the 1990s by Korisettar, Fuller and Boivin.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The type-site of the South Indian Neolithic, and the location of stone axe production on an industrial scale.
points: The hills carry dolerite quarries and workshop floors covered in flaking debris where ground and polished stone axes were made in very large numbers - far beyond local need, implying production for exchange across the peninsula. Few Indian sites document craft specialisation this early so clearly.

Circular huts with post-holes on terraced hill slopes, burnished grey, buff and brown pottery, black-and-red ware, terracotta bull and bird figurines, and cattle-dominated faunal remains complete the settlement picture.

Ashmounds nearby - great heaps of vitrified cattle dung - and rock art showing humped cattle on the same hills make the case that the southern Neolithic was organised around cattle, with periodic ritual burning of pens.

Archaeobotany from the recent work identified indigenous millets and pulses - browntop millet, horsegram, mungbean - showing an independent South Indian centre of crop domestication rather than borrowing from the north.

location.summary: Sarai Nahar Rai, Pratapgarh district, Uttar Pradesh, on the bank of a dried oxbow lake in the Ganga plain between the Ganga and the Gomti - lake-margin country that attracted repeated Mesolithic settlement.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by G. R. Sharma of Allahabad University. A radiocarbon determination of c. 8400 BCE is often quoted, though the date is disputed and several scholars place the occupation considerably later, in the 5th-4th millennia BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The first excavated Mesolithic cemetery in the Ganga plain, and the site that produced direct evidence of violence between hunter-gatherers.
points: Eleven burials were found in oblong pits dug inside the habitation area rather than in a separate cemetery - the dead kept among the living, which is the pattern across the Ganga plain Mesolithic.

One skeleton has a bone arrowhead embedded in its rib. It is among the earliest physical evidence of inter-personal violence in South Asia, and is the usual counter to the assumption that foraging societies were peaceable.

The microliths are geometric and very small, worked on chert, chalcedony and agate that had to be brought from the Vindhyas, since the alluvial plain has no stone at all. Raw material moving over long distances is the site's other significant finding.
Animal bones - bison, rhinoceros, stag, fish - and charred remains show a broad-spectrum diet, and some bones were placed in graves.
Read it with Mahadaha and Damdama nearby, which together form the Ganga plain Mesolithic complex.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 2; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; G. R. Sharma, *Beginnings of Agriculture*

location.summary: Selbalgre, West Garo Hills district, Meghalaya, on a hill slope in the Garo uplands of the north-east - the record is filed under the spelling *Sebalgiri*.

periodLevel.summary: A Mesolithic and Neolithic occupation in the Garo hills, broadly Holocene, excavated as part of the north-eastern prehistory programme. The region's Neolithic is generally placed in the 3rd-2nd millennia BCE, with the earlier microlithic phase preceding it.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of very few excavated prehistoric sites in the north-east, and evidence for animal keeping in the hills.
points: Microliths and bones of domesticated cattle were recovered, extending to the north-east the pattern seen at Bagor and Tilwara - foraging communities keeping animals without settled agriculture.

The Garo hills sites, with Daojali Hading in the North Cachar hills, define the north-eastern Neolithic. Its diagnostic tools are shouldered celts and cord-impressed pottery, forms that connect the region to Southeast Asia and southern China rather than to the Indian Neolithic traditions.

That external orientation is the analytical point. The north-east is best understood as the western end of a Southeast Asian cultural province, not as a distant periphery of the Gangetic world, and these sites are the evidence for it.

The region's *jhum* cultivation, and the possibility that root and tuber crops rather than cereals were the first domesticates here, make it important in arguments about multiple independent agricultural origins in South Asia.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; T. C. Sharma, *Prehistoric Archaeology of North-East India*

location.summary: Sundargarh district, north-western Odisha, in the upper Brahmani and Ib valleys on the margin of the Chhotanagpur plateau - hill and forest country bordering Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh. This record is duplicated as *Sudergarh* in the missed-PYQ chapter, and the two should be merged.

periodLevel.summary: A district-wide prehistoric sequence rather than a single site: Palaeolithic and Mesolithic surface industries on the river terraces, painted rock shelters at Ushakothi, Vikramkhol and elsewhere, and Neolithic and later occupation.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the principal prehistoric regions of eastern India, and the source of a famously contested inscription.
points: Microlithic industries on the Brahmani terraces place the district within the eastern Indian Mesolithic, alongside Kuchai in Mayurbhanj, and its rock shelters carry paintings in red ochre and white showing animals, human figures and geometric designs.

The Vikramkhol shelter bears a long line of incised signs which K. P. Jayaswal in 1933 read as a script transitional between the Indus signs and Brahmi. The reading has not been accepted: most scholars regard the marks as natural or as undeciphered scratchings, and no sequence linking Indus signs to Brahmi has been demonstrated. Present it as a rejected hypothesis, because it still circulates in note-sets as established fact.

The surrounding hills are rich in iron ore, worked by local communities long before modern mining, and the district's Munda-speaking populations make it relevant to arguments about the antiquity of Austroasiatic settlement in India.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 2 and 3; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; *Indian Archaeology - A Review*

location.summary: Thenmala, Kollam district, Kerala, on the Kallada river in the Western Ghats - a forested valley on the road over the Ariankavu pass between Kerala and the Tamil plain.

periodLevel.summary: A Mesolithic occupation with wood charcoal dated to about 5000 BCE, among the earliest absolute dates for prehistoric occupation in Kerala. The Ghats interior has yielded far fewer prehistoric sites than the peninsular uplands, so the sequence here is thinly documented.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the few dated Mesolithic sites in Kerala, and evidence that the Western Ghats forests were occupied rather than merely crossed.
points: Wood charcoal and worked wood recovered from the deposits gave the radiocarbon determination. Organic preservation of this kind is rare in Indian prehistory, where almost all dating rests on associated material rather than on the artefacts themselves.

Kerala's prehistory is dominated by the megalithic period - the laterite chambers, umbrella stones and urn burials of the Iron Age - and by the Edakkal petroglyphs in Wayanad. Thenmala pushes occupation of the state back several millennia before those.

The Ghats were long treated as a barrier between the Malabar coast and the Tamil country. Sites in the passes suggest instead that the forest belt was inhabited and that the passes were routes, which matters later for the trade through Muziris and the Palghat gap.
The evidence remains limited, and the honest position is that Kerala's Mesolithic is known from a handful of localities rather than a regional sequence.

location.summary: Tilwara, Barmer district, western Rajasthan, on the bank of the Luni - the only substantial river of the Thar, draining south-west into the Rann of Kutch.

periodLevel.summary: A Mesolithic settlement with two cultural phases, excavated by V. N. Misra. Period I is aceramic with microliths; Period II carries pottery and later material, the sequence running into the historic period.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: With Bagor, the evidence base for animal domestication among Mesolithic communities of western India.
points: The faunal remains include domesticated humped cattle, *Bos indicus*, alongside wild species - goat, canine, pig, spotted deer and hog. Humped cattle at a Mesolithic site in the Thar margin is a significant datum for the Indian domestication of zebu cattle, which is independent of West Asian cattle domestication.
Period I has stone-paved living floors and hearths, with an extensive geometric microlithic industry on locally available chert and chalcedony.

The Luni valley sequence - Tilwara with Bagor to the east - is the framework for prehistoric occupation of the Thar, and matters for reconstructing when and how the desert became arid. The faunal and pollen evidence indicates a wetter early Holocene.
The site is also cited in discussions of how foraging and pastoral ways of life persisted in western Rajasthan long after farming had been established elsewhere in India.

location.summary: The Tirunelveli region of southern Tamil Nadu, on the Thamirabarani river between the Western Ghats and the Gulf of Mannar - the belt of red sand dunes known locally as *teris* stretching towards the coast at Thoothukudi.

periodLevel.summary: Microlithic industries on and within the teri dunes, broadly Mesolithic and running into the later Holocene. Studied by F. E. Zeuner and B. Allchin in the 1950s and 60s, whose work defined the *teri industry*.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The type-region of the teri microlithic industry - the distinctive Mesolithic of the far south.
points: The teris are fossil dunes of red, iron-stained sand formed when the coastline and climate differed from today. Microliths occur both on their surfaces and stratified within them, so the dunes date the industry and the industry dates the dunes - a rare reciprocal control in Indian prehistory.

The tools are worked largely on quartz, which fractures poorly, and the industry is accordingly less refined than the chert-based assemblages of Rajasthan and the Ganga plain. Raw material constraining technology is the clearest lesson of the teri sites.
Their distribution along the palaeo-coastline is used to reconstruct sea-level and shoreline change in the far south during the Holocene.

The same tract later carries Adichanallur, the great urn-burial site, and the Pandya port of Korkai, so the region has an unusually continuous archaeological record from the Mesolithic to the early historic period.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 2; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; B. Allchin, *The Stone-Tipped Arrow*

location.summary: Thoothukudi, on the Gulf of Mannar coast of southern Tamil Nadu - the seaward end of the teri dune belt that runs inland towards Tirunelveli.

periodLevel.summary: Mesolithic microlithic scatters on the coastal teri dunes, part of the same industry defined for the Tirunelveli region and broadly Holocene in date.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A coastal Mesolithic locality, and the point at which the teri dune sites meet the sea.
points: The assemblage is a flake industry worked predominantly on quartz, the only abundant raw material in the tract. Its coarseness relative to the chert industries of northern and western India reflects that constraint rather than any difference in skill.

Coastal sites of this period are scarce in India because Holocene sea-level rise drowned most of the contemporary shoreline. The teri dunes survive because they lie slightly inland of the present coast, which makes them unusually valuable for studying coastal foragers.
The sites are used with the Tirunelveli teris to map shoreline change: their positions mark where the coast stood when they were occupied.

The same stretch of coast later carries the Pandya pearl fishery at Korkai and the port of Kayal, so Thoothukudi's archaeological record runs from Mesolithic foragers to Roman-period pearl exports along one shoreline.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 2; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; B. Allchin, *The Stone-Tipped Arrow*

location.summary: Amri, Dadu district, Sindh, Pakistan, on the west bank of the Indus below the Kirthar range - on the route between the Indus plain and the Baluchistan uplands.

periodLevel.summary: Four periods, excavated by N. G. Majumdar in the 1920s and by Jean-Marie Casal in the 1960s. Period I is the pre-Harappan Amrian culture, c. 3600-3000 BCE; Period II transitional; Period III Mature Harappan; Period IV the post-urban Jhukar phase.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The type-site of the Amri-Nal culture, and one of the few places where the whole sequence from pre-Harappan to post-Harappan is stratified in one mound.
points: Period I has mud-brick houses with small cellular compartments, usually interpreted as storage or granary bases, along with chert blades and stone balls. The compartmented plan anticipates Harappan practice.

Amrian pottery is fine buff ware, largely wheel-made, painted in black and brown with geometric designs - chevrons, chequers, hatched triangles - and with humped bulls and ibex. It defines, with Nal ware, the Amri-Nal complex of Sindh and southern Balochistan.

The value of the sequence is that it shows the Harappan civilisation arriving at Amri as a cultural transformation of an existing settlement rather than as a foundation on empty ground. That is the standard argument against invasion or migration accounts of Harappan origins.
Period IV's Jhukar material, with distinctive pottery and seals, documents what happened after the cities declined - continuity of population with loss of urban form.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Casal, *Fouilles d'Amri*

location.summary: Anjira, in the Surab valley of Kalat district, Balochistan, Pakistan - an upland valley in the Jhalawan region between Quetta and the Makran.

periodLevel.summary: A Chalcolithic settlement of roughly the 4th and early 3rd millennia BCE, excavated by Beatrice de Cardi in 1957. Four periods were distinguished, giving the Kalat-Surab region its ceramic sequence.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The reference sequence for central Balochistan, and a demonstration that prehistoric Balochistan was a mosaic of regional cultures rather than one.
points: Anjira ware and the associated Togau ware, with their distinctive friezes of stylised animals reduced almost to abstraction, define a ceramic province separate from the Amri-Nal complex of the south and the Quetta valley wares of the north.

De Cardi's work is important methodologically: small, carefully stratified soundings at several sites, rather than one large excavation, are what built the Balochistan framework, and much of what is known of the region still rests on that pattern.

The settlements are small stone-and-mud-brick villages in upland valleys, farming with the help of *gabarband* check dams that trapped silt and runoff - an adaptation to a landscape too dry for unaided agriculture.
Balochistan matters in the syllabus as the zone through which the Iranian plateau and the Indus were connected, and as the setting in which the Early Harappan regional cultures developed.

location.summary: Brahmagiri, Chitradurga district, Karnataka, on a granite hill in the dry southern Deccan - in the Maski-Raichur belt where the Mauryan frontier met the peninsula.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by Mortimer Wheeler in 1947. Three periods: I, the South Indian Neolithic or Stone Axe Culture, c. 2000 BCE; II, the Megalithic Iron Age, from about 1000 BCE; III, the early historic Andhra or Satavahana phase. Ashokan Minor Rock Edicts I and II are inscribed on a boulder at the site.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The excavation that established the chronological framework for the whole of south Indian archaeology.
points: Wheeler's three-period sequence gave the south its first stratigraphic chronology, and the terms he defined - Stone Axe Culture, Megalithic, Andhra - organised the field for decades. Whatever has since been revised, Brahmagiri is where south Indian prehistory acquired a spine.

Period I has wattle-and-daub huts on stone-chip floors, ground and polished stone axes, blade microliths and burnished grey pottery, with adults buried extended and children in urns beneath house floors.
Period II brings iron weapons and implements, black-and-red ware with graffiti, shell bangles and beads of terracotta, shell and jasper, with stone cist burials - the classic megalithic package.

The Ashokan edicts are addressed to the *mahamatras* of Isila from the prince at Suvarnagiri and mark the southernmost extent of Mauryan authority. A site with both a Neolithic village and an Ashokan edict lets prehistory and the Mauryan empire be taught from one place.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3 and 7; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Wheeler, *Ancient India* 4

location.summary: Budihal, Kalaburagi (Gulbarga) district, northern Karnataka, on the dry Deccan plateau in the upper Bhima basin - within the ashmound belt.

periodLevel.summary: A South Indian Neolithic settlement of roughly the 2nd millennium BCE, excavated by K. Paddayya of Deccan College across four separate localities within one site.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The excavation that reinterpreted ashmounds as parts of living settlements, and the best evidence in Indian prehistory for communal food sharing.
points: Paddayya exposed a large area rather than a trench, and recovered a functioning settlement plan: an ashmound at the centre formed by cattle penning and dung burning, separate dung disposal areas, living floors, a chert blade workshop on the sandstone boulders nearby, and burials within the habitation.

The most striking feature is a communal butchering floor - a paved area scattered with the bones of cattle, sheep and goat, with blades and choppers, where animals were dismembered and the meat apparently distributed. Organised meat processing on this scale implies collective activity and sharing beyond the household, which is very hard to demonstrate archaeologically.

The work shifted the ashmound debate decisively. Allchin had shown what ashmounds were made of; Paddayya showed where they sat in the life of a community - at the centre of settlements, not apart from them.
Red and grey pottery, ground stone axes, chert blades and bone tools complete the assemblage.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; K. Paddayya, *Man and Environment*

location.summary: Burudih, Singhbhum district, Jharkhand, on the Chhotanagpur plateau in the Subarnarekha basin - lateritic upland country rich in copper and iron ore.

periodLevel.summary: A Neolithic settlement of the eastern Indian tradition, with material that also includes wheel-made pottery and iron slag from the same levels - a compression that has complicated its dating.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A site that illustrates both the eastern Indian Neolithic and the interpretive problem of shallow, mixed deposits.
points: Neolithic celts and microliths occur together with wheel-made pottery and iron slag in what excavators recorded as a single horizon. Either the site was occupied over a long period with little accumulation, or later material has worked down into earlier levels. Thin stratigraphy of this kind is common on the plateau and makes eastern Indian prehistory harder to date than the Ganga plain's.

The honest reading is that Burudih shows a Neolithic community in a region where stone tool use persisted alongside metal, rather than a neat sequence of ages. The three-age scheme fits the plateau poorly.

Singhbhum's copper ores were exploited from the Chalcolithic period - the copper hoards of the Ganga-Yamuna doab are argued to draw on this belt - so the district connects to the wider question of where early Indian metal came from.
The surrounding region remains home to Munda-speaking communities, which is why plateau prehistory features in discussions of Austroasiatic settlement.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; *Indian Archaeology - A Review*

location.summary: Burzahom, about 16 km from Srinagar, Kashmir, on a *karewa* - a raised lacustrine terrace - overlooking the Jhelum valley and the Dal lake.

periodLevel.summary: Four periods, from about 2900 BCE to the early historic era. Period I and II are Neolithic, Period III Megalithic, Period IV Early Historic. Excavated by the ASI from the 1960s.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The most distinctive Neolithic in India - pit dwellings, a great bone industry, and burial practices found nowhere else in the subcontinent.
points: Period I people lived in pits dug into the karewa, narrow at the mouth and widening towards the base, up to 4 m deep, with steps cut into the side, mud-plastered walls and hearths both inside and outside. Pit dwellings are unknown elsewhere in India but common in the Neolithic of northern China and Central Asia, and they are the main evidence for Kashmir's trans-Himalayan connections.
The bone and antler industry - harpoons, needles, awls, points and daggers - is the richest of any Indian Neolithic site, matched only at Chirand.
Dogs were buried with their masters, and wild animals including ibex and wolf were given separate burials. Animal burial of this kind occurs nowhere else in Indian prehistory.
A stone slab engraved with a hunting scene shows two bright objects in the sky, which some read as a record of a supernova. It is a speculative reading and should be given as such.
A Harappan-type pot containing 950 agate and carnelian beads shows contact with the Indus world, and Period III menhirs mark a megalithic phase.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; ASI

location.summary: Chirand, Saran district, Bihar, on the north bank of the Ganga close to its confluence with the Ghaghara - in the fertile middle Ganga plain opposite Patna.

periodLevel.summary: One of the longest continuous sequences in the Ganga valley, running from the Neolithic of about 2500-1500 BCE through Chalcolithic, Iron Age and NBPW levels to the Kushana and Pala periods.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The type-site of the middle Ganga Neolithic, and the possessor of a bone industry rivalled only by Burzahom.
points: Bone and antler tools were recovered in great quantity - points, arrowheads, needles, borers, scrapers and ornaments, many finely polished. That two sites at opposite ends of northern India, Chirand and Burzahom, both specialise in bone while most Indian Neolithic sites do not, is a standing question in the literature.

The crop package is unusually full: rice, wheat, barley, lentil and moong together, showing summer and winter cropping in the same settlement. That combination is the strongest evidence for a developed agricultural regime in the Ganga plain by the later 3rd millennium.

Terracotta figurines of humped bulls, birds and snakes, along with beads of semi-precious stone and steatite, indicate craft production; the pottery includes red, grey, black and black-and-red wares, some with painted linear and geometric designs in ochre.
The continuity of occupation into the historic period makes Chirand valuable for tracing how Neolithic villages of the region became the settlements of the mahajanapada age.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; ASI

location.summary: Daojali Hading, Dima Hasao district - the former North Cachar Hills - of Assam, on a low hill above the Langting valley in the hill country between the Brahmaputra plain and Manipur.

periodLevel.summary: A Neolithic settlement generally placed around 2700-2000 BCE, excavated by T. C. Sharma of Gauhati University in the 1960s. It is the type-site of the north-eastern Neolithic.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The site that placed the north-east in a Southeast Asian rather than an Indian cultural province.
points: The tool kit is dominated by shouldered celts and rounded-butt axes - forms characteristic of southern China, Burma and Southeast Asia and absent from the Indian Neolithic traditions of Kashmir, the Ganga plain and the peninsula. That typology is the basis for treating the north-east as the western end of a Southeast Asian world.
Cord-marked and stamped pottery, made by beating the clay with a carved paddle, reinforces the link: the technique is standard across Southeast Asia and rare elsewhere in India.

Grinding stones, mortars and pestles indicate plant food processing, and jadeite among the stone objects points to contact with sources in Burma or China - long-distance exchange reaching the Assam hills.

No direct evidence of cereal agriculture was recovered, and it has been argued that the region's first cultivation was of roots, tubers and tree crops under *jhum* shifting cultivation - which would leave little archaeological trace. That possibility is worth stating, since it bears on how many independent agricultural origins South Asia had.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3; Thapar, *Early India*; T. C. Sharma, *Prehistoric Archaeology of North-East India*

location.summary: Golbai Sasan, Khordha district, Odisha, on the bank of the Mandakini river in the coastal plain south of Bhubaneswar - between the Eastern Ghats and the Chilika lagoon.

periodLevel.summary: Three periods excavated by the Odisha state archaeology department: Period I Neolithic from about 2300 BCE, Period II Chalcolithic from about 1700 BCE, and Period III an Iron Age phase from about 900 BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The reference sequence for coastal Odisha, and one of the few Indian sites where Neolithic, Chalcolithic and Iron Age levels follow each other without a break.
points: Period I has ground stone celts and bone tools with handmade red and grey pottery; Period II introduces wheel-made ware and copper objects - a chisel, a bangle, a fish-hook and a ring; Period III brings iron.
The bone tool industry is substantial, and includes points and awls comparable to those from Chirand, tying coastal Odisha to the eastern Indian pattern.

Some of the polished stone tools have been interpreted as adzes and gouges suited to woodworking and boat building, and this has been used to argue that the maritime tradition later visible in Odisha's Southeast Asian trade - the *Bali Jatra* memory of voyages to Java and Bali - has prehistoric roots. The inference is plausible but not demonstrated, and should be given as such.
The site's position near Sisupalgarh and Dhauli means the region's record continues unbroken from village farming to Kharavela's Kalinga.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3; Thapar, *Early India*; *Indian Archaeology - A Review*

location.summary: Gufkral, Pulwama district, Kashmir, on a karewa terrace in the Jhelum valley about 41 km south of Srinagar. The name means "cave of the potter".

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by A. K. Sharma. Period IA is aceramic Neolithic, IB and IC ceramic Neolithic, Period II Megalithic and Period III Early Historic - a sequence running from before 3000 BCE into the historic period.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The Kashmir Neolithic with an aceramic phase - farming before pottery, as at Mehrgarh, which makes it the more informative of the two Kashmir sites.
points: Period IA has pit dwellings, storage pits and hearths but no pottery at all, with domesticated sheep, goat and cattle and cultivated wheat, barley and lentil. An aceramic farming phase shows that pottery is not a prerequisite for agriculture - a point the three-age scheme tends to obscure.

The pit dwellings repeat the Burzahom pattern, and the use of pits declines in the later Neolithic as above-ground mud-brick structures take over, so the transition can be watched in one stratigraphy.
Bone and antler tools, steatite beads and terracotta objects were recovered, with handmade pottery in IB giving way to some wheel-made ware later.

The crop package - wheat, barley and lentil - is West Asian, while the pit dwellings are Central Asian and Chinese in affinity. Kashmir's Neolithic drew on both, which is what makes the valley's prehistory distinct from the rest of India.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; ASI
