location.summary: Gumla, Dera Ismail Khan district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, in the Gomal valley where the river leaves the Sulaiman range for the Indus plain - the pass route from Afghanistan into the middle Indus.

periodLevel.summary: Six periods excavated by A. H. Dani. Period I is aceramic, Period II Neolithic, Periods III-IV Early Harappan with Kot Dijian pottery, Period V shows Mature Harappan contact and Period VI belongs to the Gandhara Grave Culture of the early 1st millennium BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A long sequence on one of the main routes between Central Asia and the Indus, covering the whole span from first settlement to the Iron Age.
points: Period II has pit dwellings and hand-made pottery; Period III-IV bring mud-brick architecture, the wheel-made Kot Dijian ware with its distinctive horizontal bands and fish-scale motifs, terracotta figurines and copper.
A burnt layer separates the Early Harappan from the following phase, and was once read as a destruction; as at Rana Ghundai, that interpretation is no longer accepted without corroborating evidence.

Gumla's value is in showing the Gomal valley as an active corridor. Material from Afghanistan and Central Asia reached the Indus this way, and the Gandhara Grave Culture levels at the top mark the later movement of people associated in some accounts with Indo-Aryan speakers - a connection to be stated cautiously.
It is read with Rehman Dheri, a few kilometres away, which gives the same valley's urban phase.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3 and 4; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; A. H. Dani, *Ancient Pakistan*

location.summary: Hallur, Haveri district, Karnataka, on the bank of the Tungabhadra in the northern Karnataka plain - at the western edge of the southern Deccan Neolithic province.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by M. S. Nagaraja Rao. Period I is Neolithic-Chalcolithic, from about 2000 BCE; Period II is an overlap phase in which iron appears, with dates around 1100 BCE; the sequence continues into the Megalithic.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the earliest dates for iron in peninsular India, and the site that established millet farming in the southern Neolithic.
points: Iron objects - arrowheads, spearheads and blades - occur in levels dated to about 1100 BCE, earlier than the conventional 1000 BCE threshold for the Indian Iron Age. Hallur is a principal citation in the argument that iron working began in the peninsula earlier than the Gangetic sequence implies, and that it was not introduced from the north.

The plant remains are equally important: finger millet (*ragi*) and horsegram, with browntop millet. Ragi is of African origin, and its presence here in the 2nd millennium BCE is evidence of contact across the Indian Ocean long before the Roman trade - one of the more striking claims in Indian archaeobotany, and one to state carefully as an inference from crop origins.
Round wattle-and-daub huts with floors of stone chips and river sand, black-quartzite blades, small copper axes and fish-hooks make up the material record.
Cattle bones dominate the fauna, consistent with the pastoral emphasis seen across the ashmound belt.

location.summary: Kili Gul Mohammad, in the Quetta valley of Balochistan, Pakistan, below the Bolan pass. A duplicate record exists in the missed-PYQ chapter under the spelling *Kile Gile Mohammed*, and the two should be merged.

periodLevel.summary: The type-site for the Quetta valley sequence, excavated by Walter Fairservis in the 1950s. Period I is aceramic Neolithic from about the 5th millennium BCE; Periods II-IV carry the successive painted wares - Kili Gul Mohammad, Kechi Beg and Damb Sadaat - running to roughly 2500 BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The ceramic sequence by which the Baluchistan Chalcolithic is dated - the chronological framework for everything preceding the Harappans in the north-west.
points: Period I has mud-brick houses, blade tools, bone points and domesticated sheep, goat and cattle, but no pottery. Aceramic farming horizons are rare in South Asia and occur only here, at Mehrgarh and at Gufkral in Kashmir.

The painted wares of the later periods - black-on-red geometric designs, then the finer Kechi Beg and Damb Sadaat types - give the relative chronology used to correlate sites across Balochistan, Sindh and the Indo-Iranian borderlands.

Read with Mehrgarh, a short distance away and far older, the Quetta valley shows the long local development from early village farming to the regional cultures that fed into the Harappan civilisation. It is the standard evidence against deriving the Harappans from a West Asian migration.
The valley's position at the head of the Bolan explains the Iranian and Central Asian contacts visible in its material.

location.summary: Kunjhun, in the Son valley of Sidhi district, Madhya Pradesh, on a tributary of the Son below the Kaimur escarpment - the Vindhyan uplands south of the Ganga plain.

periodLevel.summary: A prehistoric locality in the Son valley sequence, with Mesolithic microlithic and later Neolithic material. The valley was investigated by the joint Allahabad University and University of California project under G. R. Sharma and J. Desmond Clark.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Part of the Son valley sequence - one of the few places in India where Palaeolithic, Mesolithic and Neolithic occupation can be traced along a single river with dated geological deposits.
points: The Son valley project's importance is methodological. By tying artefact horizons to river terraces, volcanic ash layers and pollen records, it established a framework for the Indian Stone Age that rested on geology rather than on typology alone.

The volcanic ash found in the valley deposits has been identified with the Toba eruption of about 74,000 years ago, giving Indian prehistory a rare absolute marker and a way to test whether human occupation continued across that event.

Kunjhun's microlithic and Neolithic material places it in the later part of that sequence, in the same Vindhyan cultural province as Baghor and the Belan valley sites at Chopani Mando, Koldihwa and Mahagara.
The Vindhyan belt is also where the great painted rock shelters occur, so settlement evidence and rock art can be studied together in one region.

location.summary: Lahuradewa, Sant Kabir Nagar district, eastern Uttar Pradesh, on the bank of an ox-bow lake in the middle Ganga plain north of the river - the record is filed under the spelling *Lahrudeva*.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by Rakesh Tewari for the Uttar Pradesh State Archaeology Department from the late 1990s. Period IA yielded pottery and rice from the 7th millennium BCE, with later periods running through the Chalcolithic and into the NBPW phase.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The strongest current claim for very early rice in India, and the site that reopened the question of an independent Gangetic agricultural origin.
points: Radiocarbon dates of roughly 6400-6000 BCE were obtained for levels containing rice, supported by a sediment core from the adjoining lake showing rice pollen and phytoliths from an even earlier date. Crucially, the evidence comes from lake cores as well as from the mound, which gives it a stratigraphic independence the earlier Belan valley claims lacked.

Whether the rice is fully domesticated or intensively exploited wild rice is still argued, and the honest position is that Lahuradewa demonstrates very early rice *use* in the Ganga plain while the domestication question remains open.

If the dates hold, the middle Ganga plain becomes an independent centre of early agriculture contemporary with Mehrgarh, which would make Indian farming a story of at least two separate origins rather than one spreading east from Balochistan.
The site also produced early handmade cord-impressed pottery, placing ceramic use in the region well before the Harappan period.

location.summary: Mahagara, Prayagraj district, Uttar Pradesh, in the Belan valley where the Vindhyan plateau meets the Ganga plain - a few kilometres from Koldihwa and Chopani Mando.

periodLevel.summary: A Neolithic village excavated by G. R. Sharma of Allahabad University. Radiocarbon determinations cluster around 2000-1600 BCE, though the site is bound up with a much-disputed claim for far earlier dates in the valley.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The clearest direct evidence of cattle penning in the Indian Neolithic, and the centre of the longest-running controversy in Indian prehistory.
points: An enclosure ringed by post-holes contained a compacted surface covered with cattle hoof impressions - a pen whose occupants left their prints in the mud. Direct physical evidence of animal management of this kind is exceptionally rare.
The site has round huts with post-holes, ground stone celts, microliths, bone tools and handmade cord-impressed pottery, with rice husk used as temper in the clay.

Sharma's excavations at neighbouring Koldihwa produced rice-tempered sherds dated to the 7th millennium BCE, which would have made the Belan valley the earliest rice-farming region in the world. The claim has not survived scrutiny: the association between the dated charcoal and the rice levels is insecure, and most specialists now reject the early chronology. Lahuradewa has since taken over as the better-founded case.
Present Mahagara as good evidence for Neolithic pastoralism and as a cautionary tale about dating - both are examinable.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; G. R. Sharma, *Beginnings of Agriculture*

location.summary: Mahishadal, Purba Medinipur district, West Bengal, near the Rupnarayan river in the lower deltaic plain west of the Hooghly.

periodLevel.summary: A Chalcolithic settlement dated to roughly 1600-1400 BCE in its earlier phase, with a later level carrying iron. Excavated as part of the programme that followed Pandu Rajar Dhibi in establishing the Bengal Chalcolithic.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the small group of sites that define the Bengal Chalcolithic, and a good illustration of how early iron reached eastern India.
points: The assemblage includes microliths, bone tools, black-and-red ware, beads of steatite and semi-precious stone, terracotta bangles and a copper celt - a modest Chalcolithic kit consistent with a farming village rather than a centre.

Rice was the staple, as the plant remains and the deltaic setting both indicate, which distinguishes the Bengal Chalcolithic from the wheat-and-barley cultures of the north-west and aligns it with the middle Ganga plain.

Iron appears in the upper levels at a date that, with Malhar and Raja Nala ka Tila in eastern Uttar Pradesh, contributes to the argument that iron was worked in eastern India earlier than the conventional 1000 BCE - a live debate worth citing rather than settling.
Terracotta figurines and objects bearing incised symbolic marks have been recovered, and are used cautiously in discussions of pre-literate sign use.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3 and 5; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; *Indian Archaeology - A Review*

location.summary: Maski, Raichur district, Karnataka, on the Maski river, a tributary of the Tungabhadra, in the Raichur doab - the granite and ashmound country of the southern Deccan.

periodLevel.summary: A long sequence from the Palaeolithic through the South Indian Neolithic and Chalcolithic to the Megalithic Iron Age and early historic periods. Ashoka's Minor Rock Edict I is inscribed on a rock at the site, discovered in 1915 by C. Beadon.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The inscription that identified Ashoka - the single most consequential epigraphic discovery for Mauryan history.
points: All the other edicts call their author *Devanampiya Piyadasi*, beloved of the gods, of pleasing appearance - a title, not a name. The Maski edict is the first found that uses the personal name, reading *Devanampiyasa Asokasa*, and so proved that the Piyadasi of the inscriptions was the Ashoka of the Buddhist chronicles. Without it, the edicts and the literary tradition could not have been securely joined.
Later finds at Gujarra, Nettur and Udegolam confirmed the identification, but Maski was first and is the one to cite.

The archaeology is substantial in its own right: polished stone tools, microlithic blades, a copper rod, dull red and pinkish-buff wares, black-and-red pottery with incised designs, and beads of carnelian, agate, amethyst, chalcedony, shell, coral and glass.

The megalithic phase has pit burials and stone alignments not associated with burials, and rock paintings in the vicinity show horse riders carrying metal axes - imagery belonging to the Iron Age rather than the Neolithic.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3 and 7; Thapar, *Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas*; ASI

location.summary: Mehrgarh, on the Kachi plain of Balochistan, Pakistan, where the Bolan river leaves the hills for the Indus lowland - at the foot of the pass that is the second great route from Iran into South Asia.

periodLevel.summary: Occupied from about 7000 BCE to 2600 BCE, excavated by Jean-Francois Jarrige from 1974. Period I is aceramic Neolithic; Periods II-III add pottery and copper; Periods IV-VII run into the Early Harappan, after which the population shifts to Nausharo nearby.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The earliest farming settlement in South Asia, and the site that settled the question of where Indian agriculture came from.
points: Period I has mud-brick houses divided into small rectangular compartments, domesticated barley and wheat, and, in its later phases, domesticated cattle, sheep and goat - with the evidence showing zebu cattle domesticated locally rather than imported. Farming developing in the Indus borderlands undercuts any account of the Harappan civilisation as a West Asian transplant, and this is the single most important point in the chapter.

Burials are in flexed position in oval pits with grave goods - shell, turquoise and lapis lazuli beads, and in some cases young goats - showing long-distance material reaching a Neolithic village from Badakhshan and the coast.
A cotton thread preserved on a copper bead from the 6th millennium BCE is the earliest cotton anywhere in the world.
Human molars with neat cylindrical drill holes, dated to about 7000 BCE, are the earliest evidence of dentistry known.
Later periods add wheel-made pottery, terracotta female and humped-bull figurines, and compartmented structures read as granaries - the technological package that the Harappans inherit.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3 and 4; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Jarrige, *Mehrgarh: Field Reports*

location.summary: Mundigak, about 55 km north-west of Kandahar in southern Afghanistan, on the Kushk-i-Nakhud river - an oasis mound on the routes linking Iran, Central Asia and the Indus.

periodLevel.summary: Seven periods excavated by Jean-Marie Casal, running from about 4000 BCE to the early 2nd millennium, with later reoccupation. The site's peak is Period IV, in the middle of the 3rd millennium.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A major regional centre outside the Indus system, and evidence that monumental building was not a Harappan monopoly.
points: The lowest levels have no structures at all, only hearths and pits, indicating a semi-nomadic camp that later became permanent - one of the clearer archaeological records of sedentarisation.

Period IV has a large building with a facade of engaged pilasters, usually called the palace, and a massive walled structure read as a temple, on a scale unmatched in the region. Monumental architecture here, contemporary with the Harappan cities, shows comparable social complexity developing along the Helmand and Kandahar routes.
Finds include alabaster vessels, terracotta humped bulls, copper needles and blades, and a carved stone head sometimes compared with the Mohenjo-daro priest-king.
Wheat and ber among the plant remains, with bones of domesticated animals, complete the subsistence picture.
Mundigak is normally studied with Shahr-i-Sokhta in Iran and the Helmand civilisation as part of the world that supplied the Indus with lapis, tin and turquoise.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3 and 4; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Casal, *Fouilles de Mundigak*

location.summary: Sohr Damb, near the village of Nal in Khuzdar district, Balochistan, Pakistan - in a valley of the Jhalawan uplands between the Indus plain and the Makran coast.

periodLevel.summary: A Chalcolithic settlement of roughly the 4th and 3rd millennia BCE, first excavated by Harold Hargreaves in 1925 and re-investigated more recently by a German team. It gives its name to the Nal ware that defines, with Amri, the Amri-Nal cultural complex.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The source of the finest painted pottery in South Asian prehistory.
points: Nal ware is polychrome - a rarity in the subcontinent. A cream or buff slip carries designs outlined in black and then filled with red, blue, yellow and green, in geometric panels and with naturalistic ibex, fish, birds and bulls. Nothing else in Indian prehistory is painted in this many colours, and the technique required firing in stages.

Burials are fractional: bones were defleshed or exposed and the collected remains placed in pots, sometimes with rich grave goods. One child burial included a necklace and a crystal pendant. Fractional burial distinguishes this tradition from the extended inhumations of the Harappans.
Beads of agate, carnelian, crystal and lapis lazuli show the site drawing on Badakhshan and Gujarat sources.

Embankments and channels at the site have been read as water management, appropriate to the *gabarband* tradition of Balochistan, where check dams trapped silt and runoff for cultivation in a dry landscape.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3 and 4; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Hargreaves, *Excavations in Baluchistan*

location.summary: Paiyampalli, Tirupattur district, northern Tamil Nadu, in the dry hill country near the Karnataka and Andhra borders - the southernmost extension of the Deccan Neolithic province.

periodLevel.summary: A South Indian Neolithic settlement with a Megalithic phase above it, broadly of the 2nd millennium BCE, excavated by the ASI. It is among the few excavated Neolithic sites in Tamil Nadu.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The southern limit of the Neolithic cattle-keeping culture, and a key site for the domestication of Indian pulses.
points: Horsegram and green gram (*mung*) were recovered from the Neolithic levels - among the earliest evidence for either crop in India. Both are indigenous South Asian domesticates, and Paiyampalli is a principal citation for the argument that peninsular India was an independent centre of crop domestication alongside the West Asian cereals of the north-west and the rice of the Ganga plain.
Cattle bones dominate the faunal assemblage, showing the same pastoral emphasis as the ashmound sites further north, though no ashmound occurs here.
Ground and polished stone axes, blade tools and burnished grey ware place it firmly in the southern Neolithic tradition rather than in any separate Tamil sequence.
The Megalithic levels above, with iron and black-and-red ware, connect the site to the Iron Age culture that spreads across Tamil Nadu and is the immediate background to the Sangam age.
Tamil Nadu's prehistory is otherwise dominated by the megaliths and by the Palaeolithic at Attirampakkam, so a Neolithic village here fills a real gap.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; *Indian Archaeology - A Review*

location.summary: Palavoy, in the Anantapur region of Andhra Pradesh, on the dry Rayalaseema plateau in the Penna basin - the eastern part of the southern Deccan ashmound belt.

periodLevel.summary: A South Indian Neolithic site with four ashmounds, and a later Megalithic phase. It belongs to the same cultural horizon as Utnur, Piklihal, Kupgal and Budihal, broadly the 3rd and 2nd millennia BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: An ashmound cluster, and the evidence that these were regional gathering places rather than single-village features.
points: Four ashmounds at one locality is unusual. Most sites have one, and the concentration here has been read as marking a regional centre where herds from a wider area were brought together - for seasonal grazing, for exchange, or for the collective ceremonies that the dung burning seems to represent.

That reading bears on the long-running question of whether the ashmounds are functional or ritual. The evidence from Utnur and Budihal shows they are physically the residue of cattle pens; the scale and repetition at sites like Palavoy suggest the burning was also ceremonial. Both can be true, and the sensible answer holds them together rather than choosing.
The Megalithic remains above show the same landscape reused by Iron Age communities, as at Maski and Brahmagiri.

The ashmound belt runs across Karnataka, Telangana and Rayalaseema, and its distribution maps the extent of the southern Neolithic cattle economy - the single most distinctive feature of prehistoric peninsular India.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; *Indian Archaeology - A Review*

location.summary: Pandu Rajar Dhibi, Barddhaman district, West Bengal, on the bank of the Ajay river in the Rarh plain west of the Bhagirathi - the name means "the mound of King Pandu".

periodLevel.summary: A Chalcolithic settlement excavated by P. C. Dasgupta from 1962, with four periods running from roughly 1500 BCE into the early historic era. Period I is Chalcolithic; Period II adds iron.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The type-site of the Bengal Chalcolithic, and the first excavation to establish that Bengal had a pre-iron settled culture at all.
points: Before this excavation, Bengal's archaeological record effectively began with the historic period. Pandu Rajar Dhibi pushed it back more than a thousand years and created the Chalcolithic framework into which Mahishadal, Mangalkot and Bharatpur were later fitted.

Period I yielded microliths, ground stone tools, bone tools, and black-and-red ware with painted designs; Period II added beads of semi-precious stone, terracotta figurines, copper and then iron with slag and ovens.

Burials were found in the habitation area, extended and with grave goods, and the excavator argued from the bead and copper material that the settlement traded over long distances - an interpretation that has been questioned as over-reading a modest assemblage.

The site's identification with the Mahabharata is folk etymology and carries no historical weight; it is worth naming as an example of how epic names attach themselves to mounds across northern India.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3 and 5; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; ASI

location.summary: Piklihal, Raichur district, Karnataka, on granite hills near the Krishna in the Raichur doab - in the same ashmound belt as Maski, Kupgal and Budihal.

periodLevel.summary: A South Indian Neolithic settlement dated from about 2700 BCE, excavated by F. R. Allchin, with a Megalithic Iron Age phase above. Allchin's work here and at Utnur established the southern Neolithic as a distinct culture.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the two sites on which the interpretation of the southern Neolithic as a cattle-keeping culture was built.
points: Allchin distinguished settlement areas from ashmound areas and argued that the ashmounds were the burnt residue of cattle pens - the thesis confirmed by his excavation at Utnur and refined later at Budihal.

The settlement has circular huts, microlithic blades, ground stone axes, and a range of pottery - handmade grey burnished ware, black, buff and red-brown wares - along with terracotta figurines of humans, cattle and birds.

Rock paintings and bruisings on the surrounding granite show humped cattle, human figures and, in later layers, horse riders carrying metal axes. The cattle imagery belongs with the Neolithic occupation; the riders belong to the Iron Age, and separating the two is essential when the art is used as evidence.
Iron appears early in the sequence here, contributing to the argument that the southern Deccan worked iron by the early 1st millennium BCE or before.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; F. R. Allchin, *Piklihal Excavations*

location.summary: Rana Ghundai, Loralai district, north-eastern Balochistan, Pakistan - a mound in a valley of the Toba Kakar ranges on the route between the Zhob valley and the Indus.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by Brigadier E. J. Ross in 1946. Five phases, RG I to RG V, spanning roughly the 4th to the 2nd millennia BCE - the first stratified prehistoric sequence established anywhere in Balochistan.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The excavation that gave Balochistan its first chronology, and the origin of a long-running argument about destruction levels.
points: RG I produced bones of oxen, ass and sheep with no structures, read as a camp of semi-nomadic herders. RG II introduces pottery painted with friezes of humped bulls; RG III black-on-red designs with ibex and antelope. The bull and ibex friezes are the diagnostic motifs of the region.

Ross identified burnt layers between phases and interpreted them as destructions by invaders, an argument taken up by Mortimer Wheeler in support of his reading of the end of the Harappan civilisation. That interpretation has since been abandoned: burnt layers at village sites usually record accidental fire or rebuilding, and there is no supporting evidence of conflict.

The episode is worth citing as an example of how mid-twentieth-century archaeology reached for invasion to explain change in the material record, a habit that also produced the Aryan invasion reading of Mohenjo-daro.
The Zhob valley figurines from nearby sites belong to the same cultural province.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3 and 4; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Ross, *A Chalcolithic Site in Northern Baluchistan*

location.summary: Rehman Dheri, Dera Ismail Khan district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, on the west bank of the Indus near the mouth of the Gomal valley.

periodLevel.summary: An Early Harappan town of about 3300-2100 BCE, excavated by Farzand Ali Durrani. Three periods; the settlement covers roughly 22 hectares and is enclosed by a boundary wall.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the earliest planned settlements in South Asia - laid out on a grid several centuries before the Mature Harappan cities.
points: The town is rectangular, oriented broadly north-south, divided by a central street with subsidiary lanes at right angles and houses in regular blocks, the whole within a wall. Because this precedes Mohenjo-daro and Harappa by centuries, it shows that town planning was an Early Harappan development that the cities inherited rather than invented - the key point the site is cited for.
Kot Dijian pottery with graffiti and potter's marks was found in quantity, along with beads of lapis lazuli and turquoise brought from Afghanistan and Iran.

A bone or ivory seal with incised signs, including what appear to be a scorpion and other motifs, is among the earliest seals from the region and is used in discussions of the origins of the Indus script.
The site was never built over by a Mature Harappan town, so its Early Harappan plan survives uncomplicated - the reason it is more legible than Kot Diji or Kalibangan for this period.

location.summary: Sarai Khola, in the Taxila valley of Punjab, Pakistan, on the Potwar plateau close to the later city sites of Bhir Mound and Sirkap.

periodLevel.summary: Four periods excavated by the Pakistan Department of Archaeology. Period I is Neolithic, from about the 4th millennium BCE; Period II is Early Harappan with Kot Dijian pottery; Period III belongs to the Gandhara Grave Culture; Period IV is early historic.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The only site that carries the Taxila region from its Neolithic beginnings through to the historical city - a four-thousand-year sequence in one mound.
points: Period I has hand-made plain red and brown burnished pottery, ground and polished stone celts, blades, microliths and a large number of bone points, with pit dwellings. Its affinities are with the Kashmir Neolithic at Burzahom rather than with Balochistan, which places the Potwar plateau in a northern rather than a western cultural sphere.
Period II shows the transition from pit dwellings to mud-brick houses and the arrival of wheel-made Kot Dijian pottery - a technological and architectural shift visible in a single stratigraphy.
Terracotta wheels and toy carts from the site are among the earlier evidence for wheeled transport in the subcontinent.

The Period III graves, with their crouched and cremated burials, belong to the Gandhara Grave Culture of the early 1st millennium BCE, and the sequence is therefore also used in discussions of Indo-Aryan movement into the north-west.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3 and 4; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; A. H. Dani, *Ancient Pakistan*

location.summary: Sarutaru, Kamrup district, Assam, on a low hillock in the Brahmaputra valley about 25 km from Guwahati - in the plain rather than the hills, unlike most north-eastern Neolithic sites.

periodLevel.summary: A Neolithic occupation broadly of the 2nd millennium BCE, excavated by T. C. Sharma. Its material connects it to the Daojali Hading group in the hills to the south.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The Neolithic of the Brahmaputra plain, showing that the north-eastern tool tradition extended out of the hills onto the valley floor.
points: Shouldered celts and round-butted axes occur here as at Daojali Hading, together with cord-marked pottery, so the same technological province covers hill and plain.
The site produced wheel-made pottery in fine kaolin clay, which is unusual for a Neolithic context in the region and suggests either a later phase or contact with more developed ceramic traditions.

The Brahmaputra valley's archaeology is thin because the river's shifting course and the deep alluvium bury or destroy sites, so the few excavated localities carry disproportionate weight. Sarutaru and Daojali Hading together are essentially the whole excavated basis for the north-eastern Neolithic.

The region's later history - the Varman kings of Kamarupa at Pragjyotishpura, the Da-Parbatia doorframe at Tezpur - begins many centuries after these settlements, so the gap between prehistory and history in Assam is largely unfilled.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3; Thapar, *Early India*; T. C. Sharma, *Prehistoric Archaeology of North-East India*

location.summary: Senuwar, Rohtas district, Bihar, in the Son valley at the foot of the Kaimur hills - on the southern edge of the middle Ganga plain, near Sasaram.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by B. P. Singh of Banaras Hindu University. Period IA is Neolithic, from about 2200 BCE; IB adds more crops and better pottery; Period II is Chalcolithic, c. 1300-700 BCE; Period III Iron Age with NBPW.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The best-dated and most thoroughly sampled Neolithic sequence in the middle Ganga plain - the reference against which the disputed Belan valley dates are judged.
points: The archaeobotany is the site's chief contribution. Period IA yielded rice, barley and field pea; IB adds wheat, lentil, and later millets, sesame and horsegram. Rice cultivated alongside the West Asian winter cereals in one village shows the two agricultural traditions meeting in the Ganga plain rather than remaining separate.

Because the samples were systematically floated and the levels radiocarbon dated, Senuwar's chronology is secure where the earlier claims from Koldihwa and Mahagara are not. It is the site to cite when the origins of Indian rice cultivation are at issue.
Circular and rectangular houses, ground stone celts, bone tools, microliths, and red, black-and-red and burnished grey wares make up the material record.
Its position at the junction of the Vindhyan uplands and the plain explains the mix: Vindhyan stone, Gangetic rice and West Asian cereals all present in one settlement.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; B. P. Singh, *Early Farming Communities of the Kaimur*

location.summary: Sohgaura, Gorakhpur district, Uttar Pradesh, on the bank of the Rapti in the eastern Ganga plain - in the territory of the ancient Malla and Kosala janapadas.

periodLevel.summary: A mound with early occupation, but known almost entirely for the Sohgaura copper plate: a small bronze plaque bearing four lines in Prakrit in Brahmi, generally assigned to the Mauryan period and argued by some to be pre-Ashokan.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the two earliest Brahmi records in India, and the oldest documentary evidence of state famine relief anywhere in the subcontinent.
points: The plate is an order issued by the *mahamatras* of Shravasti concerning storehouses at Manavasiti and other places. It directs that the stores of grain be used in an emergency and not withheld - an administrative instruction about relief in time of drought, not a royal eulogy.

Its significance is that it shows the Mauryan state in ordinary operation. Almost everything else known of Mauryan administration comes from Ashoka's edicts or from the *Arthashastra*; here is a working order about granaries, comparable in kind to the Mahasthan inscription from Bengal.
The plate carries symbols above the text, including what appear to be storehouses on posts, a tree in railing and a taurine mark - pictorial administrative notation, unusual in Indian epigraphy.

Whether it predates Ashoka is disputed. If it does, it would show Brahmi in official use before his reign and weaken the argument that Ashoka's chancery introduced writing to India. Present the dating as contested.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*

location.summary: Tekkalakote, Ballari district, Karnataka, among granite hills near the Tungabhadra in the Raichur doab - about 40 km from Hampi, in the ashmound and rock art country. A duplicate record exists in the rock-cut caves chapter under the spelling *Tekkalakota*.

periodLevel.summary: A South Indian Neolithic settlement of roughly 2000-1200 BCE with a Chalcolithic overlap, excavated in the 1960s by M. S. Nagaraja Rao and K. C. Malhotra.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A Neolithic hill settlement that produced gold - the earliest worked gold in the peninsula.
points: Gold objects were recovered from the Neolithic levels. The southern Deccan holds India's principal gold sources at Kolar and Hutti, both within reach of this site, and Tekkalakote is the evidence that they were being exploited in the 2nd millennium BCE. Lead-isotope studies matching gold from northern sites to southern ores rest on this kind of association.

The settlement occupies granite terraces with circular huts of mud and post construction, ground stone axes, blade tools and burnished grey and buff pottery, with copper and bronze in the later levels.
Burials occur under house floors, in pits and urns, with grave goods - the pattern also seen at Brahmagiri and Piklihal, in which the dead remain within the settlement.

Rock paintings and bruisings on the same outcrops show humped cattle and human figures. Because the habitation and the art are on the same hills and broadly contemporary, the paintings can be tied to an identified community, which is rare for Indian rock art.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Nagaraja Rao, *Excavations at Tekkalakota*

location.summary: Utnur, Adilabad district, Telangana, on the Deccan plateau in the upper Godavari basin - in the northern part of the ashmound belt that runs across the southern Deccan.

periodLevel.summary: A South Indian Neolithic ashmound excavated by F. R. Allchin in 1957, with radiocarbon dates in the 3rd millennium BCE. The excavation is the decisive one for understanding what ashmounds are.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The dig that settled a century of speculation about the Deccan ashmounds.
points: Ashmounds - great heaps of grey vitrified material, some many metres high - had been explained as volcanic, as meteoritic, as iron-smelting slag and as the residue of brick kilns. Allchin's excavation at Utnur found post-holes marking a substantial wooden stockade enclosing an area filled with accumulated cattle dung, burnt and reburnt over long periods.

Ashmounds are therefore cattle pens whose dung was periodically fired, probably as a seasonal ritual and practically to control parasites and clear the ground. The interpretation is now standard, and Utnur is the evidence for it.

The finding transformed the picture of the southern Neolithic from one of settled cereal farmers into one of cattle-keeping communities for whom herds were both wealth and religious focus - a reading supported by the cattle imagery in the rock art at Kupgal and Piklihal.
The site also produced ground stone axes, blade tools and handmade coarse pottery.
Later work by Paddayya at Budihal refined this by showing ashmounds as components of settlements rather than isolated monuments.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3; Thapar, *Early India*; F. R. Allchin, *Neolithic Cattle-Keepers of South India*

location.summary: Ahar, on the outskirts of Udaipur, Rajasthan, on the Ayad (Berach) river in the Banas system; the ancient name of the site was Tambavati, "the place that has copper". Excavated in 1953-54 and 1961-62.

periodLevel.summary: Type site of the Ahar or Banas culture, dated about 2100-1500 BCE. Period I is divided into phases Ia, Ib and Ic, with earliest calibrated dates of about 2500 BCE, 2100 BCE and 1900 BCE, and fifteen building phases identified.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The type site of one of the three great Chalcolithic cultures of Rajasthan, and the clearest Indian evidence of a Chalcolithic community practising copper smelting from the very outset.
points: The diagnostic pottery is a black-and-red ware with linear and dotted designs painted on in white; the site also produced the lustrous red ware of Rangpur type in Period Ic.

Copper objects are abundant: rings, bangles, antimony rods, a knife blade and four socketless axes, with copper sheet and slag showing that smelting was done locally. Unlike other Chalcolithic farming cultures, Ahar used virtually no microlithic tools and stone axes or blades are almost absent, because copper ore was locally available.

Ordinary houses were of mud on stone foundations, with walls strengthened by bamboo screens or quartz nodules and floors of black clay mixed with yellow silt; multiple-mouthed ovens were found, and one house was over 10 m long. Rice grains and bones of cow, buffalo, goat, sheep, deer, pig, fish, turtle and fowl were identified.

An iron ring and nail occurred in Period Ib and iron objects are common in Period Ic; whether these levels were intact or disturbed is debated, but this may be one of the earliest occurrences of iron in the subcontinent.

Etched carnelian beads, a lapis lazuli bead and Rangpur-type lustrous red ware point to contact with the Harappan sites of Gujarat; over 90 Ahar culture sites are known in the Banas and Berach systems, roughly between Udaipur and Jaipur.

location.summary: Balathal, Udaipur district, Rajasthan, in the Banas-Berach river system; excavated between 1994 and 1998.

periodLevel.summary: An Ahar (Banas) culture site of about 2 hectares. Calibrated dates place the protohistoric settlement in the late 4th millennium BCE, making it contemporary with the early Harappan phase at Kot Diji and as early as the Ganeshwar-Jodhpura culture of north-east Rajasthan.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Balathal is the Chalcolithic site that overturned the assumption that fortification and planned building were Harappan monopolies, since it produced a massive defensive wall in a purely non-Harappan village culture.
points: In the early phase of Period I there were small circular wattle-and-daub huts with mud-plastered floors and two plastered storage pits. In the later phase a massive mud fortification wall stood in the centre of the mound, reinforced in places with stone and with clear evidence of bastions; the walls ranged from 4.8 m to over 5 m wide and enclosed an area of over 500 sq m. A street 2 to 4.8 m wide running north-west to south-east, and a small lane, were exposed.

Houses in the second phase were larger rectangular units of mud, mud-brick and stone on stone foundations, in three multi-roomed complexes with identifiable kitchens and storage areas; two potters' kilns were also found.

The pottery includes thin red, tan, black-and-red and buff wares and a distinctive reserve slip ware, in which a thin red wash was covered with a thick dark red slip and combed while still wet. Copper artefacts are plentiful - choppers, knives, razors, chisels and barbed and tanged arrowheads - while stone microliths and blades are very few.

Of the large quantity of animal bones, wild animals account for only 5 per cent; cattle alone make up almost 73 per cent of the faunal remains. Plant remains include wheat, barley, at least two millets, black gram, moong, pea, linseed and jujube, stored in bins and ground on querns, with bread probably cooked on flat pans over u-shaped chulhas of the kind still used in the village.

location.summary: Bangarh, near Gangarampur in Dakshin Dinajpur district, West Bengal, in the Punarbhaba valley of the Bengal plains; identified with the ancient city of Kotivarsha.

periodLevel.summary: A long sequence whose lowest levels carry a pre-urban Chalcolithic occupation, followed by the Northern Black Polished Ware phase; the brick rampart can be assigned to the 2nd century BCE, and occupation continues into the early medieval period.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The principal excavated urban site of northern Bengal, and the main evidence that the Gangetic urban tradition extended east of Bihar.
points: Excavation revealed a settlement of some 1800 by 1000 feet enclosed by fortifications, with NBPW in the early historic levels.
It lay within the networks connecting the Bengal plains with Bihar, Tibet and the Brahmaputra valley of Assam, which explains its growth as a trading and administrative centre.

As Kotivarsha it served as an administrative headquarters (a vishaya centre) under the Guptas and later dynasties, and the site anchors the archaeological sequence of northern Bengal alongside Mahasthangarh in Bogra and Chandraketugarh in the 24 Parganas.

location.summary: Daimabad, on the left bank of the Pravara, a tributary of the Godavari, in Ahmednagar district, Maharashtra.

periodLevel.summary: A five-fold sequence covering the Savalda culture, a late Harappan phase (Period II), the Malwa culture and the Jorwe culture. At about 20 hectares it is the largest of the roughly 200 known Jorwe sites, and could have held around 4,000 people.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The largest Chalcolithic settlement of the Deccan, which with Inamgaon shows Jorwe society approaching an urban threshold; it is most famous for its bronze hoard.
points: The celebrated bronzes comprise a man standing on a chariot drawn by two bulls, a water buffalo, an elephant and a rhinoceros, solid-cast and together weighing about 60 kg; some show Harappan influence.

The settlement seems to have been fortified with a mud wall carrying stone rubble bastions. There were mud houses, some large and multi-roomed, with hearths, storage pits and jars, sometimes with courtyards in front, and a lane has been traced in one place.

Excavations yielded microliths, bone and stone artefacts, beads of shell, carnelian, steatite and terracotta, a phallus-shaped object of agate found inside a house, an elephant tusk and black-on-buff cream ware. Plant remains include wheat, barley, pea, lentil, black gram and green gram.

Pit burials, urn burials, symbolic burials and post-cremation burials all occur. The late Harappan Period II produced an extended grave lined with mud bricks, a fine red ware with linear and geometric designs painted in black, two button-shaped seals carrying Harappan writing and inscribed potsherds, which together make Daimabad the southernmost Harappan-related site known.

location.summary: Eran, Sagar district, Madhya Pradesh, on the Bina river, a tributary of the Betwa, in the Malwa-Bundelkhand borderland; ancient Airikina.

periodLevel.summary: Period I, roughly 1800-700 BCE, is Chalcolithic and belongs to the Malwa culture sequence; the site was among the earliest Chalcolithic settlements of central India and was fortified. Later occupation runs through the Saka and Gupta periods.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Eran combines an early fortified Chalcolithic village with one of the most important epigraphic sequences of the Gupta age, which is why it appears in two syllabus categories at once.
points: The Chalcolithic levels yielded stone and copper implements and Ochre-Coloured Pottery, and the settlement at Eran, like Kayatha, was established early in comparison with those of western Maharashtra and eastern India.
An inscription of about 339-368 CE is attributed to the Saka king Sridharavarman, and the site also carries an inscription of Samudragupta.
The Bhanugupta inscription of 510 CE records the death in battle of the chief Goparaja and the self-immolation of his wife, and is generally read as the earliest epigraphic record of sati in India.
Eran also preserves a colossal Varaha (boar) image inscribed in the reign of Toramana and a Vishnu pillar of the time of Budhagupta dated 484-85 CE.

location.summary: Ganeshwar, near Nim-ka-Thana in Sikar district, north-eastern Rajasthan, on the Kantli-Sahibi drainage, close to the copper ores of the Khetri belt.

periodLevel.summary: Type site, with Jodhpura, of the Ganeshwar-Jodhpura culture. Three cultural phases: Period I from about 3800 BCE, Period II from about 2800 BCE and Period III from about 2000 BCE, so the deposits largely predate the mature Harappan phase.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A small site of only 1.2 to 1.6 hectares that yielded hundreds of copper objects, marking it as a specialised copper-working centre supplying communities far beyond itself, probably including the Harappans.
points: Period I reflects a hunting-gathering community using microliths of chert and quartz, with charred bones almost all of wild animals. Period II saw the beginning of metallurgy, with a few copper objects - five arrowheads, three fishhooks, a spearhead and an awl - and people living in circular huts with floors paved with pebbles and rock fragments.
Period III is dominated by hundreds of copper objects of many types, arrowheads, spearheads, celts, chisels, rings, bangles and balls, with a corresponding decline in microliths and animal bones.

The typical pottery is a fine, wheel-made, orange to red ware with incised designs, including dish-on-stand with a thick slip; Ganeshwar-Jodhpura ware itself is poorly fired, made of micaceous clay with a bright red slip.

Harappan pottery occurs on the surface at two Ganeshwar culture sites, a reserved slip ware here is otherwise known in Harappan contexts only at Banawali and a few other places, and double spiral-headed pins from Ganeshwar recur at Harappan sites. Over 80 sites of this culture are known, concentrated in Sikar with others in Jaipur and Jhunjhunu districts. Curiously, no direct evidence of smelting - furnaces or crucibles - has been reported.

location.summary: Gilund, Rajsamand district, Rajasthan, in the Banas valley; about 10.5 hectares in extent. Excavated in 1959-60 and again by a Deccan College team in the early 2000s.

periodLevel.summary: An Ahar or Banas culture site, broadly 2100-1500 BCE, regarded as a regional centre of that culture.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Gilund is the Banas culture site that has produced the most substantial architecture, and evidence that has been read as pointing to contact with Central Asia.
points: The structural remains include a large mud-brick complex measuring about 30.48 by 24.38 m, and part of a wall of burnt bricks resting on a foundation of stone rubble - an unusually early use of burnt brick, around 1500 BCE, in a culture that generally did not use it.
A series of storage pits or bins was found, along with microliths, fragments of copper, and beads of semi-precious stones; unlike Ahar, Gilund had a stone blade industry.

Terracotta gamesmen and animal figurines, including humped bulls with long horns, were recovered; stylised bull terracottas in Malwa and Rajasthan are taken to show that the bull was the symbol of a religious cult.

A group of seal impressions recovered by the Deccan College excavations shows designs comparable to those of the Bactria-Margiana complex of Central Asia, which has been used to argue for long-distance contact.

location.summary: Gungeria, Balaghat district, Madhya Pradesh, in the Satpura uplands of the upper Wainganga basin.

periodLevel.summary: Chalcolithic, belonging to the Copper Hoard horizon of central India.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Gungeria produced the largest copper hoard ever found in India: 424 copper tools and weapons together with 102 thin sheets of silver objects.
points: The silver sheets are the single largest find of silver from a protohistoric Indian context, and the hoard's scale suggests either a merchant's stock, a votive deposit or the accumulated wealth of a community.

Copper hoards are distributed from West Bengal and Odisha in the east to Gujarat and Haryana in the west, and from Andhra Pradesh to Uttar Pradesh, but the largest concentration is in the Ganga-Yamuna doab; Gungeria is the outstanding find outside the doab.

The objects - flat celts, harpoons, antennae swords and anthropomorphic figures - served varied purposes, and the debate over whether they were tools, weapons or ritual objects, and over the identity of the people who made them, remains unresolved.

location.summary: Imlidih Khurd, on the banks of the Kuwana river in Gorakhpur district, Uttar Pradesh, in the trans-Sarayu part of the middle Ganga plain.

periodLevel.summary: Period I represents the pre-Narhan culture and goes back to about 1300 BCE; Period II belongs to the Narhan culture and is dated about 1300-800 BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The site provides the clearest evidence that a two-crop agricultural regime was already established in the trans-Sarayu plain in the first half of the 2nd millennium BCE.
points: Period I yielded a crude, handmade cord- or mat-impressed red ware, with spherical and pedestalled bowls, vases with flaring rims and handi-like and spouted vessels; there were wattle-and-daub houses, a storage pit 1.95 m across, a circular bin-like structure and ovens.

The plant remains are extremely varied - rice, barley, bread wheat, dwarf wheat, jowar, bajra, lentil, moong, field pea, grass pea, mustard and sesame, along with seeds of wild jujube, anwala and grape.
Faunal remains include domesticated cattle, sheep or goat and pig, with cattle bones the most numerous and bearing cut marks, plus freshwater turtle, fish and molluscs.

Period II saw intense structural activity with at least two successive mud floors, post-holes and ovens, and the white-painted black-and-red ware typical of Narhan, together with bone points, pottery discs, terracotta beads, a copper arrowhead, two copper beads and curious terracotta pedestals possibly used for ritual.

location.summary: Inamgaon, on the Ghod river, a tributary of the Bhima, in Pune district, Maharashtra; excavated over 1968-83 by H. D. Sankalia, M. K. Dhavalikar and Z. D. Ansari.

periodLevel.summary: A Chalcolithic sequence covering the Malwa and Jorwe phases, with the later Jorwe phase dated about 1300-1000 BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The most completely excavated Chalcolithic village in India, and the site on which almost all reconstructions of Chalcolithic social organisation, craft specialisation and religion are based.
points: Inamgaon was a large settlement of over a hundred houses with numerous graves, fortified and surrounded by a moat. In the earlier phase there were large mud houses with ovens and circular pit houses; in the later phase a house of five rooms, four rectangular and one circular, stood at the centre of the settlement and may have belonged to a chief, with a granary close by that may have stored tribute in kind.

Craft specialisation is unusually visible: besides farmers there were potters, smiths, ivory carvers, lime makers and terracotta artisans, and the craftsmen lived on the western fringe while the chief probably lived at the centre, a spatial pattern read as social distance.

The early Chalcolithic farmers obtained their food by farming, hunting and fishing; X-ray diffraction analysis of pottery indicates that Inamgaon supplied earthen pots to Walki, 27 km away, direct evidence of inter-village exchange.

A headless female figurine, comparable to mother goddess figures of western Asia, was recovered; the dead were buried in urns beneath house floors in a north-south position, an adult being buried with pottery and some copper, and there were no separate cemeteries as among the Harappans.

Plant and animal remains indicate the onset of an extremely arid phase around 1000 BCE which forced the farmers to abandon their homes and take to pastoral nomadism, the clearest Indian case of climate-driven settlement collapse.

location.summary: The Jaipur district of north-eastern Rajasthan, part of the nuclear zone of the Ganeshwar-Jodhpura culture; Jodhpura itself, on the banks of the Sahibi river, lies in this district.

periodLevel.summary: Ganeshwar-Jodhpura culture. Jodhpura is the first site at which the culture was identified, and its calibrated dates range between 3309-2709 BCE and 2879-2348 BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Jodhpura and the Jaipur district sites represent the eastern wing of the copper-working complex that supplied metal to the early and mature Harappans.
points: The typical pottery is wheel-made, orange to red in colour, with incised designs of various shapes; the forms include a dish-on-stand with a thick slip.

Over 80 sites of the culture have been identified, the largest concentration in Sikar district with further sites in the neighbouring Jaipur and Jhunjhunu districts; the distribution matches the copper ore resources of the Baleshwar and Khetri areas, where traces of ancient copper working survive.

Harappan pottery has been reported from the surface of Ganeshwar culture sites, and the profiles of these settlements show them to be part of an important process of metallurgical growth in Rajasthan whose roots go back to the 4th millennium BCE.

location.summary: Jorwe, on the left bank of the Pravara river, a tributary of the Godavari, in Ahmednagar district, Maharashtra.

periodLevel.summary: Type site of the Jorwe culture, dated about 1400-700 BCE, which covered the whole of modern Maharashtra except parts of Vidarbha and the Konkan coast.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Jorwe gives its name to the most widespread Chalcolithic culture of the Deccan, known from roughly 200 sites, which owed much to the Malwa culture while also sharing elements of the Neolithic culture of the south.
points: The diagnostic Jorwe ware is a wheel-made painted pottery with a matt surface, an orange-red slip and designs in black; flat rectangular copper axes have been found here and at Chandoli.

Although the culture was essentially rural, some of its settlements such as Daimabad and Inamgaon almost reached an urban stage, and a settlement hierarchy is visible, with sites of as much as twenty hectares alongside others of five hectares or less, implying that larger settlements dominated smaller ones.

Jorwe sites lie in semi-arid areas on brown-black soil carrying ber and babul vegetation but within riverine tracts; the culture outlasted the other Chalcolithic cultures of central and western India, which had disappeared by about 1200 BCE, continuing until about 700 BCE.

location.summary: Kayatha, Ujjain district, Madhya Pradesh, on the banks of the Chhoti Kali Sindh, a tributary of the Kali Sindh which in turn joins the Chambal.

periodLevel.summary: Type site of the Kayatha culture, placed by calibrated radiocarbon dates in the second half of the 3rd millennium BCE and commonly given as about 2000-1800 BCE; it is the earliest of the three successive Malwa sequences, followed by the Ahar and then the Malwa culture. There was an abrupt break in occupation around 1800 BCE, after which the site lay deserted for about a century before being reoccupied in an Ahar-Banas phase.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Kayatha, with Eran, represents the earliest established Chalcolithic settlement of central India, and its hoards give an unusually vivid picture of a household abandoned in haste.
points: The typical Kayatha pottery is a fine, sturdy, wheel-made ware with a thick brown slip and linear designs painted in violet or deep red on the upper part of the vessel; associated wares are a thin buff ware with linear and geometric designs in red, and a red combed ware decorated with wavy and zigzag lines.

Houses were of mud and reed with mud-plastered floors. The stone tool kit included plentiful microliths of locally available chalcedony, and a mace head or ring stone that may have been used to turn soil.

Two copper axes cast in moulds, a fragmentary chisel and 28 copper bangles in two pots show command of copper technology; the axes carry indentation marks similar to Ganeshwar specimens and may well have come from there.

Two necklaces of agate and carnelian beads, one of 175 and the other of 160 beads, were found in pots, and another pot held 40,000 steatite micro-beads strung in threads. All of these lay in a small area of what must have been a single house, suggesting the occupants left suddenly, abandoning their valuables on the floor.

location.summary: Koldihwa, Allahabad (Prayagraj) district, Uttar Pradesh, on the banks of the Belan river on the northern fringes of the Vindhyas, close to the related site of Mahagara.

periodLevel.summary: A sequence showing cultural continuity from the Neolithic through the Chalcolithic to the Iron Age; megalithic burials occur in the Chalcolithic period.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Koldihwa is at the centre of the debate on the origins of rice cultivation in India, since remains of rice and impressions of rice husk embedded in pieces of burnt clay were found here in Neolithic levels.
points: Examination of the rice imprints on pottery suggests that the people were familiar both with wild rice and with cultivated Oryza sativa; the very early dates once claimed for this rice have been questioned, but the site remains the key reference in the argument.
Rice was the staple, supplemented by meat, and the sequence records the introduction of wheel-made pottery in place of the earlier handmade wares.

Other finds include stone blades, polished stone celts and microliths. The Belan valley setting matters: wild rice still grows in the area, which falls within the natural habitat zone of the cereal, and the Neolithic here emerged directly out of a well-established Mesolithic phase seen at Chopani Mando.

location.summary: Narhan, Gorakhpur district, Uttar Pradesh, on the northern bank of the Sarayu (Ghaghara), about 30 km east of Imlidih; excavated by Purushottam Singh (1994).

periodLevel.summary: A cultural sequence stretching from the second half of the 2nd millennium BCE to the 7th century CE. Period I, which gives its name to the Narhan culture, is dated about 1300-700 BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The type site of the Narhan culture, whose sequence is repeated at many places across the middle Ganga plains, and which documents the agricultural colonisation of that region before the coming of iron.
points: Remains of wattle-and-daub houses with post-holes and hearths were found. The pottery is marked by a white-painted black-and-red ware, along with white-painted black-slipped ware, red-slipped ware and plain red ware.

Copper objects include a ring and a fishhook; chemical analysis shows they were made of a low-tin bronze, and the metalworkers were familiar with alloying, cold working, annealing and casting, the copper ore apparently coming from the Rakha mines of Bihar.

An exceptionally wide range of plant remains was recovered - cultivated rice, hulled and six-row barley, three kinds of wheat, pea, green gram, chickpea and khesari, with mustard and flax as oilseeds and seeds of jackfruit, mango, mahua, tamarind and bamboo. An impression of a fishhook and thread on a mud clod showed the hook was of iron and the thread of ramie, a strong water-resistant fibre.

Two iron pieces, including a 13 cm bar, were found in the upper deposits of Period I, with iron objects increasing in the following period; at Khairadih nearby, Period I was likewise marked by black-and-red ware, with calibrated dates of 1395-848 BCE.

location.summary: Navdatoli, on the southern bank of the Narmada opposite Maheshwar, in the Nimar region of western Madhya Pradesh; excavated by H. D. Sankalia.

periodLevel.summary: A Chalcolithic settlement of the Malwa culture, about 1700-1200 BCE, with the main occupation often given as 2000-1750 BCE; the site shows an overlap of Chalcolithic and Harappan-related material and does not show signs of planning.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Navdatoli has produced a greater variety of cereals than any other excavated site in India, which makes it the standard reference for Chalcolithic agriculture.
points: The plant remains include wheat, rice, bajra, lentil (masur), black gram, green gram, grass pea, ber and linseed, nearly the whole range of Chalcolithic crops at a single site.

The pottery has a coarse core and a thick buff fabric with an orange slip, the designs in black or dark brown depicting plants, animals and human figures, among them blackbuck, deer and peacock; Malwa ware is generally reckoned the richest of Chalcolithic ceramics.

Houses were circular or oblong wattle and daub, with chulhas and storage jars. Each household made its own tools, so the stone blade industry was widely distributed rather than concentrated in specialist hands.

Religious life is indicated by fire altars and by storage jars carrying a large female figure, which with the terracotta female figurines of other Chalcolithic sites is taken as evidence of a mother goddess cult.

location.summary: Ojiyana, Bhilwara district, Rajasthan, on the Khari river in the Banas system, on the slope of a hill rather than on a river flat.

periodLevel.summary: An Ahar or Banas culture Chalcolithic settlement, broadly of the late 3rd to mid-2nd millennium BCE; excavated by the Archaeological Survey of India at the end of the 1990s.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the more recently excavated Banas culture sites, and unusual in being built on a hill slope, which required the settlement to be terraced.
points: The pottery is the black-and-red ware characteristic of the Ahar culture, with white painted designs, alongside red and tan wares.
Terracotta animal figurines, particularly bulls, and beads of semi-precious stones were recovered, consistent with the wider Banas assemblage at Ahar, Gilund and Balathal.

The site extends the known distribution of the Ahar culture northwards towards Ajmer, part of the more than 90 sites identified in the Banas and Berach river systems roughly between Udaipur and Jaipur.

location.summary: Prabhas Patan, better known as Somnath, in Gir Somnath district (formerly Junagadh district) on the Saurashtra coast of Gujarat, near the mouth of the Hiran river.

periodLevel.summary: The Chalcolithic phase is dated about 2000-1400 BCE and gives its name to Prabhas ware; the site continues through the historic period, yielding Northern Black Polished Ware, and remained a major pilgrimage centre into medieval times.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A post-Harappan Chalcolithic culture of coastal Saurashtra that shows how Harappan traditions were absorbed into regional cultures after the decline of the cities.
points: Houses were rectangular and built of soft stone, a departure from the mud and wattle-and-daub construction usual in Chalcolithic India.
Fine painted ware was recovered along with a range of jars and bowls; gold ornaments and a steatite seal were also found, the seal pointing to continuing Harappan connections.

The site's later history is inseparable from the Somnath temple, repeatedly built and rebuilt, whose sack by Mahmud of Ghazni in 1025-26 became one of the most contested episodes in Indian historiography.

location.summary: Rangpur, on the Bhadar river in the Saurashtra peninsula of Gujarat; excavated by S. R. Rao.

periodLevel.summary: A Harappan and post-Harappan sequence. Period II is mature Harappan and Period III, the late or "Rangpur" phase, carries the lustrous red ware that marks the post-urban Chalcolithic of Gujarat.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Rangpur supplied the stratigraphic sequence on which the idea of a Late Harappan phase in Gujarat was built, showing the transition from the mature cities to smaller regional Chalcolithic communities.
points: Finds include black-and-red painted ware and high-necked jars, together with the diagnostic lustrous red ware, which also reached Ahar in Rajasthan in its Period Ic.
There is evidence of shell working, and of axes and beads of steatite and carnelian, alongside ordinary earthenware.

The absence of the full urban apparatus of the mature phase, combined with continuity of ceramic tradition, made Rangpur the type case in the debate over whether the end of the Harappan cities was a collapse or a transformation.

location.summary: Saipai, Etawah district, Uttar Pradesh, in the upper Ganga-Yamuna doab.

periodLevel.summary: Chalcolithic, belonging to the Ochre-Coloured Pottery and Copper Hoard horizon of the doab, broadly of the 2nd millennium BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Saipai is one of the few sites where Copper Hoard objects have been recovered in a stratified excavation alongside Ochre-Coloured Pottery, which is the main evidence linking the two.
points: The OCP deposits of the doab are generally shallow, from 0.5 to 1.5 m thick, and the settlements are usually small, up to 200-300 sq m, with sites spaced about 4 to 8 km apart.
Copper Hoard types associated with this horizon include harpoons, antennae swords, flat celts and anthropomorphic figures, whose function remains disputed.

Saipai belongs with Lal Qila, Atranjikhera, Ahichchhatra, Bahadrabad and Ambakheri in the group of excavated OCP sites that fill the gap in the upper doab between the Late Harappan and the Painted Grey Ware cultures.

location.summary: Savalda, in the Tapi valley of northern Maharashtra; the culture's sites lie between the Tapi and Godavari rivers.

periodLevel.summary: Type site of the Savalda culture, the earliest farming culture of the western Deccan, going back to the 3rd millennium BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Savalda ware is the diagnostic pottery of the first agricultural communities of Maharashtra, and is remarkable for painted designs that depict tools and weapons.
points: The typical Savalda ware is a wheel-made chocolate-coloured pottery of medium to coarse fabric with a thick, crackled slip; shapes include the high-necked jar, dish, dish-on-stand, bowl, basin, ring stand, vase, beaker and knobbed lid, and the designs painted over the crackled slip include tools, weapons and geometric motifs.
At the related site of Kaothe, a 20 hectare site with a shallow 50 cm deposit suggesting short-duration, semi-nomadic occupation, houses were round or oval with sloping roofs.

Bone tools were recovered together with beads of shell, opal, carnelian and terracotta; bones of wild deer and of domesticated cattle, buffalo, sheep or goat and dog were identified, and plant remains included a millet and two pulses, gram and moong.
A Savalda phase also occurs at Daimabad, where the evidence indicates a settled rather than semi-nomadic community, showing that the culture was not uniformly mobile.

location.summary: Senuar, on the banks of the Kudra river at the foot of the Kaimur range, Rohtas district, Bihar, not far from Sasaram.

periodLevel.summary: Four periods of occupation: Period I is Neolithic and Neolithic-Chalcolithic, Period II Chalcolithic, Period III belongs to the Northern Black Polished Ware culture and Period IV to the early centuries CE. The lower levels of Period IB are dated by radiocarbon to about 1770-1400 BCE, so Period IA probably begins in the latter half of the 3rd millennium BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The most important of the excavated Neolithic-Chalcolithic sites of the Bihar plains, and the clearest demonstration that double cropping was practised in the middle Ganga valley in the 3rd millennium BCE.
points: Carbonised grains show that two crops a year were grown. Rice was the main crop, with barley, dwarf wheat, sorghum millet, ragi millet, lentil, grass pea and field pea; bread wheat, chickpea and further pulses appear in Period IB.

Period IA was a 1.5 m deposit with wattle-and-daub houses and three main pottery types, red ware, burnished red ware and burnished grey ware, some rusticated and some cord-impressed; most was wheel-made though handmade pottery also occurs.

Artefacts include abundant microliths of chert, chalcedony, agate, quartz and quartzite, a few triangular polished celts, stone pestles, saddle querns, hammer stones, sling balls, bone points with use marks, and beads of semi-precious stones.

The animal bones have been carefully studied: domesticated cattle, buffalo, sheep, goat, pig, cat and dog, with wild nilgai, antelope and chital, many bearing charring and cut marks showing they were eaten. Senuar belongs with Chirand, Chechar-Kutubpur, Maner and Taradih in the group of excavated village sites that establish full agricultural settlement in the Gangetic plains of Bihar.

location.summary: Alamgirpur, Meerut district, western Uttar Pradesh, on the left bank of the Hindon, a tributary of the Yamuna; the easternmost Harappan site known.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by Y. D. Sharma (ASI) in 1958-59. Period I is late Harappan, c. 1900-1400 BCE; after a break in occupation comes Period II (Painted Grey Ware), then NBPW and early historic levels.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Marks the eastern limit of the Harappan world, in the upper Ganga-Yamuna doab, and the point where the Harappan and PGW sequences meet.
points: Late Harappan pottery of well-levigated clay with a thin cream wash or bright red slip, painted in black with geometric and naturalistic designs; dishes, cups, vases, beakers, and cubical dice. A few burnt bricks occurred, unusual for the doab.
A broken copper blade, chert blades, querns and pestles, bone points; beads and bangles of steatite, faience, carnelian, agate and terracotta; terracotta cakes, carts and wheels.

A cloth impression on a trough is taken as evidence of cotton. The break between the late Harappan and PGW levels here contrasts with the overlap at Bhagwanpura, and is central to dating the doab sequence.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4-5; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; ASI, *IAR* 1958-59

location.summary: Allahdino, about 40 km east of Karachi in Sindh, on a terrace near the Malir river, close to the Indus delta and the Arabian Sea coast.

periodLevel.summary: A single-period mature Harappan village, c. 2500-2000 BCE, excavated by Walter Fairservis (1973-77). Only 1.4 ha in extent and, unusually, unfortified.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The classic small Harappan village - no citadel, no wall - which nonetheless carries the full urban artefact repertoire and startling wealth.
points: Mud-brick houses on stone foundations laid out west-south-west to east-north-east; a large multi-roomed building on a mud-brick platform in the north-east appears to have had special importance.

Three wells with very narrow mouths (60-90 cm), apparently to make ground water rise higher under hydraulic pressure; Fairservis read the well-and-drain complex as an irrigation system, though the evidence is inconclusive.

A small terracotta jar held a hoard of gold, silver, bronze, agate and carnelian ornaments - a massive belt or necklace of 36 long carnelian beads with bronze spacers, and a multi-strand silver necklace. Seals, copper objects, toy carts and triangular terracotta cakes also occurred.
Typical black-on-red Harappan pottery formed barely 1 per cent of the finds here, a caution against assuming uniformity across the culture zone.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4; Fairservis, Allahdino excavation reports

location.summary: Balakot, Las Bela district, Baluchistan, on the Sonmiani Bay coast about 88 km north-west of Karachi, near the mouth of the Windar river.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by George F. Dales (1973-79). Period I is a pre/early Harappan horizon of the 4th millennium BCE with Nal-related pottery; Period II is mature Harappan, c. 2500-2000 BCE. Size 1-5 ha.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The best-excavated Harappan coastal village and, with Chanhudaro, one of the two principal shell-working centres of the civilisation.
points: Period I: wheel-made painted pottery, polychrome and similar to Nal ware; microliths; humped-bull figurines; terracotta objects; beads of lapis lazuli and other stones; mud-brick houses.
Period II: conch-shell bangle manufacture on a large scale, alongside classic Harappan red ware - the site supplied shell ornaments into the Indus network.
Marine shell and fish remains show a coastal subsistence base; Balakot sits at the interface of the Kulli-Nal traditions of Baluchistan and the Harappan culture of the plains.

location.summary: Balu, Kaithal district, Haryana, on the Ghaggar-Hakra (Sarasvati) tract of the Indo-Gangetic divide, near Siswal and Banawali.

periodLevel.summary: A small fortified rural settlement with early Harappan levels of the Kalibangan I type (c. 2900-2600 BCE) and a mature Harappan phase (c. 2600-1900 BCE); excavated by the Haryana Department of Archaeology.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Yields the fullest archaeobotanical record of any early and mature Harappan site, and shows that fortification was not confined to towns.
points: Crop remains studied by K. S. Saraswat and A. K. Pokharia (2001-02): several varieties of barley and wheat, rice, horse gram, green gram, chickpea, field pea, grass pea, sesamum, melon, watermelon, date and grapes - plus the earliest evidence of garlic in the subcontinent.
A fortified village rather than a town: a reminder that the Harappan defensive wall was a settlement type, not a marker of urban rank.
Mud-brick houses and pottery of the Kalibangan I range in the early Harappan level, with a continuous transition into the mature phase - part of the Ghaggar cluster that documents indigenous origins.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4; Saraswat & Pokharia, *Pragdhara* 2001-02

location.summary: Banawali (ancient Vanavali), Fatehabad district, Haryana, close to the dry bed of the Rangoi river in the Sarasvati-Ghaggar system.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by R. S. Bisht (1973-84). Period I early Harappan (c. 2900-2600 BCE), Period II mature Harappan (c. 2600-1900 BCE), Period III late Harappan/Bara. The fortified area measures about 300 x 500 m.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A fortified town whose plan departs from the standard citadel-and-lower-town formula, and one of the richest sites for reading Harappan social difference.
points: The citadel is semi-elliptical, has its own mud-brick fortification and is surrounded by a moat; a ramp led from it into the lower town. Baked bricks were used only for wells, bathing pavements and drains; houses had raised chabutaras outside.

A multi-roomed house with a kitchen and a toilet, holding many seals and weights, is read as a merchant's; another, with beads of gold, lapis lazuli and carnelian, tiny weights and a gold-streaked touchstone, as a jeweller's. Seals occur only in the lower town, never in the citadel.

A terracotta model of a plough, a cubical chert weight-blade, and fire altars in several houses - in one case attached to an apsidal structure with an apparently ritual function. The early Harappan level had mud-brick houses with hearths and plastered storage pits in the courtyards.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Bisht in ASI, *IAR*

location.summary: Bargaon, Saharanpur district, western Uttar Pradesh, in the upper Ganga-Yamuna doab beside Hulas and Ambakheri.

periodLevel.summary: A late Harappan village of c. 1900-1300 BCE. One of only three excavated late Harappan sites in the doab (with Alamgirpur and Hulas), out of 563 identified between the Yamuna and the Sutlej.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The type locality for the overlap of the late Harappan and Ochre Coloured Pottery (OCP) phases, and a marker of the copper-hoard zone.
points: Late Harappan pottery with a cream wash or bright red slip and black-painted designs occurs together with OCP. Bargaon's OCP belongs to the western zone that retains Harappan links (with Jodhpura, Siswal, Mitathal, Bara and Ambakheri), as against the eastern zone of Lal Qila, Atranjikhera and Saipai, which does not.

A fragmentary copper chisel and rings, chert blades, querns and pestles, bone points, terracotta cakes, carts and wheels; bangles and beads of terracotta, steatite, agate, carnelian and faience. Over 80 copper-hoard findspots are known in this tract.
Houses of wattle and daub, with wheat and barley continuing from the mature Harappan phase - the de-urbanised, rural face of the late Harappan.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4-5

location.summary: Bet Dwarka (Shankhodhar), an island off Okha in the Gulf of Kutch, Devbhumi Dwarka district, Gujarat.

periodLevel.summary: Late Harappan, with a thermoluminescence date of c. 1570 BCE. Explored on land and underwater by the Marine Archaeology Centre of the NIO (S. R. Rao, A. S. Gaur, Sundaresh) from the 1980s.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the very few late Harappan settlements large enough to be called urban, and the best evidence that Persian Gulf contact outlived the cities.
points: A partly submerged settlement originally about 4 x 0.5 km, with fortification remains - inner and outer walls, bastions and a large stone jetty - plus stone anchors of the type also found off Dwarka.
A rectangular conch-shell seal engraved with a three-headed animal of Persian Gulf type, and a jar inscribed in the Harappan script; lustrous red ware and black-and-red ware.
A coppersmith's stone mould and shell bangles indicate craft activity. With Kudwala in Cholistan and Daimabad in the Godavari valley, it shows that a few late Harappan places kept an urban character.
