location.summary: Bhagwanpura, Kurukshetra district, Haryana, on the right bank of the Sarasvati (modern Sarsuti).

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by J. P. Joshi (ASI, 1975-77). Period IA is late Harappan, c. 1700-1400 BCE; Period IB is the late Harappan-Painted Grey Ware overlap, c. 1400-1000 BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The type site for the overlap of the late Harappan and PGW cultures - the single most-cited evidence on the Harappan-Vedic relationship.
points: Late Harappan pot forms occur interlocked with PGW in the same levels (the same overlap appears at Dadheri in Haryana and Katpalon and Nagar in Punjab), showing the two cultures coexisted rather than simply succeeded one another.

Flourishing specialised craft: two clay tablets and nineteen sherds carry graffiti that may represent a surviving script. Faience ornaments, semi-precious stone beads, terracotta cart frames, kilns and fire altars.

A thirteen-room house of the PGW phase and horse bones from the overlap layers, dated c. 1600-1000 BCE. Burnt bricks reported here are the only late Harappan instance in the region, though R. S. Sharma questions the dating of that layer.

location.summary: Bhirrana, Fatehabad district, Haryana, on the left bank of the dry Ghaggar (Sarasvati).

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by L. S. Rao (ASI, 2003-06). Period IA Hakra ware, IB early Harappan, IIA early mature Harappan, IIB mature Harappan - one of the few sites carrying the whole sequence from Hakra ware to the mature phase. The excavators' dates reaching into the 6th-5th millennium BCE are debated.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A key witness to the indigenous, unbroken origins of the Harappan civilisation on the Ghaggar.
points: Period IA had subterranean dwelling pits cut into the natural soil with Hakra ware; Period IB brought mud-brick structures in the 1:2:3 ratio, including a six-room house with a central courtyard and chullahs, and copper arrowheads, rings and bangles.

The mature Harappan settlement was ringed by a massive mud-brick fortification. Three multi-roomed house complexes were exposed, one of ten rooms with verandah and courtyard, another of six rooms with a kitchen and four courtyards; a 4.8 m wide street ran along the wall, with three lanes off it. A circular tandoor and chullahs were found, with charred bones and a bovine skull beside one.

Beads of carnelian, jasper, steatite, shell and terracotta; terracotta gamesmen, rattle, bull figurine and bangles. A thick red-ware sherd bears an incised female figure whose pose recalls the Mohenjodaro bronze 'dancing girl'.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4; Rao et al. in ASI, *IAR* 2004-05

location.summary: Chanhudaro, Sindh, about 130 km south of Mohenjodaro on the left bank of an old course of the Indus.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by N. G. Majumdar (1930-31) and E. J. H. Mackay (1935-36). Mature Harappan c. 2500-1900 BCE (5-10 ha), followed by the late Harappan Jhukar levels and then Jhangar.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The Harappan industrial town - an unfortified craft settlement rather than a city, and the best single index of Harappan manufacturing.
points: No citadel and no fortification wall; streets with drains covered by burnt brick.

A major centre of craft production: a bead factory with furnaces, drills and beads at every stage, mostly of steatite; seal making; shell working (with Balakot, the principal centre); and the manufacture of cubical stone weights. Raw carnelian, agate, amethyst, jasper and crystal were stocked here.

Famous small finds include a bronze model of a bullock cart and a brick impressed with the footprints of a dog chasing a cat. The Jhukar levels above yielded circular stamp seals and buff ware, with writing surviving only on pottery.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Mackay, *Chanhu-daro Excavations 1935-36*

location.summary: Desalpur (Gunthli), Nakhatrana taluka, Kutch district, Gujarat, on a seasonal stream in the inland Kutch uplands, on the route between Sindh and Saurashtra.

periodLevel.summary: A mature Harappan fortified settlement of c. 2500-1900 BCE with no early Harappan level (like Lothal, Chanhudaro, Mitathal, Alamgirpur and Ropar). Excavated by P. P. Pandya and K. V. Soundara Rajan (ASI, 1963-64).

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A small fortified Harappan station holding the interior Kutch route, with unusually clear administrative evidence for its size.
points: A massive fortification wall of stone rubble and mud brick with a stone revetment, serving as flood protection as well as defence; streets and drains within.
Three seals bearing the Harappan script, together with stone weights and copper objects - a concentration of sealing and weighing equipment that implies a control or transit function.
Black-and-red ware occurs alongside classic Harappan red ware, part of the Gujarat group (with Lothal, Surkotada, Rojdi and Rangpur) in which BRW appears in a Harappan context.

location.summary: Ganweriwala, in the Cholistan desert of Bahawalpur district, Punjab (Pakistan), on the dry bed of the Hakra, roughly midway between Mohenjodaro and Harappa.

periodLevel.summary: Mature Harappan, c. 2600-1900 BCE. Discovered by M. R. Mughal in 1974 and surveyed intensively, but never excavated.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the five largest Harappan cities and the largest gap in the evidence - an unexcavated capital-scale site.
points: Over 81.5 ha, ranking with Mohenjodaro (over 200 ha), Harappa (over 150 ha), Rakhigarhi (over 80 ha) and Dholavira (about 100 ha); nearby Lurewala in Cholistan may have been as large as Mohenjodaro.
Surface finds include a terracotta tablet or seal showing a figure seated cross-legged in a 'yogic' posture, paralleled at Harappa, Mohenjodaro and Kalibangan; also pottery, kiln waste and weights.

Its position on the Hakra, in the tract where Kot Dijian and mature Harappan sites are densest, is the principal argument for a second settlement axis away from the Indus - and hence for the term 'Sindhu-Sarasvati' civilisation.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4; Thapar, *Early India*; Mughal, *Ancient Cholistan* (1997)

location.summary: Harappa, Sahiwal district, Punjab (Pakistan), on an old bed of the Ravi; about 483 km from Mohenjodaro, the two linked by the Indus system.

periodLevel.summary: Noticed by Charles Masson (1826) and Cunningham; excavated by Daya Ram Sahni (1921 - the first Harappan excavation), M. S. Vats, Mortimer Wheeler (1946), and since 1986 by the Harappa Archaeological Research Project (Meadow and Kenoyer). Period I Ravi/Hakra phase; Period II early Harappan, over 25 ha; Period III mature Harappan, c. 2600-1900 BCE, over 150 ha; Cemetery H, late Harappan, c. 1900-1300 BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The type site that names the civilisation, and the only city with a documented sequence from the Ravi phase to the late Harappan.
points: The citadel, shaped like a parallelogram, lies to the west on massive mud-brick platforms. To its north are the 'granary' of twelve rooms in two rows, circular brick working floors where wheat and barley husk survived in the crevices, and two-roomed barracks read as labourers' quarters.

Writing on pottery and seals, inscribed seals and standardised weights were already present in the early Harappan Period II, along with chert blades, terracotta female figurines and bangles, and beads of lapis lazuli, carnelian and steatite.

Cemetery R-37 of the mature phase and Cemetery H of the late phase, the latter with urn burials and distinctively painted jars. Unlike the single-craft towns, Harappa manufactured a wide range of goods; rice and millets appear in its late Harappan levels.

content.sourcesLine: Basham, *The Wonder That Was India*; Upinder Singh, ch. 4; Meadow & Kenoyer (2001)

location.summary: Jhukar, Larkana district, Sindh, on the Indus plain a short distance from Mohenjodaro.

periodLevel.summary: Type site of the Jhukar culture, the late Harappan phase of Sindh, c. 1900-1500 BCE; excavated by N. G. Majumdar in the 1930s. Jhangar culture levels follow above.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Gives Sindh its post-urban identity and shows that the transition from the mature phase was gradual, not a rupture.
points: Buff ware with a red or cream slip painted in black; urn burials; circular stamp seals with geometric designs (a form also found at Daimabad).
The diagnostic signs of de-urbanisation: writing survives only on pottery, cubical weights become infrequent, seals change in form, and female figurines and the Indus script disappear.
Pottery indicates reciprocal contact with late Harappan Lothal and Rangpur in Gujarat. The same culture is represented at Chanhudaro and Amri, so 'Jhukar' names a regional phase, not a single site.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*

location.summary: Kalibangan ('black bangles'), Hanumangarh district, northern Rajasthan, on the left bank of the dry Ghaggar (identified by many with the Vedic Sarasvati).

periodLevel.summary: Discovered by A. Ghosh (1951); excavated by B. B. Lal and B. K. Thapar (1960-69). Period I early Harappan, calibrated c. 2920-2550 BCE, about 4 ha; Period II mature Harappan, c. 2600-1900 BCE, 10-50 ha. The break between the two may have been caused by an earthquake.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The third great Harappan city dug in India and the clearest early-to-mature transition anywhere in the culture zone.
points: Period I: massive mud-brick fortification; houses built around courtyards with hearths, lime-plastered storage pits and saddle querns; bricks standardised at 3:2:1; over a hundred copper objects; distinctive red or pink pottery painted in black and sometimes white, with moustache-like scrolls, plants, fish and cattle. South of the site lay a ploughed field with north-south and east-west furrows - the earliest ploughed field known in the subcontinent.

Period II: both citadel and lower town fortified, the citadel divided in two. Its southern half held mud-brick platforms with a row of seven clay-plastered pits, read as fire altars for community ritual, with a well and bath pavements nearby; oblong fire altars with a central stele stood in lower-town houses. B. B. Lal suggested the northern half housed the officiants.

Street drains of the Mohenjodaro type are absent - house sewage went into troughs or jars sunk outside. Bangle making (terracotta, shell, alabaster, steatite, faience) was the leading craft. The burial ground, 200 m to the west-south-west, held extended burials and also circular pits with grave goods but no human remains.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Lal (1984)

location.summary: Kot Diji, Khairpur district, Sindh, on the left bank of an old flood channel of the Indus, about 160 km north-east of Amri and near the Rohri hills chert sources.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by F. A. Khan (1955-57). Early Harappan Period I dated from c. 3300 BCE, separated by a burnt deposit from the mature Harappan level above. Size 1-5 ha.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Type site of the 'Kot Dijian' horizon, the widest early Harappan cultural umbrella, from Cholistan to the Gomal and the Potwar.
points: Fortified with a massive wall of limestone rubble and mud brick, enclosing a citadel complex and a separate lower residential area - the citadel-and-lower-town plan already present before the mature phase.

The distinctive vessel is a short-necked ovoid pot painted with brownish bands and the 'horned deity', pipal leaves and fish-scale designs; the same deity recurs on jars at Rehman Dheri and incised on a terracotta cake at Kalibangan I, evidence of 'cultural convergence' in the religious sphere.

Objects of stone, shell and bone, terracotta figurines including a bull, bangles, beads and a bronze bangle fragment. The burnt deposit implies a major fire at the transition, as at Gumla; Amri and Nausharo also show burning.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4; Thapar, *Early India*

location.summary: Kunal, Fatehabad district, Haryana, on the dry Sarasvati-Ghaggar in the Indo-Gangetic divide, near Ratia and not far from Banawali.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by the Haryana Department of Archaeology (J. S. Khatri and M. Acharya, 1985-98). Period IA Hakra ware; Period IB early Harappan with Kalibangan I pottery; Period IC transitional between early and mature Harappan, c. 2600 BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Documents both the architectural shift from pit dwellings to a planned brick village and the earliest concentration of elite wealth in the Harappan tradition.
points: The below-ground houses of the earlier phases give way in Period IC to ground-level houses of standardised mud brick in the 1:2:3 and 1:2:4 ratios; sturdy red beakers and jars of Harappan type appear for the first time.
Six steatite seals and one shell seal with geometric patterns - which, with the seals from Nausharo, are the earliest sealing evidence in the tradition and are linked to traders or emerging elites.

Hoards of jewellery inside houses: two silver tiaras, gold ornaments, and beads of lapis lazuli and agate. Upinder Singh reads the tiaras as marking a concentration of wealth with possible political implications - authority before urbanism.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4; ASI, *IAR*

location.summary: Lewan (Lewan Dara), in the Bannu basin of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, on the western tributary drainage of the Indus below the Sheikh Budin hills.

periodLevel.summary: Early Harappan, going back to the early 3rd millennium BCE; excavated by the Bannu Archaeological Project (F. R. Allchin, Farid Khan and others, 1977-79).

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The clearest factory site of the Harappan age - an industrial locality rather than a settlement, and proof of specialised production before urbanism.
points: Beside a small habitation area, an expanse of about 450 x 325 m was littered with stone tools at every stage of manufacture: chert microliths, querns of various types, stone balls, long triangular stone axes, ring stones and pointed hammerstones. Heavy grinding equipment dominates.
Part of the industrial area was given over to bead making, with beads and bead-making material; ceramic bangles and beads also occurred.

Little direct evidence of agriculture at Lewan itself, but nearby Tarakai Qila yielded wheat, barley, lentil and field pea with sickle-sheened blades, and bones of cattle, water buffalo, sheep and goat - the farming base that supported the industry.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4; Allchin, Khan & Allchin, *Lewan and the Bannu Basin* (1986)

location.summary: Lothal, in the Bhal tract of Ahmedabad district, Gujarat, between the Sabarmati and its tributary the Bhogavo. The sea is now 16-19 km away, but boats from the Gulf of Khambhat could once sail up to the site.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by S. R. Rao (1955-62). Period A is mature Harappan, c. 2400-1900 BCE, in five phases; Period B is late Harappan with Lustrous Red Ware, c. 1900-1600 BCE. A modest 280 x 225 m, yet more tightly planned than Kalibangan, twice its size.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The best-planned small Harappan town and the civilisation's principal port on the Gujarat coast.
points: The dockyard on the eastern edge: a roughly trapezoidal basin walled in burnt brick (eastern and western walls 212 m and 215 m, northern and southern 37 m and 35 m), with a sluice gate and spill channel to hold a regular water level, and a mud-brick wharf along the western embankment. Leshnik's alternative reading of it as an irrigation reservoir is not generally accepted.

South of the acropolis stood a warehouse where sixty-five terracotta sealings were found, impressed with reed, matting, woven fibre and cord on one face and with Harappan seals on the other - direct evidence of packed and dispatched cargo.

The citadel (Rao's 'Acropolis') is trapezoidal and lies within the settlement rather than apart from it; the cemetery is to the north-west, outside the wall. Copper and bead workshops, a 'bazaar street' of shops, fire altars in houses, rice (with Rangpur, among the earliest at a Harappan site), and a Persian Gulf seal.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; S. R. Rao, *Lothal and the Indus Civilisation* (1973)

location.summary: Manda, Jammu district, on the right bank of the Chenab at the foot of the Pir Panjal - the northernmost Harappan site known.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by J. P. Joshi and Madhu Bala (ASI, 1976-77). Period I pre-Harappan; Period II mature Harappan, c. 2500-1900 BCE; Period III late Harappan, followed by PGW and early historic levels.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Fixes the northern frontier of the Harappan world and identifies its timber-procurement zone.
points: Harappan red ware in the full range - jars, dish-on-stand, beakers, goblets and perforated vessels - with potsherds bearing Harappan graffiti and script signs.
Its position where the Chenab leaves the hills suggests a station for procuring deodar and other Himalayan timber for the brick-and-beam architecture of the plains cities.
Bone points, copper objects, chert blades and terracotta cakes; the sequence continues into PGW, tying the Harappan occupation of the Jammu foothills to the later iron age.

location.summary: Mohenjodaro ('the mound of the dead'), Larkana district, Sindh, on the right bank of the Indus about 5 km from the present channel; in protohistoric times the river ran closer.

periodLevel.summary: Found by R. D. Banerji (1922); excavated by John Marshall, E. J. H. Mackay, Mortimer Wheeler (1950) and G. F. Dales (1964). Mature Harappan, c. 2600-1900 BCE. About 200 ha, the largest Harappan city; Fairservis (1967) estimated some 41,250 people in the lower town alone.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The fullest expression of Harappan urbanism - the benchmark against which every other site is described.
points: Two mounds: a smaller but higher western mound, the citadel, raised on an artificial mud and mud-brick platform about 400 x 200 m and rising 12 m above the plain, girt by a 6 m thick retaining wall with projections and a tower; and the larger, lower eastern mound, the lower town.

On the citadel: the Great Bath, about 14.5 x 7 m, sealed with bitumen and flanked by rooms and a well; the so-called 'granary', from which no grain was actually reported; the 'college of priests'; and a pillared hall to the south. The lower town has the DK, HR and S areas, over 700 wells, shops and workmen's quarters, and the finest drainage system of any Bronze Age city.

The bronze 'dancing girl', the steatite bearded 'priest-king', the Pashupati (proto-Shiva) seal, and seated male figures in shawls. Hoards of jewellery buried in the last levels and skulls huddled at one spot have been read as signs of insecurity, though not of the 'Aryan invasion' Wheeler once proposed.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Marshall, *Mohenjo-daro and the Indus Civilization* (1931)

location.summary: Nageshwar, near Dwarka in Devbhumi Dwarka (formerly Jamnagar) district, Gujarat, immediately on the Gulf of Kutch coast.

periodLevel.summary: A single-period mature Harappan settlement, c. 2500-2000 BCE, with no pre- or post-Harappan occupation. Surveyed and excavated by the M. S. University of Baroda (K. T. M. Hegde, K. K. Bhan and others, 1983-86). Size 1-5 ha.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The purest example of a Harappan single-craft settlement, founded to work one raw material and abandoned with it.
points: Devoted exclusively to shell working and specialising in bangles, using the Turbinella pyrum of the adjacent gulf; unfinished bangles, sawn cores and shell waste dominate the assemblage.
Pottery of reddish-yellow sandy clay with floral motifs, perforated jars, and channel-spouted bowls with a red slip and black painted designs; fire altars have also been reported.

With Balakot, Chanhudaro, Kuntasi, Bagasra, Rangpur, Nagwada, Dholavira and Lothal it defines the Gujarat shell-working network that supplied ornaments to the inland cities - the clearest case for Harappan site specialisation.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4; Hegde, Bhan et al., Nageshwar reports

location.summary: Padri (Kerala-no-dhoro), near Talaja in Bhavnagar district, Gujarat, on a tidal creek close to the Gulf of Khambhat coast of Saurashtra.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by Vasant Shinde (Deccan College) in the 1990s. Period I is an early Harappan 'Padri ware' phase, c. 3000-2600 BCE; Period II mature Harappan, c. 2600-2000 BCE; a late Harappan occupation follows.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Established that Gujarat had a well-developed early Harappan horizon of its own, indigenous and distinct from the Amri-Nal tradition of Sindh.
points: Padri ware: sturdy storage jars with painted buffalo-horn and allied motifs, a local ceramic tradition that precedes Harappan contact - the basis for treating Saurashtra as a separate early Harappan region.
Symbols akin to Harappan writing occur in the early Harappan levels here, as at Kalibangan, Dholavira and Harappa - evidence that the roots of the script lie in this phase.
Rectangular houses and workshops, huge copper fish-hooks, and salt-making installations - the earliest evidence of salt production on the Indian coast, and the likely reason for the site's position.

location.summary: Pirak, in the Kachi plain of Baluchistan near Sibi, at the southern foot of the Bolan pass on the Nari river.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by J.-F. Jarrige and M. Santoni (1968-74). Period I begins c. 1800 BCE and Periods II-III run to about 600 BCE - the post-Harappan iron age of Baluchistan, not a Harappan settlement itself.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The site that documents the beginning of double cropping and the earliest secure horse in South Asia.
points: Double cropping begins here: wheat and barley as winter crops, with rice (under irrigation), millet and sorghum as summer crops - the agricultural diversification that defines the late Harappan period as a whole.

Terracotta figurines of horses and of camels with riders. Richard Meadow, who reviewed the osteological evidence, holds the Pirak complex to show the earliest true horse in the subcontinent, about 1700 BCE, roughly contemporary with the disputed Surkotada specimen.

Mud-brick architecture with compartmented buildings and painted geometric pottery; iron appears in Period III. With the Gandhara Grave culture of Swat, Pirak anchors R. S. Sharma's account of the horse entering north India from the 18th century BCE.

content.sourcesLine: R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Upinder Singh, ch. 4; Jarrige & Santoni, *Fouilles de Pirak* (1979)

location.summary: Rakhigarhi (villages Rakhi Khas and Rakhi Shahpur), Hisar district, Haryana, on the dry Ghaggar-Drishadvati plain.

periodLevel.summary: Discovered by Suraj Bhan (1963); excavated by Amarendra Nath (ASI, 1997-2000) and Vasant Shinde (Deccan College, 2011-16). Early Harappan Period I; mature Harappan c. 2600-1900 BCE. Over 80 ha across five mounds - by some measurements the largest Harappan site of all.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The largest Harappan city in India, with all three phases represented, and the source of the first ancient genome from the civilisation.
points: Period I was already a planned settlement with mud-brick structures; it yielded uninscribed seals, pottery with graffiti, terracotta wheels, carts, rattles and bull figurines, chert blades, weights, a bone point and a muller - and a stacked set of hopscotches, suggesting a game like pithu goes back to early Harappan times.

The citadel mound is walled in mud brick and has platforms, a brick well, fire altars, streets and drains. A lapidary workshop held about 3,000 unfinished beads and roughly cut carnelian, chalcedony, agate and jasper, with polishers and a heating hearth; elsewhere bones, antlers and ivory with finished and unfinished points, combs, needles and engravers showed bone and ivory working.

A cemetery of mostly brick-lined pit burials, one with a wooden coffin. DNA from a female skeleton here produced the first Harappan genome (Shinde et al., 2019), which showed no Steppe ancestry - now central to the Aryan-origins debate.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; ASI, *IAR*; Shinde et al. (2019)

location.summary: Rojdi, Rajkot district, Gujarat, on the north bank of the Bhadar river in central Saurashtra.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by M. K. Dhavalikar, G. L. Possehl and M. H. Raval (1982-86). Rojdi A and B are mature (Sorath) Harappan, c. 2500-2000 BCE; Rojdi C is late Harappan, c. 2000-1700 BCE. Size 5-10 ha.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Type site of the Sorath Harappan of Saurashtra, and the clearest proof that the Harappan 'decline' was regional rather than universal.
points: At about the time Mohenjodaro was being abandoned, the people of Rojdi were expanding and rebuilding their settlement, adding a new stone enclosure wall - Upinder Singh's standard illustration of the eastward and southward shift of population.

Hard red-to-buff ware with the hemispherical bowl as the commonest form, and short Harappan inscriptions on the rims of potsherds; black-and-red ware also occurs, as at Lothal, Surkotada and Desalpur.
The richest millet record of any Harappan site - ragi, bajra, jowar and other summer millets - marking the shift to a monsoon-based, drought-tolerant agriculture that outlasted the cities.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Possehl & Raval, *Harappan Civilization and Rojdi* (1989)

location.summary: Ropar (Rupnagar), Punjab, on the left bank of the Sutlej where the river leaves the Siwaliks - the first Harappan site found east of the Indus system.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by Y. D. Sharma (ASI, 1953-56), the first excavation undertaken in independent India. Period I mature to late Harappan, c. 2100-1700 BCE, with no early Harappan level; Period II PGW; Period III NBPW; then Kushana-Gupta and medieval levels - a six-period sequence.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Supplies the standard stratified sequence from the Harappan to the medieval period in the Sutlej valley.
points: Harappan levels with typical red ware, chert blades, steatite seals, beads, terracotta cakes and bangles; one burial had a dog laid at the feet of the human, a rite not recorded elsewhere in the culture. Horse remains are reported from the post-urban phase.
PGW follows directly on the Harappan level, which makes Ropar - with Bhagwanpura and Alamgirpur - one of the fixed points in dating the Harappan-Vedic transition.
Early historic levels yielded punch-marked coins, uninscribed cast copper coins and a seal with a Mauryan Brahmi legend, so the site also carries the NBPW chapter.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; ASI, *IAR* 1953-56

location.summary: Shortughai, in Darqad of Takhar province, north-eastern Afghanistan, on the upper Oxus (Amu Darya) near its confluence with the Kokcha, close to the lapis lazuli mines of Badakhshan.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by Henri-Paul Francfort (1976-79). Mature Harappan, c. 2200-2000 BCE, roughly 1,100 km from the Indus heartland - an isolated Harappan colony.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The only true Harappan trading outpost outside the subcontinent, and the strongest single evidence for organised long-distance procurement.
points: A square Harappan seal with a rhinoceros motif, classic Harappan pottery, terracotta cakes, carts and figurines - a complete Harappan material kit, not a scatter of traded objects, so actual Harappan settlers are implied.
Beads and raw lapis lazuli, carnelian, agate, gold and steatite. The colony was evidently planted to secure Badakhshan lapis and central Asian tin for the cities; millets were also grown here.
Irrigation canals were found at the site - the clearest Harappan canal evidence anywhere. It lay on the northern overland route to Turkmenistan and Mesopotamia, via Tepe Hissar and Shah Tepe.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4; Thapar, *Early India*; Francfort, *Fouilles de Shortughai* (1989)

location.summary: Sotka Koh, near Pasni on the Makran coast of Baluchistan, on the Shadi Kaur river a few kilometres inland from the Arabian Sea.

periodLevel.summary: A mature Harappan coastal station, c. 2500-1900 BCE. Discovered by George F. Dales during his Makran coast survey of 1960 and tested thereafter.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the two Harappan stations on the Makran coast, plotting the sea route westward to the Persian Gulf.
points: A rectangular structure on a hill terrace within a stone and mud-brick enclosure, and open pit ovens used for firing pottery on the spot.
Black pottery with reddish bands around the neck and geometric motifs, alongside classic Harappan red ware and potsherds of Indus type.
With Sutkagendor and Balakot it marks the coastal chain linking Sindh to Oman and the Gulf; the settlement appears to have been deserted as the coastline shifted seaward and its creek silted up.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4 (Map 4.1); Dales, Makran coast survey (1962)

location.summary: Sutkagendor, Gwadar district, Baluchistan, on the Dasht river about 48 km inland from the Makran coast and close to the Iranian border - the westernmost Harappan site.

periodLevel.summary: Mature Harappan, c. 2500-1900 BCE. Noticed by Major Mockler (1875), surveyed by Aurel Stein (1927) and excavated by George F. Dales (1962).

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Fixes the western limit of the civilisation and anchors its maritime route to the Persian Gulf.
points: A citadel raised on a stone and mud-brick platform with a massive fortification wall and bastions, and a lower town below - the standard Harappan plan reproduced on the frontier. R. S. Sharma groups it with Surkotada as a 'coastal city marked by a citadel'.
Stone vessels, stone and copper arrowheads, shell beads, pottery and terracotta figurines; material is sparse compared with the inland towns.
Originally sited on a navigable creek of the Dasht, it served as a port of call on the run between Lothal and Dholavira and the Persian Gulf, before the sea receded from it.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Dales (1962)

location.summary: Surkotada, Rapar taluka, eastern Kutch district, Gujarat, on the northern fringe of the Little Rann, on the old overland route between Sindh and Saurashtra.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by J. P. Joshi (ASI, 1964 and 1970-72). Periods IA to IC, c. 2300-1700 BCE, running from the mature into the late Harappan phase with no break or desertion. Size 1-5 ha.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A fortified regional centre or garrison town, and the source of the most-debated horse evidence in Indian archaeology.
points: The citadel exists from the earliest level and is not set apart: a single stone and mud-brick fortification with a rubble revetment encloses both the residential annexe and the citadel, each with its own ramped gateway - a plan shared with Lothal rather than with Mohenjodaro.

Horse bones from the upper levels were identified as true horse (Equus caballus) by Sandor Bokonyi and disputed by Richard Meadow; R. S. Sharma treats the identification as doubtful. Bones of mongoose (kept against snakes), elephant and wolf were also found.

A cemetery with pot burials and a rock-cut chamber; new pottery types appear in the later phase although the settlement plan continues unchanged. A heap of sling stones and a soldier depicted on a potsherd have been read as pointing to a standing force. Black-and-red ware and millets occur here.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4-5; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Joshi, *Excavation at Surkotada* (1990)

location.summary: Adichanallur, Thoothukudi district, Tamil Nadu, on the north bank of the Tamiraparani river about 24 km from its mouth.

periodLevel.summary: An urn-burial field excavated by Alexander Rea (ASI, 1899-1905) and again by T. Satyamurthy (ASI, 2003-05). Iron age burials from c. 1000-900 BCE, continuing into the early historic Sangam age; a radiocarbon date for the terminal megaliths here runs as late as the 12th century CE, which Upinder Singh cites as proof that the megaliths are not one homogeneous culture.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The largest and earliest-excavated urn-burial site in Tamil Nadu, and the bridge between the iron age and the Sangam age.
points: Hundreds of large black-and-red burial urns containing extended and fractional skeletons, husked paddy and grain. Cairn circles - the standard marker further north - are absent here.

Iron implements in quantity: swords, daggers, tridents and a trident with a cock finial, read by some as an early Murugan emblem; bronze objects; and gold diadems and ornaments. Gold is not local to the area, so its presence implies external contact.
An urn sherd carrying a Tamil-Brahmi inscription, dated by the excavator to c. 500 BCE, is central to the debate on the antiquity of Tamil literacy.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5; Rea, ASI *Annual Reports*; ASI, *IAR* 2004-05

location.summary: Mahurjhari lies about 15 km north-west of Nagpur on the Vidarbha uplands; the map dot falls in the adjoining Balaghat district of Madhya Pradesh, the copper-bearing tract of the upper Wainganga that also yielded the Gungeria hoard.

periodLevel.summary: Vidarbha megalithic, c. 800-400 BCE on the calibrated dates for the group (Naikund gives 800-420 BCE), with bead manufacture continuing from the megalithic into the early historic phase. Excavated by S. B. Deo in the 1970s and by R. K. Mohanty (Deccan College) from 1998.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The richest stone-circle cemetery of Vidarbha and the bead-making capital of the megalithic Deccan.
points: Bead manufacture on a large scale in carnelian, agate and jasper - which Mohanty (1999) connects directly to the exceptional richness of the grave goods here. Production spans the megalithic-to-early-historic transition.

Horse remains with iron bits and copper ornaments occur in almost every stone circle, as at Naikund. One burial held the complete skeleton of a horse whose cut marks show it was sacrificed and buried with its owner.

Two burials speak of a warrior tradition: an adult male with his mouth gaping and an arrow embedded near the collarbone, and the upper half of a male with an iron-bladed, copper-hilted dagger resting on his chest.
Balaghat, in the same tract, carries the copper-hoard connection: the Gungeria hoard from this district - 424 copper objects with 102 thin silver plates - is the largest copper hoard found in India.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5; Thapar, *Early India*; Mohanty (1999)

location.summary: Banahalli, in the granite uplands of eastern Karnataka (the Kolar-Chikkaballapur tract), in the upper drainage of the north Pennar, close to the Andhra border.

periodLevel.summary: A neolithic-chalcolithic settlement whose upper levels merge into a megalithic phase, the pattern Upinder Singh notes for most South Indian sites of this class. The megalithic burials belong to the first half of the 1st millennium BCE; excavated by the Karnataka Directorate of Archaeology and Museums in the 1980s.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Shows the neolithic-to-megalithic continuum of the Karnataka plateau in a single section, where the earliest iron of the region appears in the overlap.
points: Pit burials and sarcophagus burials in high-necked jars - a form that links the Karnataka megaliths to the legged sarcophagi of Tamil Nadu.
Black-and-red ware as the diagnostic pottery, alongside the wheel-made grey and buff wares of the terminal neolithic phase.

Iron objects including agricultural implements, which is the significant point: in the Deccan megaliths iron appears as farming equipment - hoes, sickles - as much as weaponry, implying an agrarian rather than purely martial economy.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5 (Map 5.5); ASI, *IAR*

location.summary: Banimilia-Banhera, on the northern fringe of the Vindhyas in the Varanasi-Chandauli tract of south-eastern Uttar Pradesh, in the Chandraprabha-Karamnasa drainage.

periodLevel.summary: Part of the south-eastern Uttar Pradesh megalithic province - the group spread over Allahabad, Banda, Varanasi and Mirzapur districts, with Kakoria, Jang Mahal and Kotia. Most megaliths of this province are pre-iron: the Jang Mahal group is placed at the beginning of the 1st millennium BCE and pre-iron Kakoria is given a range from the 2nd millennium BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Belongs to the one Indian megalithic zone that is substantially pre-iron - the standing exception to the equation of megaliths with the iron age.
points: The megalith types are cairns and stone circles. Many of them contain no skeletal remains of any kind and are best understood as memorials to the dead rather than graves.
Fractional burials occur in some graves, and separate animal burials in others; the associated pottery is black-and-red ware with black-slipped and plain red wares.

Since iron is absent here while the peninsular megaliths are defined by it, this province is the key qualification in any answer on megalithic chronology: the megaliths are a burial practice of wide date range, not a single culture.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5 (Vindhyan megaliths)

location.summary: Junapani, about 10 km north-west of Nagpur in Vidarbha, Maharashtra, on the Nagpur plateau in the upper Kanhan drainage.

periodLevel.summary: First reported by J. H. Rivett-Carnac in 1879, among the earliest megaliths ever recorded in India, and later excavated by the ASI and Nagpur University (S. B. Deo). Vidarbha megalithic, c. 1000-400 BCE, the burials commonly dated around 1000 BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The type site of the Vidarbha stone-circle burial and the principal Indian site for cup-marked megalithic stones.
points: About three hundred stone circles of packed boulders. Several of the stones carry cup marks pecked into them, sometimes interpreted as alignment or astronomical markers - a trait that sets Vidarbha apart from the cists and urns of the far south.

Horse burials with iron horse bits and copper ornaments; black-and-red ware; copper and iron objects. Thapar links these cairn burials, with their BRW and horse furniture, to megalithic burials further south.
The associated habitation deposits show that these were flourishing agricultural settlements, not the camps of pastoral nomads - the standard correction to older views of megalith builders.

location.summary: Kakoria, on the northern fringe of the Vindhyas in south-eastern Uttar Pradesh; the habitation lies on both banks of the Chandraprabha river, immediately north-west of the megalithic cemetery at the base of a hillock.

periodLevel.summary: Pre-iron megalithic. A range from the 2nd millennium BCE (or earlier) to the 7th century CE has been suggested for pre-iron Kakoria, against the beginning of the 1st millennium BCE for the neighbouring Jang Mahal group and c. 800-300 BCE for Kotia.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The best-documented habitation-plus-cemetery pairing in the pre-iron megalithic province of the Vindhyas.
points: The megaliths are cairns and stone circles; some graves show fractional burial, others are associated with animal burials, and many contain no skeletal remains at all - memorials rather than graves.

Pottery from both habitation and burials is black-and-red ware, black-slipped ware and red ware, mostly wheel-made, with dishes, bowls, perforated vessels, lids, pedestalled cups and elliptical and globular jars.

Microliths of agate, chalcedony and chert in quantity; beads of terracotta and semi-precious stone; sling balls, grinding stones and a few copper objects - and no iron, which is the defining negative evidence of this province.

location.summary: Kotia, in the Belan valley of south-eastern Uttar Pradesh (the Prayagraj-Mirzapur tract), on the northern Vindhyan fringe.

periodLevel.summary: Megalithic, dated c. 800-300 BCE - later than the pre-iron megaliths around it, and the single iron-bearing exception in the province. Investigated in the Allahabad University programme of Belan valley excavations.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The exception that carries iron in a largely pre-iron megalithic region, and therefore the site that dates the arrival of iron in the Vindhyas.
points: Many iron tools - a spearhead, two sickles, an arrowhead and an adze - which Upinder Singh reads as indicating advanced metallurgical technique.
The graves yielded few human skeletal remains, but three contained the remains of domesticated sheep, pig and cattle; cut marks show the animals were killed at the time of burial.
Thick-fabric pottery: black-and-red ware, red ware, black-slipped ware and a dull coarse black or grey ware. Bones of ox, sheep and pig, some with cut marks, occur in the habitation deposit.

location.summary: Kuntitoli, on the Chotanagpur plateau of Jharkhand, in the western uplands drained by the North Koel.

periodLevel.summary: Eastern Indian megalithic - burials of the 1st millennium BCE in a region where megalith building survived as a living practice among the Munda-speaking peoples into modern times.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Represents the eastern Indian megalithic province, where archaeology and ethnography can be read together.
points: Dolmens, cists and standing stones of the type massed on the same plateau at Chokahatu, the 'place of mourning' in Ranchi district - one of the largest megalithic burial grounds in India.

Burials of the class the Mundas still call sasandiri, flat slabs raised over the collected bones of a clan's dead, which is why the eastern group is treated as evidence for what megaliths were for, not merely when they were built.
Associated black-and-red ware and iron objects tie the plateau to the Vindhyan group to the west and the Vidarbha group to the south.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5 (eastern India); ASI, *IAR* (Chotanagpur megaliths)

location.summary: Nagarjunakonda, Palnadu (formerly Guntur) district, Andhra Pradesh, in a valley on the right bank of the Krishna, now an island in the Nagarjunasagar reservoir.

periodLevel.summary: A sequence running from the palaeolithic, through a neolithic-chalcolithic farming village of the 3rd millennium BCE, to a megalithic phase of the 1st millennium BCE, and then to the Ikshvaku capital Vijayapuri of the 3rd-4th centuries CE. Salvage-excavated by R. Subrahmanyam (ASI, 1954-60) before submergence.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The one site where the megalithic phase can be read directly against both a neolithic village below it and an early historic city above.
points: Megalithic cists and pit burials with black-and-red ware, iron objects and beads - the Andhra group of megaliths, with Kadambapur, Yelleswaram, Gallapalli and Tadapatri.
Its palaeolithic levels have yielded palaeo-climatic data, and Thapar lists it among the early farming settlements of the Krishna-Tungabhadra tract alongside Hallur, Kupgal and Maski.
Above the megaliths lie the mahachaityas, viharas, an amphitheatre and Brahmanical temples of Vijayapuri, with the Ikshvaku inscriptions - treated under the Buddhist sites.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5 and ch. 8; Thapar, *Early India*; ASI Nagarjunakonda memoirs

location.summary: Naikund, about 40 km north-east of Nagpur in Vidarbha, Maharashtra, near Ramtek in the Kanhan-Wainganga tract.

periodLevel.summary: Vidarbha megalithic, with calibrated ranges of 800-420 BCE and 785-410 BCE - the firmest chronology available for the whole group. Excavated by S. B. Deo and A. P. Jamkhedkar (1978-80).

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Supplies the dates for the Vidarbha megaliths and the clearest iron-smelting workshop of the Indian iron age.
points: An iron-smelting furnace built of small curved bricks with a cylindrical terracotta pipe (tuyere); iron ore was traced to a nala about a kilometre away. This is the standard citation for local smelting rather than traded iron.

Stone-circle graves containing horse skeletons with iron bits and copper ornaments, as at Mahurjhari. The iron repertoire is wide - hoes, ladles, nails, dagger blades, arrowheads, knives, chisels, spikes, axes, double-edged adzes, bars, fishhooks, bangles, tridents, a sword and a cauldron.

The habitation had circular huts with wooden posts, black-and-red ware, and barley, rice and lentil grains lying on house floors - a prosperous agricultural village behind the cemetery. Iron hoes here are the direct evidence for iron in agriculture.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5; Deo & Jamkhedkar, *Excavations at Naikund* (1982)

location.summary: Nartiang, West Jaintia Hills district, Meghalaya, on a ridge above the Myntdu valley near Jowai - the old summer capital of the Jaintia rajas.

periodLevel.summary: A living megalithic tradition rather than a prehistoric one: the stones of the monolith park were raised by Jaintia chieftains from about the 16th century CE onwards, and the practice continued into the 19th century. The site is protected by the ASI.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The largest single collection of standing monoliths in India, and the standing proof that megalith building is not confined to prehistory.
points: Menhirs - moo shynrang or 'male stones', the tallest about 8 m and attributed to the chieftain U Mar Phalyngki - set beside flat table stones, moo kynthai or 'female stones', raised as memorials and to mark victories and market rights.
The Khasi-Jaintia custom of erecting memorial stones over ossuaries holding cremated bone makes the north-eastern group the ethnographic key to what megaliths were for.

It anchors the crucial distinction between commemorative and sepulchral megaliths, and supports Upinder Singh's warning that the megaliths cannot be treated as a single, homogeneous or contemporaneous culture.

location.summary: Porkalam, near Kunnamkulam in Thrissur district, Kerala, on the laterite uplands between the Bharathappuzha and Chalakudy drainages.

periodLevel.summary: Kerala megalithic (iron age), broadly c. 1000-100 BCE - the range established for the Kerala group at Mangadu in Kollam district. Excavated by B. K. Thapar in 1948, the first scientific excavation of a Kerala umbrella-stone megalith.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The type site for the distinctive laterite megalithic forms of Kerala, found nowhere else in India.
points: A kudakkal or umbrella stone: four clinostatic laterite slabs capped by a dressed hemispherical stone, set over a pit holding the burial urn; topikals or hat stones stand nearby.
The urn contained bones with iron implements and black-and-red ware; the iron objects include daggers and a tripod.

Kerala's repertoire - kudakkal, topikal, rock-cut chambers and hood stones, all cut from soft laterite - is a regional adaptation of the peninsular megalithic and is the standard illustration of megalithic regional variation.

content.sourcesLine: B. K. Thapar, 'Porkalam 1948', *Ancient India* 8 (1952); Upinder Singh, ch. 5 (megalith types)

location.summary: Sanur, near Tindivanam in the old Chingleput district of northern Tamil Nadu, in the Palar-Ponnaiyar interfluve.

periodLevel.summary: Iron age megalithic, placed by its excavators in the last centuries BCE and the early centuries CE, within the Tamil Nadu megalithic range of c. 1000 BCE to the early centuries CE. Excavated by N. R. Banerjee and K. V. Soundara Rajan in 1950 and 1952.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The standard published Tamil Nadu megalithic excavation, and the site that defined the dolmenoid cist with a sarcophagus - the illustration reproduced in most textbooks, including Upinder Singh's.
points: Dolmenoid cists set inside stone circles, each holding a legged terracotta sarcophagus within the chamber; several orthostats carry the characteristic port-hole cut into the slab.
Black-and-red ware and russet-coated painted ware, iron implements and beads; the excavation established the local sequence of cist, urn and pit-circle types.
With Adichanallur, Amritamangalam and Kunnattur it sets the Tamil megalithic typology, and its sarcophagus form connects the Tamil country to the jar burials of Karnataka.

location.summary: Veerapuram, Kurnool district, Andhra Pradesh, on the right bank of the Krishna near Nandikotkur, downstream of the Tungabhadra confluence.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by the Birla Archaeological and Cultural Research Institute (T. V. G. Sastry and others, 1977-80). A neolithic level, a megalithic-iron age level of the earlier 1st millennium BCE, and an early historic Satavahana level above.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A type site for the cultural sequence of the Krishna valley, chosen and published precisely for its unbroken column.
points: The neolithic-megalithic overlap, in which the earliest iron objects of the region appear - the transition Upinder Singh treats as characteristic of South India, where iron enters at the join between the neolithic and megalithic phases.

Megalithic burials with black-and-red ware, iron implements and beads, belonging to the Andhra group with Kadambapur, Nagarjunakonda, Yelleswaram and Gallapalli; habitation deposits with circular huts.
Satavahana-period levels above, with coins, beads and brick structures, carry the site into the early historic period and allow the megalithic phase to be dated by what follows it.

content.sourcesLine: T. V. G. Sastry et al., *Veerapuram: A Type Site for Cultural Study in the Krishna Valley* (Hyderabad, 1984); Upinder Singh, ch. 5

location.summary: Bargaon, Saharanpur district, western Uttar Pradesh, in the upper Ganga-Yamuna doab beside Ambakheri and Hulas, in the Hindon-Krishni drainage.

periodLevel.summary: Late Harappan to Ochre Coloured Pottery, c. 1900-1300 BCE. The OCP phase as a whole carries thermoluminescence dates of 2650-1180 BCE from Atranjikhera, Lal Qila, Nasirpur and Jhinjhina, making it a late contemporary of the mature and late Harappan cultures.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The type locality for the late Harappan-OCP overlap, and the centre of the densest OCP concentration in the subcontinent.
points: Bargaon and Ambakheri are the two sites where late Harappan and OCP levels overlap, which is the main evidence for those who read OCP as a degenerate late Harappan ware rather than an independent tradition.

Bargaon anchors the western OCP zone, which retains Harappan links (with Jodhpura, Siswal, Mitathal, Bara and Ambakheri), as against the eastern zone of Lal Qila, Atranjikhera and Saipai, which shows none.

Over 80 OCP sites have been identified in Saharanpur district alone, spaced 4-6 km apart - a dense village landscape. Finds include a fragmentary copper chisel and rings, chert blades, querns, bone points, terracotta cakes, carts and wheels, and beads of steatite, agate, carnelian and faience.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4-5; Mughal and Dikshit on the Saharanpur OCP survey

location.summary: Rajpur Parsu in Bijnor district, western Uttar Pradesh, on the upper Ganga where the river leaves the Siwaliks - the northern edge of the OCP distribution, which runs up to Bahadarabad near Hardwar.

periodLevel.summary: With Bisauli, one of the two sites where Ochre Coloured Pottery was first identified, in 1950-51, in B. B. Lal's excavations. The OCP phase runs c. 2000-1500 BCE within the wider thermoluminescence bracket of 2650-1180 BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A type site of the OCP culture - the ware that gives the whole post-Harappan doab its archaeological name.
points: The pottery is ill-fired and wheel-made, of fine to medium fabric, with a thick red slip sometimes decorated in black bands, and incised designs and post-firing graffiti on some sherds. Rubbed, it leaves an ochre smear on the fingers - from waterlogging, wind action, poor firing, or all three - which is what named it.

Rajpur Parsu also yielded a copper hoard, including nine flat celts and harpoons, making it one of the few places where the two defining traits of the culture - OCP and copper hoard objects - occur together.

B. B. Lal noted the resemblance of this ware to the ceramic industry of the lowest level at Hastinapura, where OCP is followed by a break in occupation and then Painted Grey Ware - the sequence on which doab chronology rests.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5; B. B. Lal, *Ancient India* 1950-51 and 1954-55

location.summary: Bisauli, Budaun district, western Uttar Pradesh, in the Ganga-Ramganga tract of the upper doab.

periodLevel.summary: With Rajpur Parsu (Bijnor), the site at which Ochre Coloured Pottery was first recognised, in 1950-51 by B. B. Lal. The copper hoard objects are attributed to the 2nd millennium BCE, though most were recovered without stratigraphic context.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Joint type site of the OCP culture, and the source of the anthropomorph that defines the copper hoard debate.
points: Ill-fired wheel-made pottery of fine to medium fabric with a thick red slip, decorated with black bands, carrying incised designs and post-firing graffiti.

The Bisauli copper anthropomorph: cast and then hammered, with in-curved arms sharpened on the outer edge and plain outstretched legs, the head thickened by beating. Anthropomorphs run 25-45 cm in length and 30-43 cm in breadth and weigh up to 5 kg; length normally exceeds breadth, and the Bisauli piece is the recorded exception.

The function of the anthropomorph is unsettled: D. P. Agrawal proposed a throwing weapon with a whirling boomerang effect for killing birds, while others argue for a ritual object - tiny figures of the same shape are still worshipped in north India as Shani. The 2001 find of 31 anthropomorphs at Madarpur (Moradabad), stacked in situ in a deposit with OCP, favours the second reading.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5; B. B. Lal, *Ancient India* 1950-51; D. V. Sharma et al. (2001-02)

location.summary: Bithur, Kanpur district, Uttar Pradesh, on the right bank of the Ganga in the central doab.

periodLevel.summary: The findspot of 1822 - the first copper hoard object ever recorded in India, a copper harpoon. The hoards as a class are placed between the mid-3rd and the 2nd millennium BCE, but almost all were chance finds without stratigraphy.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The discovery that created the category: every discussion of the copper hoards begins here.
points: The 1822 harpoon was followed by flat celts, shouldered celts and further harpoons from the same tract, part of a large hoard.

Since 1822 over 1,300 copper objects of this range have been found at about 90 sites, from the upper Ganga valley to Bengal and Odisha, with outliers in Haryana, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu. The greatest concentration is the Uttar Pradesh doab; hoards contain 1 to 47 objects, the sole exception being Gungeria in Madhya Pradesh with 424 copper objects weighing over 200 kg and 102 silver plates.

Because the finds are unstratified, dating rests on the rare excavated cases - Saipai in Etawah district, where copper hoard objects came from an OCP level, and Sanauli, where two antennae swords occurred in a late Harappan grave.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5; ASI, *IAR*

location.summary: Saipai, Etawah district, Uttar Pradesh, in the lower Ganga-Yamuna doab near the Yamuna, in the eastern OCP zone.

periodLevel.summary: An excavated OCP settlement of the 2nd millennium BCE, within the thermoluminescence range of 2650-1180 BCE obtained for the OCP culture. Excavated by the UP State Archaeology Department (1970s).

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The single most important copper hoard site, because here alone the objects came out of a dated, excavated OCP level rather than a chance find.
points: A copper hooked spearhead and a harpoon were recovered from the OCP deposit itself - the evidence that ties the copper hoards to the OCP culture and dates them. Anthropomorphs, harpoons, hooked swords, lance heads and thick, glossy, light-green axes are reported from the district.
Sandstone pounders, querns and pestles, and bones of domesticated Bos indicus, show a settled farming and cattle-keeping village behind the metal.

Saipai belongs to the eastern OCP zone, which - unlike Bargaon, Ambakheri and Jodhpura in the west - shows no link with the Harappan ceramic tradition. Upinder Singh singles out the site as 'especially important' for precisely this stratified association.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5; ASI, *IAR*

location.summary: Kallur, Raichur district, northern Karnataka, in the Raichur doab between the Krishna and the Tungabhadra - the southernmost copper hoard findspot on the standard distribution map.

periodLevel.summary: A neolithic-megalithic settlement of the Karnataka plateau whose copper hoard is placed in the late 2nd to early 1st millennium BCE, at the neolithic-megalithic overlap where the region's earliest metal appears.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Carries the copper hoard tradition a thousand kilometres south of the doab, and so defines the outer limit of the phenomenon.
points: Famous for its antennae swords, the longest exceeding 36 inches - the same distinctive type found in the Uttar Pradesh and Haryana hoards, and recently in a late Harappan grave at Sanauli with a copper sheath.

The presence of doab types this far south is the main evidence for Upinder Singh's conclusion that the upper Ganga valley emerged as a distinct copper-manufacturing area between the mid-3rd and 2nd millennia BCE, with interactions reaching Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, the Deccan, Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

Typology varies by region: flat, shouldered and bar celts and double axes dominate the eastern zone of Bihar, Bengal and Odisha; these occur with anthropomorphs, antennae swords, hooked swords and harpoons in Uttar Pradesh and Haryana; Rajasthan yields mainly flat and bar celts.

location.summary: Meerut district, western Uttar Pradesh, in the Ganga-Yamuna doab on the Hindon; one of the four districts - with Saharanpur, Muzaffarnagar and Bulandshahr - holding the densest OCP concentration.

periodLevel.summary: Ochre Coloured Pottery, c. 2000-1500 BCE, overlapping the late Harappan occupation of the same district at Alamgirpur. OCP deposits here are shallow, 0.5-1.5 m thick, and the settlements small, usually 200-300 sq m.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The core OCP district, and the tract that yields both the anthropomorph hoards and the late Harappan graves that date them.
points: Wattle-and-daub houses with mud floors and post-holes are the norm; at Atranjikhera the posts were of babul, sissoo, sal and chir pine, with an unlined well. Lal Qila in Bulandshahr district, the largest excavated OCP settlement at 632 sq m, gave oblong wattle-and-daub structures, a few sun-dried bricks with mud mortar, five copper objects, bone tools and terracotta anthropomorphic and animal figurines.

Lal Qila yielded wheat, barley and rice, and Atranjikhera rice, barley, gram and khesari - two crops a year, rice in summer and barley and legumes in winter. Circular fire pits at Lal Qila held charred bones of cattle, buffalo, goat, sheep, pig, horse, dog and wild deer, many with cut marks.

At Sanauli in the neighbouring Baghpat district, D. V. Sharma's excavations found a late Harappan cemetery with two copper hoard-type antennae swords, one in situ in a grave with a copper sheath - the firmest link yet between the copper hoards and a datable culture.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5; D. V. Sharma et al., Sanauli reports; ASI, *IAR*

location.summary: Shalozan, in the upper Kurram valley on the Pakistan-Afghanistan frontier (Kurram district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa), on the route from the Indus plains through the Peiwar Kotal into Afghanistan.

periodLevel.summary: A copper hoard findspot of the 2nd millennium BCE, recovered as a chance find without stratigraphy, like most hoards of this class.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Marks the westernmost extent of the copper hoard distribution, and the point at which the Indian series meets the Iranian and Central Asian one.
points: The diagnostic objects are trunnion celts - axes cast with lateral lugs or trunnions for hafting. This is a West Asian and Central Asian type, not a doab type, and its appearance here is the argument for contact across the Hindu Kush rather than for an extension of the Gangetic tradition.

The contrast with the doab hoards is instructive: those run to flat, shouldered and bar celts, harpoons, antennae swords and anthropomorphs, all largely hunting equipment, and about 46 per cent of copper hoard objects carry up to 7 per cent arsenic alloying against only 8 per cent of analysed Harappan artefacts - a different metallurgical tradition altogether.

The find bears on the open question Upinder Singh leaves standing: whether the upper Ganga valley was an independent centre of copper working, or an extension of the older centre in north-eastern Rajasthan at Ganeshwar-Jodhpura.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5; B. B. Lal on the north-western copper hoard types

location.summary: Ahichchhatra (modern Ramnagar), Bareilly district, Uttar Pradesh, in the Ramganga basin of the upper Ganga plain - the capital of North Panchala.

periodLevel.summary: The site at which Painted Grey Ware was first identified, in the ASI excavations of the 1940s (K. N. Dikshit and A. Ghosh), although its significance was only grasped after Hastinapura. Here the OCP level is followed by a break in occupation and then PGW, c. 1100-500/400 BCE; NBPW, Kushana and Gupta levels follow.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The type site of the PGW culture and one of its largest settlements, with a sequence running unbroken into the early historic city.
points: The PGW sherds from Ahichchhatra and Hastinapura are the standard published illustrations of the ware: a very fine, thin, even-coloured grey fabric, wheel-turned to eggshell thickness and painted in black with simple geometric designs.

Houses in the PGW levels are of wattle and daub and mud; burnt brick appears only in the later periods, when the site is enclosed by a great rampart and becomes one of the largest fortified mounds in the doab.

As the Ahichchhatra of the Mahabharata it is the capital of North Panchala - the half of the kingdom ceded to Drona, with Kampilya holding the south. This pairing of the PGW map with the epic geography is the core of the archaeology-and-Mahabharata argument.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5; Thapar, *Early India*; K. N. Dikshit, *Ancient India* 1 (1946)

location.summary: Atranjikhera, Etah district, Uttar Pradesh, on the left bank of the Kali Nadi, a tributary of the Ganga in the central doab.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by R. C. Gaur (Aligarh Muslim University, 1962-68). Period I OCP; Period II Black and Red Ware; Period III PGW, c. 1200-600 BCE; Period IV NBPW. PGW here is preceded by a BRW phase with a break in between - one of the four stratigraphic patterns in which PGW occurs.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The site at which a distinct BRW phase in the doab was first recognised, and the best evidence anywhere for PGW-age iron technology.
points: BRW lay sandwiched between the OCP and PGW levels. The same sequence was later found at Noh and Jodhpura in Rajasthan, and it is the basis for treating BRW as an independent doab phase rather than a stray ware.

Chemical analysis of the iron from the PGW levels showed wrought iron that had then been carburised, probably by long heating on a charcoal bed. The composition of the objects and of the slag matches the iron-rich rocks of the Agra-Gwalior hills, which identifies the ore source - rare precision for this period.

Rice, barley, gram and khesari came from the OCP levels and rice and moong from the BRW levels: two crops a year. Deep circular pits outside the habitation are read as kachcha wells of the kind still used locally for irrigation.

Jakhera, in the same district, carries the culture to a proto-urban stage - a 60 m water channel with a bund, potsherd-paved roads and lanes, storage bins implying surplus, gold and copper ornaments, 106 semi-precious stone beads, and iron sickle, hoe and ploughshare.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5; R. C. Gaur, *Excavations at Atranjikhera* (1983)

location.summary: The Bahawalpur region of Punjab (Pakistan), in the Cholistan tract along the dry Hakra-Ghaggar - the western limit of the Painted Grey Ware distribution.

periodLevel.summary: PGW, c. 1100-500/400 BCE. The north-western sites are held to be earlier than those of the Ganga valley, so this is where the culture begins rather than where it peters out.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Fixes the western extent of PGW and supplies one of the three regional settlement studies on which PGW social history rests.
points: M. R. Mughal's survey identified 14 PGW sites here, ranging from 0.5 to 13.7 ha; apart from Satwali at 13.7 ha, all are under 5 ha. This is the same two-tier hierarchy - one large site among many small ones - found in northern Haryana (one site of 9.6 ha, none other above 4.3 ha) and in Allahabad district, where Kaushambi at 10 ha stands over fifteen sites averaging 1.72 ha.

PGW occurs here on the dry Hakra, in the very tract that had earlier carried the densest Kot Dijian and mature Harappan concentration - the same river system holding two settlement systems a millennium apart.

PGW sites in the Ghaggar-Hakra area, Bhagwanpura included, have yielded no iron artefacts at all, unlike those of the doab. This is the standing regional qualification to any equation of PGW with the iron age.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5 (Map 5.7); Mughal, *Ancient Cholistan* (1997)

location.summary: Noh, near Bharatpur in eastern Rajasthan, on the Ruparel drainage at the western edge of the Ganga-Yamuna doab.

periodLevel.summary: Period I OCP; Period II BRW, carrying the first pieces of iron; Period III PGW, c. 1000-600 BCE; Period IV NBPW, with Sunga-Kushana levels above. Excavated by the Rajasthan Department of Archaeology (R. C. Agrawala) in the 1960s.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Carries the full doab sequence - OCP, BRW, PGW, NBPW - into Rajasthan, and is one of the sites where iron appears before PGW.
points: Shapeless pieces of iron occur in the BRW level, below PGW; the PGW level yielded a spearhead, an arrowhead with a socketed tang and an axe with a broad cutting edge. With Jakhera and Kaushambi, Noh is an exception to the doab norm in which the earliest iron accompanies PGW.
Burnt bricks and rice were recovered here, and terracotta gamesmen, taken as evidence of gaming as a pastime.

Noh shares its cultural sequence with the neighbouring upper Ganga valley. Together with Jodhpura - where the PGW levels produced a crucible-shaped furnace for the direct reduction of ore, with a forging platform beside it - it makes eastern Rajasthan a second centre of early iron working.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5; ASI, *IAR* 1963-67

location.summary: Chak 86, Sri Ganganagar district, northern Rajasthan, on the dry Ghaggar close to the Pakistan border and the Bahawalpur PGW cluster.

periodLevel.summary: A Painted Grey Ware findspot of c. 1100-600 BCE in the Ghaggar-Hakra belt, recorded in exploration rather than by excavation. The north-western PGW sites are taken to be earlier than those of the Ganga plains.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: With Bahawalpur across the border, one of the two westernmost points on the standard PGW distribution map.
points: It belongs to the Ghaggar-Hakra group of PGW sites which, like Bhagwanpura, have produced no iron - so at the western end the culture is defined by its pottery alone.

The ware itself is a very fine, thin, wheel-turned grey pottery painted in black with rows of lines, dots, dashes, circles, spirals, swastikas and sigmas. It forms only 3-10 per cent of the assemblage at the levels where it occurs, appearing with plain grey ware, BRW and black-slipped ware - a deluxe table ware for the well-to-do, not a household pottery.
The Ghaggar sites matter for the Vedic question: this is the Sarasvati tract where late Harappan settlement is densest, and PGW follows it in the same valley - overlapping it outright at Bhagwanpura.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5 (Map 5.7); ASI, *IAR*

location.summary: Hastinapura, Meerut district, Uttar Pradesh, on an old right bank of the Ganga in the upper doab.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by B. B. Lal in 1950-52 and published in *Ancient India* 10-11 (1954-55). Period I OCP; a break in occupation; Period II PGW, c. 1100-800 BCE; Period III NBPW, c. 600-200 BCE; Period IV c. 200 BCE-300 CE; Period V, 11th-15th centuries.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The excavation that established what PGW meant, and the classic attempt to tie Indian archaeology to the Mahabharata.
points: PGW occurs with black-slipped ware and plain red and red-slipped wares. Houses were of mud, mud brick and reed; unbaked bricks and a single baked brick were found. Also chert and jasper weights, bone needles, glass bangles, and iron slag in the upper levels.
Charred grains of rice and bones of pig, horse and cattle; the horse bones from Hastinapura are among the few securely reported from PGW levels.

Lal found that Period II ended in a heavy Ganga flood, and connected this with the Puranic tradition that Nichakshu abandoned Hastinapura and moved the Kuru capital to Kaushambi - the most-cited correlation of archaeology with the epic, and a much-contested one.
The site also gives the OCP-break-PGW pattern (shared with Ahichchhatra and Jhinjhana), one of the four stratigraphic contexts in which PGW is found.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; B. B. Lal, *Ancient India* 10-11 (1954-55)

location.summary: Kampilya (modern Kampil), Farrukhabad district, Uttar Pradesh, on an old course of the Ganga in the central doab - the capital of South Panchala.

periodLevel.summary: Occupation begins in the PGW phase, c. 1100-600 BCE, and runs on through NBPW into the early historic period. Upinder Singh lists Kampil among the excavated sites giving important evidence of PGW material culture; the early excavations exposed wattle-and-daub structures.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A Mahajanapada capital whose occupation demonstrably begins in the PGW phase - the archaeological test of the epic and Vedic geography.
points: Wattle-and-daub and mud structures in the PGW levels, the normal architecture of the culture; burnt brick arrives only with the NBPW phase and the second urbanisation.

Panchala was divided along the Ganga into North Panchala, with its capital at Ahichchhatra, and South Panchala, with its capital here. The Mahabharata sets Draupadi's svayamvara at Kampilya, at Drupada's court.
Kampil is also a Jain tirtha, traditionally the birthplace of the thirteenth Tirthankara Vimalanatha, and the later Panchala tribal coins bearing the names of local rulers come from this area.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5 (Map 5.7) and ch. 6; ASI, *IAR*

location.summary: Kaushambi (Kosam), near Prayagraj in Uttar Pradesh, on the left bank of the Yamuna - the capital of the Vatsa mahajanapada, and the eastern limit of the PGW distribution.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by G. R. Sharma (Allahabad University, 1949-66). Iron is present in the pre-PGW BRW level here; the PGW phase is followed by NBPW from c. 600 BCE, and the city runs on into the Kushana and Gupta periods.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The largest PGW settlement of the eastern doab, and the place where the PGW village landscape visibly turns into a city.
points: In Erdosy's settlement survey of Allahabad district, Kaushambi stands at 10 ha against fifteen other sites of 0.42-2.80 ha averaging 1.72 ha - an unmistakable two-tier hierarchy. Its siting on poor soil and rugged ground suggests it was placed to command the mineral resources of the Vindhyas rather than the best farmland.

Early houses of timber give way to brick. The city was planned and enclosed by a massive mud rampart with a burnt-brick revetment, bastions and gateways, which G. R. Sharma dated extremely early - a dating widely disputed.

Iron agricultural implements and weapons in quantity; later, the Ghositarama monastery and an Ashokan pillar carrying the schism edict. Puranic tradition brings the Kurus here from flooded Hastinapura under Nichakshu, which is why the two sites are always read together.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5-6; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Erdosy (1988)

location.summary: Mathura, on the right bank of the Yamuna in western Uttar Pradesh - the capital of the Surasena mahajanapada, at the crossing of the Uttarapatha and the southern route to Ujjain.

periodLevel.summary: PGW occurring with BRW, dated c. 800-400 BCE, followed by the NBPW phase and then the great Kushana city. Investigated by the ASI at the city mounds and at Sonkh nearby.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the largest PGW sites, and the clearest case of a PGW village growing without a break into a metropolis.
points: The sequence shows gradual growth from a village settlement rather than a founded city: PGW with BRW in the earliest levels, and steady expansion through the NBPW phase into a fortified early historic town.
Its position on the Yamuna at a junction of the great trunk routes made it the river port of the doab, which is why a modest PGW village became the southern capital of the Kushanas.

The later city produced the Mathura school of sculpture in spotted red sandstone, the earliest datable Buddha images in the round, the Kankali Tila Jain stupa, and the Mat devakula with its statues of the Kushana kings - all treated under the art sites.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5-6; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; ASI, *IAR*

location.summary: Rupnagar (Ropar), on the left bank of the Sutlej in Punjab, where the river leaves the Siwaliks - the north-western end of the PGW distribution in the Sutlej basin.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by Y. D. Sharma (ASI, 1953-56). Period II is PGW, following the Harappan level after a break in occupation; Period III is NBPW, c. 600-200 BCE, when urbanisation appears.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Fixes the PGW-after-a-break pattern that stands against the Bhagwanpura overlap - the two together frame the Harappan-Vedic argument.
points: The break between the Harappan and PGW levels here is shared with Sanghol in Punjab, Daulatpur in Haryana, and Alamgirpur and Hulas in western Uttar Pradesh. Against it stand Bhagwanpura, Dadheri, Katpalon and Nagar, where the two cultures overlap - so the relationship differs from valley to valley and cannot be settled by one site.
Signs of urbanisation come with the NBPW phase, c. 600-200 BCE: burnt-brick structures, punch-marked coins, uninscribed cast copper coins and a seal with a Mauryan Brahmi legend.

Its position in the Sutlej basin puts it in the Punjab-Haryana group of PGW sites, which is taken to be earlier than the Ganga valley group; the site's full six-period sequence from Harappan to medieval is treated in the Harappan chapter.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5; ASI, *IAR* 1953-56

exam.modelAnswer30: On the left bank of the Sutlej in Punjab. Period II is PGW. Fixes the PGW-after-a-break pattern that stands against the Bhagwanpura overlap, the two together frame the Harappan-Vedic argument.

location.summary: Shravasti (the twin mounds of Saheth-Maheth), on the south bank of the Rapti - the ancient Achiravati - in Shravasti and Balrampur districts, Uttar Pradesh; the capital of the Kosala mahajanapada.

periodLevel.summary: Identified by Sir Alexander Cunningham in 1863. Occupation begins in the PGW phase, c. 1000-600 BCE - the site marks the eastern edge of the PGW map - and continues through NBPW into the Kushana and Gupta periods. Excavated by K. K. Sinha (Banaras Hindu University, 1959) and by the ASI.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A Mahajanapada capital whose PGW village underlies one of the greatest Buddhist centres in India.
points: The PGW levels give wattle-and-daub and mud huts, the standard architecture of the culture; the later phases bring sturdy brick houses and the great horseshoe-shaped mud rampart around Maheth, revetted and pierced by gateways.
Iron objects, among them an elephant figure, and eye beads were recovered - the material of a settlement moving from village to town.

Saheth is the Jetavana, the grove Anathapindika bought from Prince Jeta and gave to the Buddha, who by tradition spent twenty-five rainy seasons here, more than at any other place; the Twin Miracle is set at Shravasti. It is also a Jain tirtha, the birthplace of the third Tirthankara Sambhavanatha.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5-6; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Cunningham, *ASI Reports*

exam.modelAnswer30: On the south bank of the Rapti, the ancient Achiravati. Identified by Sir Alexander Cunningham in 1863. A Mahajanapada capital whose PGW village underlies one of the greatest Buddhist centres in India.

location.summary: Thapli, in the Garhwal Himalaya of Uttarakhand, on a terrace above the Alaknanda-Ganga system near Srinagar (Garhwal) - one of the few excavated prehistoric sites in the Indian central Himalaya.

periodLevel.summary: A Neolithic settlement with later occupation, broadly assigned to the 2nd millennium BCE, excavated by the ASI and Garhwal University. It belongs with Malari, Ranihat and the Kumaon rock shelters in the small corpus of Himalayan prehistory.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Evidence that the Himalayan valleys were settled by farming communities, not merely crossed by them.
points: The site has yielded ground and polished stone tools, including the shouldered and harvester types that link the central Himalaya to the north-eastern Neolithic rather than to the Gangetic or southern traditions, together with handmade cord-impressed and burnished pottery.

That tool typology is the analytical point. The Indian Neolithic is usually taught as three or four regional groups - the north-west, the Vindhyan-Gangetic, the southern and the north-eastern - and the Himalayan sites sit awkwardly across them, sharing traits with Kashmir's Burzahom and Gufkral and with the shouldered celts of Assam and Meghalaya.

Burzahom's pit dwellings and bone tools make the Kashmir group the best known; Thapli and Malari extend the picture eastward along the mountain belt and show the Garhwal valleys were occupied continuously from prehistory.
The region's rock shelters at Lakhudiyar and elsewhere belong to the same broad horizon and are the art to set beside this settlement evidence.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; *Indian Archaeology - A Review*
