location.summary: Amaravati with the adjoining fortified mound of Dharanikota, Guntur district, Andhra Pradesh, on the right bank of the Krishna near the head of its delta.

periodLevel.summary: Dharanikota (ASI, R. Subrahmanyam, 1962-65) opens with an NBPW level of c. 400-300 BCE behind a mud rampart. The Satavahana capital Dhanyakataka and the Mahachaitya run c. 200 BCE-250 CE, with Ikshvaku patronage after; the carved railing and drum slabs are of the 1st-2nd centuries CE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A stratified NBPW level lying directly under a Satavahana capital - the clearest Deccan evidence that the second urbanisation reached the Krishna.
points: Dharanikota yielded a brick-lined navigational channel with a wooden wharf on the Krishna, tying the stupa's wealth to river and sea trade rather than to land revenue.

The Mahachaitya (Dipaladinne) had a drum of about 50 m faced in white Palnad limestone, with ayaka platforms carrying five pillars on each of the four sides - the diagnostic feature of Andhra stupas, absent at Sanchi and Bharhut.

The Amaravati school: high-relief narrative medallions, slender swaying figures and crowded compositions, with both aniconic and iconic Buddha images side by side. Recorded by Colin Mackenzie in 1797 and 1816; slabs are now in the Government Museum, Chennai, and the British Museum.
Tibetan tradition places the Buddha's first teaching of the Kalachakra at Dhanyakataka, and Nagarjuna is associated with this stretch of the Krishna.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8; Thapar, *Early India*; ASI, *IAR* 1962-65; Robert Knox, *Amaravati* (1992)

location.summary: Ayodhya (ancient Saketa), Ayodhya - formerly Faizabad - district, Uttar Pradesh, on the right bank of the Sarayu (Ghaghara), the northern capital of Kosala.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by B. B. Lal for the ASI's Archaeology of the Ramayana Sites project (1975-80) and again by the ASI in 2003. Period I is NBPW, with radiocarbon dates reaching back to c. 700 BCE - among the earliest NBPW horizons anywhere - running to c. 200 BCE; Shunga-Kushana and Gupta levels follow.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the sites that pushes the beginning of NBPW back before 600 BCE, and a rare case of the ware arriving before monumental building.
points: NBPW occurs with a grey ware bearing linear designs. Houses in this level are of wattle and daub; there are no baked-brick structures, so the deluxe ware precedes urban architecture here.
Broken votive tanks, wheel-made terracotta discs and animal figurines; ring wells and burnt brick appear only in the later levels.

Post-Mauryan coins were struck here by the local Deva kings, and the Dhanadeva inscription of the 1st century BCE records that his ancestor Pushyamitra performed two ashvamedhas - one of the few epigraphic notices of the Shungas.
Saketa is one of the six great cities (mahanagaras) of the Digha Nikaya, and a Jaina tirtha as the birthplace of five Tirthankaras including Rishabhanatha.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 6; B. B. Lal in ASI, *IAR* 1976-77; Thapar, *Early India*

location.summary: Champa (Champanagar-Champapur), near Bhagalpur, Bihar, where the Champa river joins the Ganga - capital of the Anga mahajanapada.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by B. P. Sinha for Patna University in the 1970s. A pre-NBPW black-and-red ware level at the base; NBPW c. 600-200 BCE, the phase of the rampart and moat; occupation continues into the Gupta period.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The fortified nagara of the Buddhist texts, and the first mahajanapada to be swallowed by Magadha.
points: Defended by a mud rampart with a moat, and listed among the six mahanagaras of the Digha Nikaya - the excavated defences confirm the textual picture of a walled city rather than a village capital.

A monarchy under Brahmadatta, annexed by Bimbisara in the mid-6th century BCE. Anga's absorption is the opening move in Magadha's rise and the standard first example of imperial expansion in the Ganga plain.
Champa was the Ganga's river port for the eastern trade; the Jatakas send merchants downstream from here towards Suvarnabhumi.
A major Jaina tirtha: the twelfth Tirthankara Vasupujya was born and attained nirvana here, and Mahavira spent three rainy seasons in the city.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 6; Thapar, *Early India*; ASI, *IAR*

location.summary: Berachampa, North 24 Parganas, West Bengal, on the Bidyadhari - a former Ganga distributary - about 35 km north-east of Kolkata, in the lower delta.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by Calcutta University under K. G. Goswami, 1956-68. A pre-NBPW level; NBPW c. 400-200 BCE; Mauryan; a rich Shunga-Kushana phase of c. 200 BCE-200 CE on the Khana Mihirer Dhipi mound; then Gupta and Pala levels.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The finest terracotta corpus of early historic India, and the delta's inland answer to the port of Tamralipti.
points: Mould-made terracotta plaques of women in elaborate headdresses and jewellery, with male figures, dwarfs, winged humans and carts. The fabric is red to reddish-brown and the moulds range from single to multiple - a technique suited to mass production for a market, not to one-off votive work.
Rouletted ware and Roman-type objects, punch-marked and Kushana coins, seals and sealings, and ivory, wood and bronze figurines - an emporium drawing on both the Ganga route and the Bay of Bengal.
Frequently identified with the capital of the Gangaridai of the Greek writers, or with the port Gange of the *Periplus*; neither identification is proven, and no inscription names the site.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8; Thapar, *Early India*; ASI, *IAR*

location.summary: The Purana Qila mound, Delhi, on the old west bank of the Yamuna; the village of Indrapat stood on it until 1913.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by B. B. Lal in 1954-55 and 1969-73, and again by the ASI in 2013-14 and 2017-18. PGW in the lowest level, c. 1000 BCE; NBPW from c. 300 BCE; then Shunga, Kushana, Gupta, Rajput, Sultanate and Mughal levels - a near-continuous sequence of some 2,500 years.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the few north Indian mounds with an unbroken PGW-to-Mughal sequence, and the archaeological anchor for the Pandava capital.
points: The NBPW level gives mud-brick and burnt-brick houses, drains built of rectangular and wedge-shaped bricks, and terracotta ring wells used as soak pits - the standard signature of the second urbanisation.
Terracotta figurines including a horse with an armoured rider, and a clay sealing.

The Mahabharata's Indraprastha, raised on the cleared Khandava forest. The PGW basal level is what allows the identification to be argued at all, but nothing found here names the site, so the equation stays traditional rather than proved.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5-6; B. B. Lal in ASI, *IAR*; Basham, *The Wonder That Was India*

location.summary: Kasia, Kushinagar district, Uttar Pradesh, on the Hiranyavati (the Little Gandak), in the tract between the Rapti and the Gandak.

periodLevel.summary: Identified by Cunningham and excavated by A. C. L. Carlleyle in 1876, later by Hirananda Sastri and J. Ph. Vogel. NBPW levels of c. 600-200 BCE underlie the monastic complex; the Nirvana temple and its great image are Gupta, 5th century CE, with Pala-period repairs above.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The place of the Buddha's Mahaparinirvana, and the capital of one of the two Malla republics.
points: Capital of the Malla gana-sangha, a republican oligarchy among the sixteen mahajanapadas - the Mallas of Kushinara and of Pava - later absorbed by Magadha.
The Buddha died here c. 483 BCE between two sal trees; one of the four great pilgrimage places with Lumbini, Bodh Gaya and Sarnath, and the site of Ashoka's Nirvana stupa, enlarged under the Guptas.
Carlleyle recovered the 6.1 m reclining Buddha in red sandstone in 1876; its pedestal inscription names the donor Haribala and the craftsman Dinna, dating it to the reign of Kumaragupta I.
The Ramabhar stupa (Mukutabandhana chaitya) marks the cremation spot, from which the relics were divided into the eight shares that produced the first stupas.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 6-7; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; ASI reports (Carlleyle, Vogel)

location.summary: Potali or Potana, usually identified with Bodhan on the Godavari in Nizamabad district, Telangana - capital of Assaka (Asmaka), the only one of the sixteen mahajanapadas lying south of the Vindhyas.

periodLevel.summary: A mahajanapada capital of the 6th-4th centuries BCE, known from texts rather than from a stratified NBPW excavation. Assaka appears in the Anguttara Nikaya list of sixteen, and the Parayanavagga of the Sutta Nipata sends the brahmana Bavari's pupils north from the Godavari to the Buddha.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Marks the southern limit of the mahajanapada map and the Deccan end of the Dakshinapatha.
points: A monarchy rather than a gana, it fought Avanti over the Godavari valley and was eventually absorbed by it - the one mahajanapada whose politics run south rather than east.
Its position fixes the Dakshinapatha, the southern high road running from Rajagriha through Ujjayini to Pratishthana; Assaka is the link in that chain between the Vindhyas and the Deccan plateau.

Some texts give Paithan (Pratishthana) rather than Potali as the Assaka capital, and the identification with Bodhan is not certain; the entry rests on literature, not on a dig, which is the honest thing to say about it in an answer.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 6; Thapar, *Early India*; H. C. Raychaudhuri, *Political History of Ancient India*

location.summary: Prahladpur, Varanasi district, Uttar Pradesh, in the Ganga plain a short distance south of Varanasi.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by A. K. Narain and T. N. Roy for Banaras Hindu University in 1963 and published as *Excavations at Prahladpur* (1968). Period I is a pre-NBPW black-slipped ware phase; Period II is NBPW, c. 600-200 BCE; the later levels run into the early centuries CE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A small dig of large consequence - one of the excavations that fixed the ceramic sequence of the middle Ganga.
points: It showed that black-slipped ware precedes NBPW rather than simply accompanying it, and with Rajghat and Chirand it gives the stratigraphic frame against which every other NBPW site in the middle Ganga is read.

NBPW itself is a deluxe ware: thin, wheel-made, with a lustrous black to steel-grey surface produced by a fine slip and a controlled firing. It was valuable enough that broken vessels were repaired with copper rivets - a detail recovered from sites of this group.
It occurs with iron, punch-marked coins, burnt brick and terracotta ring wells, the standard package of the second urbanisation, c. 600-200 BCE.
Its importance is stratigraphic, not monumental: cite it for the sequence, not for a city.

content.sourcesLine: A. K. Narain and T. N. Roy, *Excavations at Prahladpur* (BHU, 1968); Upinder Singh, ch. 6

location.summary: Pushkalavati - the mounds of Bala Hisar and Shaikhan Dheri at Charsadda, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan - at the confluence of the Swat and Kabul rivers, capital of Gandhara.

periodLevel.summary: Bala Hisar excavated by Mortimer Wheeler in 1958, Shaikhan Dheri by A. H. Dani in 1963-64. Occupation from c. 1400 BCE; the Achaemenid-to-Mauryan city of the 6th-3rd centuries BCE carries local imitations of NBPW; Shaikhan Dheri is the Indo-Greek to Kushana city, 2nd century BCE-2nd century CE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The north-western terminus of the NBPW map, and a city planned on a grid two centuries before Sirkap.
points: Mud fortifications with a defensive ditch; the city laid out on a rectangular plan with parallel streets and blocks of houses, individual rooms having a fireplace in the middle.
The NBPW here is a local copy rather than an import - the ware travels as a fashion along the Uttarapatha, not as a traded commodity, which is the point to make about its western distribution.
Alexander's general Hephaestion took the city after a thirty-day siege in 327 BCE and left a Macedonian garrison; Arrian describes it as a great city of the north-west.
Panini, the grammarian, belongs to Shalatura nearby in the 4th century BCE, and Pushkalavati traded with Taxila along the Uttarapatha before becoming a Gandhara art centre under the Kushanas.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 6 and 8; Wheeler, *Charsada* (1962); A. H. Dani, *Ancient Pakistan* II (1965-66)

location.summary: Rajgir (Rajagriha, earlier Girivraja), Nalanda district, Bihar, in a valley ringed by five hills on the Banganga - the first capital of Magadha.

periodLevel.summary: Explored by Cunningham and Marshall, excavated by A. Ghosh for the ASI in 1950 and later. The old city of Girivraja with its cyclopean stone wall is pre-Mauryan; NBPW runs c. 600-200 BCE. The capital moved to Pataliputra under Udayin, c. 460 BCE, after which the city survives as a religious centre.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The capital from which Magadha's ascendancy was built, and the only major mahajanapada capital defended by stone.
points: A cyclopean wall of undressed stone about 40 km long runs along the hill crests, with Ajatashatru's inner fortification below - the largest surviving pre-Mauryan defence work in India, and unusual in a plain where mud ramparts are the rule.
Capital under Bimbisara and Ajatashatru. Excavation has exposed the Jivakamravana - the physician Jivaka's mango-grove monastery - along with Venuvana, the Griddhakuta and Maniyar Math.
The First Buddhist Council met in the Saptaparni cave immediately after the parinirvana, under Mahakassapa and with Ajatashatru's patronage, Ananda reciting the Sutta and Upali the Vinaya.
Mahavira spent fourteen rainy seasons at Rajgir and Nalanda, and the twentieth Tirthankara Munisuvrata was born here; Xuanzang describes the site in the 7th century.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 6; Thapar, *Early India*; ASI, *IAR* 1950

location.summary: Rajapura, generally identified with Rajouri in the Pir Panjal foothills of Jammu and Kashmir, on the Rajouri river - capital of the Kamboja mahajanapada, on the route from the Punjab plains into Kashmir.

periodLevel.summary: A mahajanapada of the 6th-4th centuries BCE, known from texts; no NBPW sequence has been excavated at the site. Kautilya's Arthashastra classes the Kambojas as a varta-shastropajivin sangha, living by both agriculture and arms, and Ashoka's Rock Edicts V and XIII name them with the Yonas and Gandharas on the empire's frontier.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The north-western corner of the mahajanapada map, and a corporation of the frontier rather than a kingdom of the plains.
points: The Mahabharata records Karna's defeat of the Kambojas at Rajapura, the main textual fix for locating the capital here.
Kalhana's Rajatarangini calls it Rajapuri and shows its raja as a tributary of Kashmir in the 11th-12th centuries - the name and the polity survive unbroken into the medieval period.
Kamboja was famous for its horses; the Kamboja horse trade is the standard example of the north-western supply on which armies in the Ganga plain depended.
The sources disagree on whether Kamboja was a monarchy or a sangha, and the capital is unexcavated - a literary entry, and best presented as such.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 6; Kalhana, *Rajatarangini*; Raychaudhuri, *Political History of Ancient India*

location.summary: Sirpur (ancient Shripura), Mahasamund district, Chhattisgarh, on the left bank of the Mahanadi - capital of Dakshina Kosala, the southern half of the Kosala tradition.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by M. G. Dikshit (1953-57) and by A. K. Sharma for the Chhattisgarh government from 2000. It enters the maps as the mahajanapada-era capital of Dakshina Kosala; the excavated city is Panduvamshi (Somavamshi), 6th-8th centuries CE, at its height under Mahashivagupta Balarjuna (c. 595-655 CE), and in decline after the 12th century.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A capital where Buddhist, Jaina and Brahmanical establishments stood together, and the finest surviving brick temple of the Deccan fringe.
points: Xuanzang visited in 638-639 CE and reports about a hundred monasteries with some ten thousand Mahayana monks. The excavated Anandaprabhu Kuti and Swastika viharas, with bronze and monolithic stone Buddhas, bear the account out.

The Lakshmana temple, c. 625-650 CE, built in brick by Queen Vasata in memory of Harshagupta, stands on a jagati with a circumambulatory path and a Nagara shikhara; its carved walls carry the incarnations of Vishnu together with mithuna figures.
The Puranas name the Ikshvakus as the first rulers of Dakshina Kosala, overthrown by Mahapadma Nanda - the Nanda conquest reaching south of the Vindhyas.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; A. K. Sharma, *Excavations at Sirpur*; ASI, *IAR*

location.summary: Sisupalgarh, on the southern edge of Bhubaneswar, Khordha district, Odisha, between the Daya and the Gangua about 20 km from the coast - very probably the Kalinga capital Tosali, and adjacent to Ashoka's Dhauli rock.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by B. B. Lal in 1948 (*Ancient India* 5) and re-excavated by R. K. Mohanty and Monica Smith, 2005-07. Period I, c. 400-200 BCE, before the defences; Period II, c. 200 BCE-100 CE, when the rampart was raised; Period III to c. 350 CE, after which the city was abandoned.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The best-preserved planned fortified city of early historic India - the one whose full plan can still be walked.
points: A near-perfect square about 1.1 km on a side, enclosing some 130 ha within a rammed-earth rampart revetted in laterite, pierced by eight gateways, two on each face, with guardrooms - a scale of public works that implies an organised state, not a chiefdom.
Streets run parallel and cross at right angles with the houses aligned to them, and a pillared structure of sixteen monolithic laterite pillars stands at the centre.
NBPW, rouletted ware, punch-marked and later coins, glass and semi-precious stone beads, and the distinctive terracotta ear ornaments - a city drawing on both the Ganga route and Indian Ocean trade.
The 2005-07 work showed the settlement was large and densely occupied from the start, revising the older picture of gradual growth behind the walls.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 6 and 8; B. B. Lal, *Ancient India* 5 (1949); Mohanty and Smith (2008)

location.summary: Suktimati (Sotthivati), capital of the Chedi mahajanapada in the Bundelkhand-Baghelkhand tract between the Yamuna and the Narmada. Raychaudhuri and Pargiter place it near Banda in Uttar Pradesh on the Ken; D. K. Chakrabarti identifies it with Rewa in Madhya Pradesh. The map dot follows the Banda identification.

periodLevel.summary: A mahajanapada capital of the 6th-4th centuries BCE; no excavated NBPW sequence has been tied to the name. The Mahabharata credits its founding to King Uparichara Vasu.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The one mahajanapada capital that archaeology has never located - which is itself the examinable point about the limits of the list of sixteen.
points: Chedi's importance is locational: it lay astride the routes from the Ganga plain to the Deccan, controlling the Vindhyan passes rather than a rich agrarian core.

Shishupala, killed by Krishna at Yudhishthira's rajasuya, is the Chedi king of the epic; Kharavela of Kalinga later styles himself of the Chedi line in the Hathigumpha inscription, carrying the name into the 1st century BCE.
A monarchy. When asked for the sixteen mahajanapadas and their capitals, give Chedi-Suktimati, but note that the capital is a textual name without a site.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 6; Raychaudhuri, *Political History of Ancient India*; D. K. Chakrabarti, *The Archaeology of Ancient Indian Cities*

location.summary: Taxila (Takshashila), Rawalpindi district, Punjab, Pakistan, in the Haro valley between the Indus and the Jhelum, where the Uttarapatha from the Ganga plain met the roads to Bactria and Central Asia.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by John Marshall, 1913-34, and by Mortimer Wheeler, 1944-45. Three successive cities: Bhir Mound, c. 6th-2nd centuries BCE (Achaemenid and Mauryan, with local NBPW and silver punch-marked coins); Sirkap, c. 2nd century BCE-1st century CE (Indo-Greek, rebuilt by Shakas and Parthians); Sirsukh, 1st-2nd centuries CE (Kushana).

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The textbook contrast between an organic Indian town and a Hellenistic grid, standing 500 m apart.
points: Bhir Mound has winding irregular lanes and rubble houses; Sirkap is laid out on a grid, a main street with blocks at right angles inside a wall of some 5.5 km - the clearest surviving case of Greek town planning in South Asia.

Capital of the Gandhara satrapy under the Achaemenids and a Mauryan provincial capital. Ashoka was viceroy here, and the city revolted twice, once under Bindusara and again in Ashoka's reign. Marshall found an Aramaic inscription of Ashoka at the site in 1915.

The great centre of higher learning of the Buddhist texts, above all for medicine: Panini, the physician Jivaka and Kautilya are all associated with it, and the Jatakas send students here for the eighteen silpas. Teaching was by individual teachers taking pupils - there was no corporate university, which is what distinguishes it from Nalanda.
The Dharmarajika stupa and the Jaulian and Mohra Moradu monasteries make it a first-rank Gandhara art site; UNESCO World Heritage since 1980.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 6-8; John Marshall, *Taxila* (1951); Thapar, *Early India*

location.summary: Ujjayini, on the right bank of the Shipra, Madhya Pradesh - capital of the Avanti mahajanapada, where the Dakshinapatha met the route down to the Gujarat ports.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by N. R. Banerjee for the ASI, 1955-58. Period I begins c. 700 BCE with black-and-red ware behind a massive mud rampart; Period II is NBPW, c. 500-200 BCE; the city continues through the Shunga, Shaka-Kshatrapa and Gupta periods.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The largest and earliest urban defence work in central India, and a manufacturing city rather than an agrarian capital.
points: The mud embankment, faced and moated, encloses about 0.9 sq km - a scale of fortification unusually early for the region and the strongest single argument that Avanti urbanised alongside the Ganga plain, not after it.
Iron arrowheads, spearheads and crowbars, terracotta spindle whorls, punch-marked coins, terracotta ring wells and a large burnt-brick tank for water storage.

Avanti under Pradyota was one of the four great powers of the 6th century BCE with Magadha, Kosala and Vatsa, and was absorbed by Magadha under Shishunaga. Ashoka governed here for Bindusara, and it was on this posting that he married Devi of Vidisha.

It stood on the southern high road running from Rajagriha to Pratishthana; later it becomes the seat of the Vikramaditya legend, of Kalidasa, of the Mahakala jyotirlinga, and the prime meridian of Indian astronomy.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 6; Basham, *The Wonder That Was India*; ASI, *IAR* 1956-58

location.summary: Basarh, Vaishali district, Bihar, in the tract between the Gandak and the Ganga north of Patna - capital of the Licchavis and head of the Vajji confederacy.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by T. Bloch (1903-04), D. B. Spooner (1913-14), Krishna Deva and Vijayakanta Mishra (1950), and A. S. Altekar (1957-62). NBPW of c. 600-200 BCE at Raja Vishal ka Garh, with Shunga, Kushana and Gupta levels above.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The best-documented gana-sangha in Indian history, and the site of the earliest excavated Buddhist stupa.
points: Government was by an assembly of Licchavi rajas, not a king. The Buddha's seven aparihaniya dhammas - the conditions on which a republic does not decline - are addressed to the Vajjis, and Ajatashatru needed years of preparation and his minister Vassakara's intrigue to break them, which is the standard illustration of monarchy overcoming the republics.

Altekar's 1958 excavation of the relic stupa recovered a soapstone casket with ashes, held to be the Licchavis' share of the Buddha's relics; if so, this is the oldest Buddhist stupa yet excavated, in mud brick, later enlarged four times.
The Ashokan pillar at Kolhua carries a single lion capital and stands beside a tank and stupa - one of the few pillars still in situ on its original spot.

The Second Buddhist Council met here c. 383 BCE over ten disputed Vinaya points, the dispute that opened the Sthaviravada-Mahasamghika split. Mahavira was born at Kundagrama, a suburb of Vaishali, and the courtesan Amrapali gave her mango grove to the Buddha.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 6-7; A. S. Altekar, *Report on Vaishali Excavations*; Thapar, *Early India*

location.summary: Varanasi (Kashi), on the left bank of the Ganga between the Varuna and the Assi, Uttar Pradesh; the excavated early city is the Rajghat plateau at the Varuna confluence.

periodLevel.summary: Rajghat excavated by Banaras Hindu University under A. K. Narain and T. N. Roy from 1957. The earliest level begins c. 800 BCE with black-slipped ware; NBPW from c. 600 BCE, the phase to which the mud rampart belongs; occupation runs through the Kushana and Gupta periods without a break.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Among the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, and the capital of a mahajanapada that lost the contest it was best placed to win.
points: The NBPW levels give a mud rampart, a burnt clay floor, terracotta ring wells and brick revetments on the river front - a city, not a village, by the 6th century BCE.

Kashi was famous in the Jatakas for its fine textiles, the kasika vastra, and for its wealth; it is one of the six mahanagaras of the Digha Nikaya. It fought Kosala, Anga and Magadha, was absorbed by Kosala, and passed with Kosala to Magadha - the classic case of a rich city state losing to a territorial power.
A teaching centre for Brahmanas, Buddhists and Jainas alike, with the Vedas and Upanishads taught here and Sarnath 10 km away; the twenty-third Tirthankara Parshvanatha was born at Varanasi.
Later the Kashi Vishvanatha jyotirlinga and the Banaras gharana of Hindustani music.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 6; A. K. Narain and T. N. Roy, *Excavations at Rajghat*; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*

location.summary: Vidisha (ancient Besnagar), at the confluence of the Betwa (Vetravati) and the Bes, Madhya Pradesh, 10 km from Sanchi, on the route from the Ganga plain to Ujjayini and the Deccan.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by H. H. Lake (1910), D. R. Bhandarkar (1913-15) and M. D. Khare (1963-65). NBPW levels of c. 500-200 BCE below a fortified early historic city; its great phase is Shunga and early Satavahana, 2nd-1st centuries BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Carries the earliest epigraphic evidence for Bhagavata worship, and the earliest named craft guild in Indian art.
points: The Heliodorus pillar (Garuda-dhvaja), c. 113 BCE: set up in Prakrit in the Brahmi script by Heliodorus, a Greek of Taxila and ambassador of the Indo-Greek king Antialkidas to the Shunga king Kashiputra Bhagabhadra. Heliodorus calls himself a Bhagavata and a devotee of Vasudeva - a foreigner adopting an Indian cult, and the first inscriptional evidence for Vaishnavism.

Ashoka was viceroy at Vidisha for Bindusara and married Devi, a merchant's daughter of the city and the mother of Mahendra and Sanghamitra - the link joining Vidisha to Sanchi and to the Sri Lanka mission.
The southern gateway of Sanchi Stupa 1 carries an inscription recording that it was the work of the ivory carvers of Vidisha - rare direct evidence of a guild at work on a monument.
The colossal Besnagar yakshi and the nearby Udayagiri caves belong to the same cluster of sites.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7-8; D. R. Bhandarkar, *ASI Annual Report* 1913-14; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*

location.summary: Bairat (Viratnagar), Jaipur district, Rajasthan, in a valley of the Aravallis on the route from the Ganga-Yamuna doab to Gujarat - capital of the Matsya mahajanapada.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by D. R. Sahni (1936-37) and N. R. Banerjee (1962-63). NBPW and punch-marked coins in the early levels; the Buddhist monastery and circular temple on Bijak-ki-Pahari are Mauryan, 3rd century BCE; Indo-Greek coins of Menander come from the levels above.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The earliest free-standing structural Buddhist shrine in India, and the only Ashokan edict that names Buddhist scripture.
points: The circular chaitya on Bijak-ki-Pahari, built of brick and timber with twenty-six octagonal wooden pillars set around a small stupa inside a circular ambulatory - the structural counterpart of the rock-cut chaityas of the Deccan, and proof that the circular plan was not an accident of rock-cutting.

Two Ashokan Minor Rock Edicts. The Bairat or Bhabru edict, now in the Indian Museum, Kolkata, is addressed to the Sangha, declares Ashoka's faith in the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha, and recommends seven Buddhist texts by name - the only edict to cite scripture, and the strongest evidence for his personal Buddhism. A second Minor Rock Edict survives on a boulder at the site.
Matsya, a monarchy, is the Virata of the Mahabharata where the Pandavas passed their year of concealment; it was absorbed by Magadha and then by the Mauryas.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 6-7; D. R. Sahni, *Archaeological Remains and Excavations at Bairat* (1937); Thapar, *Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas*

location.summary: Ajanta, Aurangabad (Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar) district, Maharashtra, cut into a horseshoe-shaped basalt scarp above the Waghora, a tributary of the Tapi system, on the route from Pratishthana to the northern trade towns.

periodLevel.summary: Thirty caves in two phases separated by some five centuries. Phase I is Hinayana under the Satavahanas, c. 2nd-1st centuries BCE - Caves 9 and 10 (chaityas) and 8, 12, 13 and 15A (viharas). Phase II is Mahayana under the Vakatakas, c. 460-480 CE, in the reign of Harishena, and the site was abandoned soon after his fall. Rediscovered in 1819 by John Smith, an officer of the Madras Army.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The only place where Indian painting of the classical age survives in quantity, and where the shift from aniconic to iconic Buddhism can be read on the walls.
points: The paintings are not true fresco but tempera on a dry ground of mud, cow dung and rice husk finished with lime - drawn in outline, filled in, then burnished. Five mineral colours dominate: red and yellow ochre, lime white, lamp black, terre verte, and lapis lazuli blue imported from Central Asia.

Subjects are Jataka and Avadana tales, not doctrine: Cave 1 has the Padmapani and Vajrapani bodhisattvas and the Mahajanaka Jataka; Cave 17 the Vessantara and Simhala Jatakas; Cave 16 the "Dying Princess", and an inscription of Varahadeva, Harishena's minister, recording its excavation.

Caves 19 and 26 are the Mahayana chaityas: apsidal halls with carved pillars, a stupa carrying a standing Buddha on its face, and elaborately carved facades. Cave 26 adds a seven-metre reclining Mahaparinirvana Buddha and the Temptation of Mara.
The narrative idiom descends from Sanchi and Bharhut; the Ajanta manner travels on to Bagh, Badami, Sittanavasal and Sigiriya. UNESCO World Heritage, 1983.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 9; Walter Spink, *Ajanta: History and Development*; ASI

location.summary: Alchi, Leh district, Ladakh, on the left bank of the Indus about 70 km downstream of Leh - the one major Ladakhi gompa built on the valley floor rather than a crag.

periodLevel.summary: Founded in the late 10th or early 11th century, its temples built and painted c. 1000-1200 CE in the Kashmiri idiom; inscriptions name the founder as Kal-dan Shes-rab and the tradition credits Rinchen Zangpo, the Great Translator of the Guge kingdom. Abandoned as a working monastery and now maintained by Likir; Gelugpa.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The oldest surviving wall paintings in Ladakh, and the last substantial body of Kashmiri Buddhist art anywhere, Kashmir's own having been destroyed.
points: The Sumtsek, a three-storeyed temple, holds three colossal clay bodhisattvas - Maitreya, Avalokiteshvara and Manjushri - whose painted dhotis carry miniature scenes of palaces, pilgrimage and courtly life, a documentary record of 12th-century dress and architecture.
The Dukhang (assembly hall) has a Vairochana mandala and a carved wooden doorway; the third temple, the Manjushri lhakhang, contains a wood-carved Buddha.

The style is Indian and Kashmiri rather than Tibetan - slim modelled figures, rich reds and blues - which is why Alchi is used as the type site for the "second diffusion" of Buddhism into the western Himalaya.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Snellgrove and Skorupski, *The Cultural Heritage of Ladakh*; Roger Goepper, *Alchi* (1996)

location.summary: Bagh, Dhar district, Madhya Pradesh, cut into a sandstone hill on the left bank of the Baghani, a Narmada tributary, on the route between Malwa and the Gujarat coast.

periodLevel.summary: Nine rock-cut Buddhist caves of the late Gupta period, c. 5th-6th centuries CE, of which five survive; an inscription mentions Maharaja Subandhu, who ruled the region in the 5th-6th centuries. Contemporary with the second phase at Ajanta and abandoned by the 7th century.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The best evidence outside Ajanta for Gupta-age mural painting, and the surviving link in the chain west to Gujarat.
points: Cave 4, the Rang Mahal, carried the principal murals - processions, dancers and musicians, a royal cavalcade - painted in tempera on a mud-plaster ground, technically identical to Ajanta but more secular in subject, with Jataka and Avadana scenes.
The caves are viharas with a stupa chamber at the rear rather than true chaityas, showing how the vihara absorbed the shrine in the later phase.
The rock is friable and the paintings decayed early; copies made in 1921-22 are preserved in the Gwalior museum and are now the main record of what was there.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 9; ASI; Marshall, Ghosh and others, *The Bagh Caves* (1927)

location.summary: The Bamiyan valley in the Hazarajat of central Afghanistan, at 2,500 m on the Bamiyan river in a pass of the Hindu Kush, on the Silk Road link between Balkh, Gandhara and the Tarim basin.

periodLevel.summary: A monastic complex of the 3rd-8th centuries CE under Kushana and Hephthalite patronage. The two colossal Buddhas carved into the cliff are radiocarbon-dated to c. 544-595 CE (the 38 m eastern figure) and c. 591-644 CE (the 55 m western figure). They were destroyed by the Taliban in March 2001.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The largest standing Buddha images ever carved, and the meeting point of Gandharan, Sasanian and Gupta form.
points: The figures were cut from the conglomerate cliff, their robes modelled in mud-and-straw stucco over wooden armatures and painted; the folds follow Gandharan convention but the scale and the niche setting are local.

About fifty caves survive around them, twelve with wall paintings - and analysis after 2001 showed some used oil-based binders in the 7th century, the earliest known oil painting anywhere, made by or for travellers on the silk road.
Xuanzang visited c. 630 CE, described the two figures and a third, reclining Buddha of some 300 feet not yet found, and recorded several thousand monks of the Lokottaravada school.

content.sourcesLine: Xuanzang, *Da Tang Xiyu Ji*; UNESCO World Heritage documentation (2003); Upinder Singh, ch. 8

location.summary: Belum, Kolimigundla mandal, Nandyal (formerly Kurnool) district, Andhra Pradesh - a limestone cave system in the Erramala hills of the Nallamala country, dissolved out by an underground stream of the Chitravati drainage.

periodLevel.summary: Used by Jaina and Buddhist monks in the early centuries BCE-CE; vessels recovered from the caves have been assigned to around 4500 BCE. Brought to notice by the British geologist H. B. Foote in 1884 and surveyed by a German team under H. D. Gebauer in 1982-84.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The second longest natural cave system in India, at 3,229 m, and a rare instance of a karst cavern taken over as a monastic retreat.
points: Buddhist relics and earthen vessels were found in the chambers, now in the museum at Anantapur; the caves have stalactite and stalagmite formations throughout, with a "meditation hall" (Dhyan Mandir) named from the seats cut near the entrance.
It illustrates the pattern of the Andhra Buddhist landscape, where natural caves and hill sites near the Krishna-Penna corridor housed monks before masonry viharas were built.

content.sourcesLine: ASI; Geological Survey of India records; Upinder Singh, ch. 8 (for the Andhra Buddhist context)

location.summary: Bhaja, near Lonavala in Pune district, Maharashtra, cut into a spur above the Indrayani valley beside the Bhor Ghat - the pass carrying goods from the Konkan ports of Kalyan and Sopara up to Junnar and Paithan.

periodLevel.summary: Twenty-two caves of c. 2nd-1st centuries BCE, Hinayana, under the Satavahanas - among the earliest rock-cut Buddhist architecture in India. Later additions run to the 5th century CE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The earliest surviving chaitya hall that still keeps its wooden fittings - the direct transcription of a timber building into rock.
points: Cave 12 is an apsidal chaitya griha with a horseshoe-arched sun window, twenty-seven plain octagonal pillars raked inward as timber posts would be, and actual wooden ribs set into the vault, with a wooden umbrella surviving over the stupa. Nothing shows the timber origins of the form more plainly.

A group of fourteen stupas, five inside and nine outside, are funerary memorials to resident monks; several carry inscriptions naming the theras commemorated - among the earliest evidence for the cult of the monastic dead.

The reliefs in Cave 19 - a figure on an elephant and another driving a four-horse chariot over a demon, usually read as Indra and Surya - are the earliest large narrative sculptures in the Deccan caves.
Patronage is recorded from merchants and householders, not kings: the caves sit on a trade route, and the donors are the people who used it.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8; Thapar, *Early India*; ASI

location.summary: Bharhut, Satna district, Madhya Pradesh, in the Baghelkhand uplands on the old road from Kaushambi towards the Deccan, midway between the Ganga plain and Vidisha-Sanchi.

periodLevel.summary: A brick stupa of the Mauryan period, probably Ashokan in origin. The stone railing (vedika) and gateways are Shunga, c. 125-100 BCE; an inscription on the eastern torana records its erection during the rule of the Shungas by Vatsiputra Dhanabhuti. Discovered by Alexander Cunningham in 1873.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The earliest extensive narrative relief sculpture in India, and the only one that labels its own scenes.
points: Jataka and life-of-the-Buddha scenes are carved on the railing medallions in shallow, flat, frontal relief, each with a Brahmi label naming the story - which is how the Jataka repertoire of early Buddhist art was first identified at all.
The Buddha is never shown in human form: he is indicated by the empty throne, the footprints, the bodhi tree, the wheel and the stupa. Bharhut is the standard example of aniconic representation.

Large yaksha and yakshi figures stand on the railing uprights - Chulakoka Devata, Sudarshana, Sirima Devata - folk deities absorbed into a Buddhist monument, and among the first monumental stone figures of Indian art.
Donative inscriptions record gifts by monks, nuns, merchants and villagers rather than by a king - collective, non-royal patronage. Most of the remains are now in the Indian Museum, Kolkata.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8; Cunningham, *The Stupa of Bharhut* (1879); Basham, *The Wonder That Was India*

location.summary: Bodh Gaya, Gaya district, Bihar, on the west bank of the Niranjana (Phalgu/Lilajan) - the ancient Uruvela, where Sujata is said to have offered the milk-rice.

periodLevel.summary: Ashoka built the Vajrasana (diamond throne) and a shrine around the bodhi tree in the 3rd century BCE - a structure depicted in a Bharhut relief. The stone railing is Shunga, 1st century BCE. The present Mahabodhi temple is Gupta, 5th-6th centuries CE, with Pala and Burmese repairs and a restoration by Cunningham and Beglar in the 1880s.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The place of the enlightenment - the first of the four great pilgrimage sites, and the oldest brick temple in India still in use.
points: The Mahabodhi temple rises about 55 m in a straight-edged pyramidal shikhara over a high plinth, with four small corner towers - a form with no close parallel in India, and the model copied at Bagan, Chiang Mai and Beijing.
Ashoka's Vajrasana slab, polished sandstone with a palmette and geese frieze, survives between the temple and the bodhi tree - one of the very few Mauryan objects still in its original position.
The Shunga railing pillars carry medallions of yakshas, Surya in a chariot and Lakshmi, in the same flat idiom as Bharhut; much of the original is in the site museum and in Kolkata.

Faxian and Xuanzang both describe the site; the Sinhalese king Meghavarna built a monastery here in the 4th century with Samudragupta's leave, and later Pala kings and Burmese missions repaired it. UNESCO World Heritage, 2002.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7-9; Cunningham, *Mahabodhi* (1892); Thapar, *Early India*

location.summary: Sankaram, comprising the twin hills of Bojjannakonda and Lingalakonda, near Anakapalli in Visakhapatnam district, Andhra Pradesh, a few kilometres inland from the coast on the Sarada river.

periodLevel.summary: Occupied from about the 3rd century BCE to the 9th century CE, with the main rock-cutting of the Satavahana to Vishnukundin period, c. 1st-7th centuries CE. Excavated by Alexander Rea for the ASI in 1907.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the few sites where all three phases of Buddhism - Hinayana, Mahayana and Vajrayana - can be seen on a single hill.
points: A large brick stupa crowns Bojjannakonda, surrounded by rock-cut cells and chaityas with seated Buddha figures carved in the rock face; Lingalakonda is covered with rows of monolithic votive stupas cut from the living rock, one of the densest such groups in India.
Relic caskets in earthen pots, Satavahana lead coins and stucco fragments were recovered; the name Sankaram derives from Sangharama.
Its interest is regional: it shows the Andhra coast maintaining Buddhist establishments long after the Krishna valley centres at Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda had declined.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8 and 10; Alexander Rea, *ASI Annual Report* 1907-08

location.summary: Rangiri Dambulla, Matale district, central Sri Lanka, on a 160 m granite outcrop overlooking the dry-zone plain, near the ancient road between Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa.

periodLevel.summary: The caves were monastic shelters with drip-ledges and Brahmi inscriptions from the 3rd-2nd centuries BCE. King Valagamba (Vattagamani Abhaya) sheltered here for fourteen years and, on regaining Anuradhapura in the 1st century BCE, converted them into a temple. Enlarged and gilded by Nissanka Malla in the 12th century; the surviving paintings are largely Kandyan, 18th century, under Kirti Sri Rajasinha.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The largest and best-preserved cave temple complex in Sri Lanka, and a continuous record of Theravada image-making over two millennia.
points: Eighty documented caves, five of them developed as shrines, holding 153 Buddha statues along with images of Sri Lankan kings, Vishnu and Saman - the absorption of Hindu deities into a Theravada setting.
About 2,100 sq m of painted ceiling and wall, following the rock's natural contour; the 14 m reclining Buddha in Cave 1 is cut from the living rock.
Read with Sigiriya and Ajanta, it completes the picture of a shared painting tradition across the Bay of Bengal. UNESCO World Heritage, 1991.

content.sourcesLine: UNESCO World Heritage documentation; Senake Bandaranayake, *Sinhalese Monastic Architecture*; the *Mahavamsa*

location.summary: Ghantasala, Krishna district, Andhra Pradesh, near the lower Krishna a short way from the coast - Ptolemy's port of Kantakossyla, on the sea route to South-East Asia.

periodLevel.summary: A Satavahana and Ikshvaku Buddhist centre, c. 2nd century BCE-3rd century CE. Reported by Boswell in 1870, examined by Alexander Rea and excavated by Gabriel Jouveau-Dubreuil in 1919-20.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A stupa of unique plan, and the clearest link between Andhra Buddhism and the maritime trade that paid for it.
points: The mahastupa is built of solid brick with a wheel-shaped internal plan - radiating spoke walls dividing the drum into compartments filled with earth - a structural device found in the Andhra stupas and not in the north; a separate vihara stood beside it.

A carved slab with the twelve zodiac signs was recovered here, evidence of Hellenistic astronomical ideas reaching the Andhra coast, along with relics including a lotus, limestone sculpture in the Amaravati manner, and Roman coins.
As a port it exported the Buddhism of the Krishna valley eastwards; the Andhra stupa plan reappears in South-East Asia.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8; Jouveau-Dubreuil, *L'archeologie du sud de l'Inde*; ASI

location.summary: Hemis, Leh district, Ladakh, in a side gorge on the west bank of the Indus about 45 km south-east of Leh, hidden from the valley floor - which is why it survived raids that destroyed other gompas.

periodLevel.summary: A monastery existed on the site before the 11th century; the present establishment was founded in 1672 by King Sengge Namgyal of Ladakh for Stagsang Raspa Nawang Gyatso, and belongs to the Drukpa Kagyu lineage.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The wealthiest and largest monastery in Ladakh, and the standard example of royal patronage creating a monastic order's dominance.
points: Sengge Namgyal's endowment made the Drukpa Kagyu the state church of Ladakh; Hemis held revenue villages and controlled subsidiary gompas - monastic landholding as an instrument of Himalayan kingship.
It holds a copper-gilt Buddha, gold and silver stupas, and a thangka of Padmasambhava of several storeys, unfurled once every twelve years.
The Hemis Tse-chu, held on Padmasambhava's birth anniversary, is the best-known cham masked dance festival of the western Himalaya.

content.sourcesLine: Luciano Petech, *The Kingdom of Ladakh*; Snellgrove and Skorupski, *The Cultural Heritage of Ladakh*

location.summary: Jagaddala, Dhamoirhat upazila, Naogaon district, north-west Bangladesh - in Varendra, the Pala heartland between the Karatoya and the Mahananda.

periodLevel.summary: A Pala mahavihara founded by Ramapala, c. 1077-1120 CE, flourishing into the early 13th century; destroyed in the Ghurid raids of c. 1207. Excavated by the Department of Archaeology, Bangladesh, from 1996.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The last of the five great Pala mahaviharas to rise, and the bridge by which Vajrayana learning passed to Tibet.
points: It came into prominence as Nalanda and Vikramashila declined, and specialised in Vajrayana; Vibhutichandra, Danashila and Mokshakaragupta taught here, and Shakyashribhadra fled from here to Tibet in 1204, carrying texts that shaped the Tibetan canon.
Vidyakara compiled the *Subhashitaratnakosha*, the great Sanskrit verse anthology, at Jagaddala - the main literary product of the Pala monasteries.
Excavation has exposed a large brick monastery with cells around a courtyard and ornamental terracotta plaques, on the standard Pala plan shared with Somapura and Vikramashila.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Taranatha, *History of Buddhism in India*; Department of Archaeology, Bangladesh

location.summary: Junagadh, Gujarat, at the foot of the Girnar hills in Saurashtra, on the route from the Kathiawar ports to Malwa - three separate cave groups plus the inscribed rock on the Girnar road.

periodLevel.summary: Khapra Kodiya, cut into living rock near the Sudarshana lake, is the oldest, Mauryan, c. 3rd century BCE. Baba Pyara comprises thirteen caves of the 1st-2nd centuries CE, Buddhist with later Jaina use. The Uparkot caves, three storeys with a pillared court and cistern, are 2nd-3rd centuries CE, Kshatrapa.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The caves are Gujarat's Buddhist record; the rock beside them carries three inscriptions that between them span seven centuries of Indian history on one surface.
points: The Girnar rock holds Ashoka's fourteen Major Rock Edicts; Rudradaman I's Sanskrit inscription of c. 150 CE; and Skandagupta's of 455-458 CE - the only place where Mauryan, Shaka-Kshatrapa and Gupta records stand together.

Rudradaman's record is the first long inscription in Sanskrit and in ornate kavya prose, and it states that the Sudarshana reservoir was built by Pushyagupta, provincial governor of Chandragupta Maurya, and provided with conduits by Tushaspha the Yavana under Ashoka - our best evidence for Mauryan provincial administration and public works.

The Uparkot caves are unusual for their carved pillars with Kshatrapa-period motifs and an elaborate water-management system, showing Buddhist monasticism in a region better known for its Jaina establishments on Girnar above.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7-8; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; ASI

location.summary: Junnar, Pune district, Maharashtra, on the Kukadi river below the Naneghat pass - the gateway from the Konkan ports of Kalyan and Sopara to the Satavahana capital at Pratishthana.

periodLevel.summary: More than two hundred caves in five groups - Tulja Lena, Manmodi, Lenyadri (Ganesh Lena), Shivneri and Bhutling - cut between the 1st century BCE and the 3rd century CE, Hinayana, under the Satavahanas and the Kshatrapa Nahapana.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The largest concentration of rock-cut caves in India, and the clearest case of Buddhist establishments following a trade route rather than a capital.
points: Tulja Lena has a circular chaitya with a stupa ringed by twelve plain octagonal pillars - a domed circular plan found nowhere else in the western caves, and the rock-cut counterpart of the structural circular shrine at Bairat.

The inscriptions name the donors: Yavana (Greek-named) traders, the Kshatrapa Nahapana's officers, guilds of bamboo workers and braziers, and Saka settlers - a cross-section of the western Deccan's commercial society in the 1st-2nd centuries CE.
Lenyadri Cave 7 was converted into a Ganesha shrine and is now one of the Ashtavinayaka temples; Shivneri fort above is Shivaji's birthplace, so the hill carries three religious and political layers.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8; Thapar, *Early India*; ASI

location.summary: Kanganahalli, near Sannati village, Chitapur taluk, Kalaburagi (Gulbarga) district, Karnataka, on the left bank of the Bhima - a bend of the river in the northern Karnataka plain.

periodLevel.summary: A mahastupa, called the Adholoka Maha Chaitya in its inscriptions, built c. 3rd century BCE and encased with carved limestone slabs in the Satavahana period, 1st century BCE-3rd century CE. Excavated by the ASI under K. P. Poonacha, 1994-98.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The only known portrait of Ashoka, and a royal gallery of the Satavahana dynasty in stone.
points: A limestone slab shows a king under a parasol flanked by female attendants, labelled in Brahmi "Ranyo Ashoka" - "King Ashoka". No other representation of Ashoka identified by name exists anywhere.
Other slabs carry labelled portraits of Satavahana rulers including Simuka and Pulumavi, making the site a primary source for the dynasty's own self-representation rather than a later account of it.
About sixty carved drum and dome slabs survive, with Jataka scenes, stupa worship panels and both aniconic and iconic Buddhas, in a limestone idiom close to Amaravati.
Satavahana lead coins and donative inscriptions were recovered; the Ashokan Major Rock Edicts and both Separate Edicts found at Sannati, 3 km away, tie the complex to the Mauryan south.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7-8; K. P. Poonacha, *Excavations at Kanaganahalli* (ASI Memoir, 2011)

location.summary: Kanheri, in the basalt hills of Salsette island inside Sanjay Gandhi National Park, Mumbai, Maharashtra - within reach of the ports of Sopara, Kalyan and Chaul.

periodLevel.summary: About 110 caves cut continuously from the 1st century BCE to the 10th century CE - the longest unbroken occupation of any Buddhist cave site in western India, spanning Satavahana, Kshatrapa, Traikutaka, Rashtrakuta and Shilahara patronage.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A complete Buddhist university-monastery in rock, and the one site where the full sequence Hinayana to Mahayana to Vajrayana is visible in a single complex.
points: Cave 3 is the great chaitya of the 2nd century CE, from the reign of Yajna Sri Satakarni, with thirty-four pillars and colossal standing Buddhas over 6 m at the entrance - the last of the great chaitya halls, and the point at which the Buddha image enters a form that had been aniconic.

Cave 41 has an eleven-headed Avalokiteshvara, unique in India and paralleled only in China and Japan; Cave 90 carries the Litany of Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva saving devotees from eight perils - the mature Mahayana iconography.

Rock-cut cisterns, channels and a dam supplied the settlement, an engineering system as impressive as the sculpture; over a hundred inscriptions record gifts by merchants of Sopara and Kalyan, and later Pahlavi inscriptions of 1009 CE mark visits by Parsis.
A large gallery of memorial stupas over the ashes of resident monks lies on the hillside.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8 and 10; S. Gokhale, *Kanheri Inscriptions*; ASI

location.summary: Capital of the Shakya gana, claimed by two sites: Tilaurakot in Kapilvastu district, Nepal, on the Banganga, and Piprahwa-Ganwaria in Siddharthnagar district, Uttar Pradesh, 15 km south. The map dot follows the Nepal identification.

periodLevel.summary: Tilaurakot, excavated by Debala Mitra (1962) and later Nepali, Japanese and Durham teams, is a fortified town with NBPW from about the 6th century BCE. Piprahwa, opened by W. C. Peppe in 1898 and excavated by K. M. Srivastava for the ASI in 1971-77, has a stupa and monastery of the 5th century BCE onwards.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The Buddha's home for his first twenty-nine years, and the one major Buddhist site whose location is still genuinely in dispute.
points: The Piprahwa relic casket of 1898 carries a Brahmi inscription describing it as the receptacle of the relics of the Buddha of the Shakyas, deposited by his kinsmen - very probably the Shakya share of the eight divisions of the relics.

Srivastava's excavation recovered monastic sealings reading "Om devaputra vihare Kapilavastu bhikshu sanghasa", which he took as proof that Piprahwa is Kapilavastu; Tilaurakot's defences, NBPW and position relative to the Ashokan pillars at Niglihawa and Gotihawa support the Nepali claim. Faxian's and Xuanzang's distances have been read both ways.
The Shakyas were a gana-sangha, not a kingdom - Shuddhodana was an elected chief, not a king, a point often got wrong in answers.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 6-7; K. M. Srivastava, *Excavations at Piprahwa and Ganwaria*; Debala Mitra, *Excavations at Tilaura-kot*

location.summary: Karla, near Lonavala in Pune district, Maharashtra, on the Bhor Ghat above the Indrayani valley, a few kilometres from Bhaja - on the same Konkan-to-Deccan trade road.

periodLevel.summary: Developed from the 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE. The Great Chaitya (Cave 8) is c. 50-120 CE, in the period of the Kshatrapa Nahapana and Gautamiputra Satakarni; associated with the Mahasamghika sect, and taken over for Hindu worship in later centuries.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The largest and most perfectly finished rock-cut chaitya hall in India - the form at its height, just before the Buddha image displaces the stupa.
points: The hall is about 45 m long and 14 m high, with thirty-seven octagonal pillars carrying bell-shaped Persepolitan capitals surmounted by kneeling elephants ridden by mithuna couples; the original wooden ribbed vault and the wooden umbrella over the stupa survive, an extraordinary case of timber lasting two thousand years.
The facade carries a great horseshoe sun window and panels of donor couples, the most monumental figure sculpture in the western caves; a free-standing lion pillar stands in front.

The dedicatory inscription names Bhutapala, a setthi of Vaijayanti (Banavasi), and calls it the most excellent rock mansion in Jambudvipa. Other inscriptions record Nahapana's gifts and Gautamiputra Satakarni's grant of the village of Karajika to the monks, and name Yavana donors from Dhenukakata.
The alternation of Nahapana's and Gautamiputra's donations here is primary evidence for the Satavahana-Kshatrapa struggle over the western Deccan.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8; Thapar, *Early India*; ASI

location.summary: Kesariya, East Champaran district, Bihar, on an old bank of the Gandak (Narayani), on the ancient road from Vaishali to Kushinagar.

periodLevel.summary: A stupa with a possibly Mauryan core, its surviving terraced structure built and rebuilt between about the 2nd and the 8th centuries CE, in the Gupta and Pala periods. Reported by Cunningham in 1861-62 and excavated by the ASI under K. K. Muhammed from 1998.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The tallest Buddhist stupa in India, and the closest Indian parallel to the terraced mandala stupas of South-East Asia.
points: It stands about 31.5 m high on a base roughly 400 ft across, rising in polygonal terraces ringed with niches holding life-size Buddha images in bhumisparsha mudra - a plan compared with Borobudur, which it precedes.

Tradition holds that the Buddha, on his last journey, gave his alms bowl to the Licchavis here when they would not let him go on, and that they raised a stupa on the spot; Xuanzang notes a stupa at this stage of the route.
It shows the Pala-period transformation of the stupa from a solid relic mound into an ascending image-bearing structure, the architectural expression of the bodhisattva path.

content.sourcesLine: ASI, *IAR*; Cunningham, *ASI Reports* vol. I; Upinder Singh, ch. 10

location.summary: Key (Ki) Gompa, Spiti valley, Lahaul and Spiti district, Himachal Pradesh, on a conical hill at about 4,150 m above the Spiti river, 12 km from Kaza.

periodLevel.summary: Founded c. 1100 CE by Dromton, a pupil of Atisha, as a Kadampa monastery; it passed to the Gelugpa after the 14th century. Sacked repeatedly - by Mongol raiders in the 17th century, by Ladakhi and Mongol forces in the 1630s, by Zorawar Singh's Dogra army in 1841, and damaged by fire and by the 1975 earthquake.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The largest monastery in Spiti and its principal training centre for lamas, and a building whose form was dictated by warfare.
points: Its architecture is fort-like, a pasada of low boxes piled irregularly up the hill with windowless outer walls - the result of repeated sacking, and quite unlike the courtyard plan of Tabo below it in the same valley.
It preserves Buddhist manuscripts and thangkas, wall paintings and stucco images, and a collection of wind instruments used in cham performance; the murals show Chinese influence alongside Tibetan.

Its history is the political history of Spiti in miniature - Kadampa foundation, Gelugpa takeover, Mongol and Dogra raids - and is the usual example of how the western Himalayan monasteries changed sect with the fortunes of their patrons.

content.sourcesLine: Snellgrove and Skorupski, *The Cultural Heritage of Ladakh*; ASI; Tucci, *Indo-Tibetica*

location.summary: Kuda, near Mandad in Raigad district, Maharashtra, in a hill above the Rajapuri creek of the Konkan coast - beside the ancient port of Mandagora named in the *Periplus*.

periodLevel.summary: Twenty-six small caves of c. 1st century BCE-3rd century CE, Hinayana, under the Mahabhojas as feudatories of the Satavahanas; Mahayana images were added after the 5th-6th centuries.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Modest caves with first-rate inscriptions - the record of a Konkan feudatory house and of the ordinary people who paid for Buddhist monuments.
points: The caves are small viharas and chaityas with stupas, carrying reliefs of the Buddha, the lotus, the wheel, elephants and nagas.

The inscriptions record gifts by the Mahabhoja family - Mandava Khandapalita, Sadageri Vijaya and their kin - and by physicians, blacksmiths, gardeners and merchants with their wives, one of the best cross-sections of donor society in the western Deccan.
Their position beside a Konkan creek port shows the same pattern as Kanheri and Karle: Buddhist establishments sit on the trade arteries, and their donors are the traders.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8; S. Nagaraju, *Buddhist Architecture of Western India*; ASI

location.summary: Lalitgiri, Cuttack district, Odisha, on the Birupa river in the Assia range - with Ratnagiri and Udayagiri it forms the "Diamond Triangle" of Odishan Buddhism.

periodLevel.summary: The earliest Buddhist complex in Odisha, occupied from about the 1st century BCE to the 13th century CE, with Kushana-period Brahmi inscriptions in its lowest levels. Excavated by the ASI, 1985-92.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The rare case of an excavated stupa yielding what are claimed as corporeal relics of the Buddha.
points: The hilltop mahastupa produced a khondalite stone casket containing a steatite box, which held a silver casket and inside that a gold casket with bone relics - one of only a handful of intact multiple-casket deposits found in India.

A large brick apsidal chaitya-griha and four monasteries have been exposed, with colossal standing Buddha images and Mahayana and Vajrayana sculpture - Tara, Avalokiteshvara, Jambhala - showing the Odishan transition from Mahayana to Tantric Buddhism under the Bhaumakaras and Somavamshis.
The complex is one of the candidates for the Pushpagiri mahavihara that Xuanzang describes in Odra, though the identification is unsettled.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; ASI, *IAR* 1985-92; Debala Mitra, *Buddhist Monuments*

location.summary: Lamayuru (Yuru Gompa), Leh district, Ladakh, on a crag at about 3,510 m on the Srinagar-Leh road, above the eroded lake-bed badlands known as the moonland.

periodLevel.summary: One of the oldest and largest gompas in Ladakh, founded in the 11th century in the period of Rinchen Zangpo, with the Naropa cave at its core; originally Kadampa, and now Drikung Kagyu.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The western Himalayan monastery that best preserves the memory of the "second diffusion" of Buddhism from India into Tibet.
points: The oldest surviving building, the Seng-ge-sgang, is attributed to Rinchen Zangpo, the translator sent by the Guge kings to bring Indian texts and craftsmen north - the channel through which late Indian Buddhism entered Tibet as Indian Buddhism itself was ending.

The cave where the siddha Naropa is said to have meditated is enclosed within the complex; Naropa, a scholar of Nalanda and Vikramashila, is the link between the Pala mahaviharas and the Kagyu lineage.
It holds thangkas, murals and a large library, and hosts the Yuru Kabgyat masked dance festival.

content.sourcesLine: Snellgrove and Skorupski, *The Cultural Heritage of Ladakh*; Luciano Petech, *The Kingdom of Ladakh*

location.summary: Lumbini, Rupandehi district, Nepal, in the Terai below the Churia hills near the Telar stream, between Kapilavastu and Devadaha.

periodLevel.summary: The birthplace of Siddhartha Gautama, c. 563 BCE by the conventional reckoning. Ashoka visited in his twentieth regnal year, c. 249 BCE, and set up the Rummindei pillar. The pillar was found by A. Fuhrer and Khadga Shumsher in 1896; excavations by Debala Mitra, by the Japanese Buddhist Federation, and by Robin Coningham's team, which in 2013 reported a timber structure under the Mayadevi temple dated to the 6th century BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The first of the four great pilgrimage places, and the only Ashokan inscription that records a tax concession.
points: The Rummindei pillar inscription states that Ashoka came in person and worshipped because "here the Buddha Sakyamuni was born" (hida budhe jate sakyamuniti), and that he made the village of Lumbini free of bali and liable to only one-eighth of the produce as bhaga - the single most direct evidence we have of Mauryan revenue terms.
The pillar also fixes the site itself, and is the earliest surviving epigraphic confirmation that the Buddha was a historical person.
The Mayadevi temple, the marker stone said to locate the exact birthplace, the Puskarini tank and the surrounding monastic remains complete the complex. UNESCO World Heritage, 1997.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; Thapar, *Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas*

location.summary: Mahasthangarh, Bogura (Bogra) district, Bangladesh, on the west bank of the Karatoya - ancient Pundranagara, capital of Pundravardhana and the oldest urban site in Bangladesh.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by K. N. Dikshit from 1928-31 and since 1993 by a Bangladesh-France mission. Occupation runs from the 3rd century BCE (Mauryan, with NBPW) to the 18th century CE, through Shunga, Gupta, Pala and Sena levels.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The eastern limit of Mauryan administration on the ground, proved by an inscription rather than inferred from a map.
points: The Mahasthan stone plaque inscription, Prakrit in Brahmi of about the 3rd century BCE, is the earliest epigraph found in Bangladesh. It is an order to the mahamatra stationed at Pundranagara directing that people in distress be relieved by distributing paddy (dhanya) from the state granary (koshthagara) and by a loan in gandaka coins, the stock to be replenished afterwards.

That single text gives us a Mauryan provincial officer, a state granary, famine relief as an administrative duty and a coined loan - the best independent check on the Arthashastra's account of famine policy.
The citadel is a rampart-enclosed rectangle roughly 1.5 by 1.4 km rising 5 m above the plain, with suburban mounds around it including Govinda Bhita temple and Vasu Vihara.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; Department of Archaeology, Bangladesh

location.summary: Bargaon, Nalanda district, Bihar, about 10 km north of Rajgir in the Magadhan plain - a mahavihara on the road between Rajagriha and Pataliputra.

periodLevel.summary: Founded by Kumaragupta I in the 5th century CE (c. 415-455), enlarged under Harshavardhana and the Palas, and functioning until it was sacked by Bakhtiyar Khalji c. 1199-1203 - some 700 years of continuous teaching. Identified by Cunningham in 1861 and excavated by the ASI, 1915-37 and 1974-82.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The first residential university in the world, and the institution that separates monastic learning from the individual-teacher tradition of Taxila.
points: Eleven monasteries and six brick temples stand in a planned row along a central alley, the monasteries built to a uniform plan of cells around a courtyard with a shrine opposite the entrance - deliberate architecture for an institution, not an accumulation of donations.

Temple Site 3, the Sariputta stupa, was rebuilt seven times, each casing enclosing the last, with stucco Buddha and bodhisattva figures in its corner towers - a stratigraphy of Gupta-to-Pala sculpture in one monument.

Seals reading "Sri-Nalanda-Mahavihariya-Arya-Bhikshu-Sanghasya" confirm the identification; the Nalanda copper plate of Devapala records a grant made at the request of the Shailendra king of Suvarnadvipa, evidence of international endowment.

Xuanzang studied here in the 630s under Shilabhadra and Yijing in 673-685; both describe an admissions examination at the gate, a curriculum of Mahayana with grammar, logic, medicine and Samkhya, and residential students. Dharmapala, Shantarakshita and Dharmakirti taught here; tradition also links Nagarjuna and Aryabhata to it. UNESCO World Heritage, 2016.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 9-10; Xuanzang and Yijing's accounts; ASI, *Nalanda* excavation reports

location.summary: The Trirashmi hills, about 8 km south of Nashik, Maharashtra, above the Godavari - on the route from the Konkan ports through the ghats to Pratishthana.

periodLevel.summary: Twenty-four caves cut between the 1st century BCE and the 3rd century CE, Hinayana, with later Mahayana additions to the 6th century. Patrons were the Satavahanas, the Kshatrapa house of Nahapana, and merchants and monks.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The single most important epigraphic site of the Deccan - the caves are read for their inscriptions more than for their architecture.
points: The Nasik prashasti of Gautami Balashri in Cave 3 praises her son Gautamiputra Satakarni as the destroyer of Shakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas, as ekabrahmana, as the one who crushed the pride of the Kshatriyas and stopped the mixing of the four varnas - the fullest statement of Satavahana royal ideology, and the key text on the brahmanical claims of a dynasty that patronised Buddhism.

Ushavadata (Rishabhadatta), son-in-law of Nahapana, records gifts of villages, of 3,000 cows, of money invested with weavers' guilds at fixed interest to feed and clothe the monks, and of a free ferry on the Barnasa - among the earliest land grants and the earliest recorded permanent endowments in India.

Cave 10 (Nahapana vihara), Cave 3 (Gautamiputra vihara) and Cave 18, the chaitya of the 1st century BCE, are the principal excavations; a rock-cut water management system of cisterns serves the whole group.
The alternation of Kshatrapa and Satavahana donations on the same hill records the see-saw of control over the western Deccan in the 1st-2nd centuries CE.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; Thapar, *Early India*

location.summary: Paro Taktsang, the Tiger's Nest, in the Paro valley of western Bhutan, clinging to a granite cliff about 900 m above the valley floor at roughly 3,120 m.

periodLevel.summary: The Taktsang Senge Samdup cave is held to be where Padmasambhava meditated in the 8th century CE. The monastery around it was built in 1692 by Gyalse Tenzin Rabgye, the fourth Druk Desi; gutted by fire in 1998 and restored by 2005. Nyingma and Drukpa Kagyu.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The defining monument of Bhutanese Buddhism, and the eastern end of the Padmasambhava tradition that began in Indian Vajrayana.
points: Tradition holds that Padmasambhava - Guru Rinpoche, a tantric master associated with Uddiyana in the north-west of the subcontinent - flew here on the back of a tigress and meditated for three years, three months, three weeks, three days and three hours, subduing the local deities; this is the founding story of Buddhism in Bhutan.
The complex of four temples and residences is built into the rock face at several levels, connected by stairways cut in the cliff - a building whose whole design is an act of devotion to a cave.
Its importance for the syllabus is as evidence of the outward transmission of Indian Vajrayana into the Himalaya, alongside Tabo, Alchi and Tawang.

content.sourcesLine: Michael Aris, *Bhutan: The Early History of a Himalayan Kingdom*; Upinder Singh, ch. 10 (for the Vajrayana background)

location.summary: Pitalkhora, in a ravine of the Satmala range of the Western Ghats near Kannad, Aurangabad district, Maharashtra - Ptolemy's Petirgala, on the road from Pratishthana to the Tapi valley.

periodLevel.summary: Fourteen caves - four chaityas and ten viharas - of c. 2nd century BCE, among the earliest rock-cut excavations in the Deccan, Hinayana; Mahayana images and paintings were added in the 5th-6th centuries CE. The rock is friable and much of the site has collapsed.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The earliest monumental sculpture in the western Deccan caves, older than Karle and contemporary with Bhaja.
points: The great yaksha dvarapalas, the elephant frieze supporting the terrace, a gaja-lakshmi and a horseman in high relief are the site's chief works, and are among the first attempts at large-scale figure carving in the western caves; the best pieces are now in the National Museum, Delhi.
An inscription records the gift of a physician (vaidya) of Pratishthana - a professional donor from the Satavahana capital, showing where the patronage came from.
Rock-cut channels carry rainwater through the complex, an early example of the water engineering that made long occupation of these sites possible.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8; M. N. Deshpande, *The Rock-Cut Caves of Pitalkhora* (Ancient India 15, 1959); ASI

location.summary: Sanghol (Uchcha Pind), Fatehgarh Sahib district, Punjab, on an old course of the Sutlej between the Sutlej and the Ghaggar - on the route from Mathura to Taxila.

periodLevel.summary: A multi-period mound with late Harappan, PGW and NBPW levels; its great phase is Kushana, 1st-2nd centuries CE, when the stupa and monastery were built. Excavated by the Punjab Department of Archaeology from 1968 under S. S. Talwar and R. S. Bisht, with the decisive discovery by G. B. Sharma in 1985.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The largest single hoard of Mathura sculpture ever found, and the proof that Mathura workshops exported finished stone hundreds of kilometres north.
points: In 1985 a pit beside the stupa yielded 117 carved railing pillars, crossbars and coping stones in Mathura's spotted red sandstone, evidently buried for safety - complete with yakshi and salabhanjika figures at the toilet, with mirrors, birds and trees, in the fully modelled sensuous Mathura idiom.
The stupa was built on a wheel-shaped plan with a bone relic casket at its centre, and a monastery stood beside it; Kushana inscriptions, pottery and coins were recovered from the complex.

Because the stone is Mathura sandstone, the find settles a long argument about whether provincial Kushana sculpture was locally made or imported - here it was quarried, carved and shipped from Mathura.
Xuanzang's She-to-tu-lu is usually identified with Sanghol.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8; S. P. Gupta, *Kushana Sculptures from Sanghol* (1985); ASI, *IAR*

location.summary: Sankisa Basantapur, Farrukhabad district, Uttar Pradesh, on the Kali Nadi - the ancient Ikshumati - in the central Ganga-Yamuna doab.

periodLevel.summary: An early historic city mound with NBPW, occupied from about the 6th century BCE. The Ashokan pillar is 3rd century BCE. Identified by Alexander Cunningham in 1842 on the strength of Faxian's and Xuanzang's itineraries; the mound itself remains largely unexcavated.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the eight great places of Buddhist pilgrimage, and the only Ashokan pillar to carry an elephant capital.
points: The site marks the Buddha's descent from the Trayastrimsa heaven, where he had gone to preach the Abhidhamma to his mother Maya, returning by a triple ladder with Brahma and Indra at his sides - the "Descent at Sankissa", one of the eight great events (ashtamahapratiharya) of Buddhist art.
The surviving Ashokan capital is a seated elephant on a bell-shaped lotus; the shaft has gone and no inscription survives, but it is the only elephant capital still standing at its pillar site.
Faxian and Xuanzang both describe the ladders and the monasteries; today a Bisari Devi temple stands on the stupa mound, a common instance of a Buddhist site being absorbed into local Hindu worship.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7; Cunningham, *The Ancient Geography of India*; Faxian and Xuanzang's accounts

location.summary: Sarnath - ancient Isipatana, the Migadaya or Deer Park - 10 km north-east of Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh, near the meeting of the Varuna with the Ganga.

periodLevel.summary: The site of the first sermon, c. 528 BCE. Ashoka built the Dharmarajika stupa and the pillar with the lion capital in the 3rd century BCE; the Dhamekh stupa in its present form is Gupta, c. 500 CE, as is the Sarnath school of sculpture; the monasteries were destroyed by Qutb-ud-din Aibak's forces in 1194. Excavated by Jagat Singh and Duncan (1794), Cunningham (1835), F. O. Oertel (1904-05, who found the lion capital), and Marshall, Hargreaves and Daya Ram Sahni after.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Where the Sangha came into being, and where the two most reproduced objects in modern India were made.
points: The Buddha preached the Dhammachakkappavattana Sutta to the five ascetics here - the Middle Path, the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path - and the ordination of Kondanna and his companions founded the Sangha, the third of the three jewels.

Ashoka's lion capital in polished Chunar sandstone - four addorsed lions on an abacus carrying lion, elephant, bull and horse separated by wheels, over an inverted lotus - is India's state emblem, and its dharmachakra is on the national flag. The shaft carries the Schism Edict, warning that any monk or nun who splits the Sangha will be made to wear white and expelled, evidence of Ashoka's intervention in monastic discipline.

The Dhamekh stupa, 43.6 m of brick with a carved stone drum of Gupta floral and geometric ornament, marks the spot of the sermon; the Chaukhandi stupa nearby marks the meeting with the five disciples and carries a Mughal octagonal tower of 1588.

The Sarnath school of the 5th century CE - the seated Buddha preaching the first sermon, in cream Chunar sandstone with a plain transparent robe and no folds - is the classic Gupta Buddha, and the deliberate contrast to Mathura's heavy pleated drapery.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7 and 9; Daya Ram Sahni, *Catalogue of the Museum of Archaeology at Sarnath*; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*

location.summary: Saspol (Saspochhe) caves, Leh district, Ladakh, cut into a cliff on the right bank of the Indus opposite Alchi, above the village of Saspol.

periodLevel.summary: Five man-made caves painted in the 13th-15th centuries CE, in the period after the Guge kingdom and during the rise of the Ladakhi Namgyal house.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A fusion of the Indian-Kashmiri manner of Alchi with the Tibetan style that replaced it - the transition caught mid-way.
points: The walls were plastered with clay and painted in bright mineral colours, with mandalas, Shakyamuni, Avalokiteshvara, Padmasambhava and the wheel of existence, along with small miniature-scale panels.
The caves were meditation retreats rather than a monastery, so they preserve a private rather than an institutional iconography - unusual survival for the western Himalaya.
Placed on the World Monuments Watch because of severe deterioration; documentation rather than excavation is the work being done here.

content.sourcesLine: Snellgrove and Skorupski, *The Cultural Heritage of Ladakh*; World Monuments Fund documentation
