location.summary: Sigiriya, Matale district, central Sri Lanka - a 180 m granite monolith rising from the dry-zone plain, with a planned city at its foot.

periodLevel.summary: Caves around the rock carry drip-ledges and Brahmi inscriptions of c. 3rd century BCE-1st century CE, when they housed forest monks. King Kashyapa I made the rock his fortified capital in 477-495 CE; after his death it reverted to a monastery and was occupied until the 13th-14th centuries. UNESCO World Heritage, 1982.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The best-preserved example of early Asian urban planning, and the closest surviving relative of the Ajanta painting tradition.
points: The plan is symmetrical and axial: water gardens with working fountains at the west, boulder and terraced gardens rising to the rock, and the palace on the summit - hydraulic engineering and landscape design integrated on a scale not matched in South Asia for centuries.
A colossal lion of brick and plaster once framed the stairway; only the paws survive, and give the rock its name, Sinhagiri.

Of a reputed five hundred figures in the western rock pocket, twenty-one apsaras or cloud maidens survive - painted in sweeping strokes with heavier pressure on one side and deepening tone towards the edge to model the form, a technique closely comparable to Ajanta, and evidence of a shared Indian Ocean painting tradition.
The polished Mirror Wall carries some 1,800 graffiti of the 8th-10th centuries, verses left by visitors - the earliest substantial body of Sinhala poetry and a rare record of ordinary literacy.

content.sourcesLine: Senake Bandaranayake, *Sigiriya*; UNESCO World Heritage documentation; the *Culavamsa*

location.summary: Paharpur, Badalgachhi, Naogaon district, Bangladesh, in ancient Varendra between the Karatoya and the Mahananda - Somapura Mahavihara.

periodLevel.summary: Built by the Pala king Dharmapala, c. 781-821 CE, whose name appears on seals from the site; the principal monastery of the Palas through the 9th-11th centuries, damaged in the 11th century and abandoned by the 13th. Excavated by K. N. Dikshit for the ASI, 1923-34. UNESCO World Heritage, 1985.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The largest Buddhist monastery south of the Himalayas, and the source of a building form that spread across South-East Asia.
points: A square of 281 m a side, with 177 monastic cells opening on to a courtyard, and at its centre a cruciform temple rising in three receding terraces to about 21 m - the monastery and the temple are a single designed composition, not a shrine added to a residence.

About 2,000 terracotta plaques and 63 stone sculptures are set into the terrace walls - Buddhas and bodhisattvas alongside Shiva, Krishna, Balarama, animals and scenes of village life, evidence of how thoroughly Pala Buddhism shared a visual world with its Hindu neighbours.
The cruciform terraced plan travelled: it is the acknowledged model behind the temples of Bagan in Myanmar, and is compared with Chandi Loro Jonggrang in Java and with the Cambodian temple mountains.
Atisha Dipankara Shrijnana, who took Buddhism to Tibet in 1042, was associated with Somapura, which links it to Vikramashila and Jagaddala in the same network.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; K. N. Dikshit, *Excavations at Paharpur* (ASI Memoir 55); UNESCO

location.summary: Tabo, Spiti valley, Lahaul and Spiti district, Himachal Pradesh, on the left bank of the Spiti river at about 3,280 m, with meditation caves cut into the cliff above the village.

periodLevel.summary: Founded in 996 CE by Yeshe-O, the king of Guge, with his teacher Rinchen Zangpo; renovated in 1042, the year Atisha is said to have visited. In continuous use since - the oldest Buddhist establishment in India and the Himalaya still functioning without a break. Gelugpa; ASI protected.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Called the Ajanta of the Himalayas - and the best-preserved monument of the second diffusion of Buddhism from India into Tibet.
points: Nine temples, twenty-three chortens and the monks' quarters are built entirely of mud, sand and timber, with no stone - the survival of 10th-century mud architecture in the cold desert is itself remarkable.

The Tsuglakhang, the assembly hall, holds thirty-three life-size clay stucco bodhisattvas projecting from the walls, arranged as a three-dimensional mandala of Vairochana, with murals of the 10th-11th centuries below them in a Kashmiri-derived style.
The caves above the monastery served as assembly halls and retreats for monks; traces of hearths, cut seats and grain storage survive in them, evidence of how the community actually lived.
The 14th Dalai Lama has conducted the Kalachakra initiation here (1983 and 1996) and has spoken of retiring to Tabo, which keeps the site a living institution rather than a monument.

content.sourcesLine: Deborah Klimburg-Salter, *Tabo: A Lamp for the Kingdom* (1997); Tucci, *Indo-Tibetica*; ASI

location.summary: Takht-i-Bahi, Mardan district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, on a hill about 150 m above the Peshawar plain - in the heart of Gandhara, on the route between Pushkalavati and the Swat valley.

periodLevel.summary: Founded in the 1st century CE; an inscription dated in the reign of the Indo-Parthian king Gondophares points to c. 46 CE. Four building phases run to the 7th century, through the Kushana and Kidarite periods. Excavated from 1871 and by the ASI under Spooner and Hargreaves; UNESCO World Heritage, 1980.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The most complete surviving Gandharan monastery - the one where the whole plan of a Buddhist establishment can still be read.
points: It has four distinct components: the Court of Stupas, a courtyard ringed by votive stupas; the monastic quadrangle of individual cells around an open court; an assembly hall and refectory with a kitchen and water tank; and a temple complex of many stupas on a higher terrace.
A later addition is a Tantric complex of dark cells with low openings, taken as evidence of Vajrayana practice in Gandhara - a rare architectural trace of esoteric Buddhism in the north-west.

Its schist and stucco sculpture is classic Gandhara: the Buddha in Graeco-Roman drapery with wavy hair and a halo, narrative friezes of the life, and Corinthian pilasters - the fusion of Hellenistic form with Buddhist content under Kushana patronage.
Its hilltop position, away from a city, kept it out of reach of later building and is why it survives when the plain sites do not.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8; John Marshall, *The Buddhist Art of Gandhara*; UNESCO

location.summary: Tawang, Arunachal Pradesh, on a spur at about 3,050 m above the Tawang Chu valley, close to the Bhutan and Tibet borders on the old trade and pilgrimage road to Lhasa.

periodLevel.summary: Founded in 1680-81 by Merak Lama Lodre Gyatso at the instance of the fifth Dalai Lama; Gelugpa. Occupied by Chinese forces for some months during the war of 1962.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The largest monastery in India and the second largest in the world after the Potala - and the eastern anchor of the Gelugpa order's reach.
points: The complex is a walled monastic town: a three-storeyed assembly hall (Dukhang) with an 8 m gilded seated Buddha, some sixty-five residential buildings, and the Parkhang library holding the Kangyur and Tengyur, part of it in gold lettering.
The sixth Dalai Lama, Tsangyang Gyatso, was born nearby at Urgelling in 1683 - the reason the monastery holds the position it does in the Gelugpa hierarchy.

The fourteenth Dalai Lama crossed into India at Tawang in 1959; the monastery's history is inseparable from the politics of the eastern Himalayan frontier, which is the angle worth flagging in an answer.

content.sourcesLine: Michael Aris, *Hidden Treasures and Secret Lives*; ASI; Government of Arunachal Pradesh records

location.summary: Thanale (also called Nadsur), Sudhagad taluka, Raigad district, Maharashtra, in a Sahyadri ravine above the Konkan - on the ghat route from the Konkan creek ports up to the Deccan plateau.

periodLevel.summary: Twenty-three caves of c. 2nd-1st centuries BCE, Hinayana, contemporary with Bhaja and Kondane; partly unfinished, and little studied.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the oldest and least disturbed of the early Konkan cave groups - the plain monastic architecture that the great sites grew out of.
points: The chaitya has a stupa carved in relief on the rear wall rather than a free-standing one, an early and unusual solution; the viharas open off a long common verandah with a sculpted facade.
Several caves were abandoned part-cut, which leaves the working method visible - excavation proceeding from the roof downwards, so that no scaffolding was needed.
Like Kuda and Bhaja, its interest is that it sits on a trade pass: the early Buddhist caves of the western ghats map the routes linking the Konkan ports to Junnar, Nashik and Paithan.

content.sourcesLine: S. Nagaraju, *Buddhist Architecture of Western India*; ASI; Upinder Singh, ch. 8

location.summary: Thiksey, Leh district, Ladakh, on a hill on the right bank of the Indus about 19 km south-east of Leh at 3,600 m.

periodLevel.summary: Founded in the 15th century, c. 1430, by Palden Sherab Zangpo, in the line of Tsongkhapa's disciples; Gelugpa. The largest gompa in central Ladakh.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The clearest surviving example of Tibetan tiered monastic architecture in India, and the seat of the Gelugpa in Ladakh.
points: Twelve storeys of white-washed buildings climb the hill in ascending rank, monks' quarters below and temples at the summit - a plan modelled on the Potala at Lhasa, and the standard illustration of how Tibetan monastic hierarchy is expressed in building.
The Maitreya (Chamba) temple, built in 1970 to mark the fourteenth Dalai Lama's visit, holds a 15 m seated Maitreya occupying two storeys - the largest such image in Ladakh.
It holds stupas, thangkas, wall paintings, swords and an assembly hall with a Tara temple of twenty-one images; the Gustor festival with its cham dances is held annually.

content.sourcesLine: Snellgrove and Skorupski, *The Cultural Heritage of Ladakh*; Petech, *The Kingdom of Ladakh*

location.summary: Vala, Bhavnagar district, Gujarat, in eastern Saurashtra near the Gulf of Khambhat - a port-linked capital on the trade route from the western seaboard to Malwa.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of the Maitrakas, c. 475-775 CE, founded by Bhatarka, a general of the Guptas who made himself independent as the Gupta empire weakened. Destroyed in an Arab raid from Sindh c. 775 CE. Known principally from over a hundred Maitraka copper-plate grants.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The great centre of Hinayana learning, and the western counterweight to Mahayana Nalanda.
points: Its mahavihara taught the Sthaviravada and Sammitiya doctrines along with nitishastra (statecraft), law and philosophy, and drew Brahmana students as well as monks - graduates went into royal service, which is why it was funded. Gunamati and Sthiramati taught here.

Xuanzang visited c. 640 and Yijing in the later 7th century; both rank it with Nalanda, and Xuanzang counts some hundred monasteries with six thousand monks - the pairing Nalanda/Vallabhi is the standard contrast of Mahayana east and Hinayana west.

The second Jaina council of the Svetambaras met at Vallabhi under Devarddhi Kshamashramana, c. 453 or 466 CE, and there the Agamas were committed to writing - the moment the Svetambara canon became a fixed text.
The Maitraka copper plates are among the richest sources for land grants, administrative titles and religious endowment in western India.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 9-10; Xuanzang's account; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*

location.summary: Antichak, Bhagalpur district, Bihar, on a bluff above the right bank of the Ganga near Kahalgaon - sited on the river so that it commanded the route into Bengal.

periodLevel.summary: Founded by the Pala king Dharmapala, c. 783-820 CE, and functioning until destroyed by Bakhtiyar Khalji c. 1203. Excavated jointly by Patna University under B. P. Sinha and by the ASI, 1960-69 and 1972-82.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The leading centre of Vajrayana learning in India, and the source from which Buddhism was re-established in Tibet.
points: The plan is a square monastery of 208 cells around a courtyard, with a cruciform brick stupa on a terraced plinth at the centre, faced with terracotta plaques - the same Pala scheme as Somapura, and the fullest excavated example in India.

Its organisation is recorded in Tibetan sources: six colleges each with its own gate, a dvarapandita or gate-scholar appointed to examine entrants at each, and a mahasthavira over all - the most formally structured of the mahaviharas.

Atisha Dipankara Shrijnana was its abbot before leaving for Tibet in 1041 at the invitation of the Guge king - the single most consequential export of Indian Buddhism, and the foundation of the Kadampa and later Gelugpa lines. Ratnakarashanti, Jnanapada and Jetari also taught here.

A separate library building with a cooling water channel was identified in excavation, along with a tank; the destruction of Vikramashila and Nalanda within a few years effectively ends organised Buddhism in India.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Taranatha, *History of Buddhism in India*; ASI, *IAR* 1972-82

location.summary: Akota (ancient Ankottaka), a mound now inside Vadodara on the west bank of the Vishvamitri, Gujarat - on the route linking the Gujarat ports to Malwa and the Deccan.

periodLevel.summary: A hoard of sixty-eight Jaina bronzes recovered in 1951 when the mound was being levelled, ranging from the late 5th or 6th century to the 12th century CE - Maitraka, Gurjara-Pratihara and Chaulukya (Solanki) work. Published by U. P. Shah as *Akota Bronzes* (1959); the images are chiefly in the Baroda Museum.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The largest and earliest sequence of Jaina metal images in western India - the dated series against which all later Svetambara bronzes are measured.
points: Sixty-eight images of Tirthankaras with their attendant yakshas and yakshis, cast in brass and bronze by the lost-wax (cire perdue) method, many with silver and copper inlay for the eyes and the srivatsa mark on the chest.

The principal images are of Jivantasvami - Mahavira shown as a crowned prince before renunciation, standing in kayotsarga with dhoti, crown and ornaments - and of Parshvanatha under his serpent hood. The Jivantasvami type is rare in Indian art, and Akota has its earliest known examples.
Many pieces carry donative inscriptions naming the donor, which is why the group functions as a dated sequence rather than a stylistic guess; the donors are lay men and women and nuns, not kings.

With the Chausa bronzes it establishes that Jaina metal sculpture in the Gupta and post-Gupta centuries was a western and eastern Indian speciality funded by mercantile patronage - a tradition running parallel to, and independent of, the Buddhist bronzes.

content.sourcesLine: U. P. Shah, *Akota Bronzes* (1959); Upinder Singh, ch. 9; ASI

location.summary: Begram, Parwan province, Afghanistan, at the junction of the Ghorband and Panjshir rivers north of Kabul - the Kushana summer capital Kapisa, where the routes from China, India and the Roman west converged.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated by the Delegation Archeologique Francaise en Afghanistan under Joseph Hackin and Roman Ghirshman, 1936-40. The sealed Begram hoard was found in 1937 and 1939 in two walled-up rooms of the palace and dates to the 1st-2nd centuries CE, the Kushana peak under Kanishka.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The richest single assemblage of long-distance trade goods from the ancient world - the Silk Road as an object rather than an argument.
points: The two rooms held, stacked side by side: Indian carved ivories and bone furniture fittings; Roman and Alexandrian bronzes, plaster medallions and painted, gilded and millefiori glass; Chinese lacquerware; and alabaster vessels. Three civilisations' luxury goods in one sealed deposit, datable to within a century.

The ivories are the largest surviving group of early Indian ivory carving anywhere. They were carved, smoothed and lightly polished, with red and blue pigment used for colour, and show women at the toilet, standing at gateways and under trees, in an idiom close to Mathura and Sanchi - proof that the Kushana empire carried Indian craft north, not only Indian religion.
Whether the rooms were a royal treasury sealed in an emergency or a merchant's bonded warehouse is still argued; either reading makes Kapisa an entrepot rather than a consumer.
Much of the collection was looted from the Kabul Museum after 1992; a part had been hidden and was recovered in 2003.

content.sourcesLine: Joseph Hackin, *Recherches archeologiques a Begram* (1939, 1954); Upinder Singh, ch. 8; Thapar, *Early India*

location.summary: Chausa, Buxar (formerly Bhojpur) district, Bihar, on the south bank of the Ganga near the Uttar Pradesh border - better known as the field where Sher Shah defeated Humayun in 1539.

periodLevel.summary: A hoard of eighteen Jaina bronzes found in 1931 during digging near the village, spanning roughly the 2nd to the 6th centuries CE - the earlier pieces Kushana in feeling, the later ones Gupta. Now in the Patna Museum.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The earliest group of Jaina metal images in India, and the eastern counterpart to Akota.
points: Eighteen bronzes: Tirthankaras, yakshis, a makara and a kalpavriksha. The kalpavriksha and the dharmachakra are among the very few surviving Jaina cult objects that are not images of a Tirthankara, and show that the Jaina shrine held symbols as well as icons.

The physique is masculine and heavily modelled, and Adinatha (Rishabhanatha) is shown with long hair locks falling over the shoulders - the iconographic mark that distinguishes him from the other twenty-three Tirthankaras, here in one of its earliest datable appearances.

The earliest pieces stand close to Kushana Mathura in their modelling and the later ones show Gupta restraint, so the hoard records in bronze the same stylistic transition that Mathura records in stone.
It establishes that Jainism had a developed image cult in cast metal well before the Gupta period, against the older view that Jaina art begins with the medieval temple.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8-9; Patna Museum catalogue; ASI

location.summary: Dhanesar Kheda, Banda district, Uttar Pradesh, in the Bundelkhand tract between the Yamuna and the Ken - a minor mound, not an excavated city.

periodLevel.summary: Bronze images of the Gupta and post-Gupta period, c. 5th-6th centuries CE, the principal one an inscribed standing Buddha. The site is known for this group of metal sculpture rather than for a stratified sequence.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: An inscribed Gupta bronze that doubles as a historical document for a region with no dynastic record of its own.
points: The Buddha stands in abhaya mudra, the right hand raised in reassurance. The sanghati is wrapped over both shoulders and gathered in the left hand, and the modelling is deliberately thin and clinging, so the cloth reads as transparent over the body - the Sarnath convention of the fifth century translated into metal, and cast by the lost-wax process.

The dedicatory inscription on the image records the gift by the wife of one Hariraja - a named lay woman as donor, evidence that Gupta-period metal images were commissioned privately and not only by rulers or monasteries.
Because it is inscribed, the image supplies names and a date for local Gupta-period history where no copper plates or coins survive; its value is epigraphic as much as artistic.
Read it against the 2.3 m Sultanganj Buddha for the scale Gupta bronze casting could reach, and against the Akota and Chausa hoards for the parallel Jaina tradition in metal.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 9; Vidya Dehejia, *Indian Art*; ASI

location.summary: Tamluk (ancient Tamralipti), Purba Medinipur district, West Bengal, on the west bank of the Rupnarayan near its meeting with the Hooghly - the great eastern seaport of early India, and the seaward end of the Uttarapatha.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated from 1954-55 by the ASI and Calcutta University. A Chalcolithic black-and-red ware level at the base; NBPW from c. 400 BCE; the port at its height from the Mauryan to the Gupta period, c. 300 BCE-600 CE; decline after the 8th century as the river silted and shifted.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The exit point of the Mauryan trade route to the south and south-east, and one of the two great terracotta centres of early Bengal.
points: Its terracottas date from the Mauryan period and are hand modelled, with dress and accessories added separately afterwards - a technique that precedes the single and multiple moulds used at Chandraketugarh, so the two sites together give the sequence from modelling to mass production.

Pre-Mauryan pieces represent mother goddesses and fertility figures; the later range covers yakshas, toys, animals, birds, erotic motifs, nagas, naginis and apsaras - a repertoire of popular cult rather than court art.
Roman Arretine ware, rouletted ware and red polished ware confirm the Indian Ocean trade, alongside coins, beads and semi-precious stones.

It was the port from which Ashoka's mission under Mahendra and Sanghamitra is said to have sailed for Sri Lanka; Faxian spent two years here copying texts before sailing for Sri Lanka, and Xuanzang describes it. By land it was tied to Taxila along the Uttarapatha - the road that crossed the subcontinent from the north-west frontier to the Bay of Bengal.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7-9; Faxian, *Fo-kuo-chi*; ASI, *IAR*

location.summary: Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu, in the Kaveri delta on the Vadavaru branch - the Chola capital from Vijayalaya's capture of the town c. 850 CE, and the richest rice country in the peninsula.

periodLevel.summary: The Brihadishvara (Rajarajeshvara) temple was built by Rajaraja I between 1003 and 1010 CE, and the Chola murals in its inner ambulatory are of that date. Nayaka repainting over them belongs to the 16th century, after the fall of Vijayanagara; Maratha patronage runs from 1674. UNESCO World Heritage as one of the Great Living Chola Temples, 1987.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The only substantial survival of Chola mural painting - hidden for nine centuries under a later layer, and the high point of Dravida temple building.
points: The 11th-century frescoes were found in 1931 by S. K. Govindasamy in the dark circumambulatory passage, painted beneath the Nayaka layer. They show Shiva as Tripurantaka, Nataraja at Chidambaram, the saint Sundarar with Cheraman Perumal, and figures taken to be Rajaraja I with his guru Karuvurar - among the earliest royal portraits in South Indian painting.
They are true fresco: pigment laid on still-damp lime plaster so that the colour bonds into the surface, which is why the Chola layer has outlasted the Nayaka work painted over it.

The temple, called the Dakshina Meru, carries a 66 m vimana of thirteen diminishing storeys over the sanctum - the tallest of its time - with the tower, not the gateway, as the dominant mass; the gopura only overtakes the vimana in later Pandya and Nayaka building. Its walls hold the largest corpus of Chola inscriptions anywhere, recording endowments, temple servants, musicians and the four hundred dancers transferred here, which is what makes Chola social and economic history writable at all.

Thanjavur painting proper is a later and separate tradition of the Maratha period, 18th-19th centuries - gesso relief, gold foil and inset glass or stones on a wooden panel, mostly Vaishnava subjects - and the reverse glass painting of the same workshops is equally well known.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Vidya Dehejia, *Art of the Imperial Cholas*; ASI, *South Indian Inscriptions* vol. II

The only substantial survival of Chola mural painting, hidden for nine centuries under a later layer, and the high point of Dravida temple building.

location.summary: Ahraura, Mirzapur district, Uttar Pradesh, on a rock in the Vindhyan scarp south of the Ganga near Varanasi.

periodLevel.summary: Minor Rock Edict I, Brahmi script, Prakrit language, c. 258-257 BCE - the Minor Rock Edicts belong to Ashoka's twelfth or thirteenth regnal year and precede the Major Rock Edicts. Discovered in 1961.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The one version of Minor Rock Edict I that appears to mention relics of the Buddha - which is why a short provincial inscription carries weight out of all proportion to its length.
points: Minor Rock Edict I is Ashoka's personal statement: he has been a lay follower (upasaka) for more than two and a half years, was not zealous at first, but has since drawn close to the Sangha and been zealous - the most intimate thing he ever put on stone, and the text always quoted on the sincerity of his conversion.

The Ahraura version adds a clause absent elsewhere, read as referring to the relics (salila) of the Buddha being made an object of worship. If that reading holds, the edict dates the spread of the relic cult to Ashoka's own reign rather than after it.
Its position in the Vindhyan borderland, away from any city, illustrates the placement rule for the Minor Rock Edicts: they sit on routes and at frontier points where people passed, not in capitals.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; Thapar, *Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas*

location.summary: The Allahabad (Prayagraj) pillar, now standing inside the Akbar fort at the Ganga-Yamuna confluence, Uttar Pradesh. It was not made for this spot: it originally stood at Kaushambi and was moved here, probably in the Mughal period.

periodLevel.summary: Polished Chunar sandstone, c. 240s BCE. It carries Pillar Edicts I-VI (twenty-sixth to twenty-seventh regnal years, c. 243-242 BCE), the Schism or Kaushambi Edict, and the Queen's Edict - all in Brahmi and Prakrit. Later inscriptions were cut on the same shaft in the 4th century CE and the 17th.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The most heavily inscribed object in Indian history - one pillar carrying Mauryan, Gupta and Mughal records, eighteen centuries apart.
points: The Queen's Edict is the only Ashokan record to name a queen: it directs that the gifts of the second queen Karuvaki, mother of Tivara, be credited to her - evidence both of a queen's independent religious endowment and of an administration careful about attribution.

The Schism Edict, addressed to the mahamatras of Kaushambi, orders that any monk or nun who divides the Sangha be made to wear white and expelled - the state intervening directly in monastic discipline.

The Prayaga Prashasti of Samudragupta, composed by Harishena in polished Sanskrit kavya, is cut on the same surface: it lists the kings of Aryavarta uprooted, the Dakshinapatha kings captured and released, and the frontier states paying homage - the single most important source for Gupta political history. That a Gupta panegyric was added to an Ashokan pillar is itself an argument about how the Guptas saw their inheritance.
Jahangir added a Persian inscription recording his accession, completing the sequence.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7 and 9; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; *Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum* I and III

location.summary: Bahapur, near Kalkaji in south Delhi, on a rocky outcrop of the Delhi ridge - on the Uttarapatha where it crosses the Yamuna-Aravalli gap.

periodLevel.summary: Minor Rock Edict I, Brahmi script, Prakrit language, c. 258-257 BCE. Discovered in 1966, the latest major Ashokan find in north India.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Extends the Minor Rock Edict distribution into the Delhi region, and confirms the rule that these edicts follow trade roads.
points: The text is Ashoka's first personal message - his own account of becoming an upasaka, his initial lack of zeal, his drawing near to the Sangha, and his call that people should exert themselves in dhamma - not an administrative order.

Its setting is the point: Bahapur is not a city or a capital but a rock beside the Uttarapatha, the trunk road from the north-west to the Ganga plain. The Minor Rock Edicts map the empire's communications, whereas the Major Rock Edicts mark its frontiers.

Delhi holds two further Ashokan monuments, the Topra and Meerut pillars, but those were brought here by Firoz Shah Tughlaq in 1356; Bahapur is the only Ashokan inscription standing where Ashoka's officers put it.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; ASI

location.summary: Bairat (Viratnagar), Jaipur district, Rajasthan, in a valley of the Aravallis on the route from the doab to Gujarat - the Matsya country.

periodLevel.summary: Two Minor Rock Edicts, Brahmi script, Prakrit language, c. 258-257 BCE. One is cut on a boulder at the site; the other, the Bhabru or Calcutta-Bairat edict, was removed by Cunningham in 1871 and is now in the Indian Museum, Kolkata.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The Bhabru edict is the only Ashokan inscription that cites Buddhist scripture by name - the strongest evidence for his personal Buddhism.
points: It is addressed to the Sangha of Magadha, opens with Ashoka's salutation and his declaration of reverence and faith in the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha, and then recommends seven passages of scripture that monks, nuns and lay followers should hear and reflect on repeatedly.

That list separates the private Buddhist from the public ruler: in the Major Rock Edicts Ashoka preaches a non-sectarian dhamma of tolerance and social duty and never names a Buddhist text. The Bhabru edict is the counter-evidence, and the two together are the whole debate over whether Ashoka's dhamma was Buddhism.

The site also holds a Mauryan circular brick-and-timber chaitya on Bijak-ki-Pahari, the earliest free-standing structural Buddhist shrine in India, and a monastery - so the edict sits beside a Buddhist establishment Ashoka's period built.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; Thapar, *Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas*

location.summary: Three rock sites within a few kilometres of one another at Brahmagiri, Jatinga-Rameshwara and Siddapura, Chitradurga district, Karnataka, in the granite country between the Tungabhadra and the Pennar.

periodLevel.summary: Minor Rock Edicts I and II, Brahmi script, Prakrit language, c. 258-257 BCE. Brahmagiri is also a Neolithic and megalithic type site excavated by Mortimer Wheeler in 1947, whose three-period sequence became the frame for South Indian prehistory.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The southernmost limit of the Mauryan empire on the ground, and the clearest statement of how a Mauryan province was actually run.
points: The edicts are issued in the name of the aryaputra - the prince viceroy - and the mahamatras at Suvarnagiri, and addressed to the mahamatras of Isila, which is Brahmagiri itself. This gives the chain of command whole: king, prince at the provincial capital, mahamatras at the district town.

The scribe Chapada signs the Brahmagiri edict in Kharoshthi characters at the end of a Brahmi text - a north-western clerk working in the far south, and incidental proof of how the Mauryan bureaucracy moved men across the subcontinent.

Minor Rock Edict II sets out dhamma in practical terms: obedience to parents and elders, respect for teachers, kindness to living creatures and to servants - the social morality Ashoka actually preached.

The southern edict sites stop here. Below them lie the Cholas, Pandyas, Cheras and Satiyaputas, named in Major Rock Edicts II and XIII as neighbours rather than subjects - so the map, not the text, fixes the empire's edge.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; Wheeler, *Ancient India* 4 (1947-48)

exam.modelAnswer30: Three rock sites within a few kilometres of one another at Brahmagiri. C. 258-257 BCE. The southernmost limit of the Mauryan empire on the ground, and the clearest statement of how a Mauryan province was actually run.

location.summary: Two Ashokan pillars in Delhi: the Delhi-Topra pillar at Firoz Shah Kotla, brought from Topra in Yamunanagar district, Haryana, and the Delhi-Meerut pillar on the northern Ridge, brought from Meerut. Both were moved by Firoz Shah Tughlaq in 1356.

periodLevel.summary: Polished Chunar sandstone shafts of c. 243-242 BCE carrying Pillar Edicts in Brahmi and Prakrit, cut in Ashoka's twenty-sixth and twenty-seventh regnal years. Topra carries Pillar Edicts I-VII; Meerut carries I-VI.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Topra is the only pillar in India to carry Pillar Edict VII - Ashoka's own review of his reign, and the last thing he is known to have inscribed.
points: Pillar Edict VII looks back over what he had done for dhamma: banyan trees and mango groves planted along the roads, wells dug and rest houses built at intervals, the appointment of dhamma-mahamatras, and his conclusion that dhamma grows better by persuasion than by regulation. It is the only edict in which he assesses his own policy.

The transport is itself a documented event. Shams-i-Siraj Afif's *Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi* describes the pillars being wrapped in silk cotton, lowered onto a carriage of forty-two wheels, hauled by thousands of men and floated down the Yamuna on boats - the earliest detailed account of moving an ancient monument in India. Firoz Shah took them for their beauty; nobody could then read Brahmi.
The script was deciphered by James Prinsep in 1837, working from these and the Sanchi and Girnar texts, which is the moment Ashoka re-entered Indian history after sixteen centuries.

Delhi also holds the Bahapur Minor Rock Edict, the only Ashokan inscription in the city still on its original rock, and is later the seat of the Chishti saints Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki, Nizamuddin Auliya and Nasiruddin Chirag Dehlavi.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7; Shams-i-Siraj Afif, *Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi*; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*

location.summary: A granite boulder beside the road from Junagadh to the Girnar hills, Gujarat, in Saurashtra - on the route from the Kathiawar ports inland to Malwa.

periodLevel.summary: All fourteen Major Rock Edicts, Brahmi script, Prakrit language, cut in Ashoka's twelfth to fourteenth regnal years, c. 257-256 BCE. Noticed by James Tod in 1822. Two later inscriptions were added to the same rock: Rudradaman I's, c. 150 CE, and Skandagupta's, 455-458 CE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The only surface in India carrying Mauryan, Shaka-Kshatrapa and Gupta records together - seven centuries of imperial history on one stone.
points: The fourteen Major Rock Edicts here are the fullest and best-preserved set: Edict I bans animal sacrifice and the samajas; II provides medical care for humans and animals, and wells and roadside trees, in his realm and in the Chola, Pandya, Satiyaputa, Keralaputa and Tamraparni lands; XII urges restraint in praising one's own sect; XIII is the Kalinga edict, with its remorse over the 150,000 deported, 100,000 killed and many more dead, and the claim of dhamma-vijaya over the five Yona kings.

Rudradaman's inscription of c. 150 CE is the first long record in Sanskrit and in ornate kavya prose - the moment Sanskrit displaces Prakrit as the language of public inscription. It records that the Sudarshana reservoir was built by Pushyagupta, provincial governor of Chandragupta Maurya, and fitted with conduits by the Yavana Tushaspha under Ashoka, and that Rudradaman repaired it from his own treasury without a benevolence (pranaya) or forced labour (vishti) on his subjects.

Skandagupta's record of 455-458 CE reports the dam's breach and repair again - three dynasties maintaining one irrigation work, the best single case study of continuity in public works in ancient India.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7-9; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; *Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum* II

location.summary: Gujarra, Datia district, Madhya Pradesh, in the Bundelkhand uplands - on the old route from Pataliputra through Ujjayini to Bharuch (Broach) on the Gujarat coast.

periodLevel.summary: Minor Rock Edict I, Brahmi script, Prakrit language, c. 258-257 BCE. Discovered in 1953.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the handful of inscriptions that give Ashoka's personal name - without which the edicts would belong to an anonymous "Devanampiya Piyadasi".
points: The Gujarra text reads "Devanampiya Piyadasi Asoka raja", combining the titles with the name. Only five sites do this - Gujarra, Maski, Nittur, Udegolam and Panguraria (Saru Maru) - and the first of them, Maski, found in 1915, is what finally allowed the Piyadasi of the edicts to be identified with the Ashoka of the Buddhist chronicles.

Before that identification the edicts were an orphan corpus; after it, the chronicles of Sri Lanka and the Puranic king lists could be checked against contemporary epigraphy. This is the standard example in historiography answers of inscriptions correcting and anchoring literary tradition.
Its position on the Pataliputra-Bharuch road again shows the Minor Rock Edicts following routes rather than marking boundaries.

location.summary: Jaugada, Ganjam district, Odisha, on the Rishikulya river inside the earthen ramparts of an early historic fort - the southern administrative centre of conquered Kalinga.

periodLevel.summary: Major Rock Edicts 1-10 and 14, plus the two Separate Kalinga Edicts, Brahmi script, Prakrit language, c. 257-256 BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of only two sites - with Dhauli - where Ashoka replaced the standard edicts with a text written specially for a conquered people.
points: Rock Edicts 11, 12 and 13 are omitted here and at Dhauli. Edict 13 is the one describing the Kalinga war and Ashoka's remorse: he did not put an account of the conquest in front of the conquered. That deliberate omission is the single most revealing editorial decision in the corpus.

In their place stand the two Separate Edicts. The first tells the mahamatras that "all men are my children", that they must avoid harshness, envy and arbitrary imprisonment, and orders a quinquennial inspection tour to check their conduct. The second addresses the unsubdued forest peoples of the frontier, promising them that the king wishes them no harm and will forgive what can be forgiven.
Together they are the clearest evidence of Mauryan provincial administration under supervision - and of Ashoka's awareness that his own officers were the problem to be managed.
The edicts are addressed to the mahamatras at Samapa, the local capital, as Dhauli's are to those at Tosali.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; Thapar, *Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas*

location.summary: Kalsi, Dehradun district, Uttarakhand, on a quartzite boulder near the confluence of the Yamuna and the Tons at the foot of the Siwaliks - where the Doab route enters the hills.

periodLevel.summary: All fourteen Major Rock Edicts, Brahmi script, Prakrit language, c. 257-256 BCE. Discovered by John Forrest in 1860.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The northernmost Major Rock Edict site in India, and the one that carries a carved symbol alongside the text.
points: An elephant is carved beside the inscription with the word "gajatame" - the supreme elephant - cut beneath it. The elephant is a standard symbol of the Buddha, referring to Maya's dream, and this is a rare instance of Ashoka using an image rather than words to make a point.

The Major Rock Edicts occur at only about nine places, all of them peripheral - Kalsi, Girnar, Sopara, Dhauli, Jaugada, Yerragudi, Sannati, Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra. Their distribution outlines the empire, while the Minor Rock Edicts fill its interior along the roads.
Kalsi commands the route into the hills towards the Tibetan plateau, and is usually cited as the marker of the empire's northern reach in the central Himalaya.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; ASI

location.summary: Old Kandahar (Shar-i-Kuna), southern Afghanistan, in the Arghandab valley on the road from the Iranian plateau to the Indus - probably Alexandria in Arachosia, and the western limit of the empire.

periodLevel.summary: Three groups of texts. The Greek-Aramaic bilingual rock inscription, found in 1958, is dated "ten years after the consecration", c. 258 BCE. A Greek inscription found in 1963 carries a translation of parts of Major Rock Edicts 12 and 13. Further Aramaic inscriptions come from the same region.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The only Ashokan texts in Greek - proof that the empire administered in the languages of its subjects, not only its own.
points: The bilingual calls the king "Piodasses" and announces that from the tenth year he made men pious, that all living things prosper, that he abstains from killing, and that hunters and fishermen have ceased - the Greek rendering translating dhamma as eusebeia, piety, a Greek religious concept.
That translation choice is the evidence usually cited for dhamma being a broad ethical idea capable of being carried across cultures, rather than a sectarian Buddhist doctrine.

Aramaic was the Achaemenid chancery language and Greek the language of the Seleucid successor population; their use here shows a Mauryan administration inheriting and working through Persian and Hellenistic bureaucratic practice in the north-west.

Major Rock Edict XIII names five Hellenistic kings - Antiochus II, Ptolemy II, Antigonus, Magas and Alexander - as recipients of Ashoka's dhamma missions, and this is the region through which those embassies would have passed.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; Thapar, *Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas*

location.summary: Laghman province, eastern Afghanistan, on the Alishang and Alingar rivers north of Jalalabad - on the road linking Bactria and the Kabul valley to the Khyber and the Indus.

periodLevel.summary: Aramaic inscriptions of Ashoka's period, c. 260-250 BCE, found in 1969-70 (Laghman I) and 1973 (Laghman II), cut on rock beside the route.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The furthest north-west that Mauryan authority is attested in writing, and the only Ashokan texts that read like road markers.
points: The Laghman inscriptions are in Aramaic, the Achaemenid administrative language still in use across the region a century after Persian rule ended - so Mauryan officials here worked in the script and language their predecessors had left behind.

Laghman I records a distance measured in a local unit along the road and mentions Tadmor (Palmyra), an extraordinary reference linking a Mauryan wayside inscription to the caravan cities of the Syrian desert.
Their content is thin on dhamma and heavy on administration, which supports reading the north-western texts as the work of a provincial chancery rather than direct royal proclamations.
Note for the maps: Lampaka is the Sanskrit name for Laghman, so this site and the Lampaka entry are the same place.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; Thapar, *Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas*

location.summary: Lampaka - the Sanskrit name for the Laghman region of eastern Afghanistan, on the Alishang and Alingar rivers north of Jalalabad, between the Kabul valley and the Khyber.

periodLevel.summary: Aramaic inscriptions of c. 260-250 BCE, the same group recorded under Laghman; found on rock faces beside the highway in 1969-70 and 1973.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Fixes the north-western administrative frontier of the Maurya empire, in the province the Sanskrit sources call Lampaka.
points: Lampaka appears in the Puranas and in Sanskrit geographical literature as a country of the far north-west, and Xuanzang later describes it as Lan-po; the Aramaic inscriptions show it inside Mauryan control in the 3rd century BCE.

This is the tract Chandragupta obtained from Seleucus Nikator in the treaty of c. 303 BCE, along with Gandhara, Arachosia and Gedrosia, in exchange for 500 elephants - the north-western inscriptions are the physical evidence that the cession was real and held.
Aramaic here, Greek and Aramaic at Kandahar, Kharoshthi at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra, Brahmi everywhere else: the north-west is where the empire's multilingual character is visible.
Note for the maps: this entry and the Laghman Minor Rock Edict entry refer to the same site under two names, and should be merged or plotted as one dot.

location.summary: Two pillars about 25 km apart in West Champaran district, Bihar - Lauriya Nandangarh and Lauriya Araraj - standing in the plain north of the Gandak on the royal road from Pataliputra to Nepal.

periodLevel.summary: Polished Chunar sandstone shafts carrying Pillar Edicts I-VI, Brahmi script, Prakrit language, cut in Ashoka's twenty-sixth and twenty-seventh regnal years, c. 243-242 BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The best-preserved Ashokan pillar still standing on its original site, and the model for what a complete pillar looked like.
points: The Lauriya Nandangarh shaft is a single piece of sandstone about 10 m high, tapering, with the celebrated Mauryan polish, carrying a bell-shaped lotus capital, a circular abacus with a row of geese (hamsa), and a seated lion on top - the only pillar where shaft, capital and animal all survive in place.

Nandangarh beside it is a large brick stupa mound, excavated by Theodor Bloch and N. G. Majumdar, with a series of earthen burial mounds nearby - so the pillar stands in a monumental landscape, not alone.
The Lauriya Araraj pillar carries the same six edicts but has lost its capital.

Pillar Edicts I-VI set out the working of dhamma: Ashoka's concern for the next world, the appointment of officers, the list of animals protected from slaughter, the three-day respite granted to condemned prisoners, and his instruction that officials review and instruct the people every five years.

location.summary: The pillar standing in the sacred garden at Lumbini, Rupandehi district, Nepal, beside the Mayadevi temple - the Rummindei pillar.

periodLevel.summary: Erected in Ashoka's twentieth regnal year, c. 249 BCE, in Brahmi and Prakrit, to mark his pilgrimage to the Buddha's birthplace. Found by A. Fuhrer and Khadga Shumsher Rana in 1896.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The only Ashokan inscription that records a specific tax concession - the single most concrete piece of evidence for Mauryan land revenue.
points: The text states that Ashoka came in person, worshipped because "here the Buddha Sakyamuni was born", had a stone wall and a stone pillar set up, and made the village of Lumbini free of bali and liable to pay only an eighth share (atha-bhagiya) of the produce as bhaga.

Bali and bhaga are the two terms the whole discussion of Mauryan revenue rests on. Bhaga is the king's share of the produce, the normal rate being a sixth, reduced here to an eighth. Bali is a separate levy, usually read as a tax tied to the area of land cultivated, and it is remitted outright.

Because a religious site is being rewarded with a fiscal privilege, the inscription is also the earliest evidence in India of tax exemption used as an instrument of royal patronage - the practice that later becomes the agrahara and the land grant.
Note for the maps: this entry and the Rummindei entry describe the same pillar and should be merged or plotted as one dot.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*

exam.modelAnswer30: The pillar standing in the sacred garden at Lumbini, Rupandehi district, Nepal. C. 249 BCE. The only Ashokan inscription that records a specific tax concession, the single most concrete piece of evidence for Mauryan land revenue.

location.summary: Mansehra, Hazara division, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, on three large boulders beside the road through the Pakhli plain - on the route from Kashmir and the upper Indus down to Taxila.

periodLevel.summary: All fourteen Major Rock Edicts, cut in the Kharoshthi script in Prakrit, c. 257-256 BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: With Shahbazgarhi, one of only two Ashokan sites written in Kharoshthi - the evidence that Mauryan administration adapted to the script its subjects already used.
points: Kharoshthi runs right to left and derives from Aramaic, the chancery script of the Achaemenid empire, which held Gandhara until Alexander. Its use here is direct evidence of a century and a half of Persian administrative habit surviving under the Mauryas.

Brahmi, by contrast, runs left to right and is used everywhere else in the empire. That one emperor issued the same fourteen edicts in two scripts, at the same time, is the standard illustration of Mauryan administrative pragmatism.
The edicts are cut on three separate boulders rather than one face, the text distributed across them - a practical response to the rock available.
Mansehra sat on a live trade route and its edicts mark the empire's north-western frontier zone, along with Shahbazgarhi, Kandahar and Laghman.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; Thapar, *Early India*

location.summary: Nittur and Udegolam, two rock sites a few kilometres apart in Bellary district, Karnataka, in the granite country north of the Tungabhadra - close to the Raichur doab gold belt.

periodLevel.summary: Minor Rock Edicts I and II, Brahmi script, Prakrit language, c. 258-257 BCE. Discovered in 1977-78, the last major addition to the Ashokan corpus.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Two of the five inscriptions that name Ashoka outright, and a reminder that the corpus is still growing.
points: Both texts read "Devanampiya Asoka", giving the personal name beside the title. With Maski, Gujarra and Panguraria these are the only places that do so, and they are the basis on which the Piyadasi of the edicts is identified with the Ashoka of the Buddhist tradition.

Minor Rock Edict I is the personal statement about his becoming a lay follower and his zeal; Minor Rock Edict II gives dhamma its practical content - obedience to mother and father, respect for elders and teachers, compassion to living beings, truthfulness.

The Minor Rock Edicts are earlier than the Major Rock Edicts, and their dense concentration in northern Karnataka and the Raichur-Kurnool tract - Nittur, Udegolam, Maski, Palkigundu, Gavimath, Brahmagiri, Siddapura, Jatinga-Rameshwara, Rajula-Mandagiri, Yerragudi - is usually explained by the gold and other mineral resources of the region, which gave the Mauryas a reason to hold it.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; ASI, *Epigraphia Indica*

location.summary: Palkigundu and Gavimath, two rock sites near Koppal in Koppal district, Karnataka, among granite hills north of the Tungabhadra - Palkigundu on a hilltop boulder, Gavimath on a low rock beside the plain.

periodLevel.summary: Minor Rock Edict I, Brahmi script, Prakrit language, c. 258-257 BCE. Recorded in the late 19th century and edited by Buhler.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Part of the dense southern cluster of Minor Rock Edicts, and a pair that shows how the same text was cut twice within sight of each other.
points: Minor Rock Edict I preaches dhamma and the duty of exerting oneself in it. Ashoka states how long he has been an upasaka, admits he was not zealous at first, and declares that through his effort even the humble can attain heaven - the levelling claim that is the most quoted line of the edict.

He also orders that the proclamation be carried far, engraved on rock where rock is available, and that officers tour the countryside to spread it - the edicts themselves describe the mechanism of their own distribution, and the southern cluster is that instruction carried out.
Koppal is ancient Kopana, a Jaina centre of note in later centuries, and the tract belongs to the mineral-rich Raichur doab that drew Mauryan attention southward.

location.summary: Panguraria, at the foot of the Saru Maru hills in Sehore district, Madhya Pradesh, on the north bank of the Narmada in the Vindhyas - on the road from Vidisha towards Ujjayini.

periodLevel.summary: Two inscriptions in Brahmi and Prakrit. One is Minor Rock Edict I, c. 258-257 BCE; the second is a separate royal record cut in a rock shelter, referring to Ashoka's visit here while he was still a kumara, before his accession.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The only Ashokan inscription that looks back to the emperor's life before he was emperor.
points: The second text records that the king, "when he was a prince, came to this place on a pleasure tour" from Ujjayini - where Ashoka served as viceroy for Bindusara. No other edict mentions his pre-accession career, which is otherwise known only from the Buddhist chronicles.
The Minor Rock Edict here names him as Asoka, one of the five sites in the whole corpus to give the personal name, alongside Maski, Gujarra, Nittur and Udegolam.

Natural caves and rock shelters around the site were used by Buddhist monks, and stupas stand nearby; some shelters carry prehistoric paintings, so the hill has a Mesolithic and a Mauryan layer together.
Note for the maps: Panguraria and Saru Maru are the same site under two names, and the two entries should be merged or plotted as one dot.

location.summary: Pataliputra, modern Patna, Bihar, on the strip between the Ganga and the Son - the excavated mounds are Kumrahar, Bulandi Bagh and Agam Kuan.

periodLevel.summary: Founded as a fort by the Magadhan king Udayin c. 460 BCE and made the capital in place of Rajagriha. Imperial capital of the Nandas and Mauryas, c. 345-185 BCE, then of the Shungas and the Guptas. Excavated by D. B. Spooner (1912-15, funded by the Tatas), L. A. Waddell, and A. S. Altekar and S. Mishra (1951-55).

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The capital of the first Indian empire - and the one place where Megasthenes' description can be checked against the ground.
points: At Bulandi Bagh, a double row of enormous upright sal-wood beams was found, the remains of the wooden city wall. Megasthenes, as quoted by Arrian and Strabo, described Palibothra as 9.5 miles long and 1.75 miles wide, enclosed by a timber palisade with 570 towers and 64 gates, and fronted by a moat - the excavated palisade is that wall, and is the most direct confirmation of a Greek account of India anywhere.

At Kumrahar, an eighty-pillar hall was found: rows of monolithic sandstone pillars with the Mauryan polish, set on a wooden platform, with a wooden approach channel. It is generally identified as a Mauryan assembly or audience hall, the only Mauryan palace structure excavated.

Ashoka replaced the timber city with stone, according to both the excavated evidence and Faxian, who saw the palace still standing in the 5th century CE and thought it the work of spirits rather than men.

The Third Buddhist Council met here c. 250 BCE under Moggaliputta Tissa, in Ashoka's seventeenth regnal year; it compiled the Kathavatthu and dispatched the dhamma missions, including Mahendra's to Sri Lanka. Sher Shah Suri later rebuilt the city as Patna.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 6-7; Megasthenes via Arrian and Strabo; ASI, Kumrahar excavation reports

location.summary: Rajula-Mandagiri, near Pattikonda in Kurnool district, Andhra Pradesh, on a granite hill in the Rayalaseema uplands between the Tungabhadra and the Krishna.

periodLevel.summary: Minor Rock Edicts I and II, Brahmi script, Prakrit language, c. 258-257 BCE. Discovered in 1953.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the southern pair of sites - with Yerragudi, 40 km away - that carries both Minor Rock Edicts together.
points: Minor Rock Edict II is the more important of the two for the content of dhamma. It is cast as an instruction relayed through officials and lists the duties: obedience to mother and father, respect for elders, kindness to living creatures, truthfulness, and proper treatment of teachers, relatives, slaves and servants.

Its phrasing is close to the household duties of the Sigalovada Sutta, and it is the text that best supports reading dhamma as a civic and social ethic drawn from a shared moral vocabulary rather than a Buddhist creed - the central question in any Ashoka answer.
The concentration of Minor Rock Edicts across Kurnool, Bellary, Raichur, Koppal and Chitradurga marks the Mauryan south as a governed province, not a nominal claim, run from Suvarnagiri.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; ASI, *Epigraphia Indica*

location.summary: Rampurva, West Champaran district, Bihar, near the Nepal border in the swampy plain north of the Gandak - on the royal road running from Pataliputra towards the Himalayan foothills.

periodLevel.summary: Two polished Chunar sandstone pillars, c. 243-242 BCE. One carries Pillar Edicts I-VI in Brahmi and Prakrit and is crowned by a lion; the second is uninscribed and carries a bull capital. Excavated by A. C. L. Carlleyle in 1877 and Daya Ram Sahni in 1907-08.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The finest surviving Mauryan animal capital, and the clearest evidence of Achaemenid and Hellenistic motifs in Mauryan art.
points: The Rampurva bull, carved in the round in sandstone with the characteristic Mauryan polish, stands on an abacus decorated with a honeysuckle and palmette frieze - motifs of Greek and West Asian origin, not Indian - above a bell-shaped inverted lotus derived from Achaemenid Persepolis. It is now at Rashtrapati Bhavan, New Delhi.

That borrowed ornament is the heart of the long argument over Mauryan court art: whether the polish, the free-standing monolithic column and the animal capital were learnt from Persia after the fall of Achaemenid Iran, or developed from an Indian wooden tradition. The honeysuckle frieze is the strongest single piece of evidence for the foreign side.
The second pillar's lion is squatter and cruder than the Sarnath lions, which is used to argue a development within Mauryan sculpture rather than a single imported style.
The Champaran pillars - Rampurva, Lauriya Nandangarh, Lauriya Araraj - stand in a line and are usually read as marking a processional or pilgrimage route towards Lumbini and the Buddha's country.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7; Niharranjan Ray, *Maurya and Post-Maurya Art*; ASI

location.summary: Rupnath, Katni district, Madhya Pradesh, at the foot of the Kaimur range near a spring and waterfall below the Vindhyan scarp - on the route from the Ganga plain to the Narmada valley and the Deccan.

periodLevel.summary: Minor Rock Edict I, Brahmi script, Prakrit language, c. 258-257 BCE. Reported by Captain James Franklin in 1834.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the three texts James Prinsep worked on when he deciphered Brahmi - the site belongs to the history of Indology as much as to Ashoka's.
points: Prinsep's decipherment of Brahmi in 1837, using Rupnath, Sahasram, Bairat and the Delhi and Girnar texts, recovered a king called Devanampiya Piyadasi whose identity was then unknown. Only the Maski edict of 1915 supplied the name Ashoka.

The edict is addressed to the local sangha and records Ashoka's declaration of faith in the Buddha and the Dhamma, his admission that he was at first not zealous, and his instruction that the message be spread widely and cut on rock wherever rock is found.

It also carries the line that through exertion even the lowly can reach heaven, and closes with a dating formula counted in nights spent on tour - the sort of detail that lets the edicts be sequenced against one another.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; Thapar, *Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas*

location.summary: Sanchi, Raisen district, Madhya Pradesh, on a hill above the plain 10 km from Vidisha - beside the route from the Ganga plain to Ujjayini and the western ports.

periodLevel.summary: Stupa 1 was commissioned by Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE as a brick mound; the Shungas encased it in stone and doubled its size in the 2nd century BCE, adding the balustrade and stairway; the four carved toranas were added under the Satavahanas, c. 1st century BCE. An Ashokan pillar with a Schism Edict stands beside it, and a Gupta-period temple (Temple 17) and inscription belong to the 5th century CE. Rediscovered in 1818; restored by John Marshall, 1912-19. UNESCO World Heritage, 1989.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The best-preserved and most complete early Buddhist stupa in India, and the standard case study of how a Mauryan mound became a Satavahana picture gallery.
points: The Ashokan pillar beside the southern gateway is of finely polished sandstone with a four-lion capital - the same design as Sarnath, here weathered - and carries the Schism Edict, warning that a monk or nun who divides the Sangha is to be expelled in white robes. A Gupta inscription was later added to the same shaft.

The four gateways are the great achievement: architraves and uprights covered with Jataka scenes, the Buddha's life, the war over the relics, and Ashoka's own visit to the bodhi tree. The Buddha is still shown aniconically here - by the wheel, the tree, the empty throne, the footprints - so Sanchi is the fullest surviving statement of the aniconic phase.

An inscription on the southern gateway records that it was the work of the ivory carvers of Vidisha, and the several hundred short donative records on the railing name monks, nuns, artisans and villagers - collective, non-royal funding, which is the point to make about early Buddhist patronage.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7-8; John Marshall, *A Guide to Sanchi*; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*

location.summary: Sannati, Chitapur taluk, Kalaburagi (Gulbarga) district, Karnataka, on the left bank of the Bhima - the northernmost Deccan plain, with the Kanganahalli stupa immediately adjacent.

periodLevel.summary: Major Rock Edicts 12 and 14 and both Separate Kalinga Edicts, Brahmi script, Prakrit language, c. 257-256 BCE. Found in 1986 when a slab serving as the pedestal of the image in the Chandralamba temple was lifted and proved to be inscribed; published from 1989.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The only place outside Kalinga where the two Separate Edicts have been found - a discovery that overturned what the Separate Edicts were thought to be.
points: They had been read as a special message written for the Kalingans after the war, and their presence at Dhauli and Jaugada alone supported that. Sannati shows the same text in the Deccan, so they are better understood as a standing instruction to mahamatras in any newly acquired or frontier province - general administrative policy, not a one-off act of contrition.

Major Rock Edict 12 is the tolerance edict: honour other sects, restrain praise of your own, for whoever extols his own sect while disparaging others injures his own sect - the text always quoted on Ashoka's religious policy.

The find also extends the Major Rock Edict distribution into the Deccan interior, and it came from a temple pedestal, not an excavation, which is the standard example of how much of the corpus surfaces by accident.
The Kanganahalli stupa beside it yielded the "Ranyo Ashoka" relief portrait, so the two sites together give both Ashoka's words and his only known likeness.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7; K. V. Ramesh, *Epigraphia Indica*; ASI

location.summary: Shahbazgarhi, Mardan district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, on two boulders at the foot of a hill in the Peshawar valley - in the heart of Gandhara, near Takht-i-Bahi, on the road from the Khyber to the Indus.

periodLevel.summary: All fourteen Major Rock Edicts, cut in the Kharoshthi script in Prakrit, c. 257-256 BCE - the largest and best-preserved Kharoshthi version of the edicts.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The north-western limit of the Major Rock Edicts, and the fullest evidence that the empire published in the local script.
points: The text is divided between two rocks on the hillside, the first carrying edicts 1-12 and the second 13 and 14, written right to left in Kharoshthi, a script derived from Aramaic and used only in Gandhara and the north-west.

Major Rock Edict XIII, the Kalinga edict, is best preserved in the north-western versions. It gives the casualty figures, Ashoka's remorse, his declaration that the chief conquest is conquest by dhamma, and the naming of the five Hellenistic kings - Antiochus, Ptolemy, Antigonus, Magas and Alexander - to whom he claims to have sent missions. Those names are what allow the Mauryan chronology to be fixed against Greek dates, and they are the foundation of all ancient Indian dating.
Gandhara was an Achaemenid satrapy before it was Mauryan, and the choice of script here, as at Mansehra, records that inheritance.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; Thapar, *Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas*

location.summary: The Dhauli rock, on a low hill beside the Daya river about 8 km south of Bhubaneswar, Odisha - overlooking the plain traditionally identified as the battlefield of the Kalinga war, with the fortified city of Sisupalgarh a few kilometres away.

periodLevel.summary: Major Rock Edicts 1-10 and 14, together with the two Separate Kalinga Edicts, Brahmi script, Prakrit language, c. 257-256 BCE. The elephant carved above the inscription is of the same date. The modern Shanti Stupa on the hill was built in 1972.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The earliest rock-cut sculpture in India stands above the edicts that are Ashoka's answer to the war he fought here.
points: Major Rock Edicts 11, 12 and 13 are omitted, as at Jaugada. Edict 13 is the one that narrates the Kalinga conquest and his remorse - it was not shown to the Kalingans themselves. In its place stand the two Separate Edicts addressed to the mahamatras at Tosali.

Separate Edict I contains the line "all men are my children", instructs officers against harshness, jealousy and arbitrary imprisonment, and orders an inspection tour every five years to see that they comply. Separate Edict II addresses the unconquered forest peoples of the frontier, telling them the king wishes them no harm.

The forepart of an elephant is carved out of the living rock above the text, emerging from the boulder - the earliest example of rock-cut sculpture in India, and a Buddhist symbol placed deliberately over an edict about conquest and its aftermath.
Sisupalgarh nearby, almost certainly the Tosali the edicts address, is the excavated square fortified city of the same period, with eight gateways and a grid of streets.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; Thapar, *Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas*

location.summary: Nala Sopara, Palghar district, Maharashtra, on the Konkan coast north of Mumbai - ancient Shurparaka, the Souppara of the *Periplus* and Ptolemy's Soupara, the chief port of the western Deccan.

periodLevel.summary: Fragments of Major Rock Edicts 8 and 9, Brahmi script, Prakrit language, c. 257-256 BCE. The edict 9 fragment was found in the stupa mound by Bhagwanlal Indraji in 1882 and a further fragment in 1956. The stupa itself is Mauryan in origin with later rebuilding; the port flourished from the Mauryan period through the Satavahanas and Guptas and is still named in Arab sources.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The only Major Rock Edict site on the western seaboard - the empire's window on the Arabian Sea trade.
points: Major Rock Edict 8 records that Ashoka gave up the royal pleasure tour (vihara-yatra) of hunting and replaced it with the dhamma-yatra, visiting shramanas and brahmanas, giving gifts and instructing the countryside - the single clearest statement of what changed in his practice of kingship.

Major Rock Edict 9 attacks the ceremonies performed at births, marriages and journeys, especially those performed by women, as of little fruit, and sets against them the ceremony of dhamma - proper treatment of slaves and servants, respect for elders, restraint towards living beings.
Indraji's excavation of the stupa recovered a stone coffer holding relic caskets and eight bronze images of the Buddha of a later date, confirming continuous Buddhist use.

The Sri Lankan chronicles record that Ashoka's mission to Aparanta under Dharmarakshita went to this coast, and in later centuries Sopara was the port serving Kanheri, Kalyan and the ghat caves inland.

location.summary: Suvarnagiri, the "golden mountain" - the southern provincial capital of the Maurya empire, generally identified with Kanakagiri near Maski in the Raichur-Koppal tract of Karnataka, between the Krishna and the Tungabhadra.

periodLevel.summary: A Mauryan provincial headquarters of the 3rd century BCE. It is named not by an inscription of its own but in the Minor Rock Edicts at Brahmagiri, Siddapura and Jatinga-Rameshwara, c. 258-257 BCE, which are issued from it.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The clearest evidence for the structure of Mauryan provincial government - a capital known entirely from being quoted in other people's edicts.
points: The Brahmagiri group opens with an order sent from the aryaputra and the mahamatras at Suvarnagiri to the mahamatras at Isila. Aryaputra means a prince of the blood, so the southern province was governed by a kumara of the royal house - as were Tosali in Kalinga, Ujjayini in Avanti and Taxila in the north-west, with Pataliputra as the centre. That is the whole administrative map of the empire, and it comes from this formula.

Its name and its location in the Raichur doab tie it to the gold-bearing country around the Hatti mines, which is the usual explanation for why the Mauryas pushed this far south and held it with a prince rather than an officer.

Kanakagiri is a Sanskrit calque of Suvarnagiri, which is the main argument for the identification; the site has not been excavated to confirm it, so treat the location as probable rather than settled.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; Thapar, *Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas*

location.summary: Yerragudi (Erragudi), near Gooty in Kurnool district, Andhra Pradesh, on a granite outcrop in the Rayalaseema uplands south of the Tungabhadra.

periodLevel.summary: All fourteen Major Rock Edicts, c. 257-256 BCE, and Minor Rock Edicts I and II, c. 258-257 BCE - all in Brahmi script and Prakrit.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The only site in the empire carrying both the Major and the Minor Rock Edicts - which is what lets the two series be dated relative to each other.
points: Because both sets appear on one rock, their sequence can be established directly: the Minor Rock Edicts are the earlier, and the Major Rock Edicts follow in the twelfth to fourteenth regnal years. Every relative dating of the Ashokan corpus rests ultimately on sites like this.

The engraving is famously irregular. The lines run in varying directions, some right to left, the text crowded and fitted to the rock's surface rather than to a ruled plan - taken as evidence of a scribe working from dictation or from a Kharoshthi-trained hand unused to Brahmi, and a reminder that the edicts were cut by ordinary craftsmen, not a uniform imperial workshop.
Ashoka is named here as Piyadasi, with the title Devanampiya, not by his personal name.
Yerragudi is the southernmost Major Rock Edict site, and with Rajula-Mandagiri 40 km away it anchors the Andhra end of the southern edict cluster.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; ASI, *Epigraphia Indica*

location.summary: Aihole (ancient Ayyavole), Bagalkot district, Karnataka, on the left bank of the Malaprabha, with Badami and Pattadakal within 35 km - the first seat of the Early Chalukyas.

periodLevel.summary: Temple building spans c. 450-750 CE, the site's floruit under the Early Chalukyas of Badami. The Aihole Prashasti, cut on the east wall of the Meguti temple, was composed by Ravikirti, court poet of Pulakesin II, and dated Shaka 556 = 634 CE, in Sanskrit in old Kannada script.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The cradle of Indian temple architecture - the workshop in which Nagara and Dravida forms were tried out - carrying a dated inscription that fixes Deccan chronology.
points: The prashasti records Pulakesin II's victories over the Kadambas, Gangas, Malavas and Gurjaras, his capture of Vatapi, and his defeat of Harshavardhana on the Narmada, with Ravikirti's pun that Harsha's *harsha*, his joy, melted away in fear. It is the principal source for the one check Harsha's empire received.
Its double date, in the Shaka and Kali eras, is a fixed point of early Deccan dating; Ravikirti's comparison of himself to Kalidasa and Bharavi is the earliest datable reference to Kalidasa anywhere.

The Meguti temple, 634 CE, is the earliest dated structural temple in Karnataka. The Durga temple - named from *durga*, a fort, not the goddess - is apsidal with an ambulatory, a Nagara shikhara over a Dravida-derived mandapa; the flat-roofed Lad Khan derives from timber hall construction.
Aihole was home to the Ayyavole Five Hundred, a great south Indian merchant guild, making it a trade centre as well as a capital.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; ASI

location.summary: Banskhera, Shahjahanpur district, Uttar Pradesh, in the Rohilkhand plain between the Ganga and the Gomti, near the Garra.

periodLevel.summary: A copper-plate grant of Harshavardhana dated in his regnal year 22, c. 628 CE - the middle of his reign, 606-647 CE - in Sanskrit in the northern Brahmi of the day, and carrying the king's signature in his own hand.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of only two known charters of Harsha, and the rarest kind of document in Indian history - a royal autograph.
points: The plate records the grant of a village to two brahmanas, Bhatta Vatasvamin and Bhatta Shivadevasvamin, with its revenues and the usual exemptions. That makes it a primary document for the brahmadeya and for the land-grant economy whose spread is central to the debate over early Indian feudalism.

It gives the Pushyabhuti genealogy - Naravardhana, Rajyavardhana I, Adityavardhana, Prabhakaravardhana, Rajyavardhana II and Harsha - and records Rajyavardhana's victory over the ruler of Malava, which independently confirms and dates what Bana narrates in the *Harshacharita*. Epigraphy checking a court biography is exactly the use examiners want to see.
The charter closes with the words *sva-hasto mama*, "this is my own hand", followed by Harsha's signature, written by the king himself rather than by a scribe.
It is read alongside the Madhuban copper plate of the same reign, which records a comparable grant and repeats the genealogy.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; *Epigraphia Indica* IV

location.summary: Bhitari, Saidpur tehsil, Ghazipur district, Uttar Pradesh, in the tract between the Ganga and the Gomti east of Varanasi.

periodLevel.summary: A red sandstone pillar carrying a Sanskrit inscription of Skandagupta in Gupta Brahmi, c. 455-467 CE - the closing phase of Gupta power. A brick temple of cruciform plan with a curvilinear shikhara stands at the site, which also yielded a sealing of Kumaragupta; excavated by the ASI.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The record of the two crises that broke the Gupta empire - the Pushyamitra war and the first Huna invasion.
points: It gives the Gupta genealogy from Gupta and Ghatotkacha through Chandragupta I, Samudragupta, Chandragupta II and Kumaragupta to Skandagupta, and is a standard source for the dynastic sequence.

Skandagupta is said to have restored his family's fallen fortunes by defeating the Pushyamitras, and to have made the earth shake when he met the Hunas - the earliest Indian reference to a Huna conflict, a generation before they broke through under Toramana and Mihirakula. The verse describing how he then passed a night sleeping on the bare earth is the detail always quoted to show how close-run the defence was, and the evidence used to argue that Gupta decline began in his reign rather than after it.

It closes by recording his installation of a Vishnu image and the endowment of a village for its upkeep. Read it with Skandagupta's Junagadh inscription of 455-458 CE on the repair of the Sudarshana dam: the two give the military and administrative faces of one reign.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 9; J. F. Fleet, *Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum* III; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*

location.summary: Chandragiri, the smaller of the two hills at Shravanabelagola, Hassan district, Karnataka, in the Hemavati basin; Vindhyagiri, with the colossal Bahubali (Gommateshvara), stands opposite across the tank.

periodLevel.summary: More than five hundred inscriptions on Chandragiri alone, from about the 6th century CE to modern times - Ganga, Rashtrakuta, Hoysala and Vijayanagara - with the hill's floruit in the Western Ganga period, c. 9th-11th centuries. The Bhadrabahu and Chandragupta record belongs to an inscription of c. 600 CE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The largest single body of Jaina inscriptions in India, and the epigraphic basis for the Digambara account of the great schism.
points: They record that Bhadrabahu, the last shrutakevalin, foresaw a twelve-year famine in Magadha and led a migration of Jaina monks south to Karnataka; a disciple who accompanied him, identified in later tradition with Chandragupta Maurya, performed *sallekhana* - ritual fasting to death - on this hill, at the spot shown as the Bhadrabahu cave.

That migration is the standard explanation for the split between the Digambaras, who followed Bhadrabahu and kept to nudity, and the Svetambaras, who stayed in Magadha under Sthulabhadra and convened the Pataliputra council to fix the canon.

The claim that the emperor abdicated and died here as a Jaina ascetic rests on a tradition first recorded some nine centuries after the event. Present it as tradition and weigh the evidence - that is what the question tests.
The hill carries Ganga-period basadis, among them the Chandragupta basadi and the Chamundaraya basadi of c. 982 CE, built by the minister who raised the Bahubali colossus opposite.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7 and 10; *Epigraphia Carnatica* II; Thapar, *Early India*
