location.summary: Halmidi, Belur taluk, Hassan district, Karnataka, in the upper Hemavati basin on the eastern flank of the Western Ghats.

periodLevel.summary: A stone pillar inscription of c. 450-500 CE, in the Kannada language and an early Kannada script, of the Kadamba period and referred to the reign of Kakusthavarman - the high point of Kadamba power at Banavasi. The original is now in the Government Museum, Bengaluru, with a replica at the site.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The earliest full-length inscription in the Kannada language - the point at which Kannada becomes a written language.
points: Sixteen lines on a small pillar record a grant of villages to a warrior named Vija Arasa (Vijaya) in recognition of valour in battle, made under Kadamba authority - a service grant, not a religious one, which makes it useful evidence for how land was used to reward military followers.

The text is Kannada but heavily Sanskritised, and it opens with a Sanskrit invocation to Vishnu, so it documents the transition itself: a regional language taking over the epigraphic function from Sanskrit and Prakrit while still borrowing their formulae.

It anchors the standard sequence of "earliest inscription in language X" - the Tamil-Brahmi cave records from about the 2nd century BCE, Halmidi for Kannada in the 5th century CE, and the later emergence of Telugu and Marathi.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 9-10; *Epigraphia Carnatica*; D. C. Sircar, *Indian Epigraphy*

location.summary: The Hathigumpha, or Elephant Cave, a natural cavern on Udayagiri hill about 6 km west of Bhubaneswar, Odisha, facing the Khandagiri caves; the Daya and the fortified city at Sisupalgarh lie close by.

periodLevel.summary: A seventeen-line inscription of Kharavela, king of Kalinga of the Mahameghavahana (Chedi) line, in Prakrit in Brahmi, generally assigned to the 1st century BCE - Kalinga's revival after Ashoka. The date is contested, argued between the 2nd century BCE and the 1st century CE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The fullest royal autobiography from ancient India - a year-by-year account of a reign, with no parallel in the period.
points: It runs through the regnal years in order: year 1, repairing the gates and ramparts of Kalinganagara after a storm; year 2, an army sent west against the Satavahana Satakarni; year 5, extending a canal first cut by a Nanda king three hundred years earlier - the only epigraphic reference to Nanda rule in Kalinga, and the basis for dating the Nandas backwards from Kharavela; years 8 and 12, attacks on Magadha, forcing its king to submit and recovering the Jina image a Nanda had carried off.

He calls himself a worshipper of all sects but a Jaina by allegiance, and records excavating caves on the Kumari hill for Jaina monks - the Udayagiri and Khandagiri groups - which makes this the principal record of royal Jaina patronage in eastern India.
It also notes the rajasuya, remission of taxes, public entertainments, and his training as a prince in writing, coinage, accountancy and law.
The stone is damaged, and both the Magadhan king's name and the date are disputed readings - a useful illustration of how much early Indian chronology rests on contested epigraphy.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; Thapar, *Early India*

location.summary: Kudumiyanmalai, Pudukkottai district, Tamil Nadu, in the dry country between the Kaveri delta and the Pandya lands; the inscription is cut on a rock face beside the Shiva cave temple.

periodLevel.summary: A musical inscription of about the 7th century CE, in Sanskrit in the Pallava-Grantha script, attributed to Mahendravarman I, r. c. 600-630 CE - though on script and style rather than a signature. The hill stayed in use under the later Cholas and Pandyas, who left inscriptions of their own.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The oldest treatise on Indian music surviving anywhere in the world - and a notation, not a description.
points: It is arranged in seven sections corresponding to seven parent scales, each giving sequences of svara syllables in groups of four - a systematic working through of permutations, in effect a teaching manual for students of music.

Its value is that it is a dated physical witness to the svara system from a period that has left no musical manuscripts at all, bridging Bharata's *Natyashastra* and the medieval treatises. Almost everything else known about early Indian music is theory transmitted through later copies; this is contemporary and fixed in stone.

The attribution to Mahendravarman I is plausible on other grounds: he wrote the farce *Mattavilasa Prahasana*, bore the titles Vichitrachitta and Chitrakarapuli, and is credited in the Mamandur inscription with work on music - a Pallava king who cultivated drama, painting and music together.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; ASI, *South Indian Inscriptions*; *Pudukkottai State Inscriptions*

location.summary: The Iron Pillar, now in the courtyard of the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque in the Qutb complex at Mehrauli, south Delhi, on the ridge west of the Yamuna. It was brought here; the inscription says it was raised on a hill called Vishnupada.

periodLevel.summary: A Sanskrit inscription in Gupta Brahmi of the 4th-5th century CE naming a king Chandra, generally identified with Chandragupta II, r. c. 375-415 CE - the height of Gupta power. The shaft stands about 7.2 m above ground and weighs over six tonnes.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The most famous metallurgical object of ancient India, and a political record of Gupta expansion into Bengal and the north-west.
points: It has not rusted through in some sixteen centuries. The accepted explanation is a thin protective film of crystalline iron hydrogen phosphate, formed because the iron was made by direct reduction, is high in phosphorus and free of sulphur, and because the pillar was forge-welded from lumps of wrought iron rather than cast - large-scale forging Europe did not match for another millennium.

The inscription records that King Chandra broke a confederacy of enemies in Vanga (Bengal), crossed the seven mouths of the Indus and conquered the Vahlikas (Bactrians). These campaigns are otherwise poorly documented, so the pillar is a primary source for the reach of Chandragupta II.
It was set up as a *dhvaja*, a standard of Vishnu, once surmounted by a Garuda image now lost - the Vaishnava affiliation of the Guptas made material.
Its removal to the Qutb complex makes it, with Firoz Shah Tughlaq's Ashokan pillars, a second case of a Sultanate ruler collecting an ancient monument as a trophy of legitimacy.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 9; J. F. Fleet, *Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum* III; R. Balasubramaniam, *Delhi Iron Pillar*

location.summary: The Naneghat pass through the Sahyadris, Junnar taluk, Pune district, Maharashtra - the route carrying goods up from the Konkan ports of Kalyan and Sopara to Junnar and Pratishthana, at the head of the Kukadi valley. The inscription is in a rock-cut cave beside the pass.

periodLevel.summary: A Brahmi inscription in Prakrit of about the 1st century BCE, issued by the Satavahana queen Naganika, widow of Satakarni I, during the minority of her son - the formative phase of Satavahana power in the western Deccan.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The founding document of Satavahana history, and the earliest attestation of the numerals from which modern digits descend.
points: It lists the Vedic sacrifices performed by the royal house - the rajasuya, two ashvamedhas, the agnyadheya and others - with the dakshina paid for each in thousands of cows, horses, elephants, villages and karshapanas: the fullest record of shrauta sacrifice by any historical Indian dynasty, and the best surviving index of what royal ritual cost.

That the same dynasty endowed the Buddhist caves at Nashik, Karle and Kanheri while performing ashvamedhas is the standard demonstration that royal patronage was not confined to one religion - the point to make on Satavahana religious policy.

Naganika issues the record in her own name as regent, among the earliest instances of a queen exercising political authority in Indian epigraphy. Portrait sculptures of the royal family stood in the cave; the figures are lost, but their labels survive, naming Simuka, Satakarni and others.

Its numerals are the earliest well-attested Brahmi forms, ancestral to the Indian and then the Arabic digits. A cistern at the pass collected tolls, tying inscription, trade route and revenue together in one place.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8; D. C. Sircar, *Select Inscriptions*; Thapar, *Early India*

location.summary: Rabatak, near Surkh Kotal in Baghlan province, northern Afghanistan - ancient Bactria, north of the Hindu Kush in the Kunduz drainage of the Oxus, the Kushana heartland.

periodLevel.summary: A stone inscription of Kanishka I from the first year of his reign, c. 127 CE, in the Bactrian language written in the Greek script - the opening of the Kushana empire's greatest phase. Discovered in 1993.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The find that settled the Kushana genealogy after a century of scholarly argument - the most consequential Indian epigraphic discovery of recent decades.
points: It states the succession outright: Kujula Kadphises his great-grandfather, Vima Taktu his grandfather, Vima Kadphises his father, and Kanishka himself. Vima Taktu was previously unknown, and his insertion resolved the long dispute over the order and number of the early Kushana kings.

Kanishka says he issued the edict in Greek and then put it into Aryan - that is, Bactrian. This is an explicit record of a deliberate change of administrative language, from the Greek inherited from the Bactrian Greeks to the local Iranian vernacular, and the clearest statement of language policy in ancient Indian epigraphy.

It records the founding of a sanctuary to the goddess Nana with a list of Iranian deities, and images of the king and his ancestors installed in it - a dynastic cult of the same kind as the devakula at Mat near Mathura.
It names cities brought under submission, among them Saketa, Kaushambi, Pataliputra and Champa, the main epigraphic evidence for how far Kushana authority reached into the Ganga plain.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8; Sims-Williams and Cribb, "A New Bactrian Inscription of Kanishka the Great"; Thapar, *Early India*

location.summary: Uthiramerur, Kanchipuram district, Tamil Nadu, in the Palar basin south-west of Kanchipuram - a planned *brahmadeya* village laid out on a grid, with temples at its cardinal points. The inscriptions are cut on the walls of the village sabha mandapa and the Vaikunta Perumal temple.

periodLevel.summary: Founded as a brahmadeya under the Pallavas in the 8th century; the earliest record is of Dantivarman, c. 795-846 CE. The two celebrated inscriptions are of the Chola Parantaka I, in his twelfth and fourteenth regnal years, c. 919 and 921 CE, in Tamil. Vijayanagara additions complete the complex.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The most detailed surviving account of village self-government in the ancient world - effectively the written constitution of the Chola village assembly, cut into a temple wall that served as the village's permanent statute book.
points: Parantaka's inscriptions set out the *kudavolai*, election by pot-ticket: the village was divided into thirty wards (kudumbus), each putting up candidates whose names went on palm-leaf tickets, into a pot, and were drawn out by a young boy - selection by lot from a pre-qualified pool, not open voting.

Qualifications are stated precisely: a quarter veli of tax-paying land, a house on one's own site, age between thirty-five and seventy, knowledge of a Veda with a bhashya. So are the disqualifications - anyone who had served on a committee in the previous three years without submitting his accounts was barred, with his close relatives. That accountability clause is the detail worth quoting.
Those elected formed the *variyams* - tottavariyam for gardens, eri-variyam for tanks, pon-variyam for gold - the machinery by which a brahmadeya ran irrigation, land and temple funds.

The second inscription amends the first, showing the scheme revised in light of practice; Dantivarman's earlier endowment shows the sabha already working under the Pallavas, so the Cholas codified an inherited institution.

The Vaikunta Perumal temple that carries the text is a modest Dravida structure dedicated to Vishnu with Lakshmi - the standard illustration of the south Indian temple as archive, treasury and civic centre rather than only a place of worship.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; K. A. Nilakanta Sastri, *The Colas*; ASI, *South Indian Inscriptions* VI

location.summary: Amarkantak, Anuppur district, Madhya Pradesh, on the Maikal plateau where the Vindhya and Satpura ranges meet - the source of both the Narmada, flowing west, and the Son, flowing east.

periodLevel.summary: A group of some sixteen stone temples of the Kalachuri period, the principal ones raised under Karnadeva, r. 1041-1073 CE, when Kalachuri power in Dahala-mandala was at its height. Nagara shikharas in local sandstone; later Maratha-period additions surround the older core.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A river-source tirtha whose sanctity rests on hydrography rather than on any dynasty - the point where the Narmada is born.
points: The Narmada kund and the temple cluster around it make this the head of the Narmada Parikrama, the circumambulation of the whole river from source to sea and back, one of the longest pilgrim circuits in India and evidence for how river geography organised sacred space.

The Karnadeva group - the Machhendranath and Pataleshwar temples among them - gives a dated set of Kalachuri Nagara temples, useful for placing the dynasty's architecture beside the better-known Chandela and Paramara work of the same century.
The Puranas treat the Narmada as older and purer than the Ganga, a claim that reflects the Deccan's own tirtha tradition asserting itself against the northern one.
Amarkantak sits at the watershed between the Ganga and the peninsular drainage, which is why it recurs in questions on the physical framing of early Indian regions.

location.summary: Badami, ancient Vatapi, Bagalkot district, Karnataka, in a red sandstone gorge above the Agastya tank, near the Malaprabha and within 25 km of Aihole and Pattadakal.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of the Early Chalukyas from c. 540 CE, founded by Pulakesin I, and held until the Rashtrakutas displaced them in 753. Four rock-cut caves were excavated in the later 6th century; Cave 3 carries an inscription of Mangalesha dated Shaka 500 = 578 CE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The dated anchor of Deccan rock-cut architecture, and the Chalukya capital that Narasimhavarman I burnt.
points: Cave 3, the largest and finest, is Vaishnava: a colossal Trivikrama, Varaha, Narasimha and a seated Vishnu on Ananta, with traces of painting on the ceiling. Mangalesha's inscription makes it the earliest firmly dated Hindu cave temple in India - the fixed point against which Ellora and Elephanta are placed.
Cave 1 is Shaiva, with an eighteen-armed Nataraja whose arms resolve into recognisable dance poses; Cave 2 is Vaishnava; Cave 4 is Jaina, so a single cliff carries three faiths.

The Pallava Narasimhavarman I captured and sacked Vatapi in 642 CE, taking the title Vatapikonda - the counter-stroke to Pulakesin II's earlier campaign, and the central episode of the long Chalukya-Pallava contest.
The Bhutanatha temples on the tank and the Malegitti Shivalaya show the same workshop moving from rock-cut to structural building.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; ASI

location.summary: Badrinath, Chamoli district, Uttarakhand, on the right bank of the Alaknanda at about 3,100 m, between the Nar and Narayana peaks below Nilkantha - upstream of the Alaknanda-Dhauliganga confluence at Vishnuprayag.

periodLevel.summary: A Vishnu shrine named in the *Vishnu* and *Skanda Puranas* and sung by the Alwars as a Divya Desam. Tradition credits Adi Shankara, 8th century, with recovering the image and founding the Jyotirmath nearby; the present structure is a Garhwal-kingdom rebuilding, repeatedly repaired after avalanche and earthquake.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the Char Dham, and the clearest surviving case of a pilgrimage network binding the subcontinent together.
points: Shankara's traditional foundation of four mathas at the cardinal points - Jyotirmath here in the north, Sringeri south, Dwarka west, Puri east - is the organisational claim of Advaita Vedanta, and Badrinath anchors its northern limb.

The head priest, the Rawal, is by custom a Nambudiri brahmana from Kerala. A Malayali priesthood serving a Himalayan shrine is the single most quotable illustration of the pan-Indian reach of the Shankara tradition.

The image is a black shaligram Vishnu in padmasana. A Buddhist origin for the site has been argued from the name and the seated posture, and is worth noting as a contested reading rather than a settled one.
The temple opens only between Akshaya Tritiya and Vijayadashami; for the winter the deity moves to Joshimath, a transhumance of worship matching the region's own seasonal movement.

content.sourcesLine: Thapar, *Early India*; Upinder Singh, ch. 10; *Skanda Purana*, Badarikashrama-mahatmya

location.summary: Bhitargaon, Kanpur Dehat district, Uttar Pradesh, in the Ganga-Yamuna doab south of Kanpur.

periodLevel.summary: Gupta period, c. early 5th century CE, and the best-preserved brick temple of that age. A square sanctum on a high plinth carries a tall stepped pyramidal shikhara; the whole is brick with terracotta panels, restored by the ASI in the 1890s after the upper shikhara was struck by lightning.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The earliest surviving north Indian temple with a shikhara, and the type-site for Gupta brick-and-terracotta building.
points: It shows the shikhara already present in the 5th century, which is why it sits between the flat-roofed Gupta shrines - Sanchi 17, Tigawa - and the fully developed Nagara temple of Deogarh. The vertical sequence Tigawa, Bhitargaon, Deogarh is the standard answer to how the Nagara temple evolved.

The sanctum roof uses a corbelled vault, and the doorway a corbelled arch, often cited as early Indian arch construction. The claim needs care: these are corbelled, not true voussoir arches, so they are evidence of experiment rather than of the true arch, which arrives with the Sultanate.

Large terracotta panels set into the outer wall carry Ganga and Yamuna, Shiva, Vishnu and Durga, with mythological scenes - the finest surviving Gupta terracotta in situ, and evidence that a brick region built its sculpture in the same material.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 9; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; ASI

location.summary: Bhojpur, Raisen district, Madhya Pradesh, on a sandstone spur above the Betwa, about 28 km south-east of Bhopal.

periodLevel.summary: Paramara period, raised under Bhoja, r. c. 1010-1055 CE, the scholar-king of Dhara. The Bhojeshwar temple was never finished: the sanctum stands, but the shikhara was never built and the construction ramp is still in place.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: An unfinished temple that documents how a medieval Indian temple was actually designed and built - evidence no completed building can give.
points: The linga is a single polished sandstone shaft about 5.5 m high on a platform of three superimposed limestone blocks, among the largest monolithic lingas in India, under a sanctum roofed by a corbelled dome carried on four massive pillars.

Architectural drawings are engraved on the flat rock surfaces around the site - ground plans, mouldings, pillar and shikhara profiles at working scale. These are the only surviving medieval Indian temple drawings, and they let the *vastu-shastra* texts be checked against actual practice.
The earthen and stone ramp used to haul blocks to the roof survives intact, showing the method of construction directly.

Bhoja also built the great Bhojpur dam nearby, an earth-and-stone bund impounding a lake of some 650 sq km, breached in the 15th century by the Malwa sultan Hoshang Shah. Temple and dam together make the Paramara case for royal engineering on a very large scale.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; ASI; Kirit Mankodi, *The Queen's Stepwell at Patan* (for the Paramara context)

location.summary: Bishnupur, Bankura district, West Bengal, on the Dwarakeswar river in the lateritic Rarh country west of the Damodar - the old Mallabhum.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of the Malla kings, whose temple building peaks in the 17th century: the Rasmancha under Bir Hambir, c. 1600; the Shyam Rai in 1643 and the Jor Bangla in 1655 under Raghunath Singha; the Madan Mohan in 1694 under Durjana Singha. Laterite and carved terracotta brick, the local stone being unavailable.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The fullest expression of the Bengal temple - a regional order built in brick, deriving its form from the thatched village hut.
points: The roof types are the classification itself: *chala* forms (do-chala, char-chala, at-chala) reproduce in brick the curved bamboo-and-thatch roof of a Bengali hut, while *ratna* forms (eka-ratna, pancha-ratna) add towers on a flat roof. The Jor Bangla is two char-chala huts joined; the Shyam Rai is pancha-ratna.

The walls carry moulded terracotta panels - Ramayana and Krishna-lila scenes, court processions, hunts, ships and Portuguese figures with muskets. Because the subjects include everyday and contemporary life, they are used as social evidence, not only religious.
Bir Hambir's conversion to Vaishnavism under Srinivasa Acharya ties the building programme directly to the Chaitanya movement's spread into western Bengal.
Bishnupur is also the seat of a distinct gharana of Hindustani music, patronised by the same court - a reminder that temple patronage came with a wider cultural programme.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* II; Upinder Singh, ch. 10; ASI

location.summary: Champaner, Panchmahal district, Gujarat, at the foot of the Pavagadh hill in the Vishwamitri basin, on the route from Gujarat into Malwa.

periodLevel.summary: A Chauhan Rajput stronghold under the Khichi rulers of Pavagadh until Mahmud Begada took it in 1484 after a twenty-month siege, renamed it Muhammadabad and made it his capital for some twenty-three years. Abandoned after the Mughal conquest of Gujarat in 1573. UNESCO World Heritage Site as Champaner-Pavagadh.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The only complete pre-Mughal Islamic city in India that was never built over, and the best surviving statement of the Gujarat Sultanate style.
points: The Jami Masjid of 1513 is the set piece: two minarets flanking the entrance, a prayer hall of some 170 pillars, carved jalis, and *chhajjas*, brackets and a fluted central dome taken directly from Hindu and Jain temple craft. Gujarat's sultans employed the same guilds who had built Modhera and Dilwara, and the style is the clearest instance anywhere of an Islamic form executed in an indigenous idiom.
The Kalika Mata temple at the summit of Pavagadh is an older Shakti shrine, and remains in worship. Hindu pilgrimage hill and Islamic capital occupy one site continuously.

The city retains its full plan - walls, gates, citadel, mosques, tombs, stepwells, granaries and an elaborate water-harvesting system on the hill slopes - so it is used as evidence for medieval urban form rather than for single monuments.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I; J. L. Mehta, *Advanced Study in the History of Medieval India* I; ASI

location.summary: Da-Parbatia, on the western edge of Tezpur, Sonitpur district, Assam, on the north bank of the Brahmaputra - ancient Kamarupa.

periodLevel.summary: A carved stone doorframe of the 6th century CE, Gupta idiom, belonging to the Varman dynasty of Kamarupa whose best-known king is Bhaskaravarman, the ally of Harshavardhana. A brick temple of the Ahom period was later built over the older plinth, which is how the doorframe survived.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The oldest surviving architectural sculpture in Assam, and the proof that the Gupta classical idiom reached the Brahmaputra valley.
points: The jambs carry Ganga and Yamuna standing on their vehicles with garlands and attendants, treated with the elongated grace and restrained modelling of mature Gupta work at Deogarh and Sarnath - not a provincial copy but the same language.

It anchors Kamarupa in mainstream early Indian art history, which matters because the north-east is usually treated as peripheral. Read it with Bhaskaravarman's Nidhanpur copper plates and Xuanzang's account of his court.
The superimposition is itself instructive: a 6th-century Varman doorway, an Ahom brick shrine of the 17th-18th century above it, one site carrying a thousand-year gap in Assam's building history.
Tezpur's other early remains - the Bamuni hills group and the Agnigarh sculptures - belong to the 9th-10th centuries and show the later Kamarupa style diverging from the Gupta model.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 9 and 10; ASI; *Nidhanpur* copper plates of Bhaskaravarman

location.summary: Darasuram, near Kumbakonam, Thanjavur district, Tamil Nadu, in the heart of the Kaveri delta - the old Chola core, a few kilometres from the river.

periodLevel.summary: The Airavatesvara temple, built by Rajaraja II, r. c. 1146-1173 CE, in the late Chola period. Note that the builder is Rajaraja II, not the Rajaraja I of Thanjavur. Granite; the vimana is only about 24 m, far smaller than the imperial temples. UNESCO World Heritage Site.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The last of the three Great Living Chola Temples, and the point at which Chola architecture turns from scale to refinement.
points: Where Thanjavur and Gangaikonda Cholapuram assert size, Darasuram is small and minutely worked - a shift from imperial statement to jewel-like execution that matches the dynasty's reduced political reach in the twelfth century.

The front mandapa is conceived as a chariot drawn by horses, with carved stone wheels at its base - the same device later used on the grand scale at Konark, and evidence that the idea was circulating in the south a century earlier.

A flight of steps at the southern entrance produces musical tones when struck, and miniature friezes along the base of the mandapa illustrate the *Periya Puranam*, the lives of the sixty-three Nayanmar saints - Sekkizhar's text, composed in this same period under Kulottunga II, rendered in stone.
The name comes from Airavata, Indra's elephant, said to have been cured by bathing here. The temple's dance and music sculpture is used as evidence for the temple's role in patronising performance.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; K. A. Nilakanta Sastri, *The Colas*; ASI

location.summary: Deogarh, Lalitpur district, Uttar Pradesh, on a spur of the Vindhyas above the Betwa, close to the Madhya Pradesh border.

periodLevel.summary: The Dashavatara temple, Gupta period, c. 500-525 CE - the most fully developed Gupta temple to survive. A later Jain group of the 8th-12th centuries stands on the same hill, so the site spans the Gupta to Chandela centuries.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The classic Gupta temple: the first to combine a shikhara, a sculpted programme and the panchayatana plan.
points: It is the earliest known *panchayatana* - a main shrine on a raised platform with four subsidiary shrines at the corners - the plan that governs north Indian temple building thereafter. The curvilinear shikhara survives only in part but was clearly present.

Three great relief panels on the outer walls are the finest Gupta narrative sculpture: *Sheshashayi Vishnu*, reclining on Ananta with Brahma on the lotus and the personified weapons below; *Nara-Narayana* at Badarikashrama; and *Gajendra-moksha*, Vishnu rescuing the elephant. Their composition, in balanced tiers with restrained emotion, defines the classical Gupta idiom.
The carved doorway with Ganga and Yamuna on the jambs, mithuna couples, dwarfs and foliate scrolls sets the template for the Nagara doorframe.
Despite the name the panels are not a *dashavatara* set - a nineteenth-century misnomer worth correcting, since the temple is thoroughly Vaishnava but not an avatara cycle.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 9; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; ASI

location.summary: Dilwara, on Mount Abu, Sirohi district, Rajasthan, the highest point of the Aravallis, above the West Banas basin.

periodLevel.summary: Five Jain temples in white Makrana marble built between the 11th and 13th centuries under the Chaulukya (Solanki) kings of Gujarat. The Vimala Vasahi, dedicated to Adinatha, was raised in 1031 CE by Vimala Shah, minister of Bhima I; the Luna Vasahi, dedicated to Neminatha, in 1230 CE by the brothers Vastupala and Tejpala, ministers of the Vaghela kings.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The finest marble carving in India, and the clearest case of temple building financed by merchants and ministers rather than by kings.
points: The work is in the Maru-Gurjara idiom: closed halls with a central dome carried on eight pillars, ceilings cut into concentric rings of lotus petals, and pendant marble bosses so undercut that the stone is translucent. The Luna Vasahi's rangamandapa ceiling is the acknowledged masterpiece.

Both principal temples were built by *mantris* - state officials of the Jain mercantile community. This is the standard illustration of how commercial wealth, not just royal revenue, underwrote early medieval religious architecture.
The plan is the standard Jain *chaturvimshati-jinalaya*: a central shrine ringed by a corridor of fifty-two subsidiary cells, each holding a tirthankara image.

The exteriors are deliberately plain, so that the entire effect is interior - the opposite of the sculpted outer walls at Khajuraho or Modhera, and a reminder that Jain patrons chose restraint outside and extravagance within.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I; ASI

location.summary: Ellora, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (Aurangabad) district, Maharashtra, cut into a basalt scarp of the Charanandri hills beside the Elaganga, on the route from the Deccan plateau to the western ports.

periodLevel.summary: Thirty-four excavations spanning c. 600-1000 CE: Caves 1-12 Buddhist (6th-8th centuries), 13-29 Brahmanical (7th-9th), 30-34 Jain (9th-10th). The Kailasa, Cave 16, was cut under the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I, r. 756-773 CE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The largest monolithic excavation in the world, and the clearest single demonstration of three religions patronised at one site.
points: The Kailasa was quarried from the living rock downwards, freeing a complete Dravida temple - gateway, Nandi shrine, mandapa, vimana and cloister - from the hillside. Some 200,000 tonnes of basalt were removed with no possibility of correcting a mistake. It represents Mount Kailasa, and the famous panel of Ravana shaking the mountain while Shiva stills it with his toe is carved into its own plinth.
Its model was the Virupaksha at Pattadakal, which the Rashtrakutas took over from the Chalukyas - the architectural evidence of a political succession in the Deccan.

The Buddhist group includes Cave 10, the Vishvakarma *chaitya* with a rock-cut stupa and seated Buddha, and Cave 12, the three-storeyed Tin Thal. The Jain group is led by the Indra Sabha, a smaller Kailasa in conception.
That the Buddhist, Hindu and Jain excavations overlap in date at one cliff is the standard evidence against reading early medieval religious history as a sequence of exclusions.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Thapar, *Early India*; ASI

location.summary: Gangaikonda Cholapuram, Ariyalur district, Tamil Nadu, north of the Kollidam (Coleroon) in the Kaveri delta, about 70 km from Thanjavur.

periodLevel.summary: Founded by Rajendra I c. 1025 CE after his northern campaign, and the Chola capital for some 250 years until the dynasty's fall. The Brihadisvara temple was completed c. 1035; its vimana rises about 55 m. One of the three Great Living Chola Temples inscribed by UNESCO, with Thanjavur and Darasuram.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A capital founded as a war memorial - the Chola empire at its widest, commemorated in stone and water.
points: The name means "the city of the Chola who took the Ganga". Rajendra's army marched to the Ganga, and water carried back from it was poured into the *Chola-gangam*, a huge tank beside the temple described as a liquid pillar of victory - a *jalamaya-jayastambha*. Conquest converted into ritual topography.

The vimana is lower than Thanjavur's 66 m but concave in profile rather than straight, giving a softer, more graceful silhouette; it is usually described as the feminine counterpart to Rajaraja's masculine tower.

Sculptural high points include the *Chandesa-anugraha-murti*, showing Shiva garlanding Chandesa - read as an allegory of Rajendra receiving his father's blessing - and the monolithic Nandi, the second largest in India.

The site is central to the debate on Chola polity: Nilakanta Sastri's centralised bureaucratic empire against Burton Stein's segmentary state, in which such capitals are ritual rather than administrative centres.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; K. A. Nilakanta Sastri, *The Colas*

location.summary: Gyaraspur, Vidisha district, Madhya Pradesh, in the Betwa valley on the old route linking Vidisha, Sanchi and Udayagiri - the Malwa corridor between the Gangetic plain and the Deccan.

periodLevel.summary: Pratihara period, 9th-10th centuries CE, with Paramara-era additions. The Maladevi temple, the Bajramath and the Hindola Torana all belong to this phase, when the Gurjara-Pratiharas ruled Malwa from Kannauj.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A compact set of Pratihara-period monuments that fills the gap between Gupta Malwa and Chandela Bundelkhand.
points: The Maladevi temple is built against a hillside, half rock-cut and half structural, with a Nagara shikhara, a sanctum with ambulatory and richly carved outer walls - an unusual hybrid that shows the rock-cut tradition still alive in structural building.

The Bajramath has three sanctums in a row. It was built as a Brahmanical temple - the doorway iconography is Vaishnava and Shaiva - and later taken over by the Digambara Jains, whose tirthankara images now occupy the shrines. It is the clearest local example of a building outlasting the sect that raised it.
The Hindola Torana, a free-standing gateway of two pillars and an architrave carved with Vishnu's avataras, is the best-preserved early medieval torana in central India.

Gyaraspur's value in an answer is as Pratihara evidence: the dynasty is far better attested in inscriptions and Arab accounts than in surviving buildings, and this is one of the few places where its architecture can actually be seen.

location.summary: Halebidu, ancient Dorasamudra, Hassan district, Karnataka, beside the Dorasamudra tank on the Malnad plateau above the upper Hemavati - the name means "old capital".

periodLevel.summary: Hoysala capital from the 11th century to 1327. The Hoysaleshvara temple was begun c. 1121 CE under Vishnuvardhana, the king who also built Belur, and was never finished; work continued for over eighty years. Sacked by Malik Kafur in 1311 and again by Muhammad bin Tughlaq's forces in 1327, after which the capital shifted.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The peak of Hoysala architecture - a distinct Deccan order that is neither Nagara nor Dravida.
points: The plan is stellate: a star-shaped sanctum and outer wall on a raised *jagati* platform that follows the same profile, so the visitor circumambulates a zigzag of projecting angles catching the light. The Hoysaleshvara is *dvikuta*, twin shrines for Hoysaleshvara and Shantaleshvara, the latter named for Queen Shantala.

The material determines the style. Chloritic schist - soapstone - is soft when quarried and hardens on exposure, allowing lathe-turned pillars and jewellery carved with a fineness impossible in granite or sandstone.
The outer wall carries continuous horizontal friezes in fixed order: elephants, lions, horsemen, foliage, then epic narrative - hundreds of metres of Ramayana, Mahabharata and Bhagavata scenes.

Many sculptures are signed, so individual artists such as Kedaroja and Malitamma are known by name - a rarity in Indian art history. Jain basadis nearby show Hoysala patronage extending beyond Shaivism.

location.summary: Hampi, Vijayanagara district, Karnataka, on the south bank of the Tungabhadra among granite boulder hills - a defensible site identified with Kishkindha of the *Ramayana*.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of the Vijayanagara empire from its founding in 1336 by Harihara and Bukka to its sack in 1565 after the battle of Talikota. The great building phase is the Tuluva period under Krishnadevaraya, r. 1509-1529. UNESCO World Heritage Site.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The largest medieval Hindu capital to survive as a ruin, and the type-site of the Vijayanagara architectural order.
points: The style's markers are the towering brick-and-plaster *gopuram* over the outer gate, the pillared *kalyana mandapa*, and monolithic piers carved as rearing *yali* beasts. The Vitthala temple has the stone chariot and the colonnade of musical pillars; the Virupaksha, older than the city and still in worship, was enlarged by Krishnadevaraya.

The Hazara Rama, the royal chapel, carries Ramayana friezes on its walls and outer processional scenes of elephants, horses and dancers - the Mahanavami festival depicted on the building beside the platform where it was held.

The secular quarter is what makes Hampi exceptional: the Mahanavami Dibba, the elephant stables, the Lotus Mahal, the queen's bath and an elaborate aqueduct system. Islamic arches and domes in the courtly buildings show the Deccan sultanates' idiom adopted for palace architecture while temples stayed indigenous.
Foreign accounts - Abdur Razzaq, Nicolo de' Conti, Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz - describe the city at its height and are the standard external evidence for its scale and markets.

content.sourcesLine: Basham, *The Wonder that was India*; Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I; Thapar, *Early India*

location.summary: Puri and Konark, on the Odisha coast of the Bay of Bengal - Puri on the shore itself, Konark some 35 km north-east near the old mouth of the Chandrabhaga, now silted and set back from the sea.

periodLevel.summary: Both are Eastern Ganga foundations. The Jagannath temple at Puri was begun by Anantavarman Chodaganga c. 1135 CE and completed under Anangabhima III; the Konark Sun temple was built by Narasimhadeva I, c. 1250, to mark his victories over the Bengal sultanate. Kalinga style throughout.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The culmination of Odishan architecture, and the state cult on which Ganga and Gajapati kingship rested.
points: Konark is conceived as Surya's chariot: twenty-four carved stone wheels along the plinth, drawn by seven horses, the wheels doubling as sundials. The 70 m deul collapsed, probably in the 19th century, leaving the pidha-roofed jagamohana standing. European sailors called it the Black Pagoda, using it as a navigation mark against Puri's White Pagoda.

Puri's Jagannath - with Balabhadra and Subhadra - is a wooden triad, periodically renewed in the *Navakalevara* rite. The tribal Sabara origins claimed for the deity make Jagannath the standard example of a local cult raised into a state religion; from Anangabhima III the Gangas ruled formally as deputies of Jagannath.

The *Madala Panji*, the temple chronicle, and the Ratha Yatra are the two things to cite: one a continuous indigenous historical record, the other the procession from which the word "juggernaut" entered English.
Puri is one of the Char Dham; Konark completes the trio of great Indian sun temples with Modhera and Martand.

location.summary: Kamakhya, on the Nilachal hill in Guwahati, Assam, overlooking the Brahmaputra where the river narrows - ancient Kamarupa or Pragjyotisha.

periodLevel.summary: An early shrine of the Kamarupa kingdom, referred to from about the 8th-9th centuries and elaborated under the Palas of Kamarupa. The standing temple was rebuilt in 1565 by the Koch king Nara Narayana and his general Chilarai, after destruction attributed to Kalapahar; the plinth and some sculpture belong to the older structure.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The principal Shakta pitha of eastern India and the chief centre of Tantric worship in the subcontinent.
points: It is counted among the fifty-one *shakti pithas*, and the one where Sati's *yoni* is said to have fallen. There is no anthropomorphic image: worship is offered to a natural cleft in the rock kept moist by a spring - aniconic worship at a major temple, which is itself unusual.

The *Kalika Purana*, composed in Assam around the 10th-11th century, and the *Yogini Tantra* are the textual authorities. Both are principal sources for Kaula and Vamachara tantric practice, including the rites of animal sacrifice still performed here.

The Ambubachi Mela marks the goddess's annual menstruation, when the temple closes for three days. The presence of a mainstream pilgrimage built on that symbolism is standard evidence in questions on goddess worship and on the absorption of pre-Brahmanical fertility cult.
The structure defines the *Nilachal* type: a Nagara-derived shikhara capped by a hemispherical dome, on a cruciform plan - a regional hybrid found only in Assam.

location.summary: Kanchipuram, Tamil Nadu, on the Vegavathi, a tributary of the Palar, about 70 km inland from the coast - the natural centre of Tondaimandalam.

periodLevel.summary: A city of the Sangam age, later the Pallava capital from the 6th to the 9th centuries, then held by Cholas, Vijayanagara and the Nayakas. The Kailasanatha was built by Rajasimha (Narasimhavarman II), c. 700-728 CE; the Vaikuntha Perumal by Nandivarman II Pallavamalla, c. 770.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the seven *moksha-puris*, and the place where the southern structural stone temple begins.
points: The Kailasanatha is the earliest structural stone temple in Kanchi, built in sandstone rather than granite, with a pyramidal vimana, a circuit of small cells around the courtyard, and repeated *Somaskanda* panels - Shiva, Parvati and the infant Skanda - the Pallava dynastic image. Vikramaditya II copied it for the Virupaksha at Pattadakal.

The Vaikuntha Perumal has three sanctums stacked vertically, one above the other, and a cloister whose sculpted panels narrate the disputed Pallava succession - historical narrative carved on a temple wall, which is rare anywhere in India.

Kanchi was a *ghatikasthana*, a recognised seat of learning, hosting Jain and Buddhist institutions between the 1st and 5th centuries before becoming a Shaiva and Vaishnava centre. Bharavi, author of the *Kiratarjuniya*, the Buddhist Dharmapala who became head of Nalanda, and Ramanuja are all associated with it.

Divided into Shiva Kanchi and Vishnu Kanchi, with the Ekambaranatha and Varadaraja temples enlarged under Chola and Vijayanagara rule, it shows continuous accretion over a thousand years. It was also a silk and trade centre from the Satavahana period.

location.summary: Katarmal, Almora district, Uttarakhand, on a ridge at about 2,100 m above the Kosi valley in Kumaon, facing east across the hills towards the Himalayan snow line.

periodLevel.summary: Katyuri dynasty, c. 9th century CE, built by the Katyuri ruler Katarmalla, who gives the site its name. The Katyuris ruled Kumaon and Garhwal from Baijnath and Dwarahat between roughly the 7th and 11th centuries.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The second most important sun temple in India after Konark, and the principal monument of the Katyuri kingdom.
points: A main shrine of stone in a simplified Nagara idiom stands within a group of about forty-five subsidiary shrines, the whole aligned so that the first light of sunrise falls directly on the image - the same solar orientation used at Modhera and Konark, executed with far smaller resources.

The presiding deity is Surya as Vraddha Aditya, the aged sun. Surya worship in the central Himalaya, alongside Martand in Kashmir, shows the cult was strong along the whole mountain belt and not only in Gujarat and Odisha.

The temple's elaborately carved wooden doors and panels were among the finest surviving early medieval woodwork in the hills; they were stolen in the 1980s and the recovered pieces are now in the National Museum, Delhi. The loss is regularly cited in discussions of antiquities protection.
The Katyuri temples - Katarmal, Baijnath, Jageshwar - together form the hill counterpart to plains Nagara building, adapted to stone-and-timber construction and steep sites.

location.summary: Khajuraho, Chhatarpur district, Madhya Pradesh, in Bundelkhand between the Ken and the Betwa - Jejakabhukti, the Chandela homeland.

periodLevel.summary: Chandela period, c. 900-1050 CE, with about eighty-five temples built in roughly a century and twenty-five surviving, in Western, Eastern and Southern groups. The Lakshmana temple is dated 954 CE by Yashovarman's inscription; the Kandariya Mahadeva, c. 1030, belongs to Vidyadhara's reign.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The high point of the Nagara temple, and the largest concentrated act of temple patronage by any early medieval dynasty.
points: The Kandariya Mahadeva is the fully evolved Nagara design: a high *jagati* platform, an unbroken axis of entrance, mandapa, mahamandapa and sanctum, and a shikhara of some eighty-four clustered *urushringas* rising in graded peaks to suggest Mount Kailasa. Sandstone throughout, with no enclosure wall - the opposite of the walled Dravida temple.

Patronage is Shaiva, Vaishnava and Jaina together: the Lakshmana enshrines a Vaikuntha Vishnu, the Parshvanatha and Adinatha serve the Jain community, and the granite Chausath Yogini is the oldest structure on the site - evidence of tantric yogini worship alongside orthodox cult.

The erotic sculpture, about a tenth of the total and concentrated on the junction walls, has been read as tantric, as auspicious *mithuna*, and as a fertility motif. Treat the interpretation as open; what is certain is that it is one element in a full programme of gods, apsaras, ascetics and battle scenes.
Al-Biruni and Ibn Battuta both notice Khajuraho, which helps date its continued importance after Chandela decline.

location.summary: Bhubaneswar, Odisha, beside the Bindusagar tank in the old temple city of Ekamra Kshetra, in the lower Mahanadi delta a few kilometres from the Daya.

periodLevel.summary: Begun under the Somavamshi king Jajati Keshari and completed c. 1090-1104 CE, with the natamandira and bhogamandapa added under the Eastern Gangas. Kalinga style in sandstone; the deul rises about 55 m.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The mature Kalinga temple, with all four components present for the first time - the standard against which Odishan architecture is described.
points: The four-part axial sequence is the syllabus point: *deul* (sanctum with curvilinear rekha tower), *jagamohana* (assembly porch with stepped pidha roof), *natamandira* (dance hall) and *bhogamandapa* (hall of offerings). Earlier Bhubaneswar temples have only the first two; Lingaraj completes the scheme, and Puri and Konark follow it.

The deity is Tribhuvaneshvara or Krittivasa, worshipped as Harihara - Shiva and Vishnu in one - and offerings include tulsi. The syncretism is read as Shaiva Bhubaneswar accommodating the rising Jagannath cult of Puri under Ganga patronage.

Bhubaneswar's sequence can be walked in date order: Parashurameshvara (c. 650), Mukteshvara (c. 950, the "gem of Odishan architecture" with its famous torana), Rajarani (11th century, noted for its clustered tower and figural sculpture), then Lingaraj. Few places let a regional style be traced so continuously.
The *jagati* platform, the horizontal mouldings of the *bada*, and the *amalaka* with *kalasha* finial are the diagnostic Kalinga features to name.

location.summary: Lonar, Buldhana district, Maharashtra, in the Deccan trap country of Vidarbha - a meteorite crater about 1.8 km across holding a saline, alkaline lake, with temples ringing the rim and the crater floor.

periodLevel.summary: The crater was formed by a hypervelocity impact in basalt, dated to roughly 50,000 years ago. The temples are Chalukya and Yadava work of the 12th-13th centuries CE, in the Hemadpanti manner - dressed basalt laid without mortar.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The only large impact crater in basalt anywhere in the world, and a Puranic site whose myth encodes its own geology.
points: The Daityasudana temple, dedicated to Vishnu as the slayer of the demon Lonasura, is built on an irregular star-shaped plan in black basalt with dense figural carving. The *Skanda* and *Padma Puranas* tell of the demon crushed into the earth here, a story that reads as an explanation of the crater itself.

Kamalja Devi on the lake shore and about fifteen other shrines, several now half-submerged, complete the group. Their Hemadpanti technique - mortarless interlocking basalt - is the diagnostic Yadava building method of the Deccan.
The *Ain-i-Akbari* records revenue from salt extracted at Lonar, so the lake's alkaline chemistry was already an economic resource under the Mughals.
Its interest in an answer is the combination: a geological feature, a Puranic narrative and a dated body of Deccan temple architecture at one site.

location.summary: Madurai, Tamil Nadu, on the south bank of the Vaigai - the ancient Pandya capital, laid out in concentric streets around the temple at its centre.

periodLevel.summary: A shrine of the Pandya period, sacked by Malik Kafur in 1310. The standing complex is overwhelmingly Nayaka work of the 16th-17th centuries, begun under Vishvanatha Nayaka and completed under Tirumalai Nayaka, r. 1623-1659. Fourteen gopurams, the tallest about 52 m.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The fullest realisation of the Nayaka temple-city, and the rare major temple where the goddess outranks her consort.
points: Meenakshi, the fish-eyed goddess identified with Parvati, is the presiding deity, with Sundareshvara (Shiva) secondary - her shrine is approached first and the annual *Chithirai* festival celebrates her marriage. A goddess as principal deity of a temple of this scale is unusual and is the point to make in questions on Shakta worship in the south.

The Nayaka style is visible at its height: enormous gopurams encrusted with painted stucco figures, the *Ayirakkal* thousand-pillar hall with its carved yali piers, the Potramarai golden lotus tank, and Tirumalai Nayaka's Pudu Mandapam outside the walls.

The city plan follows the temple: concentric rectangular streets named for festival months, so that processional routes structure the whole settlement - the clearest surviving example of the south Indian temple town.
Madurai is the seat of the Sangam academy in Tamil tradition, which gives the site a literary claim reaching back to the early centuries CE, long before the standing buildings.

location.summary: Mamallapuram, Chengalpattu district, Tamil Nadu, on the Coromandel coast about 55 km south of Chennai - an open surf shore with no natural harbour, serving the Pallava capital at Kanchipuram some 70 km inland.

periodLevel.summary: Two Pallava phases. The rock-cut *mandapas*, the Pancha Rathas and the great open-air relief belong to Narasimhavarman I Mamalla, r. 630-668 CE; the structural Shore Temple to Rajasimha (Narasimhavarman II), c. 700-728. The port was active into the 9th century. Known to European sailors as the Seven Pagodas. UNESCO World Heritage Site.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The site where south Indian architecture moves from rock-cut to structural building, and the harbour from which the Pallavas projected trade and culture into Southeast Asia.
points: The Pancha Rathas are five monolithic shrines cut from single granite boulders, named for the Pandavas and Draupadi. Each tries a different roof form - the Draupadi ratha a thatched hut, the Bhima a barrel vault, the Dharmaraja a stepped pyramid - so they are a set of architectural experiments, and the Dharmaraja's form becomes the standard Dravida *vimana*.

The Shore Temple is among the earliest structural stone temples in south India: three shrines, two to Shiva and one holding a reclining Vishnu, built of dressed granite and exposed to sea air for thirteen centuries.

The *Descent of the Ganga*, also read as Arjuna's Penance, is the largest bas-relief in the world - some 30 m of rock with gods, sages, animals and a famous row of elephants, split by a natural cleft down which water was made to flow. The Varaha and Krishna mandapas carry the finest Pallava narrative panels.

As a port it is the principal evidence for what is called the Indianisation of Southeast Asia - better framed as sustained exchange by merchants and monks than as colonisation. Pallava missions sailed from here to Sri Lanka, Srivijaya and Champa, and the forms worked out at Mamallapuram reappear in Southeast Asian temples. Roman and Chinese coins show the coast was on the long-distance circuit before the Pallavas.
Its decline after the 9th century, as Nagapattinam and Kaveripattinam took the Chola traffic, tracks the transfer of power from Pallava to Chola.

location.summary: Manali, Kullu district, Himachal Pradesh, at the head of the Kullu valley on the right bank of the Beas, below the Rohtang pass into Lahaul.

periodLevel.summary: The Hidimba Devi (Dhungri) temple, built in 1553 CE by Raja Bahadur Singh of Kullu around an older rock shrine. Timber-and-stone construction in the Himalayan pagoda form; the Manu temple at Old Manali belongs to the same local tradition.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The best-known example of the Himalayan timber pagoda temple, and a clear case of a local goddess absorbed into the Sanskritic epic.
points: The structure is four-tiered, three square roofs of timber and slate rising to a conical brass finial, over a sanctum enclosing a natural rock with the footprint of the deity. The technique is *kath-kuni* - alternating courses of dressed stone and cedar beams without mortar - a seismic-resistant method developed for the western Himalaya.

The deity is Hidimba, the rakshasi of the *Mahabharata* who marries Bhima. A pre-existing local mother-goddess cult is here given a place in the epic, and worshipped not as a demon but as the tutelary goddess of the Kullu royal house. This is the standard illustration of how regional cults were folded into the pan-Indian tradition without being displaced.
Elaborately carved wooden doorframes with goddesses, animals and foliate scrolls give the finest Himalayan woodcarving of the period.
Hidimba's role in the Kullu Dussehra, where local deities are carried to Kullu in procession, shows the temple's continuing political function.

location.summary: Martand, near Mattan in Anantnag district, Kashmir, on a karewa plateau commanding the whole Jhelum valley - a deliberately chosen viewpoint rather than a settlement site.

periodLevel.summary: Built by Lalitaditya Muktapida of the Karkota dynasty, r. c. 724-760 CE, the high point of Kashmiri power, when Karkota armies campaigned into the plains and embassies went to Tang China. Ruined in the early 15th century under Sultan Sikandar Shah, called But-shikan.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The definitive monument of the Kashmiri style - the one regional order in India that absorbs classical Mediterranean form.
points: The plan is a colonnaded quadrangle of eighty-four fluted columns enclosing a central shrine, a peristyle courtyard of a kind found nowhere else in Indian temple architecture. The columns are Greco-Roman in profile, and the trefoil arches within triangular pediments, with the steep double-pyramidal roof, come from Gandharan practice adapted to a snow climate.

It is the architectural expression of Kashmir's position on the routes between India, Iran and Central Asia. Lalitaditya's reign is also when the Karkotas were fielding armies across north India, so the temple is read as imperial statement as much as devotion.

Kalhana's *Rajatarangini*, written in 1149-50, records the foundation and the later destruction. That a twelfth-century Sanskrit chronicle can be checked against a standing building makes Kashmir unusually well documented for early medieval India.
Avantipur nearby, built by Avantivarman of the Utpala dynasty in the 9th century, continues the same style and is the natural comparison.

location.summary: Masrur, Kangra district, Himachal Pradesh, on a sandstone ridge above the Beas valley, facing the Dhauladhar range across the plain.

periodLevel.summary: Monolithic rock-cut complex of about the 8th century CE, contemporary with the Ellora Kailasa, carved under local rulers of the Kangra-Jalandhara region. Severely damaged in the Kangra earthquake of 1905, which brought down several of the shikharas.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The only monolithic rock-cut temple complex in north India - the Nagara counterpart of the Deccan's Dravida excavations.
points: Some fifteen shrines were cut from a single outcrop, carved from the top downwards, each carrying a curvilinear Nagara shikhara with *amalaka* and clustered *urushringas*. Where Ellora and Mamallapuram cut Dravida vimanas from rock, Masrur proves the same technique was applied to the northern form - which is why it is called the Himalayan Ellora.
The main sanctum holds images of Rama, Lakshmana and Sita, though the temple was very likely Shaiva originally; the surviving doorway and wall sculpture is Brahmanical throughout.
A rock-cut tank in front reflects the shikharas, and the whole was aligned on the Dhauladhar peaks - the mountain-temple symbolism made literal by siting rather than by carving.
Its condition is itself evidence: the 1905 earthquake damage is a reminder that seismicity, not only iconoclasm, accounts for much of what is lost in the Himalayan belt.

location.summary: Modhera, Mehsana district, Gujarat, on the left bank of the Pushpavati, a tributary of the Rupen, in north Gujarat.

periodLevel.summary: Sun temple of the Chaulukya (Solanki) dynasty, built under Bhima I; an inscription on a wall of the sanctum gives Vikrama Samvat 1083, i.e. 1026-27 CE. Maru-Gurjara style in yellow sandstone. It was raised in the years immediately after Mahmud of Ghazni's raid on Somnath in 1025-26, and was later damaged under Alauddin Khalji.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The best-preserved sun temple in western India, and a building designed around the movement of the sun itself.
points: It has three parts on one east-west axis: the *Surya Kunda*, a rectangular stepped tank lined with 108 miniature shrines; the *sabhamandapa*, an open pillared hall with fifty-two carved pillars, entered through toranas; and the *gudhamandapa* with the sanctum beyond.
The alignment is exact: at the equinoxes the rising sun passes straight down the axis to light the sanctum, where the image of Surya once stood. The plinth carries twelve adityas, one for each month.

The kunda is as important as the temple. Stepped water architecture - here, and in the Rani ki Vav at Patan built a generation later - is the distinctive Gujarati contribution, joining ritual bathing, water storage and sculpture in one structure.
Surya worship, prominent in early medieval western and eastern India (Modhera, Konark, Martand, Katarmal), fades afterwards; these temples are the main evidence for a cult that later disappears.

location.summary: Nachna Kuthara, Panna district, Madhya Pradesh, on the Vindhyan plateau north of the Ken, in the tract later held by the Chandelas.

periodLevel.summary: The Parvati temple, Gupta period, c. late 5th century CE, built under the Uchchhakalpa or Vakataka-linked feudatories of the region. The Chaumukhnath temple on the hill above is later, c. 7th-9th century.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The Gupta temple at the moment it acquires height and an ambulatory - the step between Tigawa and Deogarh.
points: The sanctum is enclosed by a covered circumambulatory passage (*pradakshina patha*) lit by pierced stone lattice windows (*jali*), and carries a second storey above - the earliest clear instance of a storeyed Gupta shrine, and the germ of the vertical massing that becomes the Nagara shikhara.

The exterior plinth is carved as rough rock-work with animals and caves, so that the building represents a mountain. For a temple of Parvati, daughter of Himalaya, the device makes the architecture itself iconographic - the earliest Indian example of this conceit.
Sculpture on the walls includes mithuna couples, ascetics and Ramayana scenes, with a famous door-guardian and river-goddess jambs in the Gupta manner.

The site is often paired with Bhumara, its neighbour, whose Shiva temple of the same period gives the other half of the picture for temple building in the Vindhyan kingdoms between Gupta and Chandela rule.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 9; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; ASI

location.summary: Pandharpur, Solapur district, Maharashtra, on the right bank of the Bhima, which is called the Chandrabhaga where it curves like a crescent past the town - in the Deccan plateau's dry interior.

periodLevel.summary: The core shrine belongs to the Yadava period; a Kannada and Sanskrit inscription on the temple dates to 1189 CE, and Hoysala patronage under Vishnuvardhana is recorded in tradition. The mandapas and enclosures are later Maratha additions. The Varkari movement takes shape here from the 13th century.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The centre of the Varkari sampradaya - the most important bhakti site in Maharashtra, and a devotional tradition organised around a pilgrimage rather than a doctrine.
points: The deity, Vitthala or Vithoba, stands on a brick with hands on hips, a form found nowhere else. He is identified with Krishna and Vishnu, but the iconography and the pastoral associations point to an older local cult of a herdsman god absorbed into Vaishnavism.

The saint-poets of the tradition span five centuries and, crucially, all social strata: Jnaneshwar the brahmana, Namdev a tailor, Chokhamela a Mahar, Savata a gardener, Janabai a maidservant, Tukaram a shopkeeper. Their *abhangas* in Marathi made vernacular devotion a vehicle for implicit criticism of caste exclusion - the standard evidence for the social reach of the bhakti movement.

The *wari*, the walking pilgrimage in which *palkhis* carrying the saints' sandals converge on Pandharpur for Ashadhi Ekadashi, still draws hundreds of thousands, and is what binds the sect together in the absence of a monastic order.
Chokhamela's samadhi stands at the foot of the temple steps, outside the shrine - the exclusion is itself part of the historical record.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I; R. C. Dhere, *Rise of a Folk God*

location.summary: Pattadakal, Bagalkot district, Karnataka, on the left bank of the Malaprabha where the river turns north - a bend held to be auspicious - with Aihole and Badami close by.

periodLevel.summary: The Early Chalukya coronation site, *Pattada-kisuvolal*, the place of the crown. Ten major temples of the 7th-8th centuries CE: the Sangameshvara under Vijayaditya (r. 696-733), the Virupaksha and Mallikarjuna under Vikramaditya II (r. 733-746). UNESCO World Heritage Site.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The one site where the Nagara and Dravida orders stand side by side, built by the same dynasty at the same time - the textbook case for the two styles as contemporaries rather than a sequence.
points: Four temples are Nagara with curvilinear shikharas - Papanatha, Galaganatha, Kashi Vishvanatha, Jambulinga - and four are Dravida with stepped vimanas: Sangameshvara, Virupaksha, Mallikarjuna, Chandrashekhara. The Papanatha mixes both. This deliberate juxtaposition is what the examiner is after.

The Virupaksha, c. 740 CE, was built by Queen Lokamahadevi to commemorate Vikramaditya II's victory over the Pallavas at Kanchipuram, and was modelled on the Kailasanatha there - a temple raised as a war memorial, copying the vanquished enemy's own building. Its inscription names the architect, Gunda, with the title *tribhuvanacharya*.
The Virupaksha in turn became the model for the Rashtrakuta Kailasa at Ellora, so a single line of descent runs Kanchi to Pattadakal to Ellora.
Two queens, Lokamahadevi and Trailokyamahadevi, were the patrons of the two largest temples - unusually well-documented female patronage.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Thapar, *Early India*; ASI

location.summary: Pushkar, Ajmer district, Rajasthan, around a lake in a hollow of the Aravallis, on the divide between the Luni drainage and the Banas - the desert edge of eastern Rajasthan.

periodLevel.summary: An ancient tirtha named in the *Mahabharata*, the *Padma Purana* and the *Ramayana*. The present Jagatpita Brahma temple is a 14th-century structure, repaired in the 18th; the lake's stone ghats were largely built by Rajput rulers, with Maratha additions of the 18th century.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The principal Brahma temple in India - the one place where a god of the classical triad has almost no independent cult.
points: Brahma is named constantly in cosmology but is worshipped almost nowhere. The *Padma Purana* explains Pushkar as the site of his yajna and accounts for the absence of other Brahma temples by Savitri's curse. The rarity is the point: it shows that a deity's textual prominence and its actual cult can diverge completely, and that Puranic myth is often composed to explain an existing situation rather than the reverse.
The temple carries the *hamsa*, Brahma's goose, on its red shikhara, and the image is four-faced (chaturmukha), with Savitri and Gayatri shrines on the surrounding hills.

Pushkar lake is one of the five sacred *sarovars* and is treated as a self-manifested tirtha, its sanctity resting on water in an arid landscape - the same logic that operates at Amarkantak and at river confluences.
The Kartik Purnima fair, joining pilgrimage to one of the largest livestock markets in India, is standard evidence for how religious assembly and commerce reinforced each other.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Thapar, *Early India*; *Padma Purana*, Srishti-khanda

location.summary: Rajim, Gariaband district, Chhattisgarh, at the confluence of the Mahanadi, the Pairi and the Sondur - called the Prayag of Chhattisgarh for that triple junction.

periodLevel.summary: The Rajiv Lochan temple, dedicated to Vishnu, founded by Vilasatunga of the Nala dynasty in about the 7th-8th century CE, with later additions under the Kalachuris of Ratanpur and repairs into the Maratha period. The Kuleshwar Mahadeva stands on a plinth in the riverbed itself.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The main surviving monument of the Nala dynasty, and a Vaishnava centre in the Mahanadi valley between the Deccan and Odisha.
points: The Nalas are known mainly from coins and a handful of inscriptions, so a dated temple foundation gives them physical presence. They ruled the Bastar-Koraput tract in the 5th-7th centuries, fought the Vakatakas, and are a standard example of the smaller dynasties that fill the gap between Gupta and early medieval power.

The temple is *panchayatana*, with a stone-pillared mandapa whose columns carry fine early sculpture of Narasimha, Varaha, Vamana and river goddesses. The garbhagriha image is a tall four-armed Vishnu in black stone.
An inscription of the Kalachuri period on the site records grants, giving the temple a documented endowment history across dynasties.

The river confluence is the reason for the location: like Prayaga, Rajim's sanctity is hydrographic, and the Kuleshwar temple standing in the water makes the point structurally. The Rajim Kumbh is held here.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 9 and 10; ASI; *Epigraphia Indica* XXVI (Rajim plates)

location.summary: Shamlaji, Aravalli district, Gujarat, on the bank of the Meshvo river where the Aravalli foothills meet the north Gujarat plain, on the old route between Gujarat and Rajasthan.

periodLevel.summary: Two distinct phases. A post-Gupta sculptural school of the 5th-6th centuries CE worked here in a soft grey schist; the standing Vishnu (Gadadhara) temple is a Chaulukya-period rebuilding of the 11th century in white sandstone.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The type-site of a recognised regional sculptural school, and a Vaishnava tirtha on a long-used trade route.
points: The "Shamlaji school" of the 6th century - Vishnu, Matrika and Skanda images in grey schist, with full modelling and heavy jewellery - is one of the named post-Gupta regional idioms, standing between Gupta classicism and the harder early medieval western Indian style. The images are now largely in the Baroda Museum.

Devnimori, a few kilometres away, held a Buddhist stupa whose inscribed relic casket is dated to the year 127 of the Kathika kings, c. 375 CE, with terracotta Buddha figures of high quality. The site was submerged by the Meshvo reservoir. Shamlaji and Devnimori together show Buddhist and Brahmanical patronage side by side in one small valley.

The present temple, carved in white sandstone with friezes of epic scenes, elephants and dancers on its outer walls, is standard Maru-Gurjara work and is still a major pilgrimage centre with a large Kartik fair drawing Bhil and Garasia communities.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 9; ASI; Baroda Museum catalogue

location.summary: Sivasagar, upper Assam, on the south bank of the Brahmaputra near the Dikhow river - the Ahom capital region, known as Rangpur in its own day.

periodLevel.summary: Ahom dynasty at its height, 18th century. The Shivadol, Vishnudol and Devidol were built in 1734 by Queen Ambika, wife of Swargadeo Siba Singha; the Rang Ghar dates to 1746 under Pramatta Singha; the Talatal and Kareng Ghar palaces span the same century. Brick with lime plaster.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The architecture of the one Indian state that held off the Mughals for a century, and a distinct Ahom building idiom.
points: The Shivadol rises about 33 m and is among the tallest Shiva temples in India, its *dol* form - a tall curvilinear tower over a square sanctum, topped by a gold-plated *kalasha* - adapting the Nagara shikhara to brick and to Assamese proportions.

The three temples stand on the bank of the Sivasagar tank, a large excavated reservoir raised above the surrounding land. Ahom statecraft ran on such public works, built through the *paik* system of compulsory labour service - the institutional fact behind the monuments.
The Rang Ghar, a two-storeyed oval pavilion for viewing buffalo fights and games, is described as the oldest surviving amphitheatre in Asia; its roof is shaped like an inverted Ahom longboat.

The Ahoms, a Tai people who entered Assam in 1228, adopted Hinduism progressively; a Tai dynasty building Shaiva temples in a Sanskritic form is the clearest case of that assimilation, recorded in their own *Buranji* chronicles.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* II; Upinder Singh, ch. 10; *Ahom Buranji*

location.summary: Prabhas Patan near Veraval, Gir Somnath district, Gujarat, on the Arabian Sea at the Triveni confluence of the Hiran, Kapila and Saraswati - a port as well as a tirtha.

periodLevel.summary: The first of the twelve *jyotirlingas*, with temple building attributed in tradition to the Yadavas of Vallabhi. The historically attested structure was sacked by Mahmud of Ghazni in 1025-26 during Bhima I's reign, rebuilt by Bhima and again by Kumarapala c. 1169, destroyed under Alauddin Khalji in 1299 and finally by Aurangzeb in 1706. The present Kailash Mahameru Prasada temple was completed in 1951.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Less an architectural site than a historiographical one - the single best case study in how a medieval raid was turned into a modern narrative.
points: Romila Thapar's *Somanatha: The Many Voices of a History* shows the sources disagreeing sharply. Turko-Persian chroniclers magnify the iconoclasm for a Ghaznavid audience; Sanskrit inscriptions from the site carry on recording grants and repairs with little sense of rupture; Jain texts and local traditions differ again.

A Sanskrit-Arabic bilingual inscription of 1264 CE records a Hormuzi shipowner, Nuruddin Firuz, being granted land at Somnath to build a mosque, with local Hindu dignitaries as parties. Trade and cohabitation continue at the very site of the raid.

The "trauma of Somnath" as a continuous Hindu memory took shape in the 1843 House of Commons debate over Ellenborough's gates proclamation, and was carried into Indian politics thereafter. Dating the memory, not just the raid, is what the question rewards.

content.sourcesLine: Thapar, *Somanatha: The Many Voices of a History*; Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I; J. L. Mehta, *Advanced Study in the History of Medieval India* I

location.summary: Srirangam, Tiruchirappalli district, Tamil Nadu, on an island formed where the Kaveri divides from the Kollidam - a river island, which is the source of the site's sanctity.

periodLevel.summary: Attested from the Sangam period and built up continuously by the Cholas, Pandyas, Hoysalas, Vijayanagara rulers and the Madurai Nayakas between the 10th and 17th centuries. The outer Rajagopuram was left unfinished for centuries and completed only in 1987, at 72 m.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The largest functioning Hindu temple complex in the world, and the doctrinal centre of Srivaishnavism.
points: The plan is seven concentric *prakaras* - rectangular enclosures with twenty-one gopurams, the outer ones containing streets, houses and markets. The temple is literally a walled town, and is the standard example of the south Indian temple as an urban nucleus, landholder and employer rather than merely a shrine.
It is the first and foremost of the 108 *Divya Desams*, the seat of Ranganatha reclining on Adishesha, and the sites of the Alwars' hymns collected as the *Nalayira Divya Prabandham*.

Ramanuja headed the temple in the 11th-12th centuries and reorganised its administration; his Vishishtadvaita was formulated here, and his shrine in the complex is said to hold his preserved body. For questions on bhakti and on the Vaishnava acharyas this is the anchor site.
Malik Kafur's raid of 1311 forced the image into hiding for some sixty years, an episode recorded in temple tradition and used to date the Vijayanagara-period rebuilding that followed.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Basham, *The Wonder that was India*; ASI, *South Indian Inscriptions*

location.summary: Tigawa, Katni district, Madhya Pradesh, near Bahuriband on the old route between Jabalpur and Bundelkhand, in the upper Narmada-Son watershed.

periodLevel.summary: Gupta period, c. 400-425 CE - among the oldest surviving structural Hindu temples in India. Of some thirty-six shrines recorded at the site, the Kankali Devi temple survives largely intact.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The first stage of the Indian temple in stone: the simplest possible form, before the shikhara.
points: It is a flat-roofed square sanctum with a small four-pillared porch, no ambulatory and no tower - Percy Brown's Class I Gupta temple, and the starting point of every architectural sequence in the syllabus. Compare it with Sanchi Temple 17, its near-twin.

The pillars carry the heavy vase-and-foliage (purna-ghata) capital with back-to-back lions above, the diagnostic Gupta order; the door jambs are plain, before the elaborately carved doorways of Deogarh.

Originally Vaishnava, with Narasimha and Chakrapurusha panels. The Chamunda or Kankali image that gave the temple its present name is a later insertion - a small but useful instance of a shrine changing affiliation while the building stays the same.
Read the sequence as a set: Tigawa and Sanchi 17 (flat roof), Bhitargaon (brick shikhara), Nachna Kuthara (storeyed sanctum with ambulatory), Deogarh (shikhara with panchayatana plan).

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 9; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Percy Brown, *Indian Architecture*

location.summary: Tirumala, above the town of Tirupati, Tirupati district, Andhra Pradesh, on the seventh hill of the Seshachalam range near the Swarnamukhi river - the old Tondaimandalam frontier.

periodLevel.summary: The Venkateshvara temple is attested by Pallava inscriptions from the 9th century and endowed successively by the Cholas, Pandyas, Hoysalas and Yadavarayas. Its great period is Vijayanagara, above all under Krishnadevaraya, r. 1509-1529, who visited repeatedly and gilded the *ananda nilaya* vimana.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The richest temple in India, and the standard case study for the temple as an economic institution.
points: Over a thousand inscriptions on its walls record gifts of villages, gold, livestock and cash. They show the temple lending money, financing irrigation, employing hundreds and holding land across several districts - the documentary basis for Burton Stein's work on the temple economy of south India.

Krishnadevaraya's portrait statues in copper, with his queens Tirumala Devi and Chinna Devi, stand in the complex. Royal images placed before the deity are a Vijayanagara statement about the relationship of king to god.

The deity, Venkateshvara or Balaji, is a form of Vishnu, and the shrine is a *Divya Desam* praised by the Alwars; Ramanuja is credited in tradition with settling its ritual order. A long dispute over whether the image was Shaiva or Vaishnava was resolved in Vaishnava favour under Ramanuja's influence.
The practice of tonsure and the *hundi* offerings make it the largest pilgrimage economy in the country, a continuity with the endowment pattern the inscriptions record.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Basham, *The Wonder that was India*; *Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanam Inscriptions*
