location.summary: The Barabar and Nagarjuni hills, Jehanabad district, Bihar, granite outcrops rising from the plain about 25 km north of Gaya, near the Phalgu - in the Magadhan heartland.

periodLevel.summary: Mauryan. Four caves at Barabar were excavated under Ashoka, the Sudama cave dated to his twelfth regnal year, c. 261 BCE; three more on the Nagarjuni hill were dedicated by his grandson Dasharatha, c. 230 BCE. Dedicatory inscriptions in Brahmi name the donor as Piyadasi.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The oldest surviving rock-cut caves in India, and the only monuments anywhere built by a state for the Ajivikas.
points: Each cave is cut into hard granite and finished to a mirror polish - the Mauryan polish also seen on the Ashokan pillars. That so fine a surface was achieved in granite, and never repeated after the Mauryas, is a standing puzzle in the history of Indian stone-working.

The Lomas Rishi facade imitates in stone a timber-and-thatch hut: a curved architrave with lattice infill and a frieze of elephants approaching a stupa. This is the earliest *chaitya* arch, and the ancestor of every later rock-cut facade from Bhaja and Karle to the Buddhist caves at Ajanta.

They were granted to the Ajivikas, the determinist sect of Makkhali Gosala who held that all events are fixed by *niyati*. Royal endowment of a sect that was neither Buddhist nor Jain nor Brahmanical is the best material evidence for Mauryan religious policy.
In several inscriptions the word Ajivika has been deliberately chiselled out - later sectarian erasure, and a rare physical trace of religious rivalry.

content.sourcesLine: Basham, *History and Doctrines of the Ajivikas*; Upinder Singh, ch. 7; Thapar, *Early India*

location.summary: Gharapuri island in Mumbai harbour, Raigad district, Maharashtra, about 10 km by sea from the Mumbai shore - a basalt island commanding the Konkan coast's finest anchorage.

periodLevel.summary: Mid-6th century CE, the great Shaiva cave usually attributed to the Kalachuris of Mahishmati under Krishnaraja, though Konkan Maurya patronage is also argued. Seven excavations in all: five Brahmanical caves on the western hill and two Buddhist on the eastern. UNESCO World Heritage Site.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The summit of Shaiva rock-cut sculpture in India - a cave conceived as a single theological argument in stone.
points: The Great Cave, about 39 m across, is planned on two axes at once, one running to the linga shrine and the other to the Sadashiva image, so the abstract and the iconic forms of Shiva are worshipped in one space.

The Trimurti or Sadashiva bust, nearly 6 m high, shows three of Shiva's five aspects: Aghora or Bhairava in wrath to one side, Vamadeva serene and feminine to the other, and Tatpurusha in meditative calm at the centre. It is usually read not as the Brahma-Vishnu-Shiva triad but as the unity of Shiva's own natures.

The surrounding panels form a deliberate sequence of opposites - Ardhanarishvara and Gangadhara, Nataraja and Yogishvara, the marriage of Shiva and Parvati against the slaying of Andhaka - setting creation beside destruction, union beside asceticism.

The Portuguese named the island from a stone elephant at the landing, now in the Bhau Daji Lad Museum, and are reported to have used the sculptures for musket practice, which accounts for much of the damage.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Basham, *The Wonder that was India*; Thapar, *Early India*

location.summary: Malayadipatti, Pudukkottai district, Tamil Nadu, in the dry rocky uplands between the Kaveri delta and the Vaigai - the same low granite country that carries Sittanavasal, Narthamalai and Tirumayam.

periodLevel.summary: Two rock-cut shrines of about the 8th century CE, excavated under the Muttaraiyar chieftains, feudatories who held this tract between Pallava and Pandya power. The Olakkanesvara cave is Shaiva, the Ranganatha cave Vaishnava. Inscriptions of the Muttaraiyars and later of the Cholas and Pandyas record endowments; the surviving paintings are later, of the Vijayanagara-Nayaka centuries.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A rare paired Shaiva and Vaishnava rock-cut group, and one of the few Tamil sites where mural painting survives over sculpture.
points: The Ranganatha cave holds a reclining Vishnu on Adishesha cut from the rock face, with Bhudevi and attendant figures - a southern counterpart to the Anantashayana at Undavalli and Mamallapuram.

Parts of the sculpture were covered in painted stucco, and traces of lime-ground painting survive on the ceilings and walls, showing birds, human figures and floral work. Because so little Tamil painting survives between Sittanavasal and the Nayaka period, even fragments here carry weight.

The Muttaraiyar patronage is the historical point. Cave excavation in the Tamil country is usually credited to Mahendravarman I and the Pallavas, but Malayadipatti shows subordinate chieftains commissioning the same work - evidence that the practice spread well below the level of the great dynasties.
Having both a Shiva and a Vishnu shrine cut at one outcrop, endowed by the same line, argues against reading Shaiva-Vaishnava rivalry into every Tamil site.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; ASI, *South Indian Inscriptions*; *Pudukkottai State Inscriptions*

location.summary: Sitabinji, Keonjhar district, Odisha, on the Sita river in the upper Baitarani basin - a wooded tract of northern Odisha, well away from the coastal temple belt.

periodLevel.summary: A natural rock shelter called Ravanachhaya, shaped like a half-open umbrella, carrying a tempera mural usually dated to the 6th-7th centuries CE. A short inscription in box-headed characters reads *Disabhanja*, tying the painting to the Bhanja dynasty of northern Odisha. A four-faced *mukhalinga* stands at the site.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The only surviving early mural painting in eastern India, and one of very few anywhere outside Ajanta, Bagh and Sittanavasal.
points: The painting shows a royal procession: a crowned figure riding an elephant under an umbrella, footmen leading, horsemen and women following, some dancing. The subject is secular and courtly, not devotional - which is what makes it unusual, since almost all surviving early Indian painting is religious.

It is executed in tempera on the rock face, in red, yellow and white earth pigments, and the drawing is closer to folk idiom than to the Ajanta court style. Together the two give a rare sense of regional variation in early painting.

The Bhanja reading gives eastern India a named dynasty for the work, and the site is read as a royal retreat or hunting camp rather than a shrine - the umbrella-shaped shelter being a natural pavilion.
The mukhalinga is evidence that Shaivism was established in Odisha well before the great Bhubaneswar temples, filling a gap between the Kharavela period and the Somavamshis.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 9 and 10; ASI; *Orissa Historical Research Journal*

location.summary: Thirunandikkara, Kanyakumari district, Tamil Nadu, near Thiruvattar in the Kodayar basin at the southern tip of the Western Ghats. The site lay in Travancore until the States Reorganisation of 1956, which is why its art belongs to the Kerala tradition though it is now in Tamil Nadu.

periodLevel.summary: A rock-cut cave temple of about the 8th-9th centuries CE, excavated under the Ay dynasty. It began as a Jaina shrine and was converted to Shaiva use as a Mahadeva temple; eleven later inscriptions of the imperial Cholas, recording endowments for the Sadaya festival, mark the period of Chola authority over Venad.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The oldest surviving murals in the Kerala style - the starting point of a painting tradition that runs to Mattancherry and Padmanabhapuram.
points: The paintings, on the cave's inner walls, carry scenes from the *Ramayana* and *Mahabharata*. The method is visible in the surviving work: the figures were first drawn in outline and then filled with mineral colour, the technique later codified in the Kerala mural manuals.
They give the region an artistic sequence it otherwise lacks, standing between the Pallava-Pandya painting of Sittanavasal and the fully formed Kerala style of the 16th century.

The Jaina-to-Shaiva conversion is the site's other value. Jainism was strong in the far south in the early centuries CE and receded before the Shaiva bhakti of the Nayanmars; a single cave that changed hands documents that displacement physically.
The Chola inscriptions matter politically: they show imperial Chola reach into Venad, and are used to date the extension of Chola administration down the west coast.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; ASI, *South Indian Inscriptions*; *Travancore Archaeological Series*

location.summary: Udayagiri, Vidisha district, Madhya Pradesh, a sandstone ridge above the Bes near its confluence with the Betwa, about 4 km from Vidisha and within sight of Sanchi. Not to be confused with the Jain Udayagiri in Odisha.

periodLevel.summary: Gupta period. Twenty rock-cut shrines cut in the late 4th and early 5th centuries CE. Cave 6 carries an inscription of Chandragupta II dated Gupta era 82, i.e. 401-02 CE, recording the visit of the king with his minister Virasena; Cave 20 has a Jain record of Kumaragupta I, GE 106 = 425-26 CE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The earliest datable Hindu cave temples in India, and the birthplace of the classical Gupta iconographic programme.
points: The colossal Varaha panel in Cave 5 shows Vishnu as the boar lifting Bhudevi from the cosmic ocean, watched by ranks of gods and sages with the personified oceans below. It is read as political allegory as much as myth - the earth rescued and restored, matching Chandragupta II's own claim to have reunified the land after the Shaka campaign.

The site is deliberately syncretic: Vaishnava, Shaiva and Shakta images together - Anantashayi Vishnu, an *ekamukha* linga, Durga Mahishasuramardini, Ganesha and the Saptamatrikas - with a Jain shrine at Cave 20.

Architecturally it is a hybrid: rock-cut sanctums given structural pillared porticos, with carved doorways and *purnaghata* capitals. The doorframe with river goddesses first takes its classical form here, and is then repeated at Deogarh and across the Nagara tradition.
That a dated royal inscription sits beside the sculpture makes Udayagiri the fixed reference point for dating all other Gupta art.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 9; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Thapar, *Early India*

location.summary: Undavalli, Guntur district, Andhra Pradesh, cut into a sandstone hillside on the south bank of the Krishna, opposite Vijayawada - in the delta country that was the core of the Andhra kingdoms.

periodLevel.summary: Excavated from about the 4th-5th centuries CE and elaborated later, associated with the Vishnukundin dynasty, who ruled the Krishna-Godavari doab between the Satavahanas and the Eastern Chalukyas. The earliest cells are Buddhist; the surviving programme is Vaishnava.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A four-storeyed rock-cut temple - the tallest such excavation in the south - and a clear record of a Buddhist site passing into Brahmanical use.
points: The facade rises in four tiers of pillared verandahs cut back into the hill, each storey set behind the one below. Nothing else in Indian rock-cut architecture is stacked this way, and it is the site's main architectural claim.

The second storey holds a colossal reclining Vishnu - Anantashayana, carved from a single block - together with panels of Vaishnava deities. It is among the largest monolithic images in southern India.

The lowest level retains plain cells and a pillared hall of the kind cut for Buddhist monks, with figures read as monastic. Andhra was the Buddhist heartland of Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda, and Undavalli shows what happened to that establishment as Vaishnavism became the dynastic religion under the Vishnukundins.
The Vishnukundins are otherwise known mainly from copper-plate grants, so Undavalli, with Mogalrajapuram nearby, supplies their architecture.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 9 and 10; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; ASI

location.summary: Armamalai, near Vellore in the Palar basin of northern Tamil Nadu - a natural cave in a granite hill in the tract between Kanchipuram and the Karnataka border.

periodLevel.summary: A Jaina cave shrine with paintings assigned to about the 8th century CE, in the Pallava-Pandya period, and Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions on the walls that belong to a considerably earlier phase of Jaina occupation.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A rare surviving example of Jaina cave painting in northern Tamil Nadu, and evidence of long monastic use of one shelter.
points: The murals were executed in fresco and tempera technique on a lime ground, showing Jaina themes and decorative motifs. With Sittanavasal and the Malayadipatti fragments they make up almost the entire surviving corpus of early Tamil painting.

The Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions place Jaina ascetics here in the early historic centuries, long before the paintings. Jainism reached the Tamil country by the last centuries BCE, and the cave shelters of Madurai, Pudukkottai and the northern districts are the material record of that.
Rock art and petroglyphs reported at the site suggest use of the shelter before the Jaina occupation, so the sequence runs from prehistoric to monastic to painted.

Jainism's retreat in the Tamil country before Shaiva and Vaishnava bhakti from the 7th century is the context for why these sites are ruins rather than living temples, and the persecution narratives in the *Periya Puranam* are the literary side of the same story - to be treated as hagiography rather than record.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8 and 10; ASI

location.summary: The Dharashiv caves, about 8 km from Dharashiv town, formerly Osmanabad, in the Balaghat hills of Marathwada, Maharashtra - basalt country on the Deccan plateau between the Godavari and the Bhima.

periodLevel.summary: Seven caves excavated between roughly the 5th and 7th centuries CE. They began as Buddhist and were converted to Jaina use, the principal shrines now holding tirthankara images, Parshvanatha among them.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A rock-cut group whose conversion from Buddhist to Jaina use is legible in the excavation itself.
points: Cave 2, the largest, follows the Buddhist vihara plan - a pillared hall with cells around it and a shrine at the rear - but the shrine now holds a seated tirthankara with attendant figures. The plan is Buddhist, the occupancy Jaina, and the sequence can be read directly off the stone.
The layout is often compared with Ajanta, and the caves are treated as a provincial member of the western Deccan rock-cut tradition that runs from Bhaja and Karle through Ajanta and Ellora.

They matter for the wider question of what became of Deccan Buddhism. Rather than sites being destroyed, several were taken over by Jaina and Brahmanical communities as patronage shifted - the same process visible at Ellora, where Buddhist, Hindu and Jaina excavations sit on one cliff.
Jaina tradition connects the caves with Karandai and the Jaina presence in Marathwada, and local legend attaches them to the Mahabharata, as the many "Pandav Leni" names across the Deccan do.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 9 and 10; Thapar, *Early India*; ASI

location.summary: Kambadahalli, Mandya district, Karnataka, in the Kaveri basin near Shravanabelagola - the name means "village of the pillar", from the free-standing column that stands before the temple.

periodLevel.summary: The Panchakuta Basadi, built under the Western Gangas between about the 9th and 10th centuries CE, with later Hoysala renovation. Dravida idiom in granite and soapstone.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The finest Ganga-period Jaina temple in Karnataka, and a rare example of the five-shrined *panchakuta* plan.
points: The complex joins five shrines - a *trikuta* group of three and a *dvikuta* pair - around shared halls, dedicated principally to Adinatha with Neminatha and Shantinatha. Multi-shrined temples are common in the Deccan but a five-celled Jaina arrangement of this quality is unusual.

The vimanas are stepped Dravida towers in tiers, showing the Ganga adaptation of the southern form, against the Nagara shikharas of contemporary Jaina building in Rajasthan and Gujarat. The regional split in Jaina architecture follows the regional split in Hindu architecture, which is the point to make.
The *Brahmadeva pillar* in front, a monolithic column crowned by a seated figure, is characteristic of Karnataka Jaina sites and recurs at Shravanabelagola.

The Western Gangas were the great Jaina patrons of the southern Deccan for six centuries - Chamundaraya's Bahubali colossus is the same dynasty's work - and Kambadahalli is their architectural counterpart to that statue.

location.summary: Kumbharia, Banaskantha district, northern Gujarat, at the foot of the Aravallis near Ambaji and close to the Rajasthan border - about 25 km from Mount Abu.

periodLevel.summary: Five Jaina temples in white marble built under the Chaulukya (Solanki) kings between the 11th and 13th centuries CE. The Mahavira temple carries an inscription of 1062; the others are dedicated to Parshvanatha, Shantinatha, Neminatha and Sambhavanatha.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The Solanki marble tradition at its earliest and best, and the immediate context for the more famous temples at Dilwara.
points: The temples are contemporary with the Vimala Vasahi at Dilwara, begun in 1031, and were built by the same regional workshops. Kumbharia is where the Maru-Gurjara marble idiom can be seen taking shape rather than in its finished form.

The ceilings are the achievement: concentric rings of carved lotus petals with deeply undercut pendant bosses, and narrative panels of scenes from the lives of the tirthankaras and of Krishna. Comparing a Kumbharia ceiling with a Luna Vasahi ceiling of 1230 shows two centuries of development in one craft.

The patrons were merchants and ministers of the Jaina mercantile community rather than kings, following the pattern of Vimala Shah and of Vastupala and Tejpala at Abu. Commercial capital, not royal revenue, paid for western India's finest architecture.
The site's proximity to the Shakta shrine at Ambaji, one of the major goddess temples of Gujarat, makes it a good illustration of adjacent and unrelated pilgrimage traditions.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I; ASI

location.summary: Mirpur, Sirohi district, southern Rajasthan, near Abu Road in the Aravalli foothills - a short distance from Mount Abu and the Dilwara group.

periodLevel.summary: The Parshvanatha temple, built in white marble and usually assigned to the 9th-10th centuries CE under Rajput patronage. It was damaged, by tradition in Mahmud Begada's Gujarat campaigns, and rebuilt in the 15th century; further restoration followed in the modern period.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Claimed as the oldest marble monument in Rajasthan, and the precursor to Dilwara.
points: If the 9th-10th century dating holds, Mirpur precedes the Vimala Vasahi at Dilwara by more than a century and represents the first use of the Makrana marble tradition that western India later made its own. That claim to priority is the reason the site matters, and it should be stated with the dating caveat attached.

The carving - pillared halls, figured brackets, deeply cut ceilings and a richly worked *torana* - is directly comparable to Dilwara, and the two are best studied together as one workshop tradition either side of the Gujarat-Rajasthan border.
The temple is dedicated to Parshvanatha, the 23rd tirthankara, whose historicity is generally accepted and who is placed roughly two and a half centuries before Mahavira.

Its cycle of destruction and rebuilding is typical of western Indian Jaina temples, and the Jaina practice of *jirnoddhara*, the meritorious restoration of decayed temples, is why so few survive in original fabric.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I; ASI

location.summary: Parasnath hill, also called Shikharji or Sammed Shikhar, Giridih district, Jharkhand, rising to about 1,365 m - the highest peak in the state, on the Chhotanagpur plateau.

periodLevel.summary: A Jaina tirtha of the greatest antiquity in tradition, associated with the historical Parshvanatha, the 23rd tirthankara, generally placed in the 8th century BCE. The *tonks* or shrines along the summit ridge are mostly of the 18th and 19th centuries, rebuilt repeatedly on older sites.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The holiest Jaina pilgrimage site of all - where twenty of the twenty-four tirthankaras are held to have attained *moksha*.
points: The concentration of liberations makes Shikharji a *siddha-kshetra* of the first rank, ahead of even Shatrunjaya for many communities. Pilgrims walk a circuit of about 27 km over the ridge, visiting each tonk.

Its position matters historically: the hill lies in the old Magadhan sphere where Jainism first took shape, and the association with Parshvanatha connects it to the pre-Mahavira phase of the religion. Parshvanatha's four vows, to which Mahavira added celibacy as the fifth, are the standard evidence that Jainism predates Mahavira rather than beginning with him.
Both Digambaras and Svetambaras hold the site sacred and have long disputed its control, a conflict that has generated litigation into the present.
The surrounding forest and the Santal communities of the plateau give the hill a second, unrelated significance in discussions of tribal Jharkhand.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 6; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*

location.summary: Pawapuri, Nalanda district, Bihar, in the plain south of the Ganga between Rajgir and Bihar Sharif - in the heartland of ancient Magadha, close to Nalanda and Rajagriha.

periodLevel.summary: The place where Mahavira attained *nirvana*, traditionally in 527 BCE by Jaina reckoning, though most modern scholars place his death nearer 468 BCE. The Jal Mandir, standing in the middle of a lotus tank, marks the cremation site; the present structure is a later rebuilding.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The site of Mahavira's death, and the eastern anchor of the Jaina sacred geography of Magadha.
points: Jaina tradition holds that so much earth was taken from around the cremation site by devotees that a tank formed, which is why the principal temple stands on an island reached by a causeway. Whatever its origin, the arrangement is unusual and memorable.

Mahavira's life joins the Magadhan sites: born at Kundagrama near Vaishali, he renounced, attained *kevala jnana* at Jrimbhikagrama on the Rijupalika, preached at Rajagriha and died here. That circuit is the geography of early Jainism, and it overlaps almost exactly with the Buddha's, in the same kingdoms and the same decades.
His death is the fixed point of the Jaina calendar, from which the Vira Nirvana Samvat era is reckoned - the era still used in Jaina inscriptions and manuscripts, beginning 527 BCE.
Tradition also holds that Pawapuri is where the Jaina community divided on the succession, and the councils that followed at Pataliputra and Valabhi attempted to fix the canon.

location.summary: Shatrunjaya hill above Palitana, Bhavnagar district, Gujarat, rising some 600 m from the Saurashtra plain near the Shetrunji river - a ridge crowned entirely by temples.

periodLevel.summary: A tirtha from early centuries in tradition, with the surviving temples built and rebuilt from the 11th century onward. Most of what stands is of the 16th to 19th centuries, following destruction attributed to Sultanate and later raids; the Adinatha temple was rebuilt in 1530.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The largest temple city in the world - some 863 shrines on one hill - and the supreme tirtha of the Svetambara Jains.
points: Jaina tradition holds that Rishabha, the first tirthankara, preached his first sermon here, and that countless ascetics attained liberation on the hill. It is a *siddha-kshetra*, a place of liberation, which is what gives it precedence over sites associated with a single teacher.

No one lives on the summit. The temples are locked at dusk and the priests descend, so the hill is a city of gods rather than of people - an arrangement that has no parallel and is the detail worth citing.
The temples are grouped in nine walled enclosures, *tuks*, each funded by a merchant family or community, in Maru-Gurjara marble work descended from the Solanki idiom seen at Dilwara and Kumbharia.

The scale of it is evidence for the wealth of Gujarati Jaina mercantile communities and for their practice of converting commercial profit into religious endowment - the same pattern that built Dilwara and Ranakpur.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I; ASI

location.summary: Shravanabelagola, Hassan district, Karnataka, between the two hills of Vindhyagiri and Chandragiri with a tank - the *belagola*, white pond - between them, in the Hemavati basin of the southern Deccan.

periodLevel.summary: A Jaina centre from about the 3rd century BCE in tradition and certainly from the Western Ganga period. The Bahubali colossus was raised about 981 CE by Chamundaraya, minister and general of the Ganga king Rachamalla IV. Some five hundred inscriptions on the two hills run from about the 6th century to modern times.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The principal Digambara Jaina site in India, and home to the tallest free-standing monolithic statue in the world.
points: The Gommateshvara or Bahubali image on Vindhyagiri stands about 57 feet, carved from a single block of light grey granite and polished to a high finish. It shows Bahubali in *kayotsarga*, standing in meditation so long that creepers have twined up his legs - the story of a prince who won a war and renounced its fruits.
The *Mahamastakabhisheka*, the anointing of the image, is performed roughly every twelve years and is one of the largest Jaina observances anywhere.

The inscriptions are the largest single body of Jaina epigraphy in India, recording grants, *sallekhana* deaths and dynastic history from the Gangas, Rashtrakutas, Hoysalas and Vijayanagara. The Bhadrabahu tradition on Chandragiri - the migration from Magadha and Chandragupta Maurya's death by ritual fasting - is treated in the Chandragiri Hill entry in the non-Ashokan inscriptions chapter.
Chamundaraya also commissioned the *Chavundaraya Purana* in Kannada prose, so the same patron funded sculpture and literature.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7 and 10; Thapar, *Early India*; *Epigraphia Carnatica* II

location.summary: Shri Mahavirji, Karauli district, eastern Rajasthan, on the bank of the Gambhir river in the tract between the Chambal and the Banas - roughly midway between Jaipur and Agra.

periodLevel.summary: A modern Digambara pilgrimage complex grown around an image of Mahavira said to have been recovered from a mound at the village of Chandangaon in the 18th century. The main temple and the five associated shrines date from the 18th and 19th centuries, with later additions.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The principal Digambara pilgrimage centre of Rajasthan, and an example of a tirtha created in the modern period rather than inherited from antiquity.
points: Most of the sites in this chapter are ancient, and Shri Mahavirji is useful precisely because it is not. It shows the mechanism by which Indian sacred places come into being: a chance find, a local cult, a community's endowment, and within two centuries a major pilgrimage with its own fair and institutions.
The complex is built in red sandstone with *shikharas* in the north Indian idiom, and includes the Kamal Mandir, the Shantinatha temple and the Bhagwan Mahavira temple with the recovered image.
It is a Digambara site, and its growth in eastern Rajasthan from the 18th century tracks the prosperity of Jaina trading communities in the region under Jaipur and Karauli patronage.

The annual Mahavir Jayanti fair draws pilgrims from across northern India, and local Meena and other communities participate - the same cross-community pattern seen at Ramdevra elsewhere in Rajasthan.

location.summary: Sittanavasal, Pudukkottai district, Tamil Nadu, in the granite uplands between the Kaveri delta and the Pandya country. The name is read as *Siddhanavasal*, the abode of siddhas. A duplicate record exists in the rock-cut caves chapter and the two should be merged.

periodLevel.summary: Two phases. The *Eladipattam* rock shelter with polished stone beds and Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions belongs to about the 2nd century BCE to the 1st century CE; the *Arivar Koil* rock-cut temple and its paintings are of the 7th century, Pandya period, with a 9th-century inscription of Srivallabha recording renovation.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The best surviving Jaina paintings in India, and evidence for Jaina monasticism in the far south from the last centuries BCE.
points: The paintings, in fresco-secco on lime plaster, show a lotus pond with elephants, buffaloes, fish, geese and men gathering flowers, with dancing figures and celestial beings on the ceiling and pillars. They are read as the *samavasarana*, the assembly where a tirthankara preaches, with the pond as the *khatika bhumi* that the liberated soul crosses.

Almost nothing else of south Indian painting survives between Ajanta and the Vijayanagara period, so with the fragments at Malayadipatti and Kanchipuram these murals carry the whole intervening tradition.

The shelter above, with seventeen polished rock beds each with a raised stone pillow and Tamil-Brahmi donative inscriptions naming monks, documents the austere Jaina monasticism of the Tamil country - the community that produced the *Tirukkural*'s intellectual milieu and later receded before Shaiva bhakti.
Those inscriptions are among the earliest written records in Tamil.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8 and 10; Thapar, *Early India*; ASI

location.summary: Sonagiri, Datia district, Madhya Pradesh, on a low hill in the Bundelkhand plateau between Gwalior and Jhansi - the name means "golden peak".

periodLevel.summary: A Digambara Jaina temple hill with some seventy-seven temples on the summit and about twenty-six more in the village below. The earliest shrines are assigned to around the 9th-10th centuries, in the Pratihara and Chandela period, with most of the present buildings of the 17th century onward.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A *siddha-kshetra* of the Digambara tradition, and a clear example of the Indian temple-hill type.
points: Tradition holds that Nanganang Kumar and five and a half crore ascetics attained liberation here, which makes it a place of liberation rather than a place associated with a single teacher - the same category as Shatrunjaya and Shikharji.

The principal temple, number 57, holds an image of Chandraprabha, the eighth tirthankara, about 11 feet high. The temples are plain whitewashed structures with tall *shikharas*, deliberately austere compared with the marble work of Dilwara and Kumbharia.

The three great Digambara temple-hills - Sonagiri and Sammed Shikhar in the north and east, with Shatrunjaya as the Svetambara counterpart in the west - map the sectarian geography of Jainism, and the split between Digambara and Svetambara is best taught through which communities hold which sites.
Bundelkhand's Jaina heritage runs from here through the Chandela Jain group at Khajuraho to the colossi at Gwalior, so the region has a continuous Jaina record from the 9th century.

location.summary: The twin hills of Udayagiri and Khandagiri, about 6 km west of Bhubaneswar, Odisha, facing each other across a ravine near the ancient city of Sisupalgarh.

periodLevel.summary: Thirty-three rock-cut caves, eighteen on Udayagiri and fifteen on Khandagiri, excavated for Jaina ascetics under Kharavela of the Mahameghavahana line, generally 1st century BCE, with some later medieval additions and Jain images of the 10th-12th centuries.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The earliest Jaina rock-cut monastic complex in India, and the physical expression of Kharavela's patronage.
points: The caves are *lena* - austere dormitories for monks, with low ceilings, sloping floors and stone pillows cut into the rock, quite unlike the spacious Buddhist viharas of the western Deccan. Comfort was not the point, and the contrast with Ajanta or Karle is worth drawing.

The Ranigumpha, Cave 1, is the largest and the exception: two storeyed, with sculpted friezes of processions, hunts, dancers and a scene often read as the abduction of a woman, and with pillared verandahs. It is the finest early sculpture in eastern India.

The Hathigumpha on Udayagiri carries Kharavela's seventeen-line inscription, the fullest royal autobiography from ancient India. See the Hathigumpha entry in the non-Ashokan inscriptions chapter for its content.

The Ganesha Gumpha, Bagha Gumpha and Sarpa Gumpha take their names from the animal forms carved at their entrances. Khandagiri's later caves hold tirthankara reliefs showing continued Jaina use for a thousand years.

location.summary: Bidar, northern Karnataka, on a laterite plateau above the Manjra basin at the edge of the Deccan trap - chosen for its healthier climate and fertile land over the drier Gulbarga.

periodLevel.summary: Bahmani capital from c. 1425-32, when Ahmad Shah I Wali moved the seat from Gulbarga; then capital of the Barid Shahis after the Bahmani kingdom broke up, until Bijapur absorbed it in 1619 and the Mughals took it in 1656. The Mahmud Gawan madrasa was built in 1472.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The finest surviving Persianate architecture of the Deccan sultanates, and a medieval college whose ruin is itself a historical document.
points: The Mahmud Gawan madrasa was a three-storeyed college with lecture halls, a mosque, student quarters and a library said to hold three thousand manuscripts, faced in coloured tile mosaic in the Timurid manner of Samarkand and Khurasan. It is the clearest architectural evidence of direct Iranian and Central Asian contact with the Deccan.

Gawan, a Persian merchant who rose to be *wakil* of the kingdom, reformed the provincial *tarafs* and the revenue system. His execution in 1481 on forged evidence was the decisive episode in the feud between the *Afaqi* or foreign nobles and the *Dakhni* old guard - the factional split that broke the Bahmani state into the five Deccan sultanates.
Bidar fort, the Rangin Mahal with its mother-of-pearl inlay, the Solah Khamba mosque and the Bahmani and Barid tombs complete the ensemble.
The town gives its name to *bidri* ware, zinc alloy inlaid with silver - a craft that fuses Persian technique with Indian production.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I; J. L. Mehta, *Advanced Study in the History of Medieval India* I; ASI

location.summary: Dwarka, Devbhumi Dwarka district, Gujarat, at the mouth of the Gomti creek on the western tip of the Saurashtra peninsula - the first Indian landfall for shipping crossing the Arabian Sea from the Gulf.

periodLevel.summary: Occupation from the late Harappan and post-Harappan centuries, attested at Bet Dwarka offshore. The Sharada matha, Shankara's western seat, is assigned to the 8th century; the Dwarkadhish or Jagat Mandir temple in its present five-storeyed form is largely of the 15th-16th centuries on older foundations.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the Char Dham and the Sapta Puri, a working port, and the most contested piece of marine archaeology in India.
points: The *paschimamnaya* matha is assigned the Sama Veda and the *mahavakya* "Tattvamasi", completing the four-matha scheme with Sringeri, Puri and Badrinath.

Offshore excavations led by S. R. Rao from the 1980s recovered stone anchors, wall alignments and pottery in the submerged area, and were presented as the Dwarka of the *Mahabharata*. The dating and the identification are both disputed, and the site is the standard example for discussing how archaeological evidence gets attached to epic narrative. Present the finds and the controversy together.

The triangular and ring stone anchors are genuine evidence of a substantial anchorage, and Bet Dwarka has yielded late Harappan material, so an early maritime settlement is not in doubt even where the epic identification is.
As a port Dwarka handled the Gujarat coasting trade and the Gulf route, and the temple economy and the harbour reinforced each other - a pattern repeated at Somnath and Prabhas.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 5 and 10; Thapar, *Early India*; S. R. Rao, *The Lost City of Dvaraka*

location.summary: Malkhed, ancient Manyakheta, Kalaburagi (Gulbarga) district, Karnataka, on the Kagina river in the northern Deccan - the dry interior plateau between the Bhima and the Godavari.

periodLevel.summary: Rashtrakuta capital from c. 814 CE, when Amoghavarsha I moved the seat here, until the dynasty fell in 973. Sacked by the Paramara Siyaka II in 972, an event that marks the Rashtrakuta collapse; the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani then held the region.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The capital of the dynasty an Arab geographer ranked among the four great kingdoms of the world, and a court that made Kannada a literary language.
points: Al-Masudi, writing in the 10th century, named the Rashtrakuta *Balhara* one of the four greatest kings on earth beside the Abbasid caliph and the rulers of China and Byzantium - the standard external testimony to Rashtrakuta power, and evidence of the dynasty's Arab trade contacts through the Konkan ports.

Amoghavarsha I is credited with the *Kavirajamarga*, the earliest surviving literary work in Kannada, and with the Sanskrit *Prashnottara Ratnamalika*. A capital that produced the first Kannada poetics is the key point for questions on regional languages entering literature.

The court was a Jain centre: Jinasena wrote the *Adipurana* here, and Mahaviracharya composed the *Ganita Sara Sangraha*, the most important Indian mathematical text between Brahmagupta and Bhaskara II. Shaiva and Vaishnava learning was patronised alongside.
Little survives above ground, so Manyakheta is known largely from copper plates and literature - a reminder that an imperial capital can leave almost no architecture.

content.sourcesLine: Basham, *The Wonder that was India*; Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Thapar, *Early India*

location.summary: Nabadwip, Nadia district, West Bengal, on the west bank of the Bhagirathi where the Ganga turns south - a river town whose channel has shifted repeatedly, carrying parts of the old settlement away.

periodLevel.summary: A seat of Sanskrit learning from the 11th century, capital of the Sena kings under Lakshmanasena until Bakhtiyar Khalji's raid of c. 1204. Its intellectual peak is the 15th-16th centuries, when the Navya-Nyaya school flourished and Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, b. 1486, d. 1533, was born and took sannyasa here.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Two distinct claims on the same town - the most rigorous school of Sanskrit logic in late medieval India, and the source of the Bengal bhakti movement.
points: Navya-Nyaya, the "new logic", was developed here by Raghunatha Siromani and Vasudeva Sarvabhauma, building on Gangesha's *Tattvachintamani*. Its technical language for stating relations was adopted across Sanskrit disciplines, and Nabadwip displaced Mithila as the school that awarded degrees in logic.

Chaitanya founded Gaudiya Vaishnavism on the doctrine of *Achintya Bheda Abheda* - inconceivable difference and non-difference between god and the world - and made *sankirtana*, congregational singing of the divine name, its central practice. He left for Puri in 1510 and spent his last twenty-four years there.

The movement's social reach is the examinable point: it admitted low castes and Muslims, Haridasa Thakur being the best-known case, and it produced a body of Bengali devotional literature, above all Krishnadasa Kaviraja's *Chaitanya Charitamrita*.
That a centre of austere scholastic logic also produced ecstatic devotionalism is the standard illustration that the two streams were not opposed in practice.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* II; Krishnadasa Kaviraja, *Chaitanya Charitamrita*; S. K. De, *Early History of the Vaishnava Faith*

location.summary: Puri, Odisha, on the Bay of Bengal coast south of the Mahanadi delta - a shore town built around its temple, with the processional Bada Danda running from the shrine to the Gundicha temple.

periodLevel.summary: The Govardhana matha is assigned to Adi Shankara in the 8th century. The Jagannath temple was built by the Eastern Gangas from c. 1135; Puri's importance as a devotional centre peaks in the 16th century, when Chaitanya Mahaprabhu settled here from 1510 until his death in 1533.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the Char Dham, Shankara's eastern seat, and the place where the Jagannath cult became the ideology of a state. This entry covers the matha and the town; for the temple architecture see the Jagannath and Konark entry in the temple chapter.
points: The *purvamnaya* matha holds the Rig Veda and the *mahavakya* "Prajnanam Brahma". That the Advaita tradition planted a seat beside a cult as distinctly regional as Jagannath's is itself evidence of how Shankara's network absorbed local religion rather than displacing it.
From Anangabhima III the Eastern Gangas ruled formally as deputies of Jagannath, and the Gajapatis after them - kingship exercised on a god's behalf, the clearest Indian instance of a state deity.
Chaitanya's long residence made Puri the meeting point of Bengali Gaudiya Vaishnavism and Odia devotion, and it drew the *Panchasakha* poets who wrote in Odia rather than Sanskrit.
The *Madala Panji*, the temple's own chronicle, is a rare continuous indigenous historical record, used to reconstruct Odisha's dynastic sequence.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* II; *Madala Panji*

location.summary: The Langudi and Assia hills of Jajpur district, Odisha, between the Birupa and the Brahmani in the northern Mahanadi delta - the three sites of Lalitgiri, Ratnagiri and Udayagiri, together called Odisha's Diamond Triangle.

periodLevel.summary: A Buddhist monastic complex active from about the 1st-3rd centuries CE to the 11th-12th, under the Bhaumakaras and Somavamshis. Usually identified with the *Pu-sie-p'o-k'i-li* that Xuanzang describes in the 7th century as a great monastery in Odra.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The principal Buddhist university of eastern India outside Bihar, and the centre where Vajrayana takes shape.
points: Lalitgiri is the oldest of the three, with an apsidal *chaitya* hall and stupas; a casket found in its main stupa held corporeal relics, claimed by the excavators as relics of the Buddha himself - among very few such finds in India.

Ratnagiri yielded large monasteries with elaborately carved doorways, hundreds of votive stupas and a mass of Vajrayana images - Tara, Heruka, Marichi and mandala figures. It is a principal source for the iconography of Tantric Buddhism, and for arguing that Vajrayana developed in Odisha as much as in Bengal and Bihar.
Udayagiri, the largest, has produced an inscribed seal reading *Madhavapura Mahavihara*, giving the establishment its own name in its own words.

Xuanzang's account, the monastic seals and the scale of the remains together show Odisha as a Buddhist centre long after Buddhism had weakened elsewhere in India, which is why it matters in questions on Buddhism's decline.

location.summary: Sharda, in the Neelum (Kishanganga) valley about 140 km from Srinagar, in the part of the erstwhile princely state of Jammu and Kashmir now administered by Pakistan. The ruined temple and college stand where the Madhumati joins the Neelum.

periodLevel.summary: A seat of learning and a Shakti shrine attested from about the 6th century CE and flourishing under the Karkota, Utpala and Lohara dynasties to the 12th. The standing temple, in dressed limestone with the trefoil arches and pediments of the Kashmiri order, is usually assigned to the 8th-9th centuries.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The centre that made Kashmir the byword for Sanskrit scholarship - *Sharada Desha*, the land of the goddess of learning.
points: The Sharada script, used for Sanskrit in Kashmir and the Punjab hills from about the 8th century and ancestral to Gurmukhi and Takri, takes its name from this shrine. A script named after a university is unusual and is the most quotable fact about the site.

Its library and its authority in adjudicating scholarship drew visitors from across the subcontinent. Tradition records both Shankara and Ramanuja consulting texts here, the latter said to have come for a commentary on the *Brahma Sutra*; Al-Biruni names the shrine, and Kalhana's *Rajatarangini* refers to it.

It is counted among the eighteen *Maha Shakti Pithas*, where Sati's right hand is said to have fallen, so a major pilgrimage and a major college occupied one site - the normal medieval arrangement, seen also at Nalanda and Sringeri.
Its decline follows Kashmir's political disruption from the 14th century; the building was largely ruined by earthquake and neglect.

location.summary: Sringeri, Chikkamagaluru district, Karnataka, on the left bank of the Tunga in the Malnad forests of the Western Ghats, upstream of the Tunga-Bhadra confluence.

periodLevel.summary: The Sharada Peetham, traditionally the first of the four mathas founded by Adi Shankara in the 8th century, with Sureshvaracharya as its first head. Its documented history runs strongly from the 14th century, when the Vijayanagara kings became its patrons; the Vidyashankara temple dates to 1338.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The southern seat of Advaita Vedanta, and the best-documented case of a monastic institution shaping the founding of a kingdom.
points: It is the *dakshinamnaya* matha, assigned the Yajur Veda and the *mahavakya* "Aham Brahmasmi". Its unbroken succession of *jagadgurus* makes it the institutional continuity of Shankara's tradition rather than merely a shrine.

Vidyaranya, the 14th-century pontiff, is credited in tradition with inspiring Harihara and Bukka to found Vijayanagara, and the dynasty took the matha's blessing for its authority. The temple-state relationship - a monastery legitimising a kingdom, a kingdom endowing a monastery - is the point examiners want.

The Vidyashankara temple is architecturally hybrid, Hoysala in its stellate base and figural carving, Vijayanagara in its pillars. Twelve zodiac pillars are arranged so that the sun strikes each in its own month.

Sringeri's copper-plate grants and correspondence, including letters from Tipu Sultan after a Maratha raid on the matha in 1791, are used as evidence for how rulers of every religion dealt with established religious institutions.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Thapar, *Early India*; J. L. Mehta, *Advanced Study in the History of Medieval India* I

location.summary: Udupi, coastal Karnataka, on the narrow Tulu Nadu plain between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea, near the Swarna river.

periodLevel.summary: The Krishna Matha was founded by Madhvacharya, c. 1238-1317 CE, who established the Dvaita school of Vedanta here and set up the *Ashta Matha*, eight monasteries under his direct disciples. The Haridasa movement flourished from the 15th-16th centuries.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The seat of Dvaita Vedanta - the systematic dualist answer to Shankara's Advaita - and the source of the Kannada devotional tradition.
points: Madhva argued for an absolute and permanent distinction between the individual soul and Brahman, and for a fivefold difference (*pancha-bheda*) running through reality. Placed against Shankara's Advaita at Sringeri and Ramanuja's Vishishtadvaita at Srirangam, the three mathas of the western Deccan and Tamil country give the full range of Vedantic positions in one region.

The eight mathas govern the temple by *paryaya*, each taking a two-year turn in rotation - a formalised sharing of authority that has worked without a single head for seven centuries, and a useful counter-example to the idea that Indian religious institutions were always hierarchical.

The image of Krishna is worshipped through the *Navagraha Kindi*, a nine-holed window. Tradition holds the wall opened for Kanakadasa, a saint of low caste refused entry at the door. The *Kanakana Kindi* is the standard illustration of bhakti's confrontation with caste exclusion, and of the compromise that followed.
Purandaradasa, called the father of Carnatic music, and Kanakadasa belong to this Haridasa tradition of Kannada *kirtanas*.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Thapar, *Early India*; B. N. K. Sharma, *History of the Dvaita School of Vedanta*

location.summary: Arikamedu, on the Ariyankuppam river about 4 km south of Puducherry town, on the Coromandel coast - a sandbar site at a river mouth, the standard setting for an east-coast anchorage.

periodLevel.summary: Occupied from about the 2nd century BCE to the 2nd century CE, with later phases. Excavated by Jouveau-Dubreuil, then Mortimer Wheeler in 1945, and later by Casal and Vimala Begley. Generally identified with the *Poduke* of the *Periplus* and Ptolemy.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The type-site of Indo-Roman trade, and the site whose reinterpretation changed how that trade is understood.
points: The Roman material is unambiguous: Arretine ware, the red-gloss Italian tableware stamped with its potters' names, amphorae that carried wine and olive oil, Roman lamps, glass and engraved gems - the largest such assemblage in India.

Alongside it lies a fully local industry. Brick-built dyeing vats, tanks and warehouse structures point to muslin being dyed and finished for export, and the site produced the rouletted ware and Black-and-Red Ware of the Tamil country.

Wheeler read it as a Roman trading station, almost a colony. Begley's later work showed a substantial Indian settlement that predated the Roman contact and continued after it, trading with Rome rather than serving it. That correction - from Roman outpost to Indian port with Roman customers - is the point to make, and a good example of how colonial-era archaeology overstated external agency.
Sangam poems describing *yavana* ships and the wine they brought corroborate the material record, letting literature and excavation be read against each other.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8; Thapar, *Early India*; Vimala Begley, *The Ancient Port of Arikamedu*

location.summary: Bharuch, ancient Barygaza or Bhrigukachchha, on the north bank of the Narmada near its mouth on the Gulf of Khambhat, Gujarat - the outlet of the whole Narmada corridor into the Arabian Sea.

periodLevel.summary: An international port from pre-Mauryan times through the Satavahana, Western Kshatrapa, Gupta and Gurjara periods, and still important under the Sultanate and the Mughals. Its classical description is in the *Periplus of the Erythraean Sea*, c. 1st century CE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The principal western port of ancient India, and the sea end of the two great overland routes.
points: Two arms of the Uttarapatha converged here: one from Taxila through the Punjab, down the Yamuna to Mathura, then Ujjain to Bharuch; the other from Taxila down the lower Indus and along the coast. A port fed by inland highways is the clearest illustration of how India's overland and maritime trade were one system.

The *Periplus* gives unusual navigational detail - the treacherous approach through shoals and the Narmada's tidal bore, with royal pilots sent out to bring ships in. It also records the exchange of gifts with the local king, evidence of state supervision of foreign trade.
Exports were cotton cloth, spices, ivory, agate and carnelian; imports wine, copper, tin, lead, coral, glass and Roman coin. Bead-making and ring-well construction are attested archaeologically.
It changed hands between the Satavahanas and the Western Kshatrapas repeatedly, so control of Bharuch is a proxy for who held the Deccan trade in the early centuries CE.

location.summary: Chattogram, on the Karnaphuli river near its mouth on the Bay of Bengal, south-eastern Bangladesh - the only deep-water harbour on the deltaic coast, where the hills reach the sea.

periodLevel.summary: A port from the early medieval period, described by Ibn Battuta in the 1340s. Contested from the 15th century between the sultans of Bengal, the Arakanese kings of Mrauk-U and Portuguese freebooters, until Shaista Khan, Aurangzeb's governor of Bengal, took it in 1666 and renamed it Islamabad.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The Bay of Bengal's principal eastern port, and the frontier where Mughal authority finally met the sea.
points: The Portuguese called it *Porto Grande*, against the *Porto Pequeno* of Satgaon, and the pair is the standard way of describing Bengal's two medieval outlets to the sea.

From the late 16th century the Arakanese and the Portuguese *Feringhi* operated a slave-raiding trade up the Bengal rivers, depopulating parts of the delta. Shaista Khan's campaign of 1665-66, using a purpose-built river fleet, ended it - one of the few Mughal operations that was genuinely naval.

Its capture completed Mughal control of Bengal's coastline and secured the revenue-richest province of the empire, which is why the episode appears in questions on Aurangzeb's eastern policy rather than only in local history.
The port linked Bengal cotton and rice to Arakan, Burma, Malacca and beyond, and remained the outlet for the eastern delta under the British.

location.summary: Debal or Daybul, at the mouth of the Indus in Sindh, Pakistan, generally identified with the excavated port of Banbhore east of Karachi on the Gharo creek - a channel the Indus has long since abandoned.

periodLevel.summary: Founded in the early centuries CE and prominent through the 7th-13th, it was the landing point of Muhammad bin Qasim's expedition in 711-712 CE and remained Sindh's chief port under Arab rule before silting and the river's shift left it stranded.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The port at which the Arab conquest of Sindh began, and the site of the earliest dated mosque in the subcontinent.
points: The *Chachnama* records that the seizure of Arab ships off Debal - carrying, in the account, gifts and Muslim women from Sri Lanka - gave Hajjaj the pretext for the invasion. The campaign opened with the storming of Debal's great temple, whose flagstaff the Arabs brought down.

Banbhore has yielded a fortified town with a congregational mosque bearing an inscription of 727 CE, the earliest dated mosque in South Asia, alongside Sassanian, Islamic and Chinese pottery and a working industrial quarter.

Its exports were cotton cloth, indigo and leather, and the town was known for sword-making; the route inland carried goods to Multan and on to Khurasan, so Debal joins the sea and the Central Asian land routes.

The site is also standard evidence in the argument that the Arab conquest of Sindh was a commercially motivated frontier operation with limited wider consequence, rather than the beginning of Muslim rule in India proper.

location.summary: Kalyan, Thane district, Maharashtra, at the head of the Ulhas creek on the Konkan coast - the inland end of a tidal inlet, reached from the Deccan through the Naneghat and Bhor passes.

periodLevel.summary: The *Kalliena* of the *Periplus*, active from the early centuries CE under the Satavahanas and Western Kshatrapas, still notable in the 6th century, and later held in turn by the Sultanate, the Portuguese, the Mughals, the Marathas and the British.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A port whose classical description records commercial warfare between two Indian dynasties - the sharpest such passage in ancient Indian sources.
points: The *Periplus* states that Kalliena was a lawful market in the time of Saraganus the elder - Satakarni of the Satavahanas - but that after Sandanes, the Western Kshatrapa power, took possession, Greek ships putting in there were seized and taken under guard to Barygaza. It is direct evidence that control of ports was a weapon in the Satavahana-Kshatrapa struggle.

Its hinterland routes tie it to the Naneghat inscription and the Buddhist caves at Kanheri, Karle and Bhaja, all of which were endowed by merchants and guilds using this corridor. Port, pass and cave monastery form a single economic unit.

Cosmas Indicopleustes in the 6th century records Kalliana as a place of trade with a resident Christian community under a bishop consecrated in Persia - early evidence of the Church of the East on the Indian coast.

location.summary: Kannur, the Cannanore of European sources, on the north Malabar coast of Kerala, with the harbour at Ayikkara and the headland later crowned by St Angelo fort.

periodLevel.summary: The port of the Kolathiri rajas of Kolathunadu, prominent in the 12th-15th centuries in trade with Persia and Arabia. The Portuguese built St Angelo in 1505 under Francisco de Almeida; the Dutch took it in 1663 and sold it to the Arakkal family in 1772; the British held it as their western-coast military headquarters until 1887.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The horse port of the Malabar coast, and the seat of Kerala's only Muslim ruling house.
points: Medieval Indian states had no domestic supply of cavalry horses, and Kannur was one of the principal points at which Arabian and Persian horses were landed for the Deccan and south Indian kingdoms. Marco Polo remarks on the traffic. The horse trade is a standard theme in questions on why coastal control mattered to inland powers.

The Arakkal Ali Rajas, based here, were the only Muslim dynasty to rule in Kerala, held the Lakshadweep islands, and maintained a fleet - an unusual case of a Muslim maritime principality within a Hindu regional order.

The Kolathiri's rivalry with the Zamorin of Kozhikode gave the Portuguese their opening: Almeida was welcomed at Kannur precisely because Calicut resisted him. European penetration exploited existing Indian rivalries rather than creating them.
Pepper, cardamom and sandalwood were the outbound cargoes.

location.summary: Karachi, Sindh, Pakistan, on the Arabian Sea west of the Indus delta, where the coast turns towards the Makran - the last sheltered anchorage before the desert shore.

periodLevel.summary: Identified with the *Krokola* from which Alexander's admiral Nearchus began his voyage back along the coast in 325 BCE. The Indus-mouth ports of the *Periplus* lie close by. The modern city grew from the fishing settlement of Kolachi in the 18th century; the British took it in 1839 and made it the port of the Indus.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The maritime gateway of the north-west, where the Indus route meets the sea and the overland Iranian routes meet both.
points: Nearchus's voyage, recorded by Arrian, is the earliest detailed account of navigation on the Indian coast and fixes the site in the historical record from the 4th century BCE.

The *Periplus* describes this stretch as the outlet for goods brought down the Indus and overland from Bactria - turquoise from Khurasan and lapis lazuli from Badakhshan passing through to Egypt, with indigo, cotton and silk going west and topaz, coral, glass and silver plate coming in.

Because lapis and turquoise reach the Mediterranean through here, the port ties Indian maritime trade to the Central Asian caravan system, and is the natural companion to Barbarikon in discussing the Indus estuary's trade.
The nineteenth-century development, with rail links to Punjab, made it the outlet for wheat and cotton and set the pattern of colonial port cities built to drain a hinterland.

location.summary: Khambhat, the Cambay of European sources, at the head of the Gulf of Khambhat where the Mahi meets the sea, Anand district, Gujarat - a funnel-shaped gulf with one of the world's highest tidal ranges.

periodLevel.summary: The dominant port of western India from about the 11th century to the 16th, under the Chaulukyas, the Gujarat Sultanate and then the Mughals. It was superseded by Surat in the 17th century as silting and the tidal bore closed the approach to larger ships.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The Mughal empire's principal outlet to the western Indian Ocean, and a bead industry with four thousand years of continuity.
points: Marco Polo, Ibn Battuta, Duarte Barbosa and Tome Pires all describe it; Pires's remark that Cambay stretched out two arms, one towards Aden and the other towards Malacca, is the standard quotation for Gujarat's double orientation towards the Red Sea and Southeast Asia.

Exports were cotton textiles, chintz, indigo and carnelian beads; the return was gold, silver and horses from the Gulf, and spices from the east. Gujarati merchant capital financed much of it, which is why the port features in arguments about pre-colonial Indian commercial organisation.

Agate and carnelian from the Rajpipla hills are still cut and polished at Khambhat by heat-treating and drilling methods continuous with those used at Harappan Lothal, a short distance up the same gulf.
Its decline is environmental rather than political - a reminder that Indian port history is largely a history of silting rivers and shifting coastlines.

location.summary: Kollam, the Quilon of European sources, on the Ashtamudi backwater near the Arabian Sea in southern Kerala - a lagoon harbour sheltered from the open coast.

periodLevel.summary: Refounded in 825 CE, the year from which the Malayalam *Kollam* era is reckoned. It was the chief port of the Venad rulers and a great emporium through the 9th-15th centuries, raided by Malik Kafur's forces in 1311 and visited by Marco Polo, Ibn Battuta and the Chinese fleets.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The port that produced the finest surviving document of multi-religious commerce in early medieval India.
points: The *Tharisapalli* copper plates of c. 849 CE, issued by Ayyanadikal Thiruvadikal of Venad, grant land and privileges to a Syrian Christian church and place it under the protection of the merchant guilds *Anjuvannam* and *Manigramam*, with Jewish and Muslim witnesses signing in Hebrew, Pahlavi and Kufic Arabic. One plate records Christians, Jews and Muslims guaranteeing a Hindu ruler's grant.
That the Kollam era is still used in Kerala shows how decisively the port's refounding reorganised regional life.
Arab writers record Chinese vessels transshipping cargo here rather than continuing west, making Kollam the pivot between the eastern and western halves of the Indian Ocean trade.

The trading guilds named in the plates are the same corporations attested across south India and Southeast Asia, so the document is used to argue for organised merchant capital in early medieval India.

location.summary: Korkai, Thoothukudi district, Tamil Nadu, on the Thamirabarani river near the Gulf of Mannar. Silting has left the site some 6 km inland from the present shore, so the ancient harbour is now dry land.

periodLevel.summary: The earliest Pandya capital and port, flourishing c. 3rd century BCE to 3rd century CE. Excavation has yielded Black-and-Red Ware, potsherds of c. 200 BCE-200 CE, and thick deposits of pearl-oyster shell. Known to the *Periplus* and Ptolemy as Kolkhoi.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The centre of the ancient pearl fishery - a port built on one commodity, and the Pandya kingdom's origin.
points: The Gulf of Mannar pearl banks made Korkai famous across the ancient world. The *Periplus* records pearls fished by condemned criminals, and Sangam poems return repeatedly to Korkai's pearls; Roman demand for them is part of the same trade that brought gold to the Tamil coast.
Beds of oyster shell in the excavated levels confirm the literary claim directly, which is why Korkai is cited as a case where Sangam poetry can be checked against material evidence.

It was the Pandya capital before the move inland to Madurai, with Kayal serving later as the port. The sequence Korkai, Kayal, Tuticorin traces one harbour system retreating seaward as the Thamirabarani silted.
Marco Polo and the Arab geographers describe the same fishery continuing into the medieval centuries, giving the industry a documented life of well over a thousand years.

location.summary: Kozhikode, the Calicut of European and Arabic sources, on the Malabar coast of Kerala between the Ghats and the Arabian Sea, with the open roadstead at Kappad a little to the north.

periodLevel.summary: A Chera-period settlement that became the seat of the Zamorin (Samoothiri) from about the 13th century and the dominant Malabar port through the 14th-16th centuries. Vasco da Gama landed at Kappad on 17 May 1498; Portuguese conflict with the Zamorin runs from 1500 to the 1560s.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The port where the European age in Indian history begins, and the best-documented case of an Indian state resisting it at sea.
points: Ibn Battuta, visiting in the 1340s, ranked it among the greatest ports in the world and described Chinese junks wintering in its harbour - evidence that the Indian Ocean was a Chinese as well as an Arab and Indian sea before the Portuguese arrived. Zheng He's fleets called here.

The Zamorin's prosperity rested on pepper and on his guarantee of security to the Muslim Mappila merchants who handled it. His refusal to exclude them is what made conflict with the Portuguese *cartaz* system inevitable, rather than any religious quarrel.

The Kunjali Marakkars, the Zamorin's admirals, fought the Portuguese at sea for nearly a century - the one sustained Indian naval resistance of the period, and the standard counter to the claim that Indian states ignored sea power.
The city's cotton cloth gave English the word *calico*.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I; J. L. Mehta, *Advanced Study in the History of Medieval India* I; Ibn Battuta, *Rihla*

location.summary: Kuntasi, Morbi district, Gujarat, on the Phulki river near the head of the Gulf of Kutch - a small mound on the Saurashtra coast, not in Maharashtra as some note-sets have it.

periodLevel.summary: Harappan, with a Mature phase of c. 2200-1900 BCE and a Late Harappan reoccupation to c. 1700 BCE. Excavated by M. K. Dhavalikar; the site covers barely two hectares.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A specialised Harappan manufacturing and shipping outpost - evidence that the civilisation's coastal network included small industrial stations, not only cities.
points: The settlement is dominated by workshops rather than housing: bead-making debris in carnelian, agate and steatite, shell-working, copper smelting, and grinding and storage areas, with a boundary wall and a watchtower.

A stone platform and a projecting structure by the creek have been read as a jetty or loading point. With Lothal's basin, it is part of the argument that the Harappans maintained deliberate maritime infrastructure on the Gujarat coast.

Raw materials came from far inland and beyond - agate from the Rajpipla hills, copper from Rajasthan or Oman - and finished beads went out by sea towards the Gulf. The site therefore documents a full production chain compressed into one small place.

Its abandonment and reduced Late Harappan reoccupation, with coarser pottery and no workshop output, is a compact illustration of the deurbanisation visible across the Harappan world after c. 1900 BCE.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; M. K. Dhavalikar, *Kuntasi: A Harappan Emporium*

location.summary: Machilipatnam, also Masulipatnam or Bandar, Krishna district, Andhra Pradesh, on the Coromandel coast just north of the Krishna delta.

periodLevel.summary: A port from the Satavahana period, named *Maisolia* by Ptolemy and *Masalia* in the *Periplus*. Its great age is the 15th-17th centuries as the principal seaport of the Qutb Shahi kingdom of Golconda; the Dutch established a factory in 1605 and the English their first Coromandel factory in 1611. It declined after the cyclone of 1779 and the rise of Madras.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The export point for the Coromandel textile trade - the industry that drew European companies to India in the first place.
points: The *Periplus* already singles out Masalia for its fine muslin, and the region's cloth is the probable origin of the word. Two thousand years of continuous textile export from one stretch of coast is the site's main claim.

*Kalamkari*, hand-painted and block-printed cotton using natural mordants and dyes, was produced in its hinterland for markets in Persia and Southeast Asia. Designs were made to order for particular foreign markets, which is early evidence of production tailored to export demand.
As Golconda's port it handled diamonds from the Kollur mines along with cloth, and its customs revenue was a major item in Qutb Shahi finances.
The Dutch and English factories here predate Madras and Calcutta, so Machilipatnam is where European commercial settlement on the east coast begins.

location.summary: Muziris, Sangam-age Muchiri, on the Periyar near Kodungallur (Cranganore), Ernakulam district, Kerala. The archaeological site is at Pattanam, north of the present river mouth; the harbour is thought to have been destroyed by the Periyar flood of 1341.

periodLevel.summary: The premier Chera port of the Sangam age, active from about the 1st century BCE to the 4th century CE and referred to into the medieval period. Pattanam excavations have yielded Roman amphorae, glass and semi-precious stone beads, and a wharf with a dugout canoe.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The western terminus of the Roman pepper trade, and the subject of the single most informative document in Indian economic history.
points: The *Muziris Papyrus*, a 2nd-century CE contract now in Vienna, records a loan between an Alexandrian financier and a merchant for a cargo carried from Muziris on the ship *Hermapollon* - pepper, ivory and nard, valued at nearly seven million sesterces, with duty and security terms spelled out. It converts a trade known from anecdote into figures.
Pliny called Muziris *primum emporium Indiae* and complained that India drained Rome of its gold; the Peutinger Table marks a Temple of Augustus here, implying a resident Roman community.
Sangam poems describe *yavana* vessels arriving with gold and departing with pepper, churning the Periyar's water - literary confirmation of the same traffic.
Kerala's early Jewish, Christian and later Muslim communities are tied to this coast, so the port also anchors questions on the entry of those religions into India.

location.summary: Mylapore, now a quarter of Chennai, on the Coromandel coast of Tamil Nadu just south of the Cooum mouth - an open shore with no natural harbour, worked by surf boats.

periodLevel.summary: An ancient settlement and port, active under the Pallavas and Cholas and trading into the medieval centuries; the Portuguese founded San Thome here in 1523, well before the English built Fort St George at Madras in 1639.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The focus of the St Thomas tradition in India, and the Portuguese settlement that Madras grew up beside.
points: Tradition places the martyrdom and burial of the apostle Thomas at Mylapore, and the San Thome basilica is one of only three churches in the world built over an apostle's reputed tomb. Whatever its historicity, the tradition is central to the self-understanding of the Syrian Christian community and to arguments about Christianity's antiquity in India.
As a Chola-period port it exported cotton textiles and muslin eastward to Malacca and Southeast Asia, and earlier traded with the Greek world; Ptolemy's coastal list is usually taken to include it.
The Kapaleeshwarar temple marks it as a Shaiva centre of the Nayanmar tradition, and Tiruvalluvar, author of the *Tirukkural*, is by tradition associated with the town.
Mylapore is a useful corrective to the idea that European port cities were founded on empty coast: Madras was built next to a settlement already more than a thousand years old.

location.summary: Nirppeyarru, a Pallava port town of the Tamil coast known from inscriptions rather than from surviving remains. It is generally placed at the mouth of the Palar, in the Kanchipuram-Chengalpattu tract, with the excavated coastal site of Vasavasamudram the most-cited candidate.

periodLevel.summary: Pallava period, c. 7th-9th centuries CE, the same phase in which Mamallapuram was the dynasty's principal harbour. It appears in Pallava and later Chola records as a port and a centre of revenue administration.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Evidence that the Pallavas worked a coastline of several harbours rather than a single port - and a caution about how much of that coastline is now lost.
points: Pallava maritime activity is usually reduced to Mamallapuram. The inscriptions name other landing places on the same stretch, of which Nirppeyarru is one, indicating a network of small anchorages at river mouths serving the capital at Kanchipuram.

Its identification is unsettled, and the honest position is that the name is secure while the place is not. Shifting river mouths and a prograding coast have buried or washed away most early Tamil harbour sites, which is why so many are known only from texts.
Vasavasamudram, at the Palar mouth, has yielded rouletted ware and Roman-period material, showing the estuary was in use; whether it is Nirppeyarru remains argued.

The wider point is methodological: for early port history the epigraphic and literary record runs well ahead of the archaeological one, and a map entry must say so rather than pretend to a fixed location.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; ASI, *South Indian Inscriptions*; *Indian Archaeology - A Review*

location.summary: Puhar or Kaveripattinam, Mayiladuthurai district, Tamil Nadu, where the Kaveri enters the Bay of Bengal - much of the ancient town now lies under the sea and the shifting river mouth.

periodLevel.summary: Port and capital of the early Cholas in the Sangam age, c. 2nd century BCE to 3rd century CE. Known to the *Periplus* as Camara and to Ptolemy; excavation has recovered brick structures, a wharf and Roman material, with offshore remains found by marine survey.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The best-described city of early Tamilakam - a place where literature gives a town plan that archaeology can then test.
points: The *Pattinappalai* describes the harbour's warehouses, the customs officers who stamped bonded goods with the tiger seal of the Cholas, and foreign merchants living in their own quarter. The tiger-seal detail is the standard evidence for organised customs administration in the Sangam period.

The fifth book of the *Silappadikaram* divides the city into Maruvurpakkam by the shore, where the yavana and other foreign traders lived, and Pattinappakkam inland, the royal and brahmana quarter - a documented segregation of commercial and courtly space.
The *Manimekalai* is set here too, and records Buddhist and Jain establishments, so the city supports questions on religion in the Tamil country as well as on trade.
Its submergence, attributed in the epics to the sea's anger, is corroborated by coastal change, and Puhar is the usual example of an ancient Indian port lost to the sea rather than to conquest.

content.sourcesLine: Thapar, *Early India*; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Upinder Singh, ch. 8

location.summary: Achalpur, formerly Ellichpur, Amravati district, Maharashtra, on the Sapan river at the foot of the Melghat hills - the historic capital of Berar, the cotton plain between the Tapti and the Wardha.

periodLevel.summary: A regional centre under the Yadavas of Devagiri, annexed by the Delhi Sultanate in the early 14th century and made a provincial seat; then Bahmani. It became the capital of the independent Imad Shahi sultanate of Berar from 1490 until Ahmadnagar absorbed it in 1572, after which it was the Mughal subah capital of Berar.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The capital of Berar through the sultanate centuries - the least studied of the five Deccan successor states.
points: When the Bahmani kingdom broke up, Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk, governor of Berar, declared independence here in 1490. The Imad Shahis were the weakest of the five Deccan sultanates and the first to be swallowed, which is why Achalpur seldom appears beside Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar and Bidar - though it completes the set.

Berar's cotton made it the revenue prize of the eastern Deccan. Its transfer to the Mughals and later its assignment to the Nizam, and then its lease to the British in 1853, make the province a recurring item in Deccan politics down to the nineteenth century.
The town retains the Achaleshwar Mahadev and Kembhaswami temples, the fort, and Sultanate-period tombs and mosques.
Note that some note-sets make Achalpur a Rashtrakuta or Paramara capital. It was neither: the Rashtrakuta seat was Manyakheta and the Paramara seat Dhar.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I; J. L. Mehta, *Advanced Study in the History of Medieval India* I; ASI

location.summary: Adam, Kuhi tehsil, Nagpur district, Maharashtra, in the Wainganga basin of eastern Vidarbha - the plateau country between the Godavari system and the Chhattisgarh plain.

periodLevel.summary: A long sequence from the Chalcolithic through the megalithic and early historic periods to the Satavahana and Vakataka centuries. Excavated by the ASI from the 1980s; the fortified early historic town yielded Northern Black Polished Ware, punch-marked and Satavahana coins, and a large body of seals and sealings.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The site that gave the Asmaka *mahajanapada* a physical location - the only one of the sixteen lying in the Deccan.
points: A sealing from the site reads *Asikasa janapadasa*, "of the Asika janapada". Asmaka or Assaka is listed among the sixteen mahajanapadas in the Buddhist *Anguttara Nikaya* but is the only southern member, and until this find it had no securely identified centre. Epigraphy fixing a textual polity on the ground is exactly the kind of evidence examiners want cited.

The defences, the NBPW and the coinage together show a fortified urban centre in Vidarbha contemporary with the second urbanisation of the Ganga plain, which complicates the usual picture of urbanism spreading outward from the north.
Megalithic burials in the vicinity link the early historic town to the preceding Vidarbha megalithic culture of Mahurjhari and Naikund, giving an unusually continuous local sequence.
Later Satavahana and Vakataka material shows the settlement surviving as a regional town well into the historic period.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 6 and 8; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; *Indian Archaeology - A Review*
