location.summary: Banavasi, Uttara Kannada district, Karnataka, on a loop of the Varada river in the Malnad country below the Western Ghats - the oldest recorded settlement in Karnataka.

periodLevel.summary: A centre under the Satavahanas and the Chutus, who left a Prakrit inscription here, and from c. 345 CE the capital of the Kadambas, founded by Mayurasharma. The Madhukeshwara temple dates from about the 9th century with Chalukya and Hoysala additions; Pulakesin I of the Chalukyas absorbed the region in the 6th century.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The capital of the first indigenous dynasty of the Kannada country - the point at which Karnataka acquires a political history of its own.
points: The Kadambas are the earliest ruling house native to the region, as against the Mauryas, Satavahanas and Chutus who ruled it from outside. Mayurasharma was, by the Talagunda inscription's account, a brahmana student slighted at Kanchi who took up arms - one of the more vivid dynastic origin stories in Indian epigraphy.

Ashoka's Rock Edict XIII names *Vanavasi* among the places to which missionaries were sent, and the Ceylonese chronicles record the monk Rakkhita being despatched here, so the site enters the record in the Mauryan period.

Kadamba rule is the setting for the Halmidi inscription, the earliest full-length Kannada text, referred to Kakusthavarman. Capital and inscription belong to the same polity, and are best answered together.
The Madhukeshwara temple preserves the Kadamba *shikhara*, a stepped pyramidal form distinct from both Nagara and Dravida, and the dynasty's name survives in that architectural label.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 9 and 10; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Thapar, *Early India*

location.summary: Bhita, on the left bank of the Yamuna about 18 km south-west of Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh - a mound beside the river a short distance above the Ganga-Yamuna confluence.

periodLevel.summary: Occupied from about the 5th-4th centuries BCE through the Mauryan, Shunga, Kushana and Gupta periods. Excavated by John Marshall in 1911-12, one of the earliest stratigraphic excavations of an Indian urban site.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The clearest excavated plan of an ordinary early historic Indian town - not a capital, but a working commercial settlement.
points: Marshall exposed a main street with houses opening off it, courtyards, drains and shops, and worked out the sequence of rebuilding levels. Because the town was neither a great capital nor a religious centre, it is the standard reference for how early historic urban India actually looked.

Seals and sealings found in the houses name individuals, guilds and corporate bodies, using the term *nigama*. They are among the best evidence for organised commercial associations - guilds acting as recognised legal entities - in the centuries around the turn of the era.
Northern Black Polished Ware, punch-marked and Kushana coins, terracotta figurines and ring wells anchor the chronology and connect it to the wider second urbanisation of the Ganga plain.
Bhita is usually set beside Kaushambi, its larger neighbour, to contrast a fortified regional capital with a subordinate market town in the same stretch of the Yamuna.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 7 and 8; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; John Marshall, *ASI Annual Report* 1911-12

location.summary: Bhokardan, ancient Bhogavardhana, Jalna district, Maharashtra, on the Kelna river in the upper Godavari basin - on the route between Pratishthana and the western ghat passes to the Konkan ports.

periodLevel.summary: A Satavahana-period trade and craft town, flourishing c. 2nd century BCE to 3rd century CE. Excavated jointly by Nagpur University and the ASI; the site has also produced Kshatrapa-period material.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A Deccan manufacturing town caught in the act of producing for the Roman trade.
points: The ivory carvings recovered here are the site's best-known finds: female figures and toilet articles in a style close to the celebrated ivory statuette found at Pompeii, and to the Begram ivories from Afghanistan. Bhokardan is the strongest candidate for the kind of Deccan workshop that supplied both.
Beads in carnelian, agate, crystal and glass, terracotta figurines, and Roman glass and pottery fragments show a settlement making high-value goods for export while consuming imports in return.

Its position matters: goods moved from Bhokardan and Paithan through the Naneghat and other passes to Kalyan and Sopara, so the town belongs to the same commercial system as the merchant endowments recorded in the western Deccan cave inscriptions.
Donative inscriptions naming residents of Bhogavardhana appear at Sanchi and in the western caves, which ties the excavated town to named individuals funding religious architecture elsewhere.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8; Thapar, *Early India*; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*

location.summary: Charsadda, ancient Pushkalavati, at the confluence of the Swat and Kabul rivers in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan - about 30 km north-east of Peshawar, in the heart of Gandhara.

periodLevel.summary: The capital of Gandhara before Purushapura, occupied from about the 6th century BCE. The mounds of Bala Hisar and Shaikhan Dheri carry the sequence: Achaemenid satrapal, Macedonian, Mauryan, Indo-Greek, Saka-Parthian and Kushana. Excavated by Mortimer Wheeler in 1958 and later by Pakistani and British teams.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The type-site for the north-west's long exposure to successive foreign powers, and the stratigraphy against which that sequence is dated.
points: Gandhara was the twentieth satrapy of the Achaemenid empire, its tribute recorded by Herodotus and its people named in Darius's inscriptions. Charsadda is where that administration was seated, making it the physical evidence for Persian rule in the subcontinent.
Alexander's forces besieged the city for thirty days in 327 BCE under Hephaestion, according to Arrian - one of the few episodes of the Indian campaign that can be attached to an excavated site.
Wheeler's work established a ceramic and stratigraphic sequence for the north-west that is still the reference framework, and the site has produced Indo-Greek and Saka coinage in quantity.
Under the Mauryas it was a provincial centre on the road to Taxila; the two cities together define the north-western frontier of Mauryan administration.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 6 and 8; Thapar, *Early India*; R. E. M. Wheeler, *Charsada*

location.summary: Dhar, Madhya Pradesh, on the Malwa plateau south-west of Indore, between the Narmada and the upper Chambal - the agricultural core of Malwa.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of the Paramaras from the 9th century, at its height under Bhoja, r. c. 1010-1055 CE. Taken by the Delhi Sultanate in 1305, it became part of the Malwa Sultanate before the seat moved to Mandu. A centre of the 1857 revolt in central India.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The court of the scholar-king Bhoja, and the site of a documented medieval college.
points: Bhoja is credited with works across an extraordinary range - the *Samarangana Sutradhara* on architecture and mechanical devices, the *Sarasvati Kanthabharana* on poetics, and texts on grammar, medicine and astronomy. Whether he wrote them all or presided over a workshop of scholars, the corpus is the standard example of royal patronage of learning in early medieval India.

The *Bhojashala* was a Sanskrit college attached to a temple of Vagdevi, Sarasvati. Slabs there carry Sanskrit and Prakrit grammatical rules engraved in serpentine coils, including a *Nagabandha* arrangement - teaching material cut into stone, which exists nowhere else.

The Vagdevi image associated with the school was removed in the colonial period and is in the British Museum; the building has since been contested between Hindu and Muslim communities, so the site also illustrates how medieval monuments become present-day disputes.
The Lat Masjid and Kamal Maula mosque, built with re-used temple material, mark the Sultanate phase.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I; J. L. Mehta, *Advanced Study in the History of Medieval India* I; Thapar, *Early India*

location.summary: Gauda, later Lakhnauti and Gaur, Malda district, West Bengal, on an abandoned channel of the Ganga astride the present India-Bangladesh border - the deltaic heartland of Bengal.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of Shashanka's Gauda kingdom in the early 7th century CE; the seat from which the Palas ruled after Gopala's election c. 750; then the Senas'; and from 1204, when Bakhtiyar Khalji took it, the capital of Muslim Bengal as Lakhnauti, held by the Ilyas Shahi and Husain Shahi sultans until Sher Shah sacked it in 1538 and plague emptied it in 1575.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One site carrying a thousand years of Bengal's history - the only recorded election of a king in early India, and the capital of an independent Bengal Sultanate.
points: The Khalimpur copper plate states that the people, worn down by *matsyanyaya* - the law of the fishes, where the strong devour the weak - chose Gopala to be king. Taranatha's later Tibetan account says the same. An elected founder is unique in Indian dynastic records and is the single most cited fact about the Palas.

The Palas ruled Bengal and Bihar for some four centuries and were the last great royal patrons of Buddhism in India, endowing Nalanda, Vikramashila and Odantapuri and sending Atisha Dipankara to Tibet. Pala bronze and stone sculpture defines the eastern Indian style.
Shashanka, who preceded them, is remembered in Buddhist sources as a persecutor and in political history as the king who killed Harsha's brother Rajyavardhana - the link between Gauda and Thanesar.

Under the sultans, Bengal was effectively independent of Delhi from 1342; distance, the monsoon and the rivers repeatedly defeated attempts at control, making it the standard example of Sultanate provincial breakaway. Its architecture is brick, not stone, because the delta has no quarries: the curved *do-chala* cornice copied from the thatched hut, terracotta ornament and squat domes seen in the Dakhil Darwaza, the Firoz Minar and the Bara Sona Masjid of 1526. The same curved roof appears on Hindu temples at Bishnupur, so the form is regional rather than religious.
Alauddin Husain Shah, r. 1494-1519, patronised Bengali literature and employed Hindu officers; Rupa and Sanatana, later two of Chaitanya's Six Goswamis, served in his administration.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Thapar, *Early India*; Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I

location.summary: Kannauj, ancient Kanyakubja, on the right bank of the Ganga in Kannauj district, Uttar Pradesh - commanding the doab where the river routes of the upper and middle Ganga plain meet.

periodLevel.summary: A Maukhari capital in the 6th century; Harshavardhana moved his seat here from Thanesar and ruled 606-647 CE. It was the prize of the tripartite struggle in the 8th-9th centuries, then the Gurjara-Pratihara capital, sacked by Mahmud of Ghazni in 1018, and finally lost by the Gahadavala Jayachandra after Chandawar in 1194.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The city that stood for paramountcy in northern India - whoever held it claimed to be the successor of Harsha.
points: The tripartite struggle between the Palas of Bengal, the Gurjara-Pratiharas of Malwa-Rajasthan and the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan was fought explicitly for Kannauj across the 8th and 9th centuries. Three dynasties from three corners of India contesting one city is the standard illustration of early medieval political fragmentation and of what legitimacy was worth.

Xuanzang, who spent time at Harsha's court, describes a long, prosperous city on the Ganga with Buddhist and Brahmanical establishments side by side, and records the assemblies Harsha held at Kannauj and Prayaga.
Bana's *Harshacharita* supplies the court narrative, which the Banskhera and Madhuban copper plates then confirm - one of the rare cases where a Sanskrit biography can be checked against epigraphy.
Its perfume industry, distilling attar from local roses and khus, survives from the medieval period and is still the town's trade.

content.sourcesLine: Thapar, *Early India*; Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I; J. L. Mehta, *Advanced Study in the History of Medieval India* I

location.summary: Kodungallur, the Cranganore of European sources, Thrissur district, Kerala, near the mouth of the Periyar at the north end of the Vembanad backwaters - the same estuary as ancient Muziris, a few kilometres away.

periodLevel.summary: Mahodayapuram, capital of the Chera Perumals from about the 9th century to the early 12th, when the kingdom broke up into the Venad, Kolathunadu and other successor states. The earlier port of Muziris, active in the Sangam and Roman periods, lies in the same estuary; see the Muziris entry in the ports chapter.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The Chera Perumal capital, and the single stretch of Indian coast where Judaism, Christianity and Islam each claim their first foothold.
points: Tradition places the arrival of Jewish settlers here after 70 CE, the landing of the apostle Thomas in 52 CE, and the building of the Cheraman Juma Masjid in 629 CE, held to be the first mosque in India and founded in the Prophet's lifetime. The traditions are of varying strength and should be presented as traditions - but the underlying fact, that all three communities entered India through Kerala's trade rather than by conquest, is solid and is the point worth making.
The Jewish copper plates and the Tharisapalli grants issued under the Cheras record privileges to these communities and to the merchant guilds, giving documentary support to the trading context.
Kulasekhara Alwar and Cheraman Perumal Nayanar, saints of the Vaishnava and Shaiva bhakti traditions, are associated with this court, so the capital matters for religious history as well as commerce.
The Kodungallur Bhagavathy temple, with its Bharani festival, preserves an older goddess cult of the region.

content.sourcesLine: Thapar, *Early India*; Upinder Singh, ch. 10; *Travancore Archaeological Series*

location.summary: Kolar, Karnataka, on the eastern edge of the Mysore plateau near the Andhra and Tamil borders, in the upper Palar basin - dry upland country underlain by the ancient greenstone belt that carries its gold.

periodLevel.summary: An early capital of the Western Gangas before they moved to Talakad, and later contested by the Cholas, who held it in the 10th-11th centuries, and by the Hoysalas and Vijayanagara. The Kolaramma temple is Chola work of the 10th-11th centuries with later additions.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: India's principal gold field, worked from antiquity, and an early Ganga seat.
points: The Kolar Gold Fields were mined long before the shafts of the colonial period. Ancient workings, and lead-isotope studies matching gold objects from Harappan and later contexts to Kolar ore, are the basis for arguing that peninsular gold reached the north from the third millennium BCE onward.

That makes Kolar the standard answer to where early Indian gold came from - a question usually left vague - and ties the Deccan interior into the exchange networks of the Harappan and early historic worlds.
The Western Gangas took their early name from this region, and Kolar's Jain and Shaiva monuments record the succession of powers that fought over it.
Under the Cholas the area was organised as Nikarilicholamandalam, and the inscriptions of the Kolaramma temple are used for Chola provincial administration in the Kannada country.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 4 and 10; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Geological Survey of India

location.summary: Madurai, Tamil Nadu, on the south bank of the Vaigai in the plain between the Palani hills and the Pandya country - walled on three sides with the river on the fourth, as the Sangam poems describe it.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of the Pandyas from the Sangam age, c. 3rd century BCE onward, through their early medieval revival to the 14th century; then the Madurai Sultanate, Vijayanagara, and from 1529 the Nayakas, whose greatest ruler was Tirumalai Nayaka, r. 1623-1659. This entry covers the city; for the temple see the Madurai Meenakshi entry in the temple chapter.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the very few Indian cities that has been a capital continuously for over two thousand years, and the seat of the Tamil literary academy.
points: Tamil tradition places the third *Sangam* here under Pandya patronage, and the surviving Sangam corpus is the earliest literature in any Indian language other than Sanskrit. The *Maduraikkanchi* describes the city's night markets, its quarters by trade, and its festivals in enough detail to be used as social evidence.
Megasthenes reports the kingdom of *Pandaia*, and the Pandyas sent an embassy to Augustus recorded by Strabo - among the earliest Indian diplomatic contacts with the Mediterranean world.
It was a manufacturing centre for textiles, goldwork, ivory and inlay, and the inland counterpart to the Pandya pearl ports at Korkai and Kayal.
Malik Kafur's raid of 1310-11 and the short-lived Madurai Sultanate that followed brought Delhi's power to the far south, and Vijayanagara's recovery of the region is what installed the Nayakas.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8; Basham, *The Wonder that was India*; Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I

location.summary: Mukhalingam, Srikakulam district, Andhra Pradesh, on the Vamsadhara river close to the Odisha border - in the tract that was historically Kalinga rather than Andhra.

periodLevel.summary: Kalinganagara, capital of the Eastern Gangas from about the 8th century until Anantavarman Chodaganga shifted the seat to Cuttack in the 12th. Three principal temples survive: the Madhukeshwara of about the 8th-9th centuries, the Someshwara of the 10th, and the Bhimeshwara of the 11th.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The capital of the dynasty that built Puri and Konark, and the place where the Kalinga temple style takes shape.
points: The Eastern Gangas ruled from here for four centuries before their great coastal phase. Anantavarman Chodaganga, who began the Jagannath temple at Puri c. 1135, belonged to this line, so Mukhalingam is where the architectural tradition that produced Puri and Konark was first worked out.

The Madhukeshwara temple shows the *rekha deul* with its curvilinear tower and the *jagamohana* porch already formed, with dense figural carving on the outer walls - the Kalinga order in an early but fully recognisable state.

The site sits on the cultural boundary between Odisha and Andhra, and its sculpture and inscriptions are used to argue about where that line lay in the early medieval period - a reminder that modern linguistic state borders map poorly onto historical regions.
The Ganga era, dated from 1038 CE and used in eastern Indian inscriptions for centuries, was instituted by this dynasty.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Thapar, *Early India*; ASI

location.summary: Nagar, also called Karkota Nagar, Tonk district, Rajasthan, in the Banas basin east of the Aravallis - a large mounded site in the tract between Rajasthan and Malwa.

periodLevel.summary: An early historic settlement of roughly the 3rd century BCE to the 4th century CE, identified with a principal seat of the Malava people. It is best known for the enormous quantity of Malava coinage recovered from it.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The type-site for the tribal republics - the *ganas* and *sanghas* that were not monarchies, known mainly through their coins.
points: Many thousands of small copper coins bearing the legend *Malavanam jaya*, "victory of the Malavas", have been found here. Coinage issued in the name of a people rather than a king is the central piece of evidence for non-monarchical polities in early India, and Nagar is where most of it comes from.

The Malavas appear in the Greek accounts of Alexander's campaign as the *Malloi* of the Punjab, and later in Rajasthan and Malwa, which gives the region its name. Their migration south-east is traced through exactly this coin distribution.

Samudragupta's Allahabad pillar inscription lists the Malavas among the frontier peoples who submitted and paid tribute, so the republics survived into the 4th century before Gupta absorption. Their disappearance after that is the standard endpoint for the history of the ganas.
The Vikrama era, from 58 BCE, was called the *Malava-gana* era in early usage, tying India's most widely used calendar to this people.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8; Thapar, *Early India*; ASI

location.summary: Nagarjunakonda, ancient Vijayapuri, in a valley of the Nallamala hills on the right bank of the Krishna, Palnadu district, Andhra Pradesh. The valley was flooded by the Nagarjunasagar reservoir in the 1960s; selected monuments were dismantled and re-erected on an island museum.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of the Ikshvakus, c. 225-325 CE, who succeeded the Satavahanas in the eastern Deccan. The site was excavated in the 1920s and then again, on a vast scale, in a salvage operation before submergence.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The most completely excavated early historic city in India - and the most completely lost.
points: More than thirty Buddhist establishments were recorded, with *mahachaityas*, *viharas* and limestone relief sculpture of the Amaravati school, alongside Brahmanical temples, a palace, and a stone-built amphitheatre unique in India.

Inscriptions record monasteries endowed for monks from Sri Lanka, Kashmir, Gandhara and even, in one reading, from beyond - the *Sihala vihara* among them. Nagarjunakonda is the best epigraphic evidence that Indian Buddhism was an international institution with resident foreign communities.

The endowments were overwhelmingly made by royal women - Chamtisri, sister of the founder Chamtamula, above all - while the kings performed *ashvamedha* and other Vedic sacrifices. Women funding Buddhism while men sacrificed to the Vedic gods, within one family, is the sharpest available illustration of plural patronage.
The name commemorates Nagarjuna, the Madhyamaka philosopher, whose association with the site is traditional rather than documented.

content.sourcesLine: Basham, *The Wonder that was India*; Upinder Singh, ch. 8; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*

location.summary: Pawaya, ancient Padmavati, Gwalior district, Madhya Pradesh, at the confluence of the Sindh and Para rivers - in the Chambal-Sindh tract between Malwa and the Ganga plain.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of the Nagas of Padmavati in the 3rd-4th centuries CE, in the interval between Kushana decline and Gupta consolidation. The mound has yielded Naga coins in quantity, a brick temple platform, and an inscribed Manibhadra yaksha image.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The seat of one of the regional powers that filled the gap between two empires, and the dynasty Samudragupta had to remove.
points: Samudragupta's Allahabad pillar inscription names Ganapatinaga among the kings of Aryavarta violently uprooted. Padmavati is therefore one of the few places where a defeated dynasty from that famous list can be located on the ground and its coinage handled.

The Naga rulers - Bharashivas in some readings - are credited in Puranic tradition with reviving Vedic sacrifice and the *ashvamedha* after the Kushana period, so the site features in arguments about Brahmanical resurgence before the Guptas.

Padmavati is the setting of Bhavabhuti's Sanskrit play *Malatimadhava*, written in the 8th century, which describes the city and its river confluence in enough detail to be read against the excavated topography.
The Manibhadra yaksha image is an important early example of yaksha worship, the popular cult stratum that runs beneath classical Hinduism and Buddhism alike.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8 and 9; Thapar, *Early India*; ASI

location.summary: Paithan, ancient Pratishthana, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar district, Maharashtra, on the north bank of the Godavari - the head of navigation and the natural centre of the Deccan plateau.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of the Satavahanas from about the 1st century BCE to the 2nd century CE, and a major market long after. Ptolemy names it *Baithana*; the *Periplus* pairs it with Tagara as the two great inland marts of the Deccan; Ashoka's Rock Edict V and XIII name the *Petenikas* among the peoples of his realm.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The southern terminus of the Dakshinapatha, and the capital of the dynasty that made the Deccan a political unit.
points: The *Periplus* describes caravans bringing onyx from Pratishthana and cotton cloth from Tagara down to Barygaza over difficult country - a rare classical description of Indian internal trade, and the reason Paithan appears in every answer on the Dakshinapatha.

As the Satavahana seat it is the political counterpart to Naneghat, Nashik and Karle: the inscriptions in those caves record the dynasty's sacrifices and the merchants' endowments, while Paithan is where the court that received both actually sat.

The *Gatha Saptashati*, an anthology of seven hundred Prakrit verses attributed to the Satavahana king Hala, is associated with this court. That a royal house patronised Prakrit rather than Sanskrit lyric is a standard point on early Deccan literary culture.
Paithani silk weaving, with its zari borders, is a craft tradition the town has carried continuously.

content.sourcesLine: R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Upinder Singh, ch. 8; Thapar, *Early India*

location.summary: Pragjyotishpura, identified with Guwahati, Assam, on the Brahmaputra where the river narrows between hills - the natural crossing and control point of the whole valley.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of the Kamarupa kingdom under the Varman dynasty, c. 350-650 CE, whose best-known ruler is Bhaskaravarman, r. c. 600-650, the ally of Harshavardhana. Later Kamarupa dynasties - the Mlechchhas and the Palas of Kamarupa - ruled from Haruppeshvara and Durjaya nearby.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The seat of the earliest historical kingdom of the north-east, and the point at which Assam enters the mainstream Indian record.
points: Bhaskaravarman's Nidhanpur copper plates, issued from a military camp, grant land to more than two hundred brahmanas and are the principal document for Kamarupa's administration and for the settlement of brahmanas in the Brahmaputra valley - the mechanism by which Sanskritic culture spread eastward.

Xuanzang visited his court at Harsha's invitation and describes the kingdom, its people and its distance from China. Bhaskaravarman's alliance with Harsha against Shashanka of Gauda places Kamarupa inside north Indian politics rather than outside it.

The *Mahabharata* and *Ramayana* refer to Pragjyotisha and its kings Naraka and Bhagadatta, so the site carries an epic identity alongside the historical one - the standard example of a frontier region being written into the pan-Indian tradition.
The Da-Parbatia doorframe at Tezpur and the Kamakhya shrine on Nilachal hill are the surviving material remains of this period and its religion.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 9 and 10; Thapar, *Early India*; *Nidhanpur* copper plates

location.summary: Awantipora, Pulwama district, Jammu and Kashmir, on the right bank of the Jhelum between Srinagar and Anantnag - on the valley floor, commanding the river route through Kashmir.

periodLevel.summary: Founded by Avantivarman of the Utpala dynasty, r. 855-883 CE, who built two temples here: the Avantisvamin, dedicated to Vishnu, and the larger Avantisvara, to Shiva. Both are in the Kashmiri order - colonnaded courtyards, trefoil arches, pediments and stone roofs - and both were ruined by earthquake and iconoclasm.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The Utpala capital, and the setting of the most celebrated feat of engineering in Kashmir's history.
points: Kalhana's *Rajatarangini* records that Avantivarman's engineer Suyya regulated the Jhelum where it was choked at Baramulla, drained the marshes, shifted the confluence of the Jhelum and Sindh, and reclaimed vast tracts for cultivation - so that the price of rice fell dramatically. The town of Sopore is named after him.

That episode is the best-documented instance of state-directed hydraulic works in early medieval India, and it is usually cited against the view that Indian kingship was ritual rather than administrative.
The temples continue the Kashmiri style established at Martand under the Karkotas a century earlier, and the two sites are normally taken together as the surviving evidence of that tradition.

Kalhana's chronicle, written in 1149-50, gives Kashmir a continuous historical narrative unmatched anywhere else in India, and Awantipora is one of the places where it can be matched to standing remains.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Thapar, *Early India*; Kalhana, *Rajatarangini* V

location.summary: Peshawar, ancient Purushapura, in the Vale of Peshawar near the Bara and Kabul rivers, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan - at the Indian end of the Khyber pass, where the routes from Bactria and Central Asia debouch onto the plain.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of the Kushana empire under Kanishka I, r. from c. 127 CE, who moved the seat here from Bactria; the city remained the centre of Gandhara through the later Kushana and Kidarite periods until the Hephthalite disruption.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The capital from which the Kushanas ruled an empire spanning Central Asia and northern India, and the centre of Gandhara Buddhism.
points: The great stupa Kanishka raised at Shah-ji-ki-Dheri was described by Faxian and Xuanzang as the tallest structure they had seen anywhere. Excavation in 1908-09 recovered the Kanishka casket from its relic chamber, inscribed in Kharoshthi and bearing the king's own name with Buddha figures - among the few Indian reliquaries that can be tied to a named ruler.

Purushapura is where the Fourth Buddhist Council is traditionally placed under Kanishka's patronage, with Vasumitra and Ashvaghosha, marking the formal emergence of Mahayana - though the council's historicity is disputed and should be presented as tradition.

Its position made it the exchange point of the Silk Route with India, which is why Gandhara sculpture fuses Hellenistic form with Buddhist subject; the first anthropomorphic Buddha images belong to this milieu.
Kanishka's coinage, naming Greek, Iranian and Indian deities together, expresses the same cosmopolitanism from the same capital.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I; Upinder Singh, ch. 8; Thapar, *Early India*

location.summary: Sambhar, Jaipur district, Rajasthan, on the shore of Sambhar Salt Lake - the largest inland salt lake in India, in the shallow basin east of the Aravallis.

periodLevel.summary: Ancient Shakambhari, capital of the Chahamanas (Chauhans) from about the 7th century until the seat moved to Ajmer under Ajayaraja in the 12th. The Chahamanas of Shakambhari end with Prithviraj III, defeated by Muhammad of Ghor at the second battle of Tarain in 1192.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The Chauhan homeland, and a salt resource that explains why the site was worth holding.
points: The lake is the single largest source of inland salt in India, producing by solar evaporation in shallow pans. Control of salt meant control of a commodity every household needed and which could be taxed at the point of production - an early and easily collected revenue base, and the reason a dynasty rose at an otherwise unpromising spot.

The Chahamanas' move from Sambhar to Ajmer, and the later shift to Delhi under Prithviraj, traces the dynasty's transformation from a regional house on the desert margin into the principal power facing the Ghurid invasions.
Sambhar has yielded terracottas and early historic material showing occupation well before the Chahamanas, and the goddess Shakambhari, from whom the capital took its name, remains the lineage deity.
Salt from Sambhar was still a major item of Rajput and later Mughal revenue, and the lake's administration under the British is part of the wider colonial salt monopoly story.

content.sourcesLine: J. L. Mehta, *Advanced Study in the History of Medieval India* I; Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I

location.summary: Sialkot, ancient Sagala or Sakala, in Punjab, Pakistan, between the Chenab and the Ravi at the foot of the Jammu hills - on the route from the Khyber into the Punjab doabs.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of the Madra kingdom in Mahabharata tradition, then of the Indo-Greek king Menander, r. c. 155-130 BCE; later held by the Sakas, the Kushanas and the Hunas under Mihirakula, who is remembered for persecuting Buddhists there.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The capital of the most successful Indo-Greek king, and the setting of the one text in which a Greek ruler debates Indian philosophy.
points: The *Milindapanha*, the Questions of Milinda, records a dialogue at Sagala between Menander and the Buddhist monk Nagasena on the nature of the self, using the famous simile of the chariot that is nothing over and above its parts. It is a Pali classic and the best evidence for Greek engagement with Indian thought.

Menander's coins, bilingual in Greek and Kharoshthi and found in great numbers across the north-west, some carrying the Buddhist wheel, support the tradition that he adopted or at least patronised Buddhism. Plutarch reports that his relics were divided between cities after his death, in the manner of a Buddha.

The Indo-Greeks matter beyond Menander for what they transmitted: the use of portrait coinage with legends, Hellenistic sculptural form feeding into Gandhara, and Greek astronomical terms entering Sanskrit.
Sialkot was also a textile centre; the *Mahabharata* and later sources refer to the fine cloth of the Madra country.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* II; Upinder Singh, ch. 8; Thapar, *Early India*; *Milindapanha*

location.summary: Ter, ancient Tagara, Dharashiv (Osmanabad) district, Maharashtra, on the Terna river in the Marathwada uplands - inland, on the caravan route between the Godavari valley and the western ghats.

periodLevel.summary: A trade town of the Satavahana period, c. 2nd century BCE to 3rd century CE, with occupation continuing later. Excavation has produced ivory, beads, terracottas, Roman material and a brick apsidal structure now enclosed within the Trivikrama temple.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the two inland markets the *Periplus* names for the whole Deccan, and the source of a famous piece of Indian export art.
points: The *Periplus* states that from Tagara came great quantities of common cotton cloth, carried by wagon over difficult roads to Barygaza. A Greek text naming a Marathwada town is striking evidence of how deep into the interior the Roman trade reached.

The ivory work found here is stylistically close to the Indian ivory statuette recovered at Pompeii, buried in 79 CE. Linking an excavated Deccan workshop to an object found in a Roman town is the most concrete demonstration available of Indian manufactured exports reaching Italy.

The brick apsidal structure is an early Buddhist *chaitya* form later converted to Brahmanical use, so the site also documents religious change at an ordinary commercial town rather than at a royal centre.
Ter and Paithan together show that the Deccan's wealth rested on textile manufacture and transit trade, not only on land revenue.

location.summary: Talakad, Mysuru district, Karnataka, on the left bank of the Kaveri where the river turns sharply east - the town now lies largely buried beneath sand dunes thrown up by the river.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of the Western Gangas from about the 6th century CE. Taken by Rajaraja Chola in 1004 and held as Rajarajapura for over a century; recovered by the Hoysala Vishnuvardhana in 1117, who took the title *Talakadugonda*. It declined under the Vijayanagara and Wodeyar periods as the sand advanced.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The Western Ganga capital, and the pivot of the long contest between Chola and Hoysala for southern Karnataka.
points: The Western Gangas ruled Gangavadi for some six centuries and are best known for their Jain patronage, above all Chamundaraya's colossal Bahubali at Shravanabelagola. Talakad is the political centre behind that religious monument.

Its capture by Rajaraja I marks the high-water mark of Chola expansion into the Kannada country, and Vishnuvardhana's recovery of it is the event that established Hoysala power - the title he took from the victory is how the dynasty dated its rise.
Five Shiva temples, the *Pancha Linga*, are exposed and reburied by the moving sand, and are worshipped together in a festival held when the astronomical conditions recur.

The sanding-over is explained locally by the curse of Alamelamma, whose lands the Mysore Wodeyars seized in 1610. The legend is a good example of how environmental change gets narrated as moral history, and should be presented as such.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Thapar, *Early India*; *Epigraphia Carnatica*

location.summary: Thanesar, ancient Sthanvishvara, Kurukshetra district, Haryana, on the bank of the Sarasvati in the Ghaggar system - within the Kurukshetra tract, between the Sutlej and the Yamuna.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of the Pushyabhuti dynasty from the 6th century CE: Prabhakaravardhana, then Rajyavardhana, then Harshavardhana, who succeeded in 606 CE and soon moved his seat to Kannauj. Raided by Mahmud of Ghazni in 1014.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The seat from which Harsha's empire began, and a tirtha whose sanctity long predates any dynasty.
points: Bana's *Harshacharita* opens here, describing Prabhakaravardhana's court, his death, Rajyavardhana's killing by Shashanka of Gauda, and Harsha's accession - the fullest narrative account of a royal succession surviving from early India, and the reason Thanesar carries weight beyond its size.

Harsha's transfer of the capital to Kannauj is itself the examinable point: it moved the centre of power from the Sarasvati region to the Ganga, following the shift of agricultural wealth eastward, and Kannauj remained the prize for four centuries afterwards.
The surrounding Kurukshetra is the *Mahabharata* battlefield and one of the great tirthas of northern India, with Brahma Sarovar and a long tradition of eclipse-bathing that Xuanzang already records.
Mahmud's raid of 1014, aimed at the wealth of the temples, belongs with Somnath in the sequence of Ghaznavid expeditions, and the Sheikh Chilli tomb later marks the town's Sufi phase.

content.sourcesLine: J. L. Mehta, *Advanced Study in the History of Medieval India* I; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Upinder Singh, ch. 10

location.summary: Tewar, ancient Tripuri, near Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh, on the north bank of the Narmada - in the Dahala country, the corridor between the Gangetic plain and the Deccan.

periodLevel.summary: An early historic settlement with Satavahana and later occupation, and from the 8th to the 13th centuries the capital of the Kalachuris of Chedi. The dynasty's peak falls under Gangeyadeva and his son Karnadeva, r. 1041-1073 CE; Tripuri fell to the Chandellas and then to the Delhi Sultanate's expansion.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The Kalachuri capital, and the origin of an era used across central India.
points: The Kalachuri or Chedi era, reckoned from 248 CE, was used in inscriptions over a wide swathe of central and western India for a thousand years - one of the major Indian dating systems, alongside the Vikrama, Shaka and Gupta eras, and the practical reason the dynasty matters for chronology.

Gangeyadeva took the title *Vikramaditya* and struck the gold *seated Lakshmi* coins that later circulated widely and were imitated by neighbouring dynasties. Karnadeva campaigned as far as Bengal and built the temple group at Amarkantak at the Narmada's source.
Tripuri's position made the Kalachuris a permanent third party in the wars of the Paramaras, Chandellas and Chalukyas, and the Bilhari and Karanbel inscriptions are the main sources for that history.
Excavation at Tewar has exposed early historic levels with punch-marked coins and Satavahana material, showing the site was a town long before it was a capital.

location.summary: Washim, ancient Vatsagulma, Washim district, Maharashtra, on the Penganga watershed in southern Vidarbha - inland Deccan, between the Godavari and the Wardha.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of the Vatsagulma branch of the Vakatakas, founded by Sarvasena, son of Pravarasena I, in the later 4th century CE and ruling until the early 6th. The senior Nandivardhana-Pravarapura branch ruled from near Ramtek; Harishena, r. c. 475-500, was the last great Vatsagulma king.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The court that paid for the later caves at Ajanta - the most consequential act of patronage in Indian art history.
points: The second, Mahayana phase of Ajanta, Caves 16, 17, 19 and 26 among them, was excavated under Harishena and his feudatories; Cave 16 was the gift of his minister Varahadeva, whose inscription records it. The paintings that define classical Indian art are therefore the product of this dynasty and effectively stop when it falls.

Walter Spink's chronology compresses the whole later Ajanta programme into roughly two decades around Harishena's reign, arguing that work was abandoned mid-chisel when the dynasty collapsed. Unfinished caves at the site support the argument, which is the standard reference for dating Ajanta.

The Vatsagulma branch patronised Sanskrit literature: Sarvasena wrote the Prakrit *Harivijaya*, and Pravarasena II of the senior line is credited with the *Setubandha*. The Vakatakas are the bridge between Satavahana Prakrit culture and Gupta-age Sanskrit.

Their marriage alliance with the Guptas, through Prabhavatigupta, daughter of Chandragupta II, who ruled as regent, is the best-documented case of a queen exercising sovereign authority in the period.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 9; Thapar, *Early India*; Basham, *The Wonder that was India*

location.summary: Pedavegi, ancient Vengi, Eluru district, Andhra Pradesh, in the fertile doab between the Krishna and the Godavari - the agricultural core of coastal Andhra.

periodLevel.summary: A centre from the Mauryan period, then capital successively of the Salankayanas (4th-5th centuries CE), the Vishnukundins (5th-6th), and from 624 CE the Eastern Chalukyas, founded by Kubja Vishnuvardhana, brother of Pulakesin II, after the Chalukya conquest of the region.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The seat of the Eastern Chalukyas, whose dynastic marriage into the Cholas reshaped south Indian politics and created Telugu literature.
points: Vengi's fertility made it a permanent object of contest - between the Pallavas and Chalukyas, then between the Cholas and the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani for two centuries. Control of the Krishna-Godavari doab is the recurring strategic question of early medieval peninsular history.

The contest was resolved dynastically: Rajaraja Narendra of Vengi married a Chola princess, and their son ascended the Chola throne as Kulottunga I in 1070, uniting the two lines. A succession dispute settled by marriage rather than conquest is a useful counter-example to purely military narratives.

Nannaya, at Rajaraja Narendra's court in the 11th century, began the Telugu *Mahabharata* - the beginning of Telugu literature, and the reason Vengi belongs in answers on regional languages as well as on dynasties.
Excavation at Pedavegi has exposed brick structures, a Buddhist stupa and Satavahana and later coinage, showing the site's depth well before the Chalukyas.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; ASI

location.summary: Vizhinjam, Thiruvananthapuram district, Kerala, on a rocky headland at the southern end of the Malabar coast - one of the few natural deep-water anchorages on India's western seaboard.

periodLevel.summary: Capital and principal port of the Ay dynasty, prominent from about the 8th to the 10th centuries CE, and repeatedly contested by the Pandyas and the Cheras. The rock-cut cave temple with its unfinished Shiva and Parvati panel belongs to the Ay period, c. 8th century.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The seat of the Ays, the third power of the far south, and the harbour that its geography made worth fighting for.
points: The Ay kingdom held the coast between the Cheras and the Pandyas, and Vizhinjam was its capital. The prolonged Pandya campaigns against it - the Vizhinjam war recorded in inscriptions and in the Sangam-successor literature - are the main evidence for the politics of the far south between the Sangam age and the Chola expansion.

Its deep water needed no river mouth and did not silt, which is precisely why the modern transshipment terminal has been built on the same spot. A harbour chosen in the 8th century and again in the 21st is a neat demonstration that port geography is a physical constant.
The cave temple, left unfinished, shows the rock-cut tradition of the Tamil country reaching the west coast, and its sculpture is among the earliest in Kerala.
The Ays were patrons of both Jainism and Hinduism, and their territory is where the Tamil and Malayalam linguistic regions began to separate.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Thapar, *Early India*; *Travancore Archaeological Series*

location.summary: Uraiyur, now a quarter of Tiruchirappalli, Tamil Nadu, on the south bank of the Kaveri where the river divides around Srirangam island - the head of the Kaveri delta.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of the early Cholas through the Sangam age, c. 3rd century BCE to 3rd century CE, and still significant later. Excavation has produced Black-and-Red Ware, Roman pottery and coins, terracottas and a dyeing vat. Ptolemy names it *Orthoura*.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The seat of the early Cholas before Thanjavur, and the cotton town of the Sangam economy.
points: Sangam poems describe Uraiyur as fortified, with burial grounds outside the walls, and celebrate its cotton cloth as fine as the slough of a snake - the literary source for Tamil textile manufacture that the excavated dyeing vat then corroborates.

Roman material here, as at Arikamedu and Puhar, places the early Chola capital inside the Indo-Roman trade network, with Uraiyur the inland manufacturing centre and Puhar its port at the Kaveri mouth.

The early Cholas of Karikala, remembered for building the Kallanai dam across the Kaveri, belong to this phase. The dynasty then disappears from view for some six centuries before Vijayalaya's revival in the 9th century - a gap that is itself a standard question.
Uraiyur, Puhar and Thanjavur in sequence trace the Chola centre of gravity moving down and across the delta over a millennium.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8; Thapar, *Early India*; Basham, *The Wonder that was India*

location.summary: Agra Fort, on the right bank of the Yamuna at Agra, Uttar Pradesh - a river-front citadel about 2.5 km upstream of the Taj Mahal, which is visible from its walls.

periodLevel.summary: A Lodi fort rebuilt in red sandstone by Akbar between 1565 and 1573; Jahangir and above all Shah Jahan replaced much of the interior in white marble in the 1630s-40s. Aurangzeb held his father prisoner here from 1658 until Shah Jahan's death in 1666. UNESCO World Heritage Site.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The whole evolution of Mughal architecture inside one enclosure - the clearest single site for the Akbar-to-Shah Jahan transition.
points: The Jahangiri Mahal, built under Akbar, uses brackets, carved beams and post-and-lintel construction taken directly from Rajput and Gujarati practice, in red sandstone. Shah Jahan's Khas Mahal, Diwan-i-Khas, Sheesh Mahal and Moti Masjid a lifetime later are marble, with cusped arches, *pietra dura* inlay and bulbous domes. Trabeate and indigenous gives way to arcuate and Persianate; the two stand a courtyard apart.
The Musamman Burj, the octagonal marble tower looking downriver, is where Shah Jahan was confined - the episode that anchors the war of succession of 1657-58 in physical memory.
The Diwan-i-Am, with its rows of cusped arches, is where *jharokha darshan* was performed, the daily public appearance that made the emperor visible to his subjects as a ritual obligation.
As the seat of empire until Shahjahanabad was founded in 1648, the fort is where the Mughal revenue and military system was administered for eighty years.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* II; J. L. Mehta, *Advanced Study in the History of Medieval India*; ASI

location.summary: Ahmednagar, western Maharashtra, on the Sina river in the upper Godavari basin - on the Deccan plateau inland from the Western Ghats, commanding the route between Pune and Aurangabad.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of the Nizam Shahi sultanate, founded in 1490 by Malik Ahmad, Bahmani governor of Junnar. It resisted Akbar's forces under Chand Bibi in 1595, was annexed by Shah Jahan in 1636, and is where Aurangzeb died in 1707.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The Deccan sultanate that produced Malik Ambar - the administrator and general whose methods the Marathas inherited.
points: Malik Ambar, an Ethiopian *Habshi* brought to India as a slave, became the effective ruler of Ahmednagar from about 1600 to 1626. He introduced a revenue settlement on the Todar Mal model - measured land, assessment by crop and soil, collection in cash - which became the basis of the system the Marathas later used in the same country.

His military method mattered more. Denied the field against superior Mughal artillery, he used light cavalry, raiding, denial of supply and constant mobility to keep the Mughals out of the Deccan for a quarter of a century. This is the *ganimi kava* that Shivaji perfected, and Ambar is its acknowledged originator.

Chand Bibi's defence of the fort against Akbar's army in 1595, personally directing the repair of a breach, is among the best-documented instances of a woman commanding in the field in Indian history.
The fort later held Jawaharlal Nehru and other Congress leaders from 1942-45, where Nehru wrote *The Discovery of India*.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I and II; J. L. Mehta, *Advanced Study in the History of Medieval India*

chapter.title: Medieval City and Sufi Saint Sites

location.summary: Ajmer, Rajasthan, in a valley of the Aravallis below Taragarh hill beside the Ana Sagar lake - the Chahamana capital after Sambhar, and a natural pass town between the desert and eastern Rajasthan.

periodLevel.summary: The dargah of Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti, who came to India in the late 12th century and died at Ajmer in 1236. The shrine buildings are largely of the Khalji, Tughlaq and Mughal periods, with Akbar and Shah Jahan adding mosques and gateways; the annual *urs* marks the saint's death anniversary.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The principal Sufi shrine in India, and the institutional centre of the Chishti order.
points: The Chishtis are defined by what they refused: state office, land grants and royal stipends. They lived on *futuh*, unsolicited offerings, kept open *langar*, and used *sama*, devotional music, as a spiritual practice - the last controversial with the orthodox ulama and the reason Chishti khanqahs drew musicians and poets.

That refusal is best understood against the Suhrawardis at Multan and Uch, who accepted office, held property and worked with the state. The Chishti-Suhrawardi contrast is the standard frame for any question on Sufism in the Delhi Sultanate.

Akbar walked to Ajmer from Agra more than once after Salim's birth, endowed the shrine and installed a great cooking cauldron. Imperial patronage of a saint who had rejected patronage is a neat illustration of how Mughal legitimacy borrowed from popular devotion.

The shrine's following has always crossed religious lines, which is why it features in discussions of composite culture - though the Chishti chain from Moinuddin through Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki, Baba Farid and Nizamuddin Auliya is what the exam usually wants.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I; J. L. Mehta, *Advanced Study in the History of Medieval India* I

location.summary: The Atia Jame Masjid at Atia, Delduar upazila, Tangail district, Bangladesh, on the bank of the old Jhenai channel in the Brahmaputra floodplain - deep in the deltaic interior, away from any stone source.

periodLevel.summary: Built in 1609 CE by Sa'id Khan Panni, a local chieftain, in memory of the Sufi Shah Baba Kashmiri. Brick throughout, with moulded terracotta ornament; repaired in the 19th century and again later, which accounts for its present condition.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A compact demonstration that Islamic architecture in Bengal is a regional idiom rather than an imported one.
points: The building is a single-aisled, three-domed mosque of the standard Bengal type, but its defining feature is the curved *do-chala* cornice - the roofline of a thatched bamboo hut reproduced in brick. The same curve appears on the Hindu temples at Bishnupur built in the same century, so the form belongs to Bengal, not to a religion.

Brick and terracotta were used because the delta has no building stone. The walls carry moulded panels of rosettes, chains, lamps and foliage in the same technique the temple builders used for narrative scenes - one craft tradition serving two faiths.

It stands between the Sultanate mosques of Gaur and the later Mughal-influenced work in Dhaka, and is usually cited to show the regional style continuing after Mughal annexation in 1576 rather than being displaced by it.
Patronage by a local chieftain, not a sultan or emperor, makes it evidence of how far down the social scale architectural ambition reached.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* II; Department of Archaeology, Bangladesh

location.summary: Fatehpur Sikri, Agra district, Uttar Pradesh, on a rocky ridge about 37 km west of Agra, above a lake that has since dried - the water supply that helped cause its abandonment.

periodLevel.summary: Built by Akbar between 1571 and 1585 and occupied as the imperial capital for roughly fourteen years, then left when the court moved to Lahore to manage the north-west frontier. Red sandstone throughout. UNESCO World Heritage Site.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A complete Mughal capital frozen at one moment, and the setting of Akbar's religious experiment.
points: Akbar built it in fulfilment of a vow to Shaikh Salim Chishti, who had foretold the birth of his son Salim, the future Jahangir. The saint's marble tomb, with its serpentine brackets and pierced *jali* screens, sits in the courtyard of the Jama Masjid - a Sufi grave at the centre of an imperial city.

The *Ibadat Khana* housed the debates Akbar convened from 1575 among Muslim theologians, and later Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians and Jesuits. Out of these came the *mahzar* of 1579, making Akbar the final arbiter in disputed religious questions, and eventually the *Din-i-Ilahi*. The whole of Akbar's religious policy can be taught from this one building.

The Diwan-i-Khas, with its single central pillar carrying a circular platform linked by radiating bridges, and the Panch Mahal, a five-storeyed open pavilion, show Gujarati, Rajput and Timurid elements combined - the architectural counterpart of *sulh-i-kul*.
The Buland Darwaza, added about 1576, commemorates the conquest of Gujarat and is among the tallest gateways in the world.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* II; Abu'l Fazl, *Akbarnama*; ASI

location.summary: Ghazni, eastern Afghanistan, on the Ghazni river on the high plateau between Kabul and Kandahar - astride the road from Khurasan to the Indian passes.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of the Ghaznavid dynasty, founded by Sabuktigin and brought to its height by Mahmud, r. 998-1030, who led some seventeen raids into India between 1000 and 1027. The city was sacked and burnt by the Ghurid Alauddin Husain in 1151, who earned the title *Jahansuz*, the world-burner.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The base from which the Ghaznavid raids on India were mounted, and an unexpected centre of scholarship funded by their proceeds.
points: Mahmud's raids - Nagarkot, Mathura, Kannauj, Somnath in 1025-26 - were expeditions for plunder rather than for territory; only the Punjab was annexed. Treating them as conquest is the commonest error, and Ghazni's own history makes the point: the wealth was carried back here to build a capital, not used to govern India.

Al-Biruni was brought to Ghazni from Khwarezm and travelled in India in Mahmud's train. His *Kitab-ul-Hind* is the most penetrating foreign account of Indian society, science and religion before the modern period, and is notable for studying Sanskrit sources directly and for its detachment - written, as it was, in the service of a raider.
Firdausi's *Shahnama* was composed for Mahmud's court, and the poet's quarrel with the sultan over payment is part of the standard picture of Ghaznavid patronage.
The two surviving victory minarets of Masud III and Bahram Shah, richly carved in brick, are the remains of the city Mahmud's Indian plunder built.

content.sourcesLine: J. L. Mehta, *Advanced Study in the History of Medieval India* I; Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I; Al-Biruni, *Kitab-ul-Hind*

location.summary: Golconda, on a granite hill on the western edge of Hyderabad, Telangana - a citadel on the Deccan plateau above the Musi basin, with the Qutb Shahi tombs on the ridge outside.

periodLevel.summary: A Kakatiya mud fort rebuilt in stone by the Qutb Shahis from 1518, when Quli Qutb Shah declared independence from the Bahmanis. It was the capital until Hyderabad was founded in 1591, and fell to Aurangzeb in 1687 after a siege of eight months ended by bribery rather than assault.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The diamond capital of the world, and the conquest that completed Aurangzeb's overextension in the Deccan.
points: Every great Indian diamond of the period - the Koh-i-Noor, the Hope, the Regent, the Orlov - came through Golconda's market from the Kollur and other mines along the Krishna. "Golconda" entered European languages as a byword for wealth. Tavernier's account of the mines and the trade is the standard source.
The fort's acoustics are famous: a clap at the Fateh Darwaza carries to the Bala Hisar pavilion at the summit, part of a designed system of defence and signalling.

Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, who founded Hyderabad and built the Charminar in 1591, wrote poetry in Dakhni Urdu, and the Qutb Shahi court is central to the emergence of Urdu as a literary language in the Deccan rather than in the north.

Aurangzeb's annexation of Golconda in 1687, after Bijapur in 1686, removed the buffer states that had contained the Marathas and committed the empire to a war it could not end - the standard argument that the Deccan campaigns caused the Mughal decline.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* II; J. L. Mehta, *Advanced Study in the History of Medieval India*; Tavernier, *Travels in India*

location.summary: Kalaburagi, formerly Gulbarga, northern Karnataka, on the dry plateau of the upper Bhima basin - a fortified town in open country between Bidar and Bijapur.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of the Bahmani sultanate from 1347, when Alauddin Bahman Shah broke from Muhammad bin Tughlaq, until the seat moved to Bidar about 1425-32. The Jama Masjid within the fort dates to 1367; the dargah of Gesu Daraz, d. 1422, stands outside it.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The first capital of the first independent Deccan sultanate, and the place where the Chishti order moved south.
points: The Bahmani secession followed Muhammad bin Tughlaq's transfer of the capital to Daulatabad and its failure - the standard case study in Sultanate overreach, since the very officers moved south to hold the Deccan founded a kingdom there instead.

The Jama Masjid is unique in India for having its entire courtyard roofed, with sixty-three small domes and open arcaded sides rather than an open *sahn*. The design is traditionally attributed to a Persian architect and compared to Cordoba; whatever its source, it shows the Bahmanis importing Iranian expertise directly rather than adapting north Indian models.

Khwaja Bandanawaz Gesu Daraz, a disciple of the Delhi Chishti line, migrated to Gulbarga in his old age and made it a spiritual centre for the whole Deccan. His arrival marks the extension of the Chishti network beyond the Vindhyas, and he wrote in Dakhni, contributing to the language's early literature.
The rivalry between *Afaqi* immigrant nobles and *Dakhni* locals that later destroyed Mahmud Gawan at Bidar begins in this court.

location.summary: Basavakalyan, ancient Kalyani, Bidar district, northern Karnataka, on the Deccan plateau between the Manjra and the Bhima - inland, roughly 80 km from Bidar. It is not to be confused with Kalyan, the Konkan port near Mumbai.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of the Western Chalukyas, the Chalukyas of Kalyani, from about 1050 CE under Someshvara I until the dynasty's fall around 1190; then briefly of the Kalachuris of Kalyani under Bijjala. Its greatest ruler was Vikramaditya VI, r. 1076-1126, who founded the Chalukya-Vikrama era.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The court that produced the standard text of Hindu inheritance law, and the town where the Lingayat movement began.
points: Vijnaneshvara wrote the *Mitakshara* here, a commentary on the *Yajnavalkya Smriti*. It became the authority on inheritance and joint family property across almost all of India apart from Bengal, where the *Dayabhaga* prevailed, and it was applied by British and Indian courts into the twentieth century. A legal text from this court still shaped property disputes eight hundred years later.

Basavanna, minister to the Kalachuri Bijjala, founded the Veerashaiva or Lingayat movement in the 12th century. Its *Anubhava Mantapa* was an open assembly where sharanas of any caste or gender debated - Akka Mahadevi and Allama Prabhu among them - and its *vachanas*, short free-verse utterances in Kannada, rejected caste, temple ritual and priestly mediation.

The movement's crisis came with a marriage between a brahmana bride and a cobbler's son around 1167, the violent reaction to which scattered the sharanas. It is the sharpest available case of a bhakti movement colliding with caste in practice rather than in principle.
Bilhana's *Vikramankadevacharita*, a Sanskrit court epic, records Vikramaditya VI's reign.

location.summary: Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan, on the left bank of the Ravi in the Bari doab - the principal city between the Khyber and Delhi, and therefore the hinge of every invasion route into India.

periodLevel.summary: The Ghaznavids' Indian capital from the 11th century after Mahmud's raids; then Ghurid and Sultanate. Akbar made it the imperial capital from 1585 to 1598 while securing the north-west. Shah Jahan built the Shalimar Gardens in 1641, Aurangzeb the Badshahi mosque in 1673, and Ranjit Singh ruled the Sikh empire from here, 1799-1839.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The Mughal empire's second capital, and the best place to see Mughal garden and mosque architecture at full scale.
points: Akbar's move here for thirteen years was strategic: Kabul, Kandahar and the Uzbek frontier all had to be managed, and Lahore was the only city from which that was possible. The episode shows Mughal capitals following military necessity rather than sentiment.

The Shalimar Gardens are the classic *charbagh* on three descending terraces with over four hundred fountains, fed by a canal cut from the Ravi - a Persian paradise-garden realised as a hydraulic engineering project.

The Badshahi mosque, with its vast courtyard and red sandstone inlaid with marble, is the last great imperial mosque of the Mughals and deliberately answers Shah Jahan's Jama Masjid at Delhi. The Wazir Khan mosque, 1634, is the finest surviving example of Mughal glazed-tile *kashi* work.

Jahangir's tomb across the river at Shahdara, with no dome at the emperor's own instruction, and the Sikh-period additions under Ranjit Singh complete a sequence running from Ghaznavid to Sikh in one city.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* II; J. L. Mehta, *Advanced Study in the History of Medieval India*; ASI

location.summary: Multan, southern Punjab, Pakistan, in the doab near the old course of the Ravi close to its junction with the Chenab - the hinge between Sindh, the Punjab and the routes to Khurasan.

periodLevel.summary: Ancient Mulasthana, famous for its sun temple, described by Xuanzang in the 7th century and by Al-Biruni before Mahmud of Ghazni destroyed it. Under Arab and then Qarmatian rule, it became a frontier province of the Delhi Sultanate; Nasiruddin Qubacha held it in the early 13th century. The shrine of Bahauddin Zakariya, d. 1262, is its Sufi centre.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The seat of the Suhrawardi order in India - the counter-model to Chishti practice - and the Sultanate's principal western trade city.
points: Bahauddin Zakariya established the Suhrawardi silsila here on the opposite principle to the Chishtis: he accepted royal patronage and office, held substantial property, maintained contact with the Sultanate, and did not practise poverty. Setting Multan against Ajmer is the cleanest way to show that Indian Sufism was not one thing.

The tomb of Shah Rukn-e-Alam, his grandson, built in the 1320s, is among the great monuments of Tughlaq architecture - an octagonal brick mausoleum with sloping buttresses and glazed blue and white tile, and the model for later Sindhi and Punjabi tomb building.
As a Sultanate province Multan controlled the caravan traffic to Khurasan and Central Asia, and was the point at which Mongol pressure on the north-west was absorbed for over a century.
The destruction of the sun temple by Mahmud, and the earlier Arab practice of leaving it standing to tax pilgrims, are often paired to show how differently rulers treated the same shrine.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I and II; J. L. Mehta, *Advanced Study in the History of Medieval India* I

location.summary: Ramdevra, also called Runicha, Jaisalmer district, Rajasthan, in the Thar desert about 12 km from Pokhran - a shrine village on the old caravan track across western Rajasthan.

periodLevel.summary: The samadhi of Baba Ramdev, a Tanwar Rajput chieftain of the early 15th century - his dates are usually given as 1352-1385 or in the 1400s, and cannot be fixed precisely. The temple over the samadhi was built later, with major additions in the 19th and 20th centuries.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A regional saint venerated across religious and caste lines - the best western Indian example of folk devotion that no orthodoxy controls.
points: Ramdev is worshipped by Hindus as an incarnation of Krishna and by Muslims as *Ramshah Pir* or *Ramapir*, and his shrine carries both a Hindu samadhi and Islamic devotional practice. That a single figure is a deity to one community and a pir to another is the standard illustration of how the Hindu-Muslim boundary worked in practice at the village level.

His following is strongest among Dalit and artisan communities, especially the Meghwals, and the tradition centres on his rejection of untouchability - the story of his taking food with Dali Bai and his refusal of caste exclusion at his own feast.

The *Kamdiya* and *terah taali* devotional performances, and the annual fair at Bhadrapada, sustain an oral tradition in Marwari with no Sanskrit text behind it - useful evidence that bhakti in western India operated largely outside the literate tradition.
The site belongs with Pandharpur and the Varkaris as an example of caste-inclusive regional devotion, though Ramdev's cult has no theological system comparable to theirs.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* II; *Rajasthan District Gazetteer*, Jaisalmer

location.summary: Sasaram, Rohtas district, Bihar, at the foot of the Kaimur hills in the Son valley - on the Grand Trunk Road, the highway its most famous son rebuilt.

periodLevel.summary: The tomb of Sher Shah Suri, r. 1540-1545, was built between about 1540 and 1545 by the architect Aliwal Khan. Red sandstone, five storeys, octagonal, about 46 m high, standing on a plinth in the middle of an artificial lake. One of Ashoka's minor rock edicts is also inscribed on a hill nearby.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The finest tomb of the Indo-Afghan tradition, and the burial place of the administrator the Mughals copied.
points: The tomb is the culmination of the Lodi-Sur octagonal type: an octagon within a square terrace, ringed by chhatris, its dome among the largest built in India before Gol Gumbaz. Setting it in the centre of a tank makes the reflection part of the design - an effect later used at the Taj by different means.

Sher Shah's five years of rule produced the framework the Mughals inherited: the *zabti* revenue settlement with measured land and rates fixed by crop, later developed by Todar Mal under Akbar; the silver *rupiya*, ancestor of the modern rupee; the rebuilt Sadak-i-Azam from Bengal to the Indus with sarais and a *dak* postal relay.
That an Afghan interregnum supplied so much of Mughal administration is the standard corrective to treating Mughal institutions as purely Mughal inventions.
The Ashokan minor rock edict on the hill above makes Sasaram a rare site carrying both Mauryan and Sur-period remains.

location.summary: The Khanqah-e-Moula or Shah-e-Hamadan mosque, on the right bank of the Jhelum in the old city of Srinagar, Jammu and Kashmir - built at the river's edge in the heart of the medieval town.

periodLevel.summary: Built in 1395 by Sultan Sikandar in memory of Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani, the Persian Kubrawi Sufi who came to Kashmir in the 1370s and died in 1384. Rebuilt after fires in the 15th and 18th centuries, always to the same design, in deodar timber.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The masterpiece of Kashmiri wooden architecture, and the monument of the Sufi credited with reshaping the valley's economy as well as its religion.
points: The structure is built of interlocking deodar beams laid without nails, on the *taq* and *dhajji* principles that give Kashmiri buildings their resistance to earthquake. The interior is finished in *papier-mache* and *khatamband* - geometric wooden ceilings assembled from small pieces without glue - and hung with painted panels.

Sayyid Ali Hamadani is said to have arrived with several hundred followers, many of them craftsmen, and Kashmiri tradition credits him with introducing or systematising shawl weaving, carpet knotting, papier-mache and woodcarving. Whether or not the attribution is exact, it records a real transfer of Persian craft into the valley, and is the standard example of Sufi networks moving technique as well as doctrine.

His son Mir Muhammad Hamadani influenced Sikandar's reign, associated with iconoclasm and conversion - so the site is also cited in the harsher account of Kashmir's Islamisation, against the accommodating reputation of Nund Rishi and the Rishi order.
The mosque stands opposite the Hindu ghats on the Jhelum, and both remain in use.

location.summary: Thatta, Sindh, Pakistan, near the eastern edge of the Indus delta about 100 km from Karachi, with the Makli ridge rising beside it - the delta's capital before the river shifted away.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of Sindh under the Sammas, Arghuns and Tarkhans from the 14th century, then a Mughal provincial seat from 1592. The Makli necropolis spans the 14th to the 18th centuries; the Shah Jahan mosque was completed about 1647.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the largest funerary landscapes in the world, and the point where Persian and Timurid tilework meets Gujarati stone carving.
points: The Makli necropolis covers roughly ten square kilometres and holds an estimated half a million graves - kings, queens, saints, scholars and soldiers across four centuries. Nowhere else in South Asia can a single regional elite be studied so completely through its tombs.

The two traditions sit side by side there. Samma-period tombs, such as Jam Nizamuddin's, are carved sandstone with Gujarati-derived brackets and floral bands; Tarkhan and Mughal tombs are brick faced in blue, turquoise and white glazed tile in the Iranian manner. The shift tracks Sindh's reorientation from the Indian west coast towards Safavid Iran and Central Asia.

The Shah Jahan mosque, built for a city that had sheltered the emperor during a revolt, has ninety-three domes and no minarets, and is designed so that a speaker at the mihrab can be heard throughout - the most sophisticated acoustic design in Mughal architecture.
Thatta declined as the Indus migrated westward and Karachi took its trade, the same river-shift that had earlier stranded Debal.

content.sourcesLine: Basham, *The Wonder that was India*; Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* II; ASI/UNESCO

location.summary: Uch Sharif, Bahawalpur district, Punjab, Pakistan, near the confluence of the Chenab and the Sutlej before they join the Indus - a river-island town on the Multan-Sindh route.

periodLevel.summary: An ancient site sometimes identified with an Alexandrian foundation on the Indus. It was Nasiruddin Qubacha's capital in the early 13th century before the Delhi Sultanate absorbed it, and thereafter a Sultanate frontier stronghold and a major Suhrawardi centre. The surviving tomb group is of the 14th-15th centuries.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: With Multan, the second pole of the Suhrawardi order, and the site of some of the finest glazed-tile architecture in the subcontinent.
points: Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari settled here in the 13th century and his descendant Jahaniyan Jahangasht, the "world traveller", made Uch a centre whose spiritual authority reached across Sindh and Gujarat. The Multan-Uch axis is where Islam spread along the Indus by persuasion and patronage rather than by campaign.

The tomb of Bibi Jawindi, c. 1493, is octagonal with sloping buttresses and faced in blue and white glazed tile, closely related to the Multan tombs and to Central Asian work at Samarkand. Half of it was carried away by flooding of the Chenab, and what remains is on the tentative World Heritage list.
Guru Nanak visited during his travels, and the shrine preserves relics associated with him - a reminder that Sufi khanqahs on the Indus were meeting points rather than closed communities.
Qubacha's brief kingdom here, squeezed between Iltutmish and the Mongols, is a useful example of how unstable the north-western frontier was in the Sultanate's first decades.

location.summary: Vijayapura, long known as Bijapur, northern Karnataka, on the dry Deccan plateau between the Krishna and the Bhima - about 100 km from Badami and Pattadakal.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of the Adil Shahi sultanate from 1490, when Yusuf Adil Khan broke away from the Bahmanis, until Aurangzeb took the city in 1686. Its architectural high point falls under Ibrahim Adil Shah II, r. 1580-1627, and Muhammad Adil Shah, r. 1627-1656.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The most accomplished architecture of the Deccan sultanates, and a court whose religious eclecticism rivalled Akbar's.
points: The Gol Gumbaz, the tomb of Muhammad Adil Shah completed about 1656, carries a dome roughly 44 m across - the largest in India and among the largest anywhere - resting on intersecting pendentive arches rather than a drum. Its Whispering Gallery, where a murmur circles the base of the dome, is the best-known acoustic feature in Indian architecture.

The Ibrahim Rauza, the tomb and mosque of Ibrahim II, is the finer building: exact proportions, deep eaves and stonework cut like filigree. It is often said to have influenced the Taj, and its architect Malik Sandal signed it.

Ibrahim II called himself *Jagadguru Badshah*, and his *Kitab-i-Nauras*, a book of songs in Dakhni, opens by invoking Saraswati and Ganesha alongside the Prophet. A Muslim sultan writing Hindustani music theory addressed to Hindu deities is the sharpest Deccan example of religious accommodation.

The Malik-e-Maidan, one of the largest bronze cannon of the medieval world, stands on the ramparts - a reminder that these sultanates were technically formidable until Mughal artillery and money outlasted them.

location.summary: Vrindavan, Mathura district, Uttar Pradesh, on the right bank of the Yamuna in the Braj country - a few kilometres from Mathura, at the centre of the Krishna landscape.

periodLevel.summary: An ancient tirtha that was effectively refounded in the 16th century, when Chaitanya Mahaprabhu sent the Six Goswamis to identify and restore the Braj sites. The great temples belong to the decades around 1590: Govind Dev, Madan Mohan, Radha Raman and Jugal Kishore.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The physical centre of Krishna bhakti, and a case of a sacred landscape being deliberately reconstructed.
points: Rupa, Sanatana, Jiva and the other Goswamis located the groves, ghats and ponds of the Krishna story on the ground and wrote the theological works - Rupa's *Bhaktirasamritasindhu* above all - that gave Gaudiya Vaishnavism its doctrine of *rasa*. Vrindavan is therefore where a devotional geography was mapped as a scholarly project.

The Govind Dev temple was built about 1590 by Raja Man Singh of Amber, Akbar's leading Rajput commander, in red sandstone on a cruciform plan with a vaulted nave. A Mughal *mansabdar* funding a Vaishnava temple with imperial approval, in an architectural idiom that borrows from mosque construction, is the clearest single illustration of Akbar's religious policy in built form; Aurangzeb later had its upper storeys taken down.

Braj bhakti produced a vernacular literature to match - Surdas of the Ashtachhap and the Vallabha sampradaya, Mirabai's songs, and the poetry of Swami Haridas - which is why Vrindavan belongs in questions on regional languages as well as religion.
