location.summary: Balkh, ancient Bactra, in northern Afghanistan on the Balkh river a little south of the Oxus (Amu Darya) - the oasis where the roads from Iran, the Central Asian steppe, China and India converge.

periodLevel.summary: An Achaemenid satrapal seat, then the core of the Greco-Bactrian kingdom from c. 250 BCE, the base from which the Yuezhi became the Kushanas, and later a great Buddhist and then Islamic centre. Destroyed by Genghis Khan in 1220 and never fully recovered. The Arabs called it *Umm al-Bilad*, the Mother of Cities.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The single most important crossroads on the northern route - the place where Greek, Iranian, Indian and Chinese worlds met.
points: The Greco-Bactrian kings, Diodotus, Euthydemus and Demetrius among them, ruled here before pushing into India as the Indo-Greeks. Their portrait coinage and Hellenistic sculptural conventions fed directly into Gandhara art, so Balkh stands behind the Buddha image itself.

The *Nava Vihara*, the great Buddhist monastery outside the city, was described by Xuanzang in the 7th century. Its hereditary abbots, after conversion, became the Barmakid family, viziers of the Abbasid caliphs at Baghdad - the channel through which Indian mathematics, astronomy and medicine reached the Arab world in the 8th-9th centuries.
Zoroastrian tradition places Zoroaster's death at Balkh, and the city was a major centre of that faith before Buddhism and Islam - three religions in succession at one site.
Rumi was born here in 1207, a few years before the Mongol destruction that drove his family west.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* II; Thapar, *Early India*; Upinder Singh, ch. 8

location.summary: Barbarikon, the port at the mouth of the Indus in Sindh, Pakistan. The *Periplus* places it on the middle of seven mouths; it is generally sought in the delta east of modern Karachi, and is sometimes identified with the site later known as Debal.

periodLevel.summary: Active in the 1st century CE, when the *Periplus of the Erythraean Sea* describes it, under Indo-Scythian (Saka) and then Indo-Parthian rule, with the Kushanas controlling the hinterland shortly after.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The one port where the maritime trade of the Indian Ocean and the overland Silk Route demonstrably meet.
points: The *Periplus* says ships anchored at Barbarikon but cargo was taken upriver to the royal capital - Minnagara - for the king's inspection, a rare description of customs procedure. Imports listed are clothing, figured linens, topaz, coral, storax, frankincense, glass vessels, silver plate and wine.

The exports are what matter: *costus*, bdellium, *lycium*, nard, turquoise, lapis lazuli, Chinese pelts, cotton cloth, silk yarn and indigo. Turquoise comes from Khurasan, lapis from Badakhshan, silk from China - none of it Indian. The goods had come down the Indus from Bactria and beyond, so this is the documentary proof that the Central Asian caravan routes emptied into the Arabian Sea trade here.
That makes Barbarikon the standard answer to how the Silk Route connected to maritime commerce, rather than running only overland to the Mediterranean.
Note that the port is often loosely equated with modern Karachi. The two are near neighbours on the same delta but not the same place, and Karachi has its own separate entry as Krokola.

location.summary: Herat, western Afghanistan, on the Hari Rud in the province of Khurasan - the junction of the roads north to Merv and Bukhara, west into Iran, east to Balkh and Kabul, and south to Kandahar and the Indian passes.

periodLevel.summary: An ancient city, sacked by the Mongols in 1221, and restored as the capital of the Timurids under Shah Rukh and his queen Gauhar Shad in the 15th century. Its cultural peak, the Herat school, falls between about 1400 and 1507, when the Uzbeks took the city.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The Timurid capital whose artistic tradition the Mughals brought to India - the aesthetic ancestor of Mughal painting.
points: The Herat atelier under Sultan Husain Bayqara, with Bihzad as its greatest master, brought Persian miniature painting to its height: individualised faces, controlled recession, and everyday incident within formal composition.

Humayun recruited two Herat-trained painters, Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd us-Samad, during his exile at the Safavid court and brought them to India. They founded the imperial atelier under Akbar, so the Mughal school begins as a Herati transplant before absorbing Indian colour and naturalism. The line from Herat to the *Hamzanama* and the *Akbarnama* is the point to make.

Babur was a Timurid prince who visited Herat and admired it, and his sense of inheritance - the *Baburnama*'s constant comparisons between Kabul, Herat and Hindustan - is why the Mughals called themselves Timurids rather than Mughals at all.
Gauhar Shad's musalla and minarets, and the Friday Mosque, are the surviving monuments of that period.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* II; J. L. Mehta, *Advanced Study in the History of Medieval India*; Babur, *Baburnama*

location.summary: Jaisalmer, western Rajasthan, on the Trikuta hill rising some 75 m above the Thar desert - built of the local yellow sandstone that turns gold at sunset, on the caravan track from Gujarat and Delhi towards Multan and Central Asia.

periodLevel.summary: Founded in 1156 CE by Rawal Jaisal of the Bhati Rajputs, who moved the seat from Lodurva. The fort was besieged by Alauddin Khalji in the early 14th century, with *jauhar* performed, and again under Firoz Shah Tughlaq. The Jain temples within the walls date from the 12th to the 15th centuries; the merchant *havelis* are 18th and 19th century.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A desert caravan city, one of the very few forts anywhere still inhabited as a town, and the keeper of one of India's most important manuscript collections.
points: Jaisalmer's wealth came entirely from transit. Caravans crossing between the Indian plains and the Indus carried opium, indigo, silk, spices and horses, and the Bhati rulers taxed them. When sea trade through Bombay and then the railways redirected that traffic in the 19th century, the town simply stopped growing - which is why its medieval fabric survives so completely.

Ninety-nine bastions ring the hill, and the defence depended on the Ghadisar tank and on the desert itself: an attacker had to bring water across the Thar, which is why sieges here were rare and short.

Roughly a quarter of the old town still lives inside the walls, with continuous drainage, wells and habitation rather than a preserved ruin. That is also its main conservation problem - modern water use has saturated the foundations and caused bastion collapses.

The Jain temples inside hold the *Jaisalmer Bhandar*, a library of palm-leaf and paper manuscripts preserved by the dry desert air, some from the 11th century, including texts that survive nowhere else. It is a principal source for medieval Indian literature and science.
The havelis, Patwon ki Haveli above all, document the Marwari commercial families whose networks later financed trade across northern India.

location.summary: Kabul, eastern Afghanistan, in a high valley on the Kabul river between the Hindu Kush passes to the north and the Khyber to the east - the gate through which almost every land invasion of India has passed.

periodLevel.summary: A Hindu Shahi centre before the Ghaznavids; taken by Babur in 1504, who ruled from it for twenty-two years before Panipat in 1526 and was buried there at his own wish. Kabul and Kandahar were Mughal provinces, Kandahar contested repeatedly with the Safavids until lost in 1649.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The Mughal dynasty's own homeland and the empire's strategic hinge - the reason so much Mughal effort went north-west rather than south.
points: Babur's *Baburnama* describes Kabul's markets in detail: caravans arriving from Ferghana, Turkestan, Khurasan and Hindustan, and the goods and fruits of each. It is one of the best first-person accounts of Central Asian trade, written by a ruler who knew the routes personally.

Retaining Kabul mattered because it commanded the passes. The Mughal obsession with Kandahar and the disastrous Balkh-Badakhshan campaign of 1646-47 under Shah Jahan, intended to recover Timur's Samarkand, both follow from this orientation - an enormous drain of treasure for territory the empire could not hold.

Babur asked to be buried at Kabul rather than in India, and the *Bagh-e-Babur* he laid out is the earliest Mughal garden, the prototype of the *charbagh* that reaches its Indian form at Agra and Lahore.
The city's position also made it the route by which Central Asian horses, essential to Indian cavalry, entered the subcontinent.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* II; J. L. Mehta, *Advanced Study in the History of Medieval India*; Babur, *Baburnama*

exam.modelAnswer30: Eastern Afghanistan. A Hindu Shahi centre before the Ghaznavids, taken by Babur in 1504. The Mughal dynasty's own homeland and the empire's strategic hinge, the reason so much Mughal effort went north-west rather than south.

location.summary: Leh, Ladakh, on the right bank of the Indus at about 3,500 m in the rain-shadow between the Zanskar and Ladakh ranges - the meeting point of the routes over the Karakoram to Yarkand, west to Kashmir, and east along the Indus to Tibet.

periodLevel.summary: A settlement of the Ladakh region from early times, and capital of the Namgyal dynasty from the 16th century. Leh Palace, a nine-storeyed structure modelled on the Potala, was built by Sengge Namgyal in the 17th century. The Treaty of Tingmosgang in 1684 fixed the Ladakh-Tibet frontier and the terms of its trade.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The hinge of the trans-Himalayan trade, and the route by which Indian Buddhism reached Tibet and survived there.
points: Leh was the entrepot of the pashmina trade. The fine underwool of the Changthangi goat, raised on the western Tibetan plateau, was brought here and channelled by treaty to Kashmir, where it was woven into shawls. An entire luxury industry in Srinagar depended on a mountain route through Leh, and the Tingmosgang terms made that monopoly explicit.
The Karakoram route to Yarkand and Kashgar linked Ladakh to the Tarim basin oases, carrying silk, tea, gold, borax and charas in exchange - the southernmost limb of the Silk Route system.

Ladakhi Buddhism, in its Tibetan form, preserves the monastic and textual tradition transmitted from Kashmir and from the Indian mahaviharas. Monasteries at Hemis, Alchi, Thiksey and Lamayuru hold manuscripts, and Alchi's 11th-12th century murals preserve a Kashmiri painting style otherwise entirely lost in Kashmir itself.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* II; Janet Rizvi, *Trans-Himalayan Caravans*

location.summary: Lhasa, in the valley of the Kyi Chu, a tributary of the Brahmaputra (Yarlung Tsangpo), on the Tibetan plateau at about 3,650 m - the political and religious centre of Tibet.

periodLevel.summary: Made the capital by Srongtsen Gampo in the 7th century CE, who founded the Jokhang and the first structure on the Potala hill. Buddhism's "first diffusion" belongs to this period; the "second diffusion" follows Atisha Dipankara's arrival from India in 1042. The Potala as it stands is a 17th-century rebuilding under the Fifth Dalai Lama.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The destination of the Indian Buddhist transmission, and the reason much of Indian Buddhist literature survives at all.
points: Srongtsen Gampo sent Thonmi Sambhota to India to devise a script for Tibetan; the alphabet he brought back derives from an Indian Gupta-period script, so Tibetan writing is an Indian export. The king's Nepali and Chinese queens, Bhrikuti and Wencheng, are credited with bringing the images around which the Jokhang was built.

Atisha Dipankara Shrijnana, abbot of Vikramashila in Bihar, went to Tibet in 1042 and reformed its monastic Buddhism. The Bengal-to-Tibet connection under Pala patronage is the key link for questions on the later phase of Indian Buddhism.

Indian Buddhist texts were translated into Tibetan on a vast scale and collected as the *Kangyur* and *Tengyur*. A large number of works whose Sanskrit originals were lost after Buddhism declined in India survive only in these translations, so Tibetan sources are now primary evidence for Indian intellectual history.
The route through Nepal and the Chumbi valley also carried trade in wool, salt, borax and gold.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Thapar, *Early India*; Taranatha, *History of Buddhism in India*

location.summary: Quetta, Balochistan, Pakistan, in a high valley ringed by mountains at the head of the Bolan pass - the second great gateway from the Iranian plateau into the Indus valley, after the Khyber.

periodLevel.summary: The Quetta valley carries one of the longest cultural sequences in South Asia. Kili Gul Mohammad and Damb Sadaat give a Neolithic-to-Chalcolithic succession from about the 5th millennium BCE, and Mehrgarh on the Kachi plain at the foot of the Bolan runs from about 7000 BCE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The corridor through which farming, and later people and goods, entered the subcontinent.
points: Mehrgarh, excavated by Jean-Francois Jarrige, is the earliest farming settlement known in South Asia: mud-brick houses, domesticated wheat, barley, cattle, sheep and goat, and in its later levels cotton, the earliest anywhere. It shows agriculture developing locally in the Indus borderlands rather than arriving fully formed from West Asia - the central point in any question on the origins of the Harappan civilisation.
Mehrgarh has also produced drilled human molars, evidence of dentistry around 7000 BCE, and fine bead-work in turquoise and lapis that anticipates Harappan craft.
The Quetta valley sites give the ceramic sequence - Kili Gul Mohammad, Kechi Beg, Damb Sadaat wares - by which the Baluchistan Chalcolithic is dated and linked to Iranian and Central Asian material.
In historic times the Bolan carried the same traffic: Achaemenid and Greek armies, and the caravan trade between Kandahar and Sindh.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; Jarrige, *Mehrgarh: Field Reports*

location.summary: Akhnoor, Jammu district, Jammu and Kashmir, on the right bank of the Chenab where the river leaves the hills for the plain - the crossing point on the old route between Punjab and Kashmir.

periodLevel.summary: The standing fort was begun by Mian Tej Singh in 1762 and completed under Raja Alam Singh about 1802. The site matters more for what lies around it: the Harappan settlement at Manda a few kilometres upstream, and the Buddhist monastic site of Ambaran, active from about the 1st century BCE to the 5th century CE.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The northernmost extension of the Harappan world, and a Kushana-period Buddhist establishment in the Jammu hills.
points: Manda, on the Chenab at the foot of the Pir Panjal, is the northernmost Harappan site known. Its pre-Harappan, Mature Harappan and Late Harappan levels extend the civilisation's map into the sub-Himalaya and are usually explained by access to Himalayan timber floated down the Chenab.

Ambaran has produced a stupa complex with a gold and silver casket containing bone relics and charred material, and a large body of terracotta heads in the Gandhara idiom - the *Akhnoor terracottas*, among the finest unbaked-clay sculpture from ancient India, now dispersed across several museums.

Together the two sites make Akhnoor evidence that the Jammu region was not peripheral: it was inside the Harappan network in the third millennium BCE and inside the Gandharan Buddhist one in the early centuries CE.
The 18th-century fort itself belongs to the Dogra rise under the Jammu rajas that culminates in Gulab Singh and the state of Jammu and Kashmir.

location.summary: Amer, about 11 km north of Jaipur, Rajasthan, on a ridge of the Aravallis above the Maota lake, with the older fortress of Jaigarh on the hill behind it.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of the Kachhwaha Rajputs, taken from the Meenas and held from the 12th century. The palace-fort as it stands was begun by Raja Man Singh I from 1592 and extended by Mirza Raja Jai Singh and Sawai Jai Singh II, who moved the capital to the new city of Jaipur in 1727.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The seat of the first Rajput house to ally with the Mughals, and the architectural record of what that alliance produced.
points: The Kachhwahas entered Mughal service in 1562 when Bharmal's daughter married Akbar. Man Singh I became one of Akbar's senior commanders, governing Kabul and Bengal and leading the imperial army at Haldighati against Mewar. Amber is therefore the counterweight to Chittorgarh: two Rajput states, alliance and resistance, and both should be given in any answer on Mughal-Rajput relations.

The palace shows the resulting hybrid - Rajput courtyards, *jharokhas* and painted ornament combined with Mughal *charbagh* gardens, *pietra dura* and the Sheesh Mahal's mirror work. Man Singh's Ganesh Pol and the Diwan-i-Am use Mughal arcading on Rajput plans.
Man Singh also built the Govind Dev temple at Vrindavan, so the same patron funded a Vaishnava temple in Braj and served a Muslim emperor - the alliance's cultural dimension.
Jaigarh above holds the Jaivana, cast in 1720 and among the largest wheeled cannon ever made.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* II; J. L. Mehta, *Advanced Study in the History of Medieval India*; ASI

location.summary: Bekal, Kasaragod district, northern Kerala, on a headland jutting into the Arabian Sea - the largest fort in Kerala, covering about 16 hectares of laterite headland with the sea on three sides.

periodLevel.summary: Built about 1650 by Shivappa Nayaka of Keladi, whose dynasty succeeded to Vijayanagara authority in coastal Karnataka after 1565. It passed to Mysore under Hyder Ali in the 1760s, was held by Tipu Sultan, and was taken by the British in 1799 after Tipu's death.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A purely military coastal fort, and evidence of Karnataka powers pressing south into Malabar.
points: Bekal has no palace, temple or residential quarter inside it - only ramparts, a magazine, an observation tower and water tanks. That makes it unusual among Indian forts, which were normally seats of government as well, and it is read as a garrison built specifically to control the Malabar coast and its shipping.

The keyhole-shaped bastion facing the sea, with tiered openings for cannon at the top and for muskets below, and the water-filled ditch cut into laterite, show the adaptation of fort design to gunpowder and to a laterite coast.

Shivappa Nayaka is better known for the *Shivappa Nayaka Shist*, a revenue settlement assessing land by its productivity, so the same ruler appears in questions on both fortification and agrarian administration.
Its later passage to Hyder Ali and Tipu ties the site into the Anglo-Mysore wars and the Company's absorption of Malabar.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* II; J. L. Mehta, *Advanced Study in the History of Medieval India*; ASI

location.summary: Chittorgarh, southern Rajasthan, on an isolated plateau about 180 m above the plain between the Berach and Gambhiri rivers - the largest hill fort in India, commanding the route from Malwa into Mewar.

periodLevel.summary: The Sisodia capital of Mewar until 1568. It was stormed three times: by Alauddin Khalji in 1303, by Bahadur Shah of Gujarat in 1535, and by Akbar in 1567-68, after which Udai Singh moved the capital to Udaipur.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The central symbol of Rajput resistance, and the site of the three *jauhars* around which that tradition is built.
points: The 1303 siege is the subject of Malik Muhammad Jayasi's *Padmavat*, written in Awadhi in 1540 - two and a half centuries after the event, by a Sufi poet, as an allegory in which Padmini represents the soul. Treating it as a contemporary record of Alauddin's motives is the commonest error; Amir Khusrau, who was present, says nothing of the kind.

Akbar's siege of 1567-68 ended in a general massacre, and Abu'l Fazl records it. It is the hardest case against the picture of Akbar as uniformly conciliatory, and should be set beside his Rajput marriage alliances rather than omitted.

The Vijaya Stambha, a nine-storeyed victory tower raised by Rana Kumbha about 1448 to mark his defeat of Mahmud Khalji of Malwa, is covered in sculpture of Hindu deities and carries an inscription giving the Sisodia genealogy. The older Kirti Stambha is Jain.
Mirabai, the bhakti poet, belonged to this court by marriage, and her rejection of it links the fort to the chapter on saints.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I and II; J. L. Mehta, *Advanced Study in the History of Medieval India*

location.summary: Cooch Behar, northern West Bengal, on the Torsa river in the duars below the eastern Himalaya - the plain between Bhutan, Assam and the Bengal delta. The building is a palace rather than a fort, despite this chapter's heading.

periodLevel.summary: The Koch kingdom was founded by Biswa Singha in the early 16th century and reached its height under Nara Narayan, r. 1554-1587, and his general Chilarai. The present Victor Jubilee Palace was built in 1887 by Maharaja Nripendra Narayan; the princely state acceded to India in 1949.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The seat of the Koch dynasty, and a textbook example of princely-state architecture built to advertise loyalty to the Raj.
points: Nara Narayan rebuilt the Kamakhya temple at Guwahati in 1565 after its destruction, so the Koch court is directly connected to the principal Shakta shrine of the north-east. He also patronised Shankaradeva, the Assamese Vaishnava reformer, who took refuge in Koch territory - a single kingdom sustaining both tantric Shaktism and neo-Vaishnavism.

Chilarai's campaigns briefly made the Koch the dominant power of the Brahmaputra valley, checking the Ahoms, before the kingdom split into Koch Bihar and Koch Hajo and fell between Mughal and Ahom pressure.

The palace, modelled on Buckingham Palace with Corinthian columns and a 38 m dome over the durbar hall, is Italianate Renaissance with no Indian element at all. Princely rulers adopting European classicism wholesale is the architectural signature of the post-1858 settlement, and stands in deliberate contrast to the Indo-Saracenic style the British themselves used for public buildings in India.

location.summary: Fort St George, on the Coromandel shore at Chennai, Tamil Nadu, beside the mouth of the Cooum - an open surf coast with no natural harbour, chosen for politics rather than geography.

periodLevel.summary: Built by the English East India Company from 1640 under Francis Day and Andrew Cogan, on a strip granted by Damarla Venkatadri, the Nayak governing for the Vijayanagara successor at Chandragiri. Completed 1644; captured by the French under La Bourdonnais in 1746 and returned in 1749 by the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The first English fortress in India, and the model for how a trading company turned into a territorial power.
points: The sequence is the point: a factory becomes a fortified factory, the fortified factory acquires jurisdiction over the settlement around it, and the settlement becomes a base for revenue and troops. Madras grew as White Town inside the walls and Black Town outside, the earliest instance of the segregated colonial city.
Madras received a municipal corporation and a mayor's court in 1688, the first in India, so the institutions of Company government were tried here before Bengal.
St Mary's Church inside the fort, consecrated in 1680, is the oldest Anglican church east of Suez; Robert Clive and Elihu Yale were both married in it, and Clive began his career here as a writer.
Its loss to the French in 1746 and recovery by treaty, not by arms, opened the Carnatic Wars and demonstrated that the European struggle for India would be settled as much in Europe as in Asia.

location.summary: Fort William, Kolkata, West Bengal, on the east bank of the Hooghly beside the Maidan - sited where the river was deep enough for ocean-going ships, about 130 km upstream from the sea.

periodLevel.summary: The old fort was built from 1696 to 1706 around the Company's factory at Sutanuti-Kalikata-Govindpur. It was stormed by Siraj-ud-Daula in June 1756; after Plassey the present star-shaped fort was built between 1758 and 1781 on a new site cleared for the purpose.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The base from which the Company conquered Bengal, and therefore India.
points: Siraj-ud-Daula's capture of the old fort, provoked by the Company's unauthorised fortification and abuse of the *dastak* trade privilege, is the immediate cause of the campaign that ended at Plassey on 23 June 1757. The Black Hole episode, as reported by Holwell, has been questioned on its numbers ever since and should be presented with that qualification.

Plassey brought the Company the *diwani* of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa in 1765 - the right to collect revenue - which converted a trading body into a territorial government with an army paid from Indian land tax. Everything that follows in the Company's expansion rests on that revenue.
The new fort was built on a scale intended never to be taken: eight bastions, a vast glacis cleared of buildings, which is how Kolkata acquired the Maidan.

Fort William College, founded in 1800 by Wellesley to train civil servants in Indian languages, produced grammars, dictionaries and the first printed prose in Bengali and Hindustani - a lasting effect on Indian vernacular literature.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* II; ASI

location.summary: Gagron, Jhalawar district, south-eastern Rajasthan, at the confluence of the Ahu and the Kali Sindh - water on three sides and a rock-cut moat on the fourth, in the Hadoti country bordering Malwa.

periodLevel.summary: Built by the Doda and later Khichi Rajputs from about the 12th century. It was besieged repeatedly from Malwa and Delhi, taken by Hoshang Shah of Malwa in 1423 and by Mahmud Khalji in 1444, held by Rana Kumbha of Mewar, and finally passed to Akbar.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The classic Indian *jaldurg* or water fort, and a frontier stronghold between Rajasthan and Malwa.
points: Indian fort typology distinguishes *giridurg* (hill), *jaldurg* (water), *vandurg* (forest), *dhanvadurg* (desert) and others, following the *Arthashastra* and later texts. Gagron is the textbook *jaldurg*: it needed no artificial defences on three sides and was reduced only by prolonged blockade.

Its position on the Rajasthan-Malwa border made it the object of repeated contest between Mewar and the Malwa Sultanate, and two *jauhars* are recorded there. The fort is useful for showing that Rajput warfare was as often against neighbouring sultanates over frontier ground as against Delhi.
The dargah of the Sufi Mitthe Shah stands below the walls, and its Muharram fair draws both communities - a shared devotional site at a contested military one.
It is among the six Hill Forts of Rajasthan inscribed by UNESCO in 2013.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I; J. L. Mehta, *Advanced Study in the History of Medieval India*; ASI

location.summary: Garhgaon, Sivasagar district, upper Assam, in the Dikhow valley south of the Brahmaputra - about 13 km from Sivasagar, in the Ahom heartland.

periodLevel.summary: Built as the Ahom capital in 1540 by Suklenmung, called the Garhgaya Raja after it, and used until the seat moved to Rangpur in the 18th century. The surviving Kareng Ghar, a seven-storeyed brick palace of which four floors remain, was rebuilt by Rajeswar Singha about 1752.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The Ahom capital through the century of Mughal invasion, and the base of the resistance that stopped Mughal expansion eastward.
points: Mir Jumla, Aurangzeb's governor of Bengal, took Garhgaon in 1662 and held it through the monsoon, but disease and the flooded country destroyed his army and he withdrew and died in 1663. The Treaty of Ghilajharighat that followed was reversed within a decade.

The decisive engagement came at Saraighat in 1671, where Lachit Borphukan destroyed a far larger Mughal fleet in a river battle on the Brahmaputra. Assam is the one region the Mughals never held, and the terrain, climate and Ahom naval capability are the reasons - a useful counter-case in any question on the limits of Mughal power.

The Ahom state ran on the *paik* system, under which every adult male owed rotational labour service organised in *khels*. It produced the embankments, tanks, roads and palaces without a cash revenue economy, and is the standard example of a non-monetised administrative system.
The *Buranjis*, Ahom chronicles first written in Tai-Ahom and later in Assamese, record all of this from the Ahom side.

location.summary: Gingee or Senji, Villupuram district, Tamil Nadu, where three granite hills - Rajagiri, Krishnagiri and Chandrayandurg - are linked by a wall enclosing about 11 square km of ground between them.

periodLevel.summary: Begun under the Konar chiefs and the Cholas, and fortified on its present scale by the Gingee Nayaks under Vijayanagara in the 16th century. It passed to Bijapur in 1649, to Shivaji in 1677, to the Mughals in 1698, then to the Carnatic Nawabs, the French in 1750 and the British in 1761.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The strongest fortress in the Deccan, and the base from which the Maratha state survived Aurangzeb's conquest of Maharashtra.
points: After Sambhaji's execution in 1689, Rajaram escaped to Gingee and ruled from here for eight years while Zulfiqar Khan besieged it. The Mughals took it only in 1698, by which time Maratha power had regenerated in the west. Gingee is therefore the answer to how the Maratha state outlasted the loss of its own homeland.

Its design uses three separate hill citadels with independent water and granaries, so that the fall of one did not end resistance - the reason the fort acquired the reputation Shivaji is said to have given it as the most impregnable in India.
The Kalyana Mahal, a square tower in the Nayak style, the granaries, and the cut-rock cisterns show what a self-sufficient garrison needed.
Raja Tej Singh, Desingh of the ballads, died in 1714 resisting the Nawab of Arcot, and the episode entered Tamil folk literature - an example of local memory preserving a minor chief's revolt.

location.summary: Gwalior, Madhya Pradesh, on an isolated sandstone plateau about 100 m above the plain in the Chambal basin - the fort that commands the route between the Ganga plain and Malwa.

periodLevel.summary: Occupied from at least the 6th century CE, when a Huna inscription of Mihirakula records a sun temple. The standing fort is largely the work of Man Singh Tomar, r. 1486-1516; the Jain colossi in the rock face are 15th century. Held afterwards by the Lodis, Mughals, Marathas and Scindias.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The home of the earliest known written zero, and of the finest pre-Mughal Hindu palace architecture in northern India.
points: An inscription of 876 CE in the Chaturbhuj temple records a land grant for a garden measuring 187 by 270 *hastas* and a daily gift of fifty garlands - and writes the 0 in both numbers. It is the oldest securely dated use of zero as a written numeral anywhere in the world, and the single most quotable fact about Indian mathematics.

The Man Mandir palace, faced in blue, green and yellow glazed tile with friezes of ducks, elephants and banana trees, is the high point of Tomar building and was admired by Babur, who otherwise found little in Hindustan to praise.
The Siddhachal Jain colossi, rock-cut tirthankaras up to 17 m high, were defaced on Babur's orders and later repaired - a visible instance of iconoclasm and restoration on one cliff.
Tansen, Akbar's musician, is buried at Gwalior beside his teacher Muhammad Ghaus, and Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi was killed here in June 1858 during the last phase of the revolt.

location.summary: The Hawa Mahal, in the walled city of Jaipur, Rajasthan, forming part of the City Palace complex and fronting onto the Sireh Deorhi bazaar - a screen wall rather than a free-standing building.

periodLevel.summary: Built in 1799 by Sawai Pratap Singh, designed by Lal Chand Ustad, in red and pink sandstone. It belongs to the later phase of Jaipur, the city founded in 1727 by Sawai Jai Singh II. Despite this chapter's heading, it is a palace facade and not a fort.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Purdah made architectural - a building whose entire design exists to let women see without being seen.
points: The facade rises five storeys and is pierced by 953 small *jharokhas* with latticed screens. Women of the zenana could watch processions and street life in the bazaar below while remaining invisible and unapproachable. Few buildings anywhere state a social rule so directly in their structure, which is why it belongs in any discussion of gender and space in Indian history.
The screens also drive airflow, cooling the interior by the venturi effect - the *hawa* of the name - so the same device serves seclusion and climate together.

Jaipur itself is the more important subject: Sawai Jai Singh II laid it out in 1727 on a nine-block grid derived from the *Shilpa Shastra*, one of the earliest planned cities of the period, with the Jantar Mantar observatory at its centre.
Jai Singh's five observatories, his astronomical tables and his correspondence with European astronomers make Jaipur the best example of Indian scientific patronage in the 18th century.

location.summary: Kangla, in the centre of Imphal, Manipur, on the west bank of the Imphal river - the historic seat of the Meitei kings, surrounded by moats within the Manipur valley.

periodLevel.summary: The traditional capital of the Ningthouja dynasty, with the *Cheitharol Kumbaba*, the Manipuri royal chronicle, beginning its record in 33 CE. Rebuilt several times, notably under Khagemba in the 17th century and Bhagyachandra in the 18th. Occupied by the British after the Anglo-Manipur War of 1891 and returned to Manipur only in 2004.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The centre of Meitei kingship, and the site of one of the last independent kingdoms absorbed into British India.
points: The *Cheitharol Kumbaba* is a continuous court chronicle maintained over centuries, comparable in kind to Kashmir's *Rajatarangini* and Odisha's *Madala Panji* - one of very few indigenous historical records of its type, and the main source for Manipur's dynastic past.
The Kangla Sha, paired heraldic lion-dragons guarding the enclosure, are the emblem of Manipuri sovereignty and were destroyed by the British in 1891 and later rebuilt.

The Anglo-Manipur War of 1891 followed a palace coup and the killing of British officers. It ended with the public hanging of Yuvraj Tikendrajit and Thangal General at Imphal and the fort's conversion into a garrison - an episode central to Manipuri political memory and generally absent from all-India narratives.
Manipur's Vaishnava turn under Bhagyachandra in the 18th century, which produced the *Raas Leela* dance tradition, was directed from this court.

location.summary: Kumbhalgarh, Rajsamand district, Rajasthan, on a spur of the Aravallis at about 1,100 m, west of Udaipur - deliberately sited on the watershed between Mewar and Marwar.

periodLevel.summary: Built by Rana Kumbha of Mewar, r. 1433-1468, largely between 1443 and 1458, with the architect Mandan. Its perimeter wall runs about 36 km, the second longest continuous wall in the world. Taken only once, by a combined Mughal, Amber and Marwar force under Akbar in 1576, and then only by poisoning the water.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The refuge fortress of Mewar - the place the dynasty retreated to when Chittor fell, and the reason it survived.
points: Rajput strategy in Mewar depended on having a second capital in the hills that no siege train could reach. Udai Singh was born here and sheltered here as an infant; Maharana Pratap was born here in 1540 and used the surrounding hills as his base after Haldighati in 1576. Kumbhalgarh is what made a policy of prolonged resistance possible.

Rana Kumbha built or rebuilt some thirty-two of Mewar's eighty-four forts. He was also a scholar - a commentator on the *Gita Govinda* and a writer on music - and the *Kumbhalgarh prashasti* records his works. The soldier-scholar king is a Rajput counterpart to Bhoja of Dhar.
The fort encloses over three hundred temples, Jain and Hindu, some predating Kumbha, showing that a fortress of this size functioned as a self-sufficient township rather than a garrison.
It is one of the six Hill Forts of Rajasthan inscribed by UNESCO, with Chittorgarh, Ranthambore, Amber, Jaisalmer and Gagron.

location.summary: Mandu, Dhar district, Madhya Pradesh, on a Vindhyan plateau about 630 m high, cut off from the tableland by a deep ravine and looking south over the Narmada valley - a natural fortress with a 45 km circuit of walls.

periodLevel.summary: The Paramara *Mandapa-durga*, fortified from the 10th-11th centuries; capital of the Malwa Sultanate from 1401 under Dilawar Khan Ghuri and his son Hoshang Shah, r. 1405-1435. Taken by Akbar in 1561 from Baz Bahadur, the last independent sultan.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The finest provincial Sultanate architecture in India, and the building the Taj Mahal's architects came to study.
points: Hoshang Shah's tomb, completed about 1440, is the earliest marble building in India: a plain domed cube with latticed screens and corner cupolas. An inscription on it records the visit of Ustad Hamid and three other architects sent by Shah Jahan - documentary evidence of a Mughal masterpiece's acknowledged model.

The Jami Masjid, said to follow the great mosque of Damascus, and the Hindola Mahal with its steeply battered walls, show the Malwa style: massive, austere, unornamented, and using coloured stone rather than surface carving.

The Jahaz Mahal, a long narrow pavilion between two tanks so that it appears to float, is the best surviving example of Sultanate pleasure architecture and of the elaborate rainwater harvesting the plateau required.

Baz Bahadur and Rupmati, the sultan and the singer, are the subject of a romance that generated its own painting and poetry tradition after Akbar's conquest - a case of a defeated court surviving as legend.

location.summary: Mehrangarh, Jodhpur, Rajasthan, on a sheer rock about 120 m above the city at the eastern edge of the Thar - the Rathore capital of Marwar, on the desert's trade frontier.

periodLevel.summary: Begun in 1459 by Rao Jodha, who moved the Rathore seat here from Mandore, and extended by successive rulers, notably Jaswant Singh and Ajit Singh in the 17th and 18th centuries. Jaswant Thada, the royal cenotaph in white marble, dates from 1899.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The Rathore stronghold of Marwar, and the centre of the longest Rajput resistance to Aurangzeb.
points: When Jaswant Singh died in 1678, Aurangzeb attempted to take Marwar under direct control and to bring up the infant heir Ajit Singh at court. Durgadas Rathore smuggled the child out of Delhi and fought a thirty-year guerrilla war until Ajit Singh was restored in 1707. The Rajput war is a principal item in the case that Aurangzeb's religious and political policies cost the empire its most useful allies.

The fort's Loha Pol carries the handprints of Maharaja Man Singh's widows who committed *sati* in 1843 - a physical record of the practice as it persisted into the colonial period, and abolished in Marwar only afterwards.
Cannonball scars from a Jaipur bombardment remain in the walls, evidence of the inter-Rajput warfare that preoccupied these states as much as any imperial threat did.
Foundation legends - Karni Mata laying the first stone, and a man buried alive in the ramparts - attach to the site and are worth reporting as tradition.

location.summary: Penukonda, Sri Sathya Sai district, Andhra Pradesh, at the foot of a steep granite hill in the dry Rayalaseema uplands - about 70 km from Anantapur, on the road between Karnataka and the Andhra plateau.

periodLevel.summary: A Vijayanagara stronghold from the 14th century, and the empire's capital after the defeat at Talikota in 1565, when Tirumala Deva Raya of the Aravidu line withdrew here from the ruined Hampi. It served as capital until about 1592, when the seat moved to Chandragiri and then to Vellore.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The proof that Vijayanagara did not end in 1565 - the standard correction to the textbook date.
points: The Aravidu dynasty ruled from Penukonda, Chandragiri and Vellore for nearly a century after Talikota, issuing grants and asserting authority over the Nayaks of Madurai, Thanjavur and Gingee. Ending the empire at the sack of Hampi misses that entire successor phase, and Penukonda is the place to anchor the correction.
The Gagan Mahal, built as a summer palace, shows the Deccan sultanate idiom - arches, stucco and domes - adopted by a Hindu court, the same borrowing visible in Hampi's secular buildings.
Jain and Hindu temples on the hill, including the Parshvanatha basadi, and the tomb of Sher Khan below, record the mixed religious landscape of a Rayalaseema garrison town.
Its eventual decline follows the Nayaks' assertion of independence and the Bijapur and Golconda advance into the Carnatic in the 1640s, which finished the Aravidu claim.

location.summary: Raigad, Raigad district, Maharashtra, on an isolated basalt hill about 820 m high in the Sahyadris, approached by a single fortified path - inland from the Konkan coast, roughly 25 km from Mahad.

periodLevel.summary: Taken by Shivaji from the Chandrarao More of Javli in 1656, rebuilt by his engineer Hiroji Indulkar, and made the Maratha capital. Shivaji's coronation was held here on 6 June 1674; he died at Raigad in 1680. The fort fell to Aurangzeb's forces in 1689 and was destroyed by British artillery in 1818.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The seat of the Maratha state, and the setting of the coronation that turned a rebellion into a kingdom.
points: The *rajyabhisheka* of 1674 is the event that matters. Shivaji was crowned *Chhatrapati* with full Vedic ritual, conducted by Gaga Bhatta of Banaras, who first had to establish a Kshatriya genealogy for him - the resistance of the local brahmanas to crowning a man they regarded as a shudra, and the lengths gone to overcome it, is the best evidence available on caste and kingship in 17th-century Maharashtra.

He also instituted the *Ashta Pradhan*, an eight-member council with defined portfolios, and commissioned the *Rajyavyavahara Kosha*, a lexicon replacing Persian administrative terms with Sanskrit ones - a deliberate assertion of independence at the level of language.

The fort's design shows Maratha military practice: hill forts chosen for inaccessibility, held by small garrisons, used as bases for mobile cavalry rather than as centres to be defended in set-piece war. Shivaji is said to have held over two hundred such forts.
The Jagadishwar temple, Shivaji's samadhi and the market street survive on the summit.

location.summary: Ranthambore, Sawai Madhopur district, Rajasthan, on an isolated hill where the Aravallis meet the Vindhyas, between the Banas and the Chambal - now within a tiger reserve.

periodLevel.summary: Founded by the Chauhans, probably in the 10th century, and their principal stronghold after the fall of Delhi in 1192. Besieged and taken by Alauddin Khalji in 1301 after the death of Hammira Deva Chauhan; later held by Mewar under Rana Sanga, and surrendered to Akbar in 1569.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The site of Alauddin Khalji's first great Rajput siege, and of the *jauhar* tradition's earliest well-documented instance.
points: Hammira Deva's refusal to surrender Mongol rebels who had taken refuge with him gave Alauddin his pretext. The year-long siege ended with Hammira killed in a final sortie and the women of the fort performing *jauhar* - the episode celebrated in Nayachandra Suri's Sanskrit *Hammira Mahakavya* a century later.

Amir Khusrau, who accompanied the campaign, describes the siege in the *Khazain-ul-Futuh*, so the event can be read from both the victor's Persian account and the vanquished's Sanskrit one. Setting the two against each other is a good exercise in source criticism, and a corrective to relying on either alone.

Alauddin's reduction of Ranthambore, Chittor, Siwana and Jalor between 1301 and 1311 broke Rajput power in eastern Rajasthan and secured the Delhi Sultanate's western flank before the Deccan campaigns.
It is one of the six Hill Forts of Rajasthan inscribed by UNESCO.

location.summary: Srirangapatna, Mandya district, Karnataka, on an island formed where the Kaveri divides - a natural moat that made it the strongest position in southern Karnataka, about 15 km from Mysuru.

periodLevel.summary: Fortified in 1454 by Timmanna Nayaka under Vijayanagara; Wodeyar capital from 1610; then the capital of Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan. It fell to the British on 4 May 1799 in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War, when Tipu was killed defending the breach.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The capital of the state that fought the East India Company four times - the most formidable Indian opponent the Company faced in the south.
points: Tipu's Mysore was a modernising state: he reorganised revenue on a *ryotwari* basis cutting out intermediaries, established state trading houses and factories, sent embassies to France, Turkey and Persia, and introduced a new calendar and coinage.

The Mysorean iron-cased rockets used at Pollilur in 1780 and afterwards were effective enough that captured examples were studied at Woolwich and developed into the Congreve rocket. Indian military technology influencing European practice is the point worth making.
The Daria Daulat Bagh, Tipu's summer palace, carries a mural of the Mysorean victory at Pollilur - one of very few Indian paintings of a battle against the British painted from the winning side.

Note that the French assisted Hyder Ali and Tipu in the 18th century; they had nothing to do with the fort's construction in 1454, which was Vijayanagara work. The Ranganathaswamy temple on the island is one of the three great Kaveri island shrines with Srirangam and Shivanasamudra.

location.summary: Warangal, Telangana, on the Deccan plateau in the upper Krishna-Godavari interfluve - a plain fortified with concentric earth and stone ramparts rather than a hill fort.

periodLevel.summary: Capital of the Kakatiyas from the 12th century, built up under Ganapatideva, r. 1199-1262, and his daughter Rudramadevi, r. 1262-1289. Malik Kafur raided it in 1309-10 and Ulugh Khan annexed it in 1323, ending Kakatiya rule under Prataparudra II.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The Kakatiya capital, with one of the very few women to rule an Indian kingdom in her own right, and a temple architecture of exceptional refinement.
points: Rudramadevi succeeded her father and ruled for nearly three decades. Inscriptions refer to her by the male name Rudradeva and depict her in male dress, and Marco Polo, who passed through her realm, praised her government. She is the standard example in questions on female sovereignty, alongside Razia and Didda.

The fort's four free-standing *kirti toranas*, carved gateways standing where the Svayambhusiva temple once was, are now the emblem of Telangana. The Thousand Pillar Temple at Hanamkonda, c. 1163, is a triple-shrined Kakatiya building in polished black basalt.

The Ramappa temple at Palampet, consecrated 1213 and inscribed by UNESCO in 2021, is the only major Indian temple named after its sculptor. It uses lightweight bricks said to float, and carries bracket figures of dancers of extraordinary quality.
Kakatiya rule rested on tank irrigation - Pakhal, Laknavaram and Ramappa lakes - built by the state and by local chiefs, which is the usual evidence for their agrarian base.

location.summary: Alwarthirunagari, Thoothukudi district, Tamil Nadu, on the Thamirabarani river in the southern Pandya country - near Tirunelveli, in the belt of nine Vaishnava shrines along that river.

periodLevel.summary: The home of Nammalwar, generally placed in the 9th century CE, the foremost of the twelve Alwars. His four works - the *Tiruviruttam*, *Tiruvasiriyam*, *Periya Tiruvandadi* and above all the *Tiruvaymoli* - make up over a third of the *Nalayira Divya Prabandham*.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The central figure of Tamil Vaishnava bhakti, and the poet whose work Srivaishnavism treats as scripture.
points: The *Tiruvaymoli*, 1,102 verses, is called the *Dravida Veda* or Tamil Veda, and Ramanuja's tradition gives it standing equal to the Sanskrit Upanishads. A vernacular text admitted to canonical parity with the Veda is the single most important development in the history of Indian devotional religion, and Nammalwar is where it happens.

His poetry speaks in many voices - lover, mother, friend - using the grammar of Tamil *akam* love poetry for religious longing. The Sangam secular tradition converted into a devotional idiom is the clearest instance of continuity between classical Tamil literature and bhakti.

The Alwar movement, with the Shaiva Nayanmars, is the earliest mass devotional movement in India, running from roughly the 6th to the 9th centuries, and precedes the north Indian bhakti movement by several hundred years - the point examiners most often want established.
Nathamuni is credited with collecting and setting to music the scattered Alwar hymns in the 10th century, which is how the corpus survived.

location.summary: Apegaon, Paithan taluk, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar district, Maharashtra, on the Godavari - the ancestral village of Jnaneshwar's family, a short distance from Paithan and from Alandi near Pune where he took *samadhi*.

periodLevel.summary: Jnaneshwar, or Dnyaneshwar, c. 1275-1296, wrote under the Yadavas of Devagiri. His *Dnyaneshwari* is dated 1290. He died at twenty-one, having taken *sanjeevan samadhi* at Alandi.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The founder of the Varkari tradition and the writer who made Marathi a language of philosophy.
points: The *Dnyaneshwari* is a commentary on the *Bhagavad Gita* in Marathi *ovi* verse, some nine thousand stanzas. Writing Vedantic philosophy in a regional language, for an audience that could not read Sanskrit, was a deliberate act: he says so in the text. It is the foundation of Marathi literature and the model for later vernacular commentary across India.
His *Amrutanubhav* is an independent philosophical work rather than a commentary, arguing a non-dual position derived from the Nath tradition in which he was initiated by his brother Nivrittinath.

He and his siblings were outcaste, their father having returned from sannyasa to family life, and were refused the sacred thread by the brahmanas of Paithan. The exclusion is the biographical fact behind the movement's later openness - the Varkari sampradaya centred on Pandharpur admitted all castes, and Namdev, Chokhamela, Eknath and Tukaram follow from this beginning.
The annual *palkhi* carrying his sandals from Alandi to Pandharpur still draws hundreds of thousands.

location.summary: Basavana Bagewadi, Vijayapura district, northern Karnataka, in the dry Deccan plateau between the Krishna and the Bhima - the birthplace of Basavanna, some 80 km from Kalyana where he worked.

periodLevel.summary: Basavanna, c. 1105-1167 CE, served as treasurer and chief minister to the Kalachuri king Bijjala II at Kalyana. The Veerashaiva or Lingayat movement he led belongs to the second half of the 12th century.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The origin of the most thoroughgoing social critique produced by any Indian devotional movement.
points: Basavanna rejected caste, image worship, temple ritual, pilgrimage and the authority of the Vedas, and replaced them with the *ishtalinga*, a personal linga worn on the body, so that each devotee carried the shrine and needed no priest. Abolishing the intermediary is what distinguishes the Lingayats from most bhakti movements, which softened caste without dismantling its ritual basis.

The *Anubhava Mantapa* at Kalyana was an assembly where *sharanas* of every background debated - Allama Prabhu presiding, Akka Mahadevi among them, along with cobblers, washermen and tanners whose *vachanas* survive under their own names.

The *vachanas* are short, unmetred, direct utterances in Kannada, deliberately plain against Sanskrit ornament. They are a major literary corpus and the earliest sustained body of prose-poetry by non-elite authors in any Indian language.

The movement's crisis came around 1167 with a marriage between a brahmana girl and an untouchable boy arranged by the sharanas, the violence that followed and the dispersal of the community. It is the best-documented case of a bhakti movement tested in practice and defeated.

location.summary: Bannur, Mysuru district, Karnataka, on the Kaveri in the southern Deccan - the birthplace of Vyasatirtha, whose working life was spent at the Vijayanagara court and at Tirupati.

periodLevel.summary: Vyasatirtha, or Vyasaraja, 1460-1539, headed the Madhva Dvaita order and served as *rajaguru* to Krishnadevaraya, r. 1509-1529. He administered the Tirupati temple for some years before moving to the capital.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The philosopher-minister of Vijayanagara at its height, and the link between Dvaita philosophy and the Haridasa devotional movement.
points: His *Nyayamrita*, *Tarkatandava* and *Tatparyachandrika* are the most rigorous statements of Dvaita logic, written against Advaita. The *Nyayamrita* provoked Madhusudana Sarasvati's *Advaitasiddhi* in reply, and that exchange is the last great philosophical debate of the Indian scholastic tradition.

He was Krishnadevaraya's preceptor, and the emperor is recorded as seating him on the throne during an inauspicious conjunction. A Dvaita pontiff holding that position illustrates how Vijayanagara kingship drew authority from religious institutions, as the Sringeri matha had done for the dynasty's founders.

He was guru to Purandaradasa and Kanakadasa, the two great Haridasa poets, so the technical philosophy of the mathas and the popular Kannada devotional songs of the *dasa* tradition run through one teacher.
He endowed and administered temples across the Vijayanagara territories, and inscriptions record his grants - useful evidence for the temple economy of the period.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I; B. N. K. Sharma, *History of the Dvaita School of Vedanta*

location.summary: Champaran, also called Champajhar, in Raipur district, Chhattisgarh, on the Mahanadi about 60 km from Raipur. Note that this is not the Champaran of Bihar: Vallabhacharya's birthplace is the Chhattisgarh village, where his family was travelling when he was born.

periodLevel.summary: Vallabhacharya, 1479-1531, a Telugu brahmana by descent, taught during the Lodi and early Mughal period. He established the Shrinathji shrine at Govardhan in the Braj country; the image was later moved to Nathdwara in Mewar to keep it from Aurangzeb.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The founder of the Pushtimarg, the most organised of the Krishna devotional sects, and of the *Shuddhadvaita* philosophy.
points: *Shuddhadvaita*, pure non-dualism, holds that the world is a real transformation of Brahman and not *maya* - an explicit rejection of Shankara's position, preserving the reality of the world so that devotion to an embodied god makes sense.

*Pushtimarg*, the way of grace, teaches that liberation comes from divine favour rather than from works or knowledge, and that the devotee serves Krishna through *seva* - the daily cycle of bathing, dressing, feeding and putting the image to rest. The sect's ritual life is unusually elaborate and domestic.

It drew its following from the trading and banking communities of Gujarat and Rajasthan, which gave it wealth and durability, and it generated its own painting tradition in the *pichhwai* hangings of Nathdwara.
The *Ashtachhap*, eight poet-musicians including Surdas, sang in its temples, so the sect is also the institutional setting for much of the finest Braj literature.

location.summary: Dehu, Pune district, Maharashtra, on the Indrayani river about 30 km from Pune - a village on the same river as Alandi, where Jnaneshwar's samadhi lies.

periodLevel.summary: Tukaram, c. 1608-1650, a grain trader of the Kunbi caste, wrote during the last years of the Nizam Shahi and the rise of Shahaji and Shivaji. He is the last of the four principal Varkari saints and the movement's greatest poet.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The peak of Marathi devotional poetry, and the sharpest voice against ritual and caste privilege in the tradition.
points: His *abhangas*, some four and a half thousand of them, are direct, colloquial and often bitter - about hunger, debt, the death of his family in the famine of the 1620s, and his own doubt. That autobiographical honesty is unusual in Indian devotional literature and is what gives the poems their standing.

Tradition records brahmana opponents, Rameshwar Bhatt among them, forcing him to sink his manuscripts in the Indrayani because a shudra had no right to expound scripture; the notebooks are said to have surfaced after thirteen days. Whatever happened, the story preserves the real conflict over who could speak for religion.

He is said to have declined Shivaji's invitation to court and sent him back to his duties, while his contemporary Ramdas accepted the role of royal preceptor. The contrast between the two is the standard question on the relationship of Maharashtra's saints to Maratha politics.
The *palkhi* from Dehu joins the Alandi procession to Pandharpur each year, binding the two founding villages of the Varkari tradition.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* II; Dilip Chitre, *Says Tuka*

location.summary: Jamb near Jalna, Maharashtra, in the Godavari basin of Marathwada, is Ramdas's birthplace; his working life was spent at Sajjangad near Satara, the fort where he died.

periodLevel.summary: Samarth Ramdas, 1608-1681, was an exact contemporary of Tukaram and lived through the rise of Shivaji. His principal work, the *Dasbodh*, was composed in the Marathi *ovi* metre at Shivthar Ghal.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The saint of activist devotion - the counter-model to the Varkari tradition, and the figure invoked to give Maratha power a religious sanction.
points: Ramdas was a devotee of Rama and Hanuman rather than of Vitthala, and he stands outside the Varkari succession. His teaching joins *bhakti* to worldly capability: the *Dasbodh* discusses statecraft, organisation, discipline and leadership as spiritual duties, which is why he is read as advocating an engaged rather than a withdrawn piety.
He founded a network of Hanuman temples and *mathas* across Maharashtra, giving the movement an institutional reach the Varkaris never sought.

His role as Shivaji's guru is the contested part. The relationship is asserted strongly in later Maratha tradition and was emphasised again by nineteenth and twentieth-century nationalist writers; contemporary evidence for it is thin, and historians treat the *guru-shishya* claim with caution. The honest answer sets the tradition out and notes the doubt rather than repeating either version flat.
The contrast with Tukaram - one declining the court, the other associated with it - is the usual frame for discussing religion and politics in 17th-century Maharashtra.

location.summary: Kalady, Ernakulam district, Kerala, on the bank of the Periyar about 45 km from Kochi - in the Chera country, on the river that also carried the Muziris trade.

periodLevel.summary: The traditional birthplace of Adi Shankaracharya, usually dated c. 788-820 CE, though the dates are disputed and some scholars place him earlier. His floruit falls in the early medieval period, after the Tamil bhakti movement and during the decline of Buddhism in the peninsula.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The birthplace of the philosopher who gave Advaita Vedanta its systematic form and gave Hinduism an institutional structure.
points: Shankara's commentaries on the *Brahma Sutras*, the ten principal Upanishads and the *Bhagavad Gita* are the foundation of Advaita: Brahman alone is real, the world as perceived is *maya*, and the individual self is not different from Brahman. The *Sri Bhashya* of Ramanuja and Madhva's Dvaita were both written against this position, so Indian philosophy for the next five centuries is largely a conversation with Shankara.

He organised the *Dashanami* monastic order and, by tradition, founded four mathas at the cardinal points - Sringeri, Dwarka, Puri and Jyotirmath at Badrinath. A network of monasteries with defined territories and a succession of heads gave Hinduism a durable institutional form it had lacked.
His debate with Mandana Mishra, and Ubhaya Bharati's adjudication of it, is the best-known story of the scholastic disputation culture of the period.

He is often credited with the decline of Buddhism in India. The claim needs care: Buddhism was already weakening for reasons of patronage and institutional concentration, and Shankara's own debt to Buddhist logic was noted by his opponents, who called him a crypto-Buddhist.

content.sourcesLine: Thapar, *Early India*; Upinder Singh, ch. 10

location.summary: Karaikal, a coastal enclave of the union territory of Puducherry on the Arasalar, a distributary of the Kaveri, surrounded by Tamil Nadu - in the delta, close to Nagapattinam.

periodLevel.summary: The home of Karaikkal Ammaiyar, born Punithavathi, usually placed in the 6th century CE - among the earliest of the sixty-three Nayanmars, and earlier than Appar and Sambandar, so her verse is some of the oldest Tamil devotional poetry to survive.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of only three women among the Nayanmars, and the author of the earliest datable Shaiva poetry in Tamil.
points: Her *Arputhat Tiruvantadi* and *Tiru Irattai Manimalai* are included in the eleventh *Tirumurai*. Because they precede the great Shaiva hymnists, they are the starting point for the Tamil bhakti movement, which is itself the earliest large-scale devotional movement in India and the model for later north Indian bhakti.

The mango story defines her: having given a fruit meant for her husband to a Shiva devotee, she produced another by prayer, and her husband, recognising her as more than human, left her. Freed of marriage, she asked Shiva not for beauty but for the form of a *pey*, a ghoul, and is depicted as an emaciated skeletal figure with bulging eyes, playing cymbals at Shiva's dance.

That request is the point worth making. Where male saints are shown as ideal devotees, she achieves sanctity by deliberately abandoning the feminine ideal - the sharpest instance in Indian religious literature of a woman escaping the roles available to her by refusing the body itself.
Her image appears in Chola bronze and in the Nayanmar friezes at Darasuram.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Thapar, *Early India*; *Periya Puranam*

location.summary: Kudki, or Kurki, in Pali district, Rajasthan, in the arid Marwar country of the Luni basin - traditionally Mirabai's birthplace, with Merta nearby as the home of her Rathore family.

periodLevel.summary: Mirabai, c. 1498-1547, was a Rathore princess of Merta married to Bhojraj, son of Rana Sanga of Mewar. Her life spans the collapse of Rajput power at Khanwa in 1527 and the early Mughal decades.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The best-known woman in the north Indian bhakti tradition, and a case of devotion used to refuse the obligations of rank and marriage.
points: She took Krishna as her husband and refused the duties owed to her marital family, including, by tradition, *sati* on Bhojraj's death and the seclusion expected of a Sisodia widow. The persecution that followed - the poisoned cup, the basket with a snake - is the standard material of her legend and of her own verse.

Her *padas*, in a Rajasthani-Braj mixture, are sung across northern and western India. As *saguna* devotion to a personal Krishna they sit opposite Kabir's formless god, and the pairing is the usual way of laying out the two streams of north Indian bhakti.

The gender argument is the point to develop: for a woman of her rank, bhakti was the one available exit from the duties of caste and household, and Mirabai's refusal - like Akka Mahadevi's in Kannada and Andal's in Tamil - shows devotion functioning as social escape as much as religious practice.
The textual position is uncertain: few of the songs attributed to her can be traced to her own century, and the corpus grew by accretion. Say so rather than treating the whole body as hers.

location.summary: Pandrethan, ancient Puranadhisthana, on the outskirts of Srinagar beside the Jhelum, Jammu and Kashmir - the old capital site, where a small 10th-century stone Shiva temple stands in a tank.

periodLevel.summary: Lal Ded, also Lalleshwari or Lalla Arifa, is placed in the 14th century, roughly 1320-1392, a generation into the Shah Mir sultanate and contemporary with the arrival of Sayyid Ali Hamadani and the spread of Islam in the valley.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The founding voice of Kashmiri literature, and a figure claimed by both Hindus and Muslims.
points: Her *vakhs*, four-line utterances, are the earliest substantial composition in the Kashmiri language and remain in oral circulation - proverbs as much as poetry. The Kashmiri literary tradition effectively begins with a woman.

Her thought is Kashmir Shaivism, the non-dual Trika system of Abhinavagupta, expressed without Sanskrit apparatus: the self and Shiva are one, the search outside oneself is futile, and ritual, caste and scripture are useless without realisation.

She left her marriage and wandered, by tradition naked, refusing both household and social respectability. Hindus call her Lalleshwari and Muslims Lalla Arifa, and she is associated with the Rishi order of Nund Rishi (Sheikh Nooruddin), whose verse echoes hers. She is the standard example of Kashmir's shared devotional culture, and of the Rishi tradition as a Kashmiri counterpart to Sufism.
Her position at the moment of religious transition makes her the best single source on how that change was experienced from inside the valley rather than from court chronicles.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I; Upinder Singh, ch. 10

location.summary: Associated with Tiruvathavur near Melur, Madurai district, Tamil Nadu, in the Vaigai basin east of Madurai - Pandya country, with the saint's later life spent at Madurai and Chidambaram.

periodLevel.summary: Manikkavachakar is generally placed in the 9th century CE, serving as chief minister to a Pandya king before renouncing office. His *Tiruvasagam* and *Tirukkovaiyar* together form the eighth *Tirumurai* of the Shaiva canon.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The finest devotional poet in Tamil, and one of the four *Samayacharyas* who shaped Shaiva Siddhanta.
points: The four teachers of Tamil Shaivism are Appar, Sambandar, Sundarar and Manikkavachakar. Note that the first three are counted among the sixty-three Nayanmars and he is not - a distinction frequently got wrong, and worth stating precisely.

The *Tiruvasagam* is built on the experience of grace rather than on ritual or scholarship: the soul's helplessness, its seizure by Shiva, and the alternation of union and abandonment. G. U. Pope's remark that those unmoved by it must have hearts of stone is the standard quotation.

Shaiva Siddhanta, the philosophical system that grew from this poetry, holds *pati*, *pashu* and *pasha* - god, soul and bond - to be eternally distinct, with release consisting in the soul's union with Shiva by grace rather than in identity with him. It is the dominant theology of Tamil Shaivism and the counterpoint to Advaita.

The story of his diverting royal funds meant for horses into temple building, and the divine intervention that followed, is the best-known episode of his life, and marks the renunciation of office for devotion.

location.summary: Bordowa in Nagaon district, Assam, on the south bank of the Brahmaputra in the central valley - Shankaradeva's birthplace, with his later work centred at Barpeta and at Patbausi in Koch territory.

periodLevel.summary: Srimanta Shankaradeva, 1449-1568, taught through the late Ahom and Koch period. His disciple Madhavadeva, 1489-1596, carried the movement forward; the Koch king Nara Narayan gave it protection after Ahom hostility.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The founder of Assamese neo-Vaishnavism, and the most complete case of a religious movement creating a regional culture whole.
points: *Ekasarana Dharma*, shelter in one name, rejected image worship, sacrifice and caste distinction in favour of *nama-kirtana*, the chanting of Krishna's name. The *sattras*, monastic establishments, and the *namghars*, village prayer houses, gave it an institutional base that still organises rural Assamese life.

What distinguishes Shankaradeva from other bhakti teachers is the sheer range of forms he created: *Borgeet* devotional songs, *Ankiya Naat* one-act dramas in Brajavali, *Sattriya* dance now recognised as a classical form, the *Kirtan Ghosha* verse anthology, and the *Vrindavani Vastra*, a woven silk tapestry depicting Krishna's life, fragments of which are in the British Museum and the Musee Guimet.

He composed in Assamese and in Brajavali, an artificial literary dialect, rather than Sanskrit, and his movement admitted Muslims, tribal groups and low castes - Chandsai, a Muslim, was among his close disciples.
The Ahom court's suspicion and the Koch court's patronage show how much these movements depended on finding a protector.

location.summary: Nankana Sahib, formerly Talwandi, in Sheikhupura district, Punjab, Pakistan, about 75 km west of Lahore in the Ravi-Chenab doab.

periodLevel.summary: The birthplace of Guru Nanak, 1469-1539. His life spans the late Lodi Sultanate, Babur's invasion of 1526 and the first Mughal decade; he settled finally at Kartarpur on the Ravi.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The origin of Sikhism, and of a religious teaching that was institutional as well as devotional from the start.
points: Nanak taught a formless god - *Ik Onkar* - reached through *nam simran*, honest work and sharing, and rejected caste, ritual, idol worship and asceticism. What separates him from Kabir, with whom he shares much vocabulary, is organisation: he established *sangat*, the congregation, *pangat* and *langar*, the common kitchen where all eat seated together regardless of caste, and appointed a successor. A named line of succession is why the teaching became a community and Kabir's did not.

His *udasis* took him across India and, by tradition, to Mecca, Baghdad and Sri Lanka; his hymns were later collected by Guru Arjan in the *Adi Granth* in 1604, alongside those of Kabir, Ravidas, Namdev and Sufi Shaikh Farid - a scripture that includes writers of other faiths and low caste, which is unique.
His *Babarvani* verses describe Babur's invasion and the suffering of the Punjab - rare contemporary comment on a political event from a religious teacher, and a useful non-courtly source on 1526.
Kartarpur, where he farmed and taught, and Nankana Sahib are both now in Pakistan, which is why the corridor opened in 2019 matters.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I and II; *Guru Granth Sahib*

location.summary: Naraina, Jaipur district, Rajasthan, in the semi-arid country south-west of Jaipur near the Sambhar salt lake - the place where Dadu Dayal settled and where his principal seat remains.

periodLevel.summary: Dadu Dayal, 1544-1603, a cotton-carder by trade, probably of Muslim birth, taught in Rajasthan during Akbar's reign and is recorded as having met the emperor at Fatehpur Sikri in 1585. Note that some note-sets place him in the 6th century; he is a 16th-century figure.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The founder of the Dadupanth, and one of the clearest cases of a *nirguna* teacher building a lasting order.
points: Dadu preached a formless god beyond the categories of Hindu and Muslim, rejecting scripture, caste, image worship and circumcision alike. He called his followers simply *parabrahmi*, of the supreme reality, refusing a sectarian name - a deliberate attempt to found a community without a religious identity.

His verses were collected by his disciple Rajjab as the *Dadu Anubhav Vani*, and the Dadupanthi scribes assembled anthologies of *nirguna* poetry - the *Panch Vani* and the Sarvangi collections - which preserve the earliest datable manuscripts of Kabir, Namdev and Ravidas. The Dadupanthi archive is therefore a principal source for the whole north Indian bhakti corpus, independent of the Sikh and Bijak traditions.
His recorded audience with Akbar belongs with the Ibadat Khana debates as evidence of how far the emperor's religious enquiry extended beyond the formal ulama.
The order later maintained an armed *naga* wing that took military service with Jaipur - a reminder that devotional sects in this period could become political and military actors.

location.summary: Paithan, on the north bank of the Godavari, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar district, Maharashtra - the old Satavahana capital of Pratishthana, for which see the separate entry in the capitals chapter. This entry concerns Eknath, who lived and wrote here.

periodLevel.summary: Eknath, c. 1533-1599, worked at Paithan during the Nizam Shahi and early Mughal period in the Deccan. He is the third of the four great Varkari figures, between Jnaneshwar and Namdev before him and Tukaram after.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The saint who recovered the Varkari textual tradition and pushed it furthest on caste.
points: His first act of scholarship was to produce a corrected text of the *Dnyaneshwari*, which had become corrupt in the two and a half centuries since Jnaneshwar wrote it. Without that edition the central text of Marathi devotion might not have survived in usable form.

The *Eknathi Bhagavata*, his Marathi commentary on the eleventh book of the *Bhagavata Purana*, was attacked by the pandits of Banaras for expounding scripture in a vernacular. That episode is the standard illustration of the resistance vernacular religious writing met from the Sanskrit establishment.

His *bharuds* - dramatic songs written in the voices of a washerwoman, a Muslim faqir, an untouchable - carried devotion into street performance, and his recorded acts of eating with Mahars and drawing water for them were public breaches of caste practice by a brahmana, not merely statements against it.
He is usually described as the bridge between the earlier and later Varkari saints, and his *samadhi* is at Paithan on the Godavari.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* II; R. C. Dhere, *Rise of a Folk God*

location.summary: Runkata, near Agra on the Yamuna in Uttar Pradesh, is one of the places named as Surdas's birthplace; his working life was spent at Gaughat and then at Parasauli near Govardhan in the Braj country.

periodLevel.summary: Surdas, c. 1478-1583 by tradition, was blind from birth or early childhood. He became a disciple of Vallabhacharya about 1510 and was one of the *Ashtachhap*, the eight poets of the Pushtimarg who sang before the image of Shrinathji at Govardhan.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The greatest poet of Braj Bhasha, and the figure through whom Krishna devotion became a literature of childhood and maternal love.
points: The *Sursagar*, attributed to him, is an enormous body of *pada* verse on Krishna's infancy and youth at Gokul and Vrindavan - butter-stealing, the games with the cowherds, and Yashoda's love. That the emotional centre of the poetry is *vatsalya*, parental affection, rather than erotic longing distinguishes it from the Radha-centred tradition.

The *Bhramargeet* section, in which the gopis rebuke Krishna's messenger Uddhava for offering them abstract philosophy in place of the god they love, is the most famous statement in Hindi of *bhakti*'s superiority to *jnana* - devotion answering back to metaphysics.
His verse fixed Braj Bhasha as the standard literary dialect of north India for the next three centuries, used by poets far outside the Vaishnava fold.

Textual scholarship has shown the *Sursagar* grew hugely by accretion, from a few hundred verses in early manuscripts to many thousands later, so the corpus is a tradition rather than one man's work. A few of his verses also appear in the Guru Granth Sahib.

location.summary: Sriperumbudur, Kanchipuram district, Tamil Nadu, in the flat country between Kanchipuram and the coast, in the upper drainage of the Adyar - about 40 km west of Chennai.

periodLevel.summary: The birthplace of Ramanuja, traditionally 1017-1137 CE. He studied at Kanchipuram under Yadava Prakasha, later headed the Srirangam temple, and spent years at Melkote in Hoysala territory after conflict with a Chola ruler.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The origin of Vishishtadvaita - the philosophy that gave devotional religion an intellectual foundation - and of a practical challenge to caste exclusion.
points: Ramanuja's *Sri Bhashya* on the *Brahma Sutras*, with the *Vedarthasangraha* and his *Gita Bhashya*, argue for qualified non-dualism: souls and matter are real and form the body of Brahman, distinct from it yet inseparable. Against Shankara's impersonal absolute this allows a personal god who can be loved, which is what made *bhakti* philosophically respectable.

He brought the Tamil hymns of the Alwars into temple liturgy alongside the Sanskrit Veda, a decision with large consequences: it gave a vernacular devotional corpus canonical standing, and it is the basis of the Srivaishnava claim to an *ubhaya vedanta*, a dual scripture.

Tradition records him admitting groups excluded by caste to temple worship, and proclaiming the secret *Tirumantra* from a temple tower so that all could hear it. Present it as tradition, but the Srivaishnava community's later division into Vadakalai and Tenkalai turned partly on exactly these questions.
At Melkote he is said to have converted the Hoysala Vishnuvardhana from Jainism - the link between his teaching and the Hoysala temple programme at Belur and Halebidu.

content.sourcesLine: Thapar, *Early India*; Upinder Singh, ch. 10
