location.summary: Srivilliputhur, Virudhunagar district, Tamil Nadu, at the foot of the Western Ghats in the dry Pandya country near the Vaippar basin - about 75 km from Madurai.

periodLevel.summary: The home of Andal, also called Kodhai, generally placed in the 8th-9th centuries CE. She is the only woman among the twelve Alwars, the Tamil Vaishnava saint-poets whose hymns were later collected as the *Nalayira Divya Prabandham*.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The one female voice in the Alwar canon, and the author of a text still recited by millions every year.
points: The *Tiruppavai*, thirty verses on the *pavai* vow, is sung daily through the Tamil month of Margazhi in temples and households across the south. Few devotional compositions anywhere have that continuity of ritual use, and it is the single most widely known piece of Alwar poetry.

Her *Nachiyar Tirumozhi* is more striking for the historian: it speaks of longing for Krishna in frankly erotic terms, in a woman's own voice, and uses the conventions of Tamil love poetry for devotion. It is the key text in any question on gender and bhakti, beside Akka Mahadevi in Kannada and Mirabai in Rajasthani.

Tradition holds that she refused a human marriage and merged into the image of Ranganatha at Srirangam. That refusal - devotion as an alternative to marriage - is the recurring pattern in the lives of women saints, and Karaikal Ammaiyar and Mirabai show the same shape.
The temple's eleven-tiered gopuram is the emblem of the Government of Tamil Nadu.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 10; Thapar, *Early India*; *Nalayira Divya Prabandham*

location.summary: Talaja, Bhavnagar district, Gujarat, on the Shetrunji river near the Gulf of Khambhat coast of Saurashtra - Narsinh Mehta's birthplace, with his later life spent at Junagadh below Girnar.

periodLevel.summary: Narsinh Mehta, c. 1414-1481, a Nagar brahmana, lived under the Gujarat Sultanate. He is counted the *Adi Kavi*, the first poet, of Gujarati literature.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The founder of Gujarati literature, and the author of the hymn that became the anthem of the national movement.
points: *Vaishnava Jana To* defines a Vaishnava entirely by conduct - one who feels another's pain, helps the suffering, is free of pride, covets nothing, treats all women as mothers, speaks no untruth. Gandhi made it a daily prayer at his ashrams, and it is the clearest instance of a 15th-century devotional lyric being carried into 20th-century politics.

His *prabhatiya* morning hymns and the *pada* cycles on Krishna and Radha established Gujarati as a literary language, and his autobiographical narrative poems - the *Hundi*, the *Mameru*, the *Shraddha* - are among the earliest sustained first-person narratives in an Indian vernacular.

He was excommunicated by his own Nagar caste for singing and eating with untouchables at Junagadh, and the episodes of divine intervention that follow in his verse are framed as vindication against that exclusion. Caste conflict recorded by the excluded party himself is rare and worth citing.
His devotion is *saguna*, to a personal Krishna, placing him with Mirabai and Surdas rather than with Kabir.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* II

location.summary: Tirthahalli, Shivamogga district, Karnataka, on the Tunga in the Malnad hills below the Western Ghats - one of the places named as Purandaradasa's birthplace, with Hampi the centre of his later life.

periodLevel.summary: Purandaradasa, c. 1484-1564, was by tradition a wealthy gem merchant who gave away his property and became a wandering singer, taking initiation from Vyasatirtha. He lived and sang at Vijayanagara in its last decades before the defeat at Talikota.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: Called the father of Carnatic music - the man who turned a performing art into a teachable system.
points: He devised the graded exercises still used to begin instruction: the *sarali varisai*, *janti varisai* and *alankaras*, set in the Mayamalavagowla raga, which every Carnatic student in south India starts with to this day. Codifying pedagogy is what earns him the title *Sangita Pitamaha*, and it is the concrete reason his name matters beyond devotion.

He composed *kirtanas* in Kannada, said to number in the thousands though far fewer survive, joining a devotional text to a fixed raga and tala - the structural ancestor of the Carnatic *kriti* that Tyagaraja and his contemporaries later perfected.

His songs belong to the Haridasa movement, the Kannada devotional stream flowing from the Madhva mathas at Udupi, and they attack caste pride, hypocrisy and ritualism in plain language while remaining within a Dvaita framework.
That a merchant's renunciation and a court philosopher's initiation lie behind the standard music syllabus of half the subcontinent is the point worth making about Vijayanagara's cultural reach.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I; B. N. K. Sharma, *History of the Dvaita School of Vedanta*

location.summary: Varanasi, on the left bank of the Ganga where the river turns north, Uttar Pradesh. For the ancient city, the Kashi mahajanapada and its NBPW levels, see the separate Varanasi entry in the NBPW chapter; this entry concerns the bhakti teachers associated with the city.

periodLevel.summary: The 15th and early 16th centuries, under the Sharqi sultans of Jaunpur and then the Lodis and early Mughals. Ramananda belongs to the late 14th and early 15th centuries; Kabir to c. 1440-1518; Ravidas to roughly the same span.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The place where north Indian bhakti became a movement that crossed caste and religion, and where the *nirguna* tradition took shape.
points: Ramananda, a Ramanandi teacher in the Ramanuja line, is credited with opening initiation to disciples of every caste and preaching in Hindi rather than Sanskrit. Tradition gives him twelve disciples including Kabir the weaver, Ravidas the leather worker, Sena the barber and Dhanna the farmer - the list itself, whatever its accuracy, states the movement's social claim.

Kabir's verse attacks the ritual of Hindus and Muslims alike, the authority of Veda and Quran, pilgrimage, caste and image worship, holding to a formless god. His work survives in three distinct recensions - the *Bijak*, the Guru Granth Sahib and the Rajasthani manuscripts - which differ enough that establishing what Kabir actually said is a genuine textual problem worth citing.

Ravidas, a *chamar* by birth, taught an equally uncompromising *nirguna* devotion and imagined *Begampura*, a city without sorrow, tax or hierarchy - one of the very few utopias in pre-modern Indian literature, and central to modern Dalit thought. Forty of his verses are in the Guru Granth Sahib.
Their shared vocabulary with Sufi teaching makes them the standard evidence in questions on syncretism, though Kabir himself refused both labels.

content.sourcesLine: Satish Chandra, *Medieval India* I and II

location.summary: Edakkal, on Ambukuthi hill near Ambalavayal, Wayanad district, Kerala, at about 1,200 m in the Western Ghats - a cleft formed where a boulder fell across a fissure, so the "cave" is a natural rock shelter rather than an excavation.

periodLevel.summary: Petroglyphs of at least two phases, the earlier assigned to the Neolithic, roughly the 4th-3rd millennia BCE, and later carvings to the early historic period. Brahmi and Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions on the same walls date to about the 3rd-5th centuries CE. Reported by Fred Fawcett in 1890.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The only substantial prehistoric petroglyph site in south India, and one of very few anywhere carved rather than painted.
points: The engravings are cut into the rock, not painted, which sets Edakkal apart from Bhimbetka, Lakhudiyar and the Vindhyan shelters. They show human figures with elaborate headdresses, wheels, carts, animals, tridents and geometric symbols.

Some signs have been compared with Indus symbols - a claim made repeatedly and never demonstrated. The honest position is that the resemblance is unproven and probably coincidental, and it should be reported as a claim rather than a finding.

The later Brahmi inscriptions, including one reading *Sri Vazhumi*, show the shelter still in use in the early historic period, so the site records continuous human attention across three thousand years.
Wayanad's position on the routes between the Malabar coast and the Deccan plateau explains why a hill shelter here attracted such sustained use; megalithic remains occur nearby.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3; R. S. Sharma, *India's Ancient Past*; ASI

location.summary: Kondana, near Karjat in Raigad district, Maharashtra, in a wooded ravine of the Sahyadris close to the Rajmachi fort - on the escarpment above the Konkan, near the passes carrying trade from the coast to the Deccan.

periodLevel.summary: A group of sixteen Buddhist excavations of the Hinayana phase, generally dated to the 1st century BCE, contemporary with Bhaja and a little earlier than Karle. They comprise a *chaitya* hall and *viharas*.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: One of the earliest western Deccan cave groups, and an unusually clear case of stone imitating carpentry.
points: The chaitya's facade and interior reproduce timber construction in rock: a horseshoe arch, ribbed vaulting and railing patterns cut to look like assembled wood, with actual wooden ribs originally fixed into the ceiling. The same translation of carpentry into stone begins at Barabar and runs through Bhaja, Bedse and Karle - Kondana is a key stage in that sequence.
Sculpture on the vihara facade includes *mithuna* couples and dancing figures of high quality, and the pillars carry the pot-and-foliage forms of the period.

Its setting explains its existence. These monasteries stood on the trade routes between the Konkan ports - Kalyan, Sopara, Chaul - and the Deccan markets at Paithan and Ter, and were endowed by merchants, guilds and Satavahana officials, as the inscriptions at Nashik, Karle and Kanheri record.
Part of the chaitya collapsed in a landslide in the 1990s, so the site is also cited in discussions of monument conservation.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 8; Thapar, *Early India*; ASI

location.summary: Kupgal, near Sanganakallu on the granite hills outside Ballari, Karnataka, in the Raichur doab between the Krishna and the Tungabhadra - the core of the South Indian Neolithic ashmound country.

periodLevel.summary: South Indian Neolithic with a Chalcolithic overlap, roughly 3000-1200 BCE. The site includes a hilltop settlement, ashmounds, thousands of petroglyphs, and the *rock gongs* for which it is best known. Re-surveyed in the 2000s by Nicole Boivin and colleagues after being lost to record for a century.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: A Neolithic ritual landscape - the clearest Indian evidence that prehistoric sites were used for ceremony as well as habitation.
points: The rock gongs are boulders bearing deep cup-shaped depressions which, when struck, ring with a loud metallic resonance. The wear on them shows sustained use, and their position beside the petroglyph concentrations argues that sound was part of whatever was performed here.

The petroglyphs, pecked rather than painted, are dominated by long-horned humped cattle, with human figures and hunting scenes. Cattle imagery, ashmounds and faunal remains together make the case that the southern Neolithic was organised around cattle herding, and that the ashmounds - great heaps of burnt cow dung - are the residue of periodic ritual burning of cattle pens rather than domestic rubbish.
Excavations at neighbouring Sanganakallu have produced ground stone axe workshops on an industrial scale, so the hills were a production centre as well as a ceremonial one.
The ceramics are burnished grey and buff wares, some painted in white, and copper and gold appear in later levels.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 3; Thapar, *Early India*; Boivin et al., *Antiquity*

location.summary: Porivarai, in the Karikkiyur complex of the Nilgiri hills near Kotagiri, Tamil Nadu - a rock shelter in the Western Ghats at about 1,500 m. The name means "the rock of writing" or "carved rock" in Tamil.

periodLevel.summary: Rock paintings assigned broadly to the late Neolithic and megalithic periods, roughly the 2nd millennium BCE to the early centuries CE, with some figures argued to be later. The Nilgiri megalithic cairns and cromlechs in the surrounding hills belong to the same broad horizon.

keyFindsAndSignificance.summary: The principal rock art site of the Nilgiris - the southern extremity of the Indian painted-shelter tradition.
points: The paintings, in white kaolin and red ochre, show human figures with headdresses and weapons, riders, cattle, deer and a range of symbols. Figures carrying what appear to be bows and standing beside horses suggest contact with the megalith-building communities of the peninsular uplands.

The Nilgiri material extends the map of Indian rock art south beyond the Deccan, and its imagery differs from both the Vindhyan hunting scenes and the cattle-centred art of the Bellary region - evidence that the tradition had distinct regional grammars rather than one subject repertoire.

The Nilgiris also hold a dense concentration of megalithic monuments excavated from the 19th century by Breeks and others, and the relationship between those burials and the shelter paintings is the site's open question.

The hills remain the home of the Toda, Kota, Kurumba and Irula communities, and Kurumba wall painting has been compared with the prehistoric work, though continuity is asserted more often than demonstrated.

content.sourcesLine: Upinder Singh, ch. 2 and 6; ASI; *Indian Archaeology - A Review*
